It devastated and overturned villages and cities, and destroyed and crushed their inhabitants within them, like grapes in a single winepress of destruction.
For thirteen cities were overturned and destroyed in it: Ephesus, Magnesia, Sardis, Maetna [?], Aegae,
Caesarea, Philadelphia, Tmolus, Temnos, Cyme, Myrina, Apollonia, and Hyrcania.
All these were devastated by this wrath because of their sins, and all their height and all their extent were destroyed. In this same year,
Pompey's theater burned down. In the year 2040, Philip built the city of Caesarea.
He also built another city, Julias. In the year 2040, Philip built the city of Caesarea.
He also built another city, Julias. In the year 2043,
Pilate was sent as governor over Judea. In the year 2044, Herod built the city of Tiberias.
To honor Caesar, he named it Tiberias. He also built the city of Livias. In this same year,
John, the son of Zechariah, was preaching in the wilderness beside the Jordan River, announcing to everyone that the Messiah, the Son of God, was among them.
Jesus himself also began the saving work of the gospel from this time, showing those who saw him the reality of divine power through words and deeds.
Herod took Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip, while Philip was still alive. He rejected his first wife, who was his lawful wife
and the daughter of Aretas, king of the [?]. He separated Herodias from her husband while her husband was still alive. On her account he went to war with King Aretas,
because Aretas's daughter had been dishonored. In this war Herod's entire army was killed. And because he was also being rebuked by John the Baptist,
that he should not marry his brother’s wife. Moreover, when Herod heard John’s words, he was afraid.
When he saw that all the people inclined to follow him, that he gathered large crowds, and that he spoke to people with authority,
he feared that this affair might lead to rebellion. For he saw that they did everything at John’s word [?] and at his command. And he considered in his mind
that it was much better to act first and have him killed before that upheaval came about through him, rather than [?] fall into remorse afterward because of the turn of events involving John.
So, because of this suspicion on Herod’s part, John was sent in chains to the prison called Machaerus, and there he was killed.
Afterward Herod and Herodias were driven out and expelled beyond the borders into exile in the city of Vienne.
There he received punishment worthy of his deeds. The years are counted from the second rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem,
which took place in the second year of Darius, king of the Persians, down to this present year, which is the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius:
548 years. From Solomon and the first building of the Temple, 1,061 years.
From Moses and the departure from Egypt, 1,541 years. From Abraham and the reign of Ninus and Semiramis,
2,044 years. From the flood to Abraham, 942 years.
And from Adam to the flood, 2,242 years.
In the year 2,046, Abgar, king of Edessa, sent a letter to Christ in the land of Jerusalem.
In the year 2,049 from Abraham, the father of the nations, and, reckoning from Alexander son of Philip the Macedonian,
in the year 342, Jesus Christ approached his suffering in accordance with the prophecy about him, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Tiberius.
At this time, we also find these events recorded individually in other Greek records: the sun grew dark; Bithynia was shaken,
and much of Nicaea fell. This bears witness to the things that happened in the time of our Savior. Phlegon, who wrote an account of the Olympiads, also wrote
about these things in his thirteenth book as follows: “In the fourth year of the 202nd Olympiad,
there was an exceedingly great eclipse of the sun, surpassing those that had occurred before it. At the sixth hour of the day it became night,
so that stars appeared in the sky. There was a great earthquake, and much of Nicaea [?].” These are the things said by the man we have mentioned.
A sign that our Savior suffered in this year is the testimony of John, which took place in the fifteenth year of Tiberius.
It attests a period of three consecutive years of our Lord’s teaching. Concerning those times, Josephus also writes
that on the day of Pentecost, a disturbance and a great shaking seized the priests. Afterward a powerful voice was heard from within the inner sanctuary,
saying, “We are departing from here.” Josephus himself recorded another event: at that same time Pilate the governor
placed an image of Caesar in the Temple at night, something he was not permitted to do. He thereby caused the beginning of great turmoil and rebellion among the Jews.
And the front of the temple entrance was torn apart. Many dead people rose from their graves and appeared to many.
An account of our Lord’s suffering and the conduct of his trial. Avitus to Antius Licinius Asprenas: greetings.

Since you asked me through my Frontontus to learn what happened in court concerning Jesus Christ, I have taken care that everything that happened in the governor’s headquarters and on the judgment seat
I should write down and confirm for you. I also ask you to repay me in turn. For Frontontus himself told me
that you invited some of Jesus’ disciples, and they gave you many things belonging to him, which you have.
Know, then, that the chief priests and scribes of the Jewish people were jealous of Jesus more than of any living person.
They arrested Jesus and brought him to my lord Pilate, because they regarded him as a blasphemer and a breaker of the laws,
and as deserving death. [?] They brought him forward and said many things against him.
But when Pilate learned that he was a Galilean and under Herod’s authority, he sent him to Herod, who was then in Jerusalem
because it was the Feast of Unleavened Bread. Herod himself, after hearing the accusations of the priests and Pharisees, also sent him to Pilate
and sent him this message: “Many things are being said against this man. And since those accusing him are inhabitants of Jerusalem,
people who are under your authority [?]” In the year 2,066 of Abraham,
there was a severe [famine] in Rome, and many perished in it. In the year 2,067, Maʿnu son of Abgar died,
the king of Edessa. His brother Maʿnu reigned for fourteen years. In the year 2,070, Claudius, emperor of the Romans, died.
Nero reigned in his place for thirteen years and eight months. During his rule, Nero plunged into many evil deeds
and took up arms against reverence for God. But to write about the nature of his wickedness
is not our task at this time. Many have given detailed accounts of him, and anyone who wishes can learn from them about this man’s madness:
how he destroyed countless tens of thousands of people and reached such murderous depravity that he did not refrain even from killing members of his own household and his relatives.
For he destroyed his mother, his brothers, his wives, and many of his family. He killed them by every kind of death, as though they were enemies and adversaries.
In the year 2,084, Saint Paul was martyred in Rome, his head being cut off with a sword.
In that same year Peter, the chief of the apostles, was also martyred, being crucified upside down.
They lived for thirty-five years after Christ. In the year 2,071, in the days of Nero,
when Felix was governor of Judea, Josephus again recounts the disputes and disturbances that arose among the priests, and writes as follows in his history:
“A dispute flared up between the chief priests and the priests and leaders of Jerusalem. Each of them gathered a band of reckless troublemakers
and became their leader. As they quarreled with one another, they spoke abusively about each other and threw stones.”
There was no one to rebuke them, and it was like a city without a governor. Again, in those days a kind of bandit appeared in Jerusalem.
In broad daylight, in the middle of the city, they killed those they encountered. Especially during the festivals, they mingled with the crowds.
They hid swords beneath their clothes and used them to stab prominent people.
When their victims fell, they themselves joined those who protested against the murderers. Because of their manner, they were not recognized.
Jonathan the high priest was killed first. After him, many were killed every day.
The fear of it was worse than the suffering that occurred continually. Everyone awaited his death as though in battle.
In the year 2072, the Jews rebelled in Caesarea, and many of them perished.
In the year 2075, Felix was relieved of his position in Judea, and Festus came as governor in his place.
In the year 2076, Paul was sent as a prisoner to Rome for the first time.
In the year 2077, Saint James, the brother of our Lord, who was the first bishop of the church of Jerusalem, was martyred.
The Jews, however, when Paul appealed to Caesar's protection and was sent to Rome by Festus,
were frustrated in the treacherous scheme they had been devising against him. They turned against James, the brother of our Lord,
who had received the episcopal throne of Jerusalem from the apostles. Their brazen attack against him happened in this way. They brought him
into their midst and tried to force him to deny faith in Christ before the whole assembly.
But contrary to everyone's wishes and expectations, he boldly confessed in a loud voice before all the people that our Lord Jesus Christ is the Son of our God.
And when they could not endure his testimony—for everyone believed that he was righteous because of the perfection of his wise conduct
and the fear of God in which he lived. For they found a suitable opportunity, because Festus had died in Judea,
and they had no governor at that time. The administration there was without a head or governor.
James, the brother of our Lord, whom everyone called the Just, led the church of Jerusalem from the time of our Lord until now.
For there were many who were likewise called James. But this man was holy from his mother's womb.
He drank neither wine nor strong drink, and he ate nothing that had life in it. No razor touched his head. He did not anoint himself with oil or use a bathhouse.
He alone used to enter the sanctuary. They would find him kneeling on his knees, asking forgiveness for the people,
until his knees became hard like a camel's, because he constantly knelt and worshiped God and asked forgiveness for the people.
Because of his outstanding righteousness, he was called the Just, the wall of the people and their righteousness, as the prophets say about him.
Some people from those seven sects among the Jews used to ask him, “What is the gate of Jesus?” He
But he said to them, “This is the Savior.” And some of them believed that Jesus was the Messiah.
But these previously mentioned sects did not believe, not even that he had risen from the dead.
Nor did they believe that he would come to repay everyone according to their deeds. Those who did believe believed because of James.
Now, when many of the leaders of the people were believing, there was an uproar among the Jews, the scribes, and the Pharisees. And they were saying,
“All the people are being compelled to await Jesus the Messiah.” So they gathered and said to James, “We ask you to restrain the people,
because they are mistaken about Jesus, thinking that he is the Messiah. We ask you to persuade everyone who has come for the day of Passover concerning Jesus.
For we all trust you. We and all the people testify that you are righteous and show no partiality to anyone.
So persuade this crowd not to be mistaken about Jesus. For all the people, and all of us, trust you. Stand, then, on the pinnacle of the temple,
so that you can be seen from there and your words can be heard by all the people. For all the tribes have come for Passover, along with the Gentiles.”
The scribes and Pharisees placed him on the pinnacle of the temple, and they shouted to him, “Righteous one, whom we all ought to trust,
since the people have gone astray after Jesus who was crucified, tell us what the gate of Jesus is.”
He answered in a loud voice, “Why are you asking me about the Son of Man? He sits at the right hand of the great Power and will come on the clouds of heaven.”
When many were strengthened and were giving praise because of James’s testimony, saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” then
those same scribes and Pharisees were again saying to one another, “We have done wrong by giving Jesus testimony like this.
But let us go up and throw him down, so that they will be afraid and not believe him.” And they shouted, “Oh, oh! The righteous one
has gone astray!” And they were fulfilling what is written in Isaiah: “Throw down the righteous man, because he is of no use to us.” Therefore they will eat the fruit of their deeds.
So they went up and threw down the righteous man. And they said to one another, “Let us stone James the righteous.”
They began to stone him, because he had not died when he fell. But he turned and knelt down, saying, “I ask you, Lord God,
forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” While they were stoning him like this, one of the priests, a descendant of Rechab [?], son of Rechabim,
one of those about whom the prophet Jeremiah bears witness, shouted, “Stop! What are you doing?
The righteous man is praying for you!” And one of them took from the fuller the wooden club with which he used to press clothes,
and struck the righteous man on the head. Thus he was martyred. They buried him on that spot, beside the temple.
After him, Simon son of Clopas became bishop in Jerusalem. Clopas was the brother of Joseph, Mary’s husband and James’s father.
This Simon, who was called Simo [?], became the leader of Jerusalem after James, his cousin. And in the year 2078,
Saint Mark, bishop of Alexandria, died, and Annianus succeeded him. In the year 2080, there was a great tremor and an earthquake.
And in it three cities in the land of Asia collapsed: Laodicea, Hierapolis, and Colossae. At this time the people rebelled—
the Jews. Josephus also recounted the calamities that overtook the Jewish people, describing them in his account along with many others:
“Many, he says, of those held in honor among the Jews were scourged in Jerusalem and then crucified
by Florus, who was governor of Judea, when the beginning of the war was stirred up,
in the twelfth year of Nero’s rule. Throughout Syria, because of the rebellion of the Jews,
bitter turmoil overtook the members of the people. Everywhere they were mercilessly killed by the inhabitants of the cities, as in war.
One could see cities filled with dead bodies, unburied and trampled together: children, old people, and women,
with not even their private parts covered. All the districts were filled with indescribable afflictions.
The onslaught of tortures was severe, as was the violence committed every day.” Josephus said these things in his account: that these things happened to the Jews.
The year 2081. Manu, king of Edessa, died, and Abgar son of Manu took the throne for twenty years.
The year 2082. Nero killed all the leading men of the Romans because of their testimony to Christ.
He also killed his wife, his three daughters, and his sons along with them. The year 2083.
Paul and Peter were martyred in Rome. The year 2084. The wrath of God began to come upon Nero.
In this same year the Jewish people rebelled. Vespasian, commander of the Roman army, came against them with a large army
and attacked Jerusalem. While they were attacking it, bad news began reaching Nero from every direction, and he killed himself
with his own hands. The year 2085. Galba and Otho took power.
The Roman army that was attacking Jerusalem proclaimed Vespasian emperor. He left his son Titus behind and went himself to take possession of the empire.
The year 2086. Galba and Otho were killed, and Vespasian became emperor.
For Josephus the historian, who is Caiaphas, says—since he remained alive until the destruction of Jerusalem—that after Nero had reigned for thirteen and a half years,
and after Galba and Otho for a year and a half, Vespasian was victorious in the war against the Jews. In Judea itself, the Roman army stationed there appointed him
king and emperor. Immediately he entrusted the war against the Jews to his son Titus and himself departed for Rome.
After our Savior’s ascension, in addition to the Jews’ insolence toward him, they devised many plots against the apostles.
First they killed Stephen with stones. Then, after him, James the son of Zebedee was beheaded, and then James, our Lord’s brother.
They devised many schemes against the rest of the apostles to bring about their death, and they were driven from the land of Judea.
But those who were sent by our Lord among the nations to proclaim the good news in his name, and also the people of the church in Jerusalem—
As, through a revelation that came to the distinguished men among them, they had been commanded before the war to leave the city
and go and settle across the river, in a city called Pella—all those in Jerusalem who believed in Christ—
so that the people would leave it completely, and then judgment would come upon it:
the judgment of retribution from God upon it, the royal city of the Jews, and upon the whole land of Judea, for what it had dared to do against Christ and his apostles,
so as to wipe out the entire generation of the wicked from that place. But what calamities befell [all the people in every] place,
and how the inhabitants of Judea were subjected to especially terrible torments, and how many tens of thousands fell together by the sword, by famine, and by many deadly afflictions,
and the captivity that befell many cities of Judea, and also the terrible calamities experienced in Jerusalem by those who had fled to take refuge there
as in a fortified city, and the course of the entire war, and everything that happened in it, event by event,
and how, in the end, the sign of the abomination of desolation stood, as spoken of in the prophet, over that renowned temple which had formerly belonged to God,
and how it was completely destroyed by fire—anyone who wishes to learn these things accurately can learn them from the history that Josephus wrote.
But it is worth pointing out that this same Josephus indicates that people had gathered from all Judea during the days of the Passover festival
and [?] entered Jerusalem and were shut up there as in a prison—about three million people.
For it was fitting that, on those very days when they had gathered and dared to act against the Savior and benefactor of all, Christ the Son of God,
they should be shut up as in a prison and receive destruction from God's just judgment.
Again, concerning the famine that seized the Jews, the sword, and other forms of suffering.
And I will speak only of the bitter afflictions that overtook them through famine, so that those who read this book may, even from a brief account,
know that punishment from God for their outrage against Christ overtook them swiftly.
Take up, then, the fifth book of Josephus's history and read what happened to them at that time, as he speaks as follows:
“For those,” he says, “who had property, remaining or perishing amounted to the same thing. For they would fabricate a charge against someone
that he wanted to surrender to the Romans, and he would perish because of his property. Along with the famine, the insolence of the rebels also grew stronger.
Every day these two evils blazed more fiercely. Grain was nowhere to be seen openly.
They would rush in and search the houses. If they found anything, they beat the people for denying that they had it.
And if they found nothing, they tortured them as people who had hidden it because of their distress.
The appearance of the bodies of these wretched people was taken as evidence of whether or not they had anything.
Those among them whose bodies remained strong were thought to have an abundant supply of food.”
But to kill those who were already close to dying of hunger would have been senseless.
Many secretly exchanged their possessions for a single measure of wheat, if they were rich;
and if they were poor, for barley. They hid themselves in the inner rooms of their houses. Some of them, because of their extreme need,
ate the wheat just as it was, without grinding it. Others baked it as necessity dictated. And a table
was nowhere set at all. They snatched the food straight from the fire and ate it before it was cooked.
That meal was a sorrowful one, and the sight deserved tears: those who were stronger snatched the food from their companions,
while those who were weak wailed. The torment of hunger overpowered every feeling, and nothing destroys shame as it does.
For things that under other circumstances deserve respect are treated with contempt under its power. Women snatched from their husbands,
and children from their fathers; and, lowest of all, mothers snatched food from the mouths of their infants.
Even when they saw their beloved children wasting away in their arms, they had no pity and took away the drops that sustained their lives. And while they were eating in this way,
they could not remain hidden. Those troublemakers came everywhere and seized whatever food the people had snatched.
For whenever they saw a closed door anywhere, this was a sign that those inside were eating some food.
They immediately broke down the doors, rushed in, and squeezed the food out of their throats.
Old men were beaten for clinging to their food, and the hair of women who hid any food was torn out.
There was no mercy for old women or infants. They would pick up the infants, lift them up as they clung to their food, and dash them to the ground.
But against those who had managed to eat their food before they entered, so that they found none, they grew bitter, as though they themselves had suffered an injustice,
and devised cruel forms of torture to search out food.
For they forced wedges into the wombs of those being tortured and drove sharp rods into their buttocks.
It was terrifying even to hear what a person suffered to make them confess to having a single small loaf or a handful of barley flour.
Their torturers were not even hungry. Yet in their eyes it was too small an act of cruelty merely to seize things by force.
They practiced cruelty and prepared provisions for themselves in advance for the days to come.
As for those who crept out at night toward the Roman guards to gather wild greens and grass,
they intercepted them; and just when they thought they had escaped their enemies, they snatched away whatever they had brought.
How often they pleaded with them, appealing to them by the fearful name of God,
to give them a small portion of what they had brought back through such toil and distress! But they gave them none of it.
But they were glad of this: that they would not perish along with their tormentors. And a little later he adds and says:
“For the Jews, he says, hope of survival was cut off along with their departure. Famine was severe in every house and every family, and was consuming the people.
For the rooftops were full of women and children lying prostrate, and the streets were full of dead old men. Boys and young women wandered about.
They roamed the marketplaces like ghosts and fell wherever suffering overtook any one of them.
Those who were suffering could not bury their loved ones. And anyone
who still had the strength hesitated because of the multitude of the dead, and did not know what would happen to him himself.
For many of them fell and died on top of those being buried, and many died before they reached the graves.
Amid these bitter afflictions there was no lamentation or weeping, for famine had overcome every emotion. With dry eyes, those suffering the agony of death
watched those who were dying before them. But a deep silence [?] they watched those who were dying before them.
A deep silence surrounded the city, and a night full of death. But the robbers were worse than all these things.
For they plundered the dead in their houses and stripped the coverings from their bodies, and went out from there laughing.
They tested the sharpness of their swords on dead bodies, and also drove them through those who lay there still alive.
Those who begged them to stretch out their right hand with the sword and release them from famine, they arrogantly ignored.
Each of those who were dying fixed his gaze on the temple, leaving the rebels alive.
At first, they ordered the dead to be buried at the expense of the public treasury, because they could not endure the stench.
But when they could no longer keep up with the burials, they threw them from the wall into the ravines. When Titus passed those ravines and saw that they were full of dead bodies
and the putrid fluid flowing from the corpses, he groaned, raised his hands on high, and called God as his witness, saying, ‘This is not my doing.’”
After saying a little more, Josephus added: “I will not hold back from saying what grief commands me to say.
I think that if the Romans had delayed coming against these shameless men, either that city would have been swallowed by a chasm or destroyed by a flood,
or fire like that of Sodom would have been sent upon it. For God endured this generation more than those who suffered these things,
godless as it was. For through their shamelessness they destroyed the entire people along with themselves.” And again, in the sixth book, he wrote as follows:
“Those who were being destroyed by famine in the city fell in vast, uncountable numbers, and their sufferings cannot be recounted.
For in every house where even a shadow of food appeared, a battle broke out, as loved ones attacked one another
and snatched away the pitiful provisions that sustained life. Yet they were not believed in their destitution, [?] as they were dying.
Instead, those robbers even searched the dying, in case any one of them had something in the folds of his clothing.
Death overtook him. Others, in their destitution, lay with their mouths hanging open, panting like dogs.
Children wandered about, straying from door to door. They staggered like drunkards, and because of the distress surrounding them,
they would rush into the very same houses two or three times in a single hour. Necessity brought everything into use as food.
They gathered and ate things that even unclean animals would not eat. In the end, they did not even refrain from eating the straps of their belts and footwear.
They stripped the hides covering shields and chewed them. Even straw from old hay became food.
People gathered stalks one by one and sold a small weight for four assaria. But why do we need to speak about
their use of lifeless things during the famine? For I have a deed to relate whose like never happened among the Greeks,
nor is it reported to have occurred among the barbarians. It is horrifying to tell and difficult for those who hear it to believe.
So that I would not seem to be inventing some new marvel for humanity, I would gladly have left this account aside and passed over it,
had I not had countless witnesses. Besides, I would have shown little kindness to my own people
if I had neglected to tell what they actually did. A woman, one of those who lived beyond the Jordan,
whose name was Mary, daughter of Eleazar, from a village called Meit-hazor [?], which means “House of Hyssop,”
was well known for her ancestry and wealth. She had fled with many others to take refuge in Jerusalem,
and was trapped there. The possessions she had brought with her into the city from beyond the Jordan
were seized by those tyrants. Whatever household utensils and provisions she still had left, and anything else they could find belonging to her,
those armed men would rush in and seize. She complained bitterly,
and often insulted and cursed them to provoke them into killing her. But when neither in anger
nor out of pity would any of them kill her, even if she managed to find some food, she was laboring for others.
Every possibility of finding anything was cut off on all sides. Hunger had taken possession of her innards and marrow, and more fiercely than hunger,
her anger blazed. This woman, taking counsel from terror and necessity, turned against nature.
She seized her son, whom she was still nursing, and said, “Poor child, amid war, famine, and rebellion, for whom am I to keep you?
Even if we survive, there is slavery under the Romans. But famine will come before slavery, and the bandits are more bitter than either.
Come, then, become food for me, madness for the rebels, and a tale for the whole world—
the one thing still missing from the sufferings of the Jews.” Having said this, she killed her son.
She roasted him and ate half, then covered and kept the rest. Immediately the rebels caught the smell of this abominable deed.
They drew their swords and threatened to kill her. But she showed them what she had prepared. Then she immediately said to them:
“I have also kept a good portion for you from what I obtained from my son.” She uncovered it and showed them. Immediately trembling seized them, and they were beside themselves.
They were paralyzed by the sight. But she said, “This was my own beloved son, and this is my own doing. Take it and eat.
I too have eaten. So do not be weaker than a woman or more compassionate than a mother. But if you are devout
and shrink from my sacrifice, I have eaten of it already, and I have kept what remains for myself.” After this,
they left that place trembling and afraid. Only with difficulty did they leave even this food for that woman.
Immediately the whole city was filled with this horrifying report. Everyone pictured this suffering before their own eyes
and shuddered at it as though they had done it themselves. Those tormented by hunger had only this desire: to die. And fortunate

were considered those who had gone before, before hearing and seeing such evils.

Again, concerning the things Christ had previously spoken and prophesied.
Such retribution had overtaken the Jews for their wrongdoing and the wickedness they committed against Christ, who is God.
It is fitting to compare these things with our Savior’s prophecy, which was not proved false, when he said: “Woe to pregnant women and nursing mothers in those days!
Pray that your flight will not take place in winter or on the Sabbath. For there will be great distress, such as has not occurred since the day the world came into being

until now, and never will again.”

On the number of those who perished through famine, plague, and the sword, and those who were also taken into captivity.
This same writer totaled the number of those who perished through famine and the sword, and said that it was one hundred and ten myriads,
that is, one million one hundred thousand. The rest of those robbers and rebels were killed after the city’s destruction,
as they pointed one another out. Those who were young, tall in stature, and outstanding in appearance
were kept for public spectacles. The rest of the people, aged seventeen and above, were bound and sent to Egypt for labor.
Many were distributed among the provinces to perish in public spectacles by swords and wild beasts. Those aged seventeen and below
were taken captive and sold. They numbered ninety thousand. These things happened in this way in the second year of Vespasian,
which was the year 2087 from Abraham, in accordance with the foreknowledge of our Savior, our Lord Jesus Christ,
who, through the great power of his divinity, foresaw and foretold the things that were going to happen, just as they happened. And he wept over the city,
as it is written in the holy Gospel, which says that he spoke to Jerusalem in this way: “If only you had known the day of your peace!
But it has been hidden from your eyes. Days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you and press you on every side.
They will level you to the ground, and your children within you.” Again, he said concerning the people: “There will be great distress upon the earth and fierce wrath upon this world.
They will fall by the edge of the sword and be taken captive among all nations. And Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations.”
Until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled. And again he said, “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army,”
“then you will know that its destruction has drawn near.” So when someone compares these words of our Savior with this historian’s account of the whole war,
how can he fail to marvel at how wonderfully glorious our Savior’s foreknowledge is, and acknowledge that it truly belongs to God?
As for the things that befell the whole Hebrew people after our Savior’s suffering, and those cries of the entire assembly of the Jews,
who shouted and demanded that the robber and murderer should live, while pleading that the giver of life should be taken away from them,
we need not add anything to these accounts. But it is right to append to them
the things that demonstrate his mercy and his gracious care: for forty whole years after their outrageous conduct against Christ,
he held off their destruction. During those years, many of his disciples and apostles, and James, our Lord’s brother,
who was the first bishop, were still alive and living in Jerusalem itself.
They remained in that place like a strong wall, since God’s judgment was still being delayed for them [?], so that perhaps

they might eventually repent and turn back from what they had done, and receive forgiveness and life.

On the signs that occurred before the war.
In addition to all this patience, marvelous signs were also given to them of what was going to befall them unless they repented.
The historian whom we mentioned earlier also considered these worthy of being recorded in his history. There is nothing to prevent us,
as we proceed with this book, from including them too. Take up, then, and read what he says in the sixth book of his history,
where he speaks as follows: “At that time, those deceivers who testified falsely about God were persuading the wicked people
not to pay attention to or believe the clear signs that gave advance warning of the destruction that was to come.
Instead, like people deprived of their reason, with neither eyes nor souls, they disregarded God’s proclamation.
First, a star resembling a spear stood above the city and remained upright for a year.
Again, before they rebelled and war broke out against them, when the people were gathered for the feast of Unleavened Bread, on the eighth of Nisan, at the ninth hour of the night,
such a light flashed over the altar and the temple that one would have thought it was bright daylight. It remained there for half an hour.
But those who knew the sacred Scriptures interpreted it beforehand as a sign of the things that were going to happen. Again, at this same feast,
someone brought a cow to the altar, and it gave birth to a lamb in the middle of the temple. Again, the eastern gate, which was made of bronze
and was heavy—twenty men could barely close it in the evening, and it was secured with iron bars, and underneath it had
deep bolts—was found standing open of its own accord at the sixth hour of the night.
A few days after the feast, on the twenty-first of Iyyar, a certain vision appeared, which seems difficult to believe.
If it were not that many who saw it tell of it, and that the consequences of the signs, too, deserve belief. For before the sun set,
chariots appeared above throughout the country, and armed forces up in the clouds. They were rushing about and surrounding the city.
Again, on the day of the festival called Pentecost, the priests entered the temple at night to perform their service, as was their custom.
They said that first they heard the sound of shaking and pounding. Afterward, a voice was suddenly heard saying, “We are leaving this place.”
And there were things even more frightening than these. There was also a certain villager named Jesus, one of the common people, who, four years before the war,
while the city was at peace and had everything in great abundance, came to the festival at which they used to make shelters for God,
as was customary. Suddenly he began crying out in the temple: “A voice from the east! A voice from the west!
A voice from the four winds! A voice against Jerusalem and against the temple! A voice against bridegrooms and brides! A voice against all the people!”
He went around through all the streets, crying this out all day and all night. Some prominent people among the population became angry with this bearer of bad news [?].
They seized this man and beat him severely. But he did not even answer them a word in his own defense,
to those who were standing there, nor did he say anything on his own behalf. Instead, he kept crying out those same cries as before.
The rulers thought that this man’s agitation came from a demon, and they brought him before the Roman governor.
There they tore his flesh with blows down to his bones. But he did not plead with them or shed any tears.
Instead, he kept returning all the more to this same cry, groaning with every blow they struck him and saying,
“Woe, woe to Jerusalem!” This historian also related other astonishing things: that a prophetic saying was found in Jerusalem,
in which it was written as follows: “At that very time someone will arise from their country and rule over the whole world.”
They thought that these words were fulfilled in Vespasian. Yet he did not rule over the whole world, but only over the Romans.
This should therefore be understood as referring to Christ, to whom it was given by the Father: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance,
and the ends of the earth as your possessions.” And again: “He will rule from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the ends of the earth.
The islands will bow down before him, and his enemies will lick the dust.” It also says, “His dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom lasts from generation to generation.”
At this very time the apostles’ good news went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world, as it is written.
Their message was heard even at the farthest reaches of the world. The total span of time up to Vespasian’s second year and the final destruction of Jerusalem,
from the fifteenth year of Tiberius and the beginning of our Savior’s preaching, was forty-two years.
From the siege in the days of Antiochus, two hundred and thirty-eight years. From the year
two of Darius, in whose days the temple in Jerusalem was built for the second time, five hundred and [?] years.
From the first building of the temple, which took place in Solomon’s days, until its final destruction,
which took place in Vespasian’s days: 1,103 years. From Alexander, king of the Macedonians: 381 years.
[?]. Two thousand and eighty-seven. In the year 2,090 of Abraham, Saint Linus received the bishopric of Rome.
He presided for twelve years. In the year 2,092, there was a severe earthquake on the island of Cyprus,
and three cities collapsed in it. In the year 2,094, Emperor Vespasian died.
His son Titus reigned after him for two years and two months. In the year 2,096, Titus died.
His brother Domitian took power after him for fifteen years and four months. He launched a persecution against the Christians after Nero,
and killed many prominent people. He also persecuted the Chaldeans and the philosophers and expelled them from Rome. He also ordered that no one should make Christians,
that is, that no one should baptize. In the year 2,100, Abilius received the bishopric of Alexandria and presided for twelve years.
In the year 2,101, Abgar son of Izates became king over Edessa for six years and nine months.
In the year 2,102, there was a war between the Romans and the Nasamones and Dacians. The Romans won.
In the year 2,106, Abgar, king of Edessa, died. Because of the desire for power, there was no agreement on a single ruler. And so
it remained in conflict for two years. Afterward, [?] Parthamaspates took the kingship for three years and ten months.
In this same year, Saint Clement took office in the church of Rome. At this time Emperor Domitian ordered
that all grapevines should be uprooted from the cities, and that no one should plant vines in a city.
This Domitian launched a persecution against the Christians and killed many members of prominent families. He persecuted and expelled many,
and also banished John the apostle to the island of Patmos, where he also received the Revelation. At this time many heresies arose.
First was the heresy called that of the Ebionites, because they held a low and impoverished view of Christ.
For they considered him an ordinary human being who became righteous through training in habitual good conduct, and who was born from the union of a man and Mary.
They said that observance of the law was required, and did not believe that they received life through faith.
There were also others called by the very same name, Ebionites, because of their great insolence.
They do not deny that he was born of a virgin and the Holy Spirit, but acknowledge, as we do, that he existed from the beginning as the Word of God and Wisdom.
They strive to maintain the impiety of those earlier people in the matter of customs. They completely reject Paul’s letters,
and call him an apostate from the law. They use only the Gospel called the Hebrew Gospel, and do not accept the others.
Like those others, they observe the Sabbath and Jewish practices. But they also observe Sunday as we do, in commemoration of our Savior’s resurrection.
Because of this way of thinking, they received the name Ebionites. For in Hebrew a poor person is called an ebion.
There was also another sect called that of Cerinthus. This Cerinthus, they say, introduced [?] into the world through visions, as though he were a great apostle.
Of the foolish words he fabricated, he said that he had learned them from angels: that after the resurrection Christ’s kingdom would be on earth.
“And we will once again serve bodily desires in Jerusalem,” he said. And because he was an enemy of the Scriptures of God,
he sought to mislead people by saying that there would be a festival of feasting lasting a thousand years. The things he himself desired were what he saw in his dream.
Because he was very worldly, he loved pleasures—that is, drinking, eating, and sexual intercourse—and the things he thought he had found
that were more respectable than these: festivals, sacrifices, and the slaughter of animals. This man opposed the apostle John the Evangelist.
One day John went into the bathhouse to bathe. When he learned that Cerinthus was there, he sprang from his place and fled to the door,
because he could not bear to be under the same roof as Cerinthus. He said this: “Get out of the bathhouse, so that it does not fall on you because of Cerinthus, the enemy
of God.” There was also another heresy called that of Nicolaus.
This Nicolaus was one of the seven who were chosen with Stephen to serve those in need.
He had a beautiful wife. After our Lord’s ascension, the apostles rebuked him for being jealous over her.
He brought her before them and gave her permission to belong to anyone she wished. What had been said with sincerity of intention,
those misguided people took as they pleased, saying that he had said this because one ought to give the body its pleasures.
They distorted this act, which had been done out of love for Christ, because he could not serve two masters—serve our Lord and his wife.
They did the opposite: all those who belong to this heresy committed sexual immorality without restraint.
But we have learned concerning this Nicolaus that from that day onward he lived out his life in chastity. His son and his daughters also grew old in virginity.
In the year 2110, Domitian ordered that all those descended from David should be killed,
so that no one would remain to inherit the kingdom of the Jews. Among them, all the relatives of Joseph, Mary’s husband, were also seized.
In the year 2112, great signs appeared in Rome and throughout the earth. In that same year,
Domitian was killed in the palace, and Nerva reigned for one year and four months. In the year 2113,
Parthamaspates reigned over Edessa for ten months. After him, Ma‘nu son of Izates reigned for nineteen years and
eight months. The bishopric of Alexandria: Cerdon became its third bishop, for eleven years. After Nerva, Trajan reigned for nineteen years
and six months. In the year 2115, John the Evangelist departed from this world and was buried in Ephesus.
At this time, Papias of Hierapolis, Polycarp, bishop of the community, and Ignatius of Antioch were well known.
who are the disciples of John. In the year 2,121, there was a great earthquake.
It overthrew four cities in Asia: Elaea, Myrina, Pitane, and Cyme. In Greece it also overthrew Spontium [?] and Oritum [?].
Wrath crushed their inhabitants within them like grapes. Primus took office as the fourth bishop of the church of Alexandria, for twelve years.
At this time Trajan stirred up persecution against the church. During it, Simeon son of Clopas, bishop of Jerusalem, was martyred.
Justus succeeded him. This Simon was the son of Clopas, the brother of Joseph, Mary's husband.
When he was 120 years old, he entered the struggle of martyrdom. After the many different tortures he endured,
he was crucified on a tree. Ignatius of Antioch was also martyred in Rome. After him, Heron became bishop in Antioch.
In the year 2,124, Trajan ordered that the persecution of the Christians should cease
and that their faith should be built up. Alexander assumed the bishopric of the church of Rome as its fifth bishop, for ten years. Now the temple in Rome
called the temple of all the gods was destroyed by lightning. Three cities in Galatia were destroyed by an earthquake. In the year 2,128,
Zacchaeus assumed the episcopal seat of the church in Jerusalem as its fourth bishop. After him came Tobias, the fifth; after him came Tobias, the fifth; and after him, Philip.
In the year 2,128, there was a great earthquake in Antioch, and it very nearly overthrew the city.
In the year 2,130, Ma'nu son of Ma'nu became king over Edessa, for twenty-four years.
He went into Roman territory. The Jews in Libya began to stir up rebellion and wage war against the pagans who lived alongside them,
as did those in Egypt, Alexandria, Cyrene, and Thebes. But the Greeks in Alexandria prevailed over them.
In the year 2,131, when the Jews of Mesopotamia rebelled, Trajan gave Lusius Quietus orders concerning them,
to clear them out of the province. Quietus armed himself and killed many tens of thousands of them,
so that the streets and houses of the cities, the roads and paths, and every place were filled with their corpses,
and there was no one to bury them. The Jews also rose up against Salamis in Cyprus. They killed the pagans within it and destroyed the city.
In the year 2,132, Trajan died of an illness at Selinus. Hadrian became emperor, for twenty-one years.
Hadrian restored Alexandria, which had been thrown into disorder by the Jews. He subdued the Jews who had rebelled against the Romans
twice. He also ordered all the Jews to leave Jerusalem and never again enter
there. At this time the heresy of Sabellius arose. Sabellius stood against the church at this time and said
that the Trinity has only one person, and that Mary is therefore the mother of the Trinity, and that the cross, too, is the cross of the Trinity.
A synod of forty-three bishops assembled against him at Ancyra in Galatia. It issued a decree, and they anathematized him and expelled him from the church.
And because he did not wish to turn back from the position he maintained. In Hadrian’s second year, he granted a remission of debts.
He burned the debt records of the cities that were in debt, and he remitted taxes for many. In his fourth year,
Sixtus became bishop of Rome for three years. In that same year, Justus took office in the church of Alexandria for eleven years.
In this same year there was a severe earthquake, in which Nicomedia and much of Nicaea collapsed. Hadrian sent gold and rebuilt them.
In Jerusalem, Seneca became bishop after Philip; after him, Justus; after him, Levi; after him, Ephres; and after him, Joseph;
and after him, Judas. All these bishops were from the circumcision, down to the siege in Hadrian’s days.
In the year 2144, Telesphorus became bishop of Rome for twenty years.
Cornelius became bishop of the church of Antioch. At that time Nicopolis and Caesarea were also overthrown by an earthquake.
In the church of Alexandria, Eumenes took office for thirteen years. At this time the river Cephissus had great and violent floods.
They inundated the city of Eleusis, bringing destruction and drowning its inhabitants. The river also swept away everything in it. At this same
time, Emperor Hadrian built a bridge over that river. In the year 2145, Eumenes became bishop in the church of Alexandria.
In the year 2149, Kokhba, the commander of the Jews, made the Christian people suffer many evils,
because they would not go with him to war against the Romans. The Romans and the Jews fought a war in the region of Palestine.
The Jews were devastated, and the Romans also took them captive, uprooting and destroying them from Jerusalem.
From this time onward, they were completely forbidden even to go up to Jerusalem: first by the will of God,
and afterward by the command of the Romans. Mark became the first bishop of Jerusalem from the Gentiles,
when the succession of those from the circumcision came to an end. In the year 2152, Hadrian died of dropsy.
After him, Titus Antoninus, who was called the Pious, reigned with his sons Aurelius and Lucius for twenty-two years
and three months. In his first year, Hyginus became bishop of Rome for four years. After him, Pius became bishop
for fifteen years. In the year 2154[?], Wael son of Sahru became king over Edessa for two years.
After him, Ma'nu son of Izates reigned for twelve years, after returning from Roman territory. The total length of his reign was thirty-six years,
not counting the years he spent in Roman territory. At this time Valentinus, the leader of a heresy, became known,
as did Cerdon, who belonged to the faith of Marcion’s followers. In the year 2157, Eros became the fifth bishop of Antioch.
In Alexandria, Mark took office and served for ten years. In the year 2169, there began to reign over Edessa
Abgar son of Ma'nu, for thirty-five years. In that same year, Celadion became bishop in Alexandria for fourteen years.
In the year 2172, Anicetus became bishop in Rome for eleven years.
In his days, Polycarp came to Rome and converted many heretics. Again, the bishops of Jerusalem: the seventeenth to take office was
Marcianus; the eighteenth, Publius; the nineteenth, Maximus; the twentieth, Julian; the twenty-first, Gaianus; and the twenty-second, Symmachus.
The twenty-third, Gaius; the twenty-fourth, Julian; and the twenty-fifth, Capito. In the year 2177,
Titus, emperor of the Romans, died. After him, his sons Lucius and Aurelius took over the empire for nineteen years
and one month. In their fourth year, Vologases, king of the Parthians, captured many towns from the Romans.
In their sixth year, Lucius conquered the Parthians and subjected them. In that same year, Agrippinus became bishop in the church of Alexandria
for twelve years. In the year 2183 of Abraham, a harsh, fierce, and merciless persecution arose against the Christians.
Many people were martyred in it, especially in the regions of Galatia. Also, Saint Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna,
and Papias, bishop of the community, disciples of John the apostle, were martyred in it. In this same year,
a severe and devastating plague broke out throughout the whole earth. It reached even Rome. In Alexandria, Agrippinus was bishop, and in the church of Rome,
Soter, for eight years. In Antioch, Theophilus became the sixth bishop. His distinguished writings also survive.
At this time, the following bishops were known in the church: Soter of Rome, Agrippinus of Alexandria, Theophilus of Antioch,
Dionysius of Corinth, and Apollinarius of Hierapolis. The latter opposed and refuted the false prophecy of the Phrygians.
Melito of Asia. In the year 2188, Antoninus was constantly arrayed against his enemies to fight them,
both when he fought in person and when he sent out military commanders. When Pertinax and those with him among the Quadi were suffering from thirst,
rain came to them from heaven, while lightning fell upon the Germans and Sarmatians who stood against them,
and destroyed many of them. They say that letters of the emperor Marcus also survive, in which he testified
that when his army was close to perishing from thirst, they were saved through the prayers of the Christians, as rain also came from heaven.
In the year 2192, Eleutherus became bishop of the church of Rome for fifteen years. In the church of Antioch, Maximus became bishop.
In the year 2194, there was an earthquake, and Smyrna in Asia collapsed. So that it could be rebuilt, it was exempted from taxes for ten years.
In the year 2195, Antoninus fell ill and died in Pannonia. After him, Commodus reigned for thirteen years.
In the church of Alexandria, Julian took office and governed for ten years. Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, was well known.
Again, the bishops of Jerusalem, those who were known in succession: the twenty-sixth to take office was Maximus; the twenty-seventh, Antoninus; and the twenty-eighth, Valens.
The twenty-ninth, Dolichianus; the thirtieth, Narcissus; the thirty-first, Dius; the thirty-second, Germanion; the thirty-third, Gordianus; and after him, that same Narcissus who had served before.
All these bishops held office in Jerusalem. We have no date by which to place each of them in order,
because the dates of their administration were not recorded. Year 2203.
Lightning struck the Capitol, and a fierce fire destroyed the libraries and many other places.
Abgar Severus reigned over Edessa with his son for one year and seven months. After him, his son Ma‘nu reigned for twenty-six years.
Serapion became bishop of the church of Antioch. In the church of Alexandria, Demetrius held office for forty-three years.
At this time the synod of Neocaesarea assembled. Also at this same time the following bishops were known: Demetrius of Alexandria,
Serapion of Antioch, Narcissus of Jerusalem, Irenaeus of Lyons, Dionysius of Corinth,
Apollinaris of Hierapolis, Victor of Rome, Alexander of Lesser Alexandria, and also Theophilus of Caesarea.
Polycrates and Bacchylides, shepherds [?], were also known. Year 2208.
Commodus stirred up persecution against the Christians and made many of them martyrs. He himself soon received punishment, dying suddenly.
He was strangled in the house of Bastianus. After him Pertinax reigned for six months, and after him Severus for eighteen years.
Year 2213. There was a war between the Jews and the Samaritans. Year two thousand two hundred
and fifteen. Zephyrinus became bishop of the church of Rome. At this time,
there was severe persecution against the church. Leonides, the father of Origen, was martyred, and Alexander was crowned for confessing the faith.
Also at this time Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, was known. This Narcissus was a powerful man who performed miracles.
During the feast of Easter, the deacons ran short of oil, and great distress seized the congregation because of this.
When the blessed man saw the congregation's distress, he instructed the deacons to bring him water.
When it was brought to him and he had prayed over it, he instructed them to pour it into these lamps with fervent faith in our Lord. When he did this [?],
that water was changed into the substance of oil through divine power and the blessed man's prayer. Because he was zealous for good deeds and opposed all evil,
three evildoers, afraid that they might fall into his hands, fabricated a charge against him and accused him slanderously before the people.
One of them said, “If this is not so, may I be burned in fire.” Another said, “If it is not true, may I fall ill with an incurable disease.”
Another of the three also said, “If it is not true, may I fall ill with an incurable disease.” Another of the three also said,
“If this has not been shown to me, may my eyes go blind.” When they said this, beloved, none of the believers believed them.
But in accordance with the sentence they had pronounced upon themselves, and with the suffering they had chosen for themselves,
punishment overtook them swiftly and soon. And because Narcissus himself was unable to minister owing to the burden of old age,
It was revealed in a vision to Alexander, bishop of Caesarea, that he should come and see the places where the work of salvation took place. And when
he reached Jerusalem, it was also revealed to the whole church there: “Go out and welcome the bishop whom God has chosen for you [?].”
When they went out, they met Alexander as he was coming. And so he was detained by the bishops: “the one who has been chosen for you by God.”
When they went out, they met Alexander as he was coming. And so he was detained by the bishops, the brothers, and the whole church there.
They did not allow him to return to his own country. Instead, he served alongside Narcissus while Narcissus was still alive. At this time the heresy of Montanus also existed.
There is a village in Mysia called Ardabau. From it came a man named Montanus, who had recently become a believer.
Satan filled this man's heart, and he spoke and prophesied strange things outside the tradition of the church. Montanus boasted
and said of himself that he was the Spirit, the Paraclete. He also appointed two women from among his own followers,
filled them with a spirit of falsehood, and called them prophetesses. One was named Prisca and the other Maximilla.
The holy Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia, fought against these people. The year 2226.
Severus died while fighting the barbarians. After him Antoninus reigned for seven years.
In the year 2127, Asclepiades became the eighth bishop (in Antioch), and Alexander became bishop in Jerusalem.
In the year 2232, there was a flood in Edessa from the river that enters the city on its western side.
In this river, called the Daisan, violent torrents of water rose during the night. While everyone was asleep, quiet and at rest inside their homes,
the river entered, full from bank to bank. Its outlets in the eastern wall became blocked by the mass of debris it carried from the mountains and the streets. And
the flood backed up. While everyone was asleep on their beds, the water came upon them through the doors and windows, and they drowned on their bedding.
The houses built of mud and bricks became waterlogged and fell, crushing their owners inside them. Suddenly they became tombs for their inhabitants.
The prophecy was fulfilled which says, “Their graves are in their houses forever.” More than two thousand people drowned in it, along with a great many animals.
When the flood pressed hard against the wall, it suddenly broke open and fell, and was swept away by the water.
It also plundered the city and carried out everything that the torrent had overwhelmed: the bodies of people and animals, timber [?], household belongings, and luxurious furnishings,
and everything in its streets and shops. It also swept away gardens [?], houses, villages, and all the property in its path
in the plains of Edessa and Harran. Beds [?] could be seen, made up and floating along in it,
and [?], with their owners inside them. In the year 2233, there was a fierce and violent battle.
The land between Edessa and [?] was drenched with human blood. In that battle Antoninus, emperor of the Romans, was killed.
After him Macrinus reigned for one year. He too was killed by Archelaus. After him Antoninus of Elagabalus reigned.
At this point the kingdom of the Edessenes also came to an end. Their royal rule had lasted 352 years.
From then onward they were subjected to Roman rule. The year 2234.
Philetus became bishop of the church of Antioch, and Callistus became bishop of the church of Rome.
In the year 2236, the city of Nicopolis was built in Palestine.
It had previously been called Emmaus. The year 2238: Antoninus was killed in the marketplace of Rome.
After him, Alexander, the son of Mamaea, took over the kingdom for thirteen years. He appeared to be the first Christian among the Roman emperors.
They also say of Mamaea, Alexander's mother, that among the women of the world there was no woman who feared God more than she did.
Indeed, there are also many accounts about her because of her good conduct.
The year 2240: Urban became bishop of the church of Rome for nine years, and Zebinus took office in the church of Antioch.
Origen was becoming known in Alexandria. The year 2246: Heraclas became bishop of the church of Alexandria for nineteen years.
At this same time there was also a great disturbance in Alexandria. Origen moved away from there and made his home in Caesarea in Palestine.
In that same year, Pontian became bishop of the church of Rome for five years.
The year 2251: Alexander was killed at Mogontiacum, and Maximinus became emperor.
He reigned for three years. He stirred up a harsh persecution against the leaders of the church, dislodging them, driving them away, and removing them from their episcopal seats.
He made many into martyrs during that persecution. God sent a small measure of wrath upon him too and took him from this life when he was killed at Aquileia.
After him, Gordian became emperor for six years. The year 2255: Anterus served in the church of Rome for one month [?].
After him, Saint Fabian served for twelve years. Now let us say a little about how this Saint Fabian came to office.
For when the holy bishop Anterus died, everyone was eagerly seeking this position of leadership, and bishops gathered from every region,
along with priests and monks, in Rome, to appoint a bishop for it. There were also well-known and distinguished men there,
in whom many placed their hopes concerning this matter. One person wanted one candidate, while another praised another.
Fabian, however, had not entered anyone's mind. He happened to come from a country estate outside the city.
Along with others who were with him, he had come forward, like everyone else, to see what was happening. When he approached and arrived,
suddenly it flew down from above in the bodily form of a dove and settled on his head.
Immediately all the people cried out as if with one voice, “He is worthy!” So they took him and seated him on the episcopal throne.
The year 2260: Gordian was killed in Parthia. After him, Philip became emperor for seven years.
During Philip’s reign, a thousand years were completed, and the millennial games were celebrated.
Wild animals were killed, and a theatrical spectacle was held on the Field of Mars for three days and three nights.
It was said of him that he was a Christian, and on another day of Easter he wanted to join the people in prayer.
Bishop Fabian would not allow him this until he confessed and counted himself among those doing penance because of their sins. He said [?] he would receive him. But
he did this because of the many accusations against him. He complied wholeheartedly, as is reported of him.
Through his actions he demonstrated the sincere devotion he had to the fear of God. Thus they received him, and he entered the church.
In the year 2264, Dionysius became bishop of Alexandria, for seventeen years.
In the year 2267, the faithful emperor Philip was killed along with his sons, and Decius reigned for one year and three months.
Now this Decius killed the faithful and God-fearing Philip and his sons because of the hostility he had toward Philip.

Because that holy man was suppressing and overthrowing the worship of idols, his hostility toward him inflamed his anger against us too. He launched a persecution against the holy shepherds of the church
and against all the people in it. He uprooted, demolished, and scattered churches and sanctuaries, and shed the blood of the church’s children. In this persecution the following suffered martyrdom:
Saint Fabian, bishop of Rome; Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem; and Dionysius of Alexandria.
Origen also suffered greatly. Priests, ascetics, and lay believers beyond counting suffered martyrdom in this year.
He also left his own place, driven by the blazing anger of the demon upon him, to travel through all the regions and persecute all the believers.
He reached as far as the city of Ephesus. There he committed more evil deeds than in any of the other cities.
So I want to pause here in my account and relate a little of the many evil deeds committed in this city of Ephesus.
The account of Ephesus and of the eight young men who suffered martyrdom there.
When the wicked Decius had become emperor and had come down to Byzantium and the city of Ephesus from the city of Carthage,
the churches of the region were closed, and the congregations of believers were dispersed. The priests and the brothers were afraid and fled from him.
When Decius entered Ephesus, his heart grew proud, and he began building altars in the middle of the city. As he grew more vehement in his paganism,
he gave orders to the city’s leaders, and they sacrificed to the idols with him. He defiled their bodies with sacrifices.
Every day dense crowds gathered from everywhere in the middle of the city of Ephesus, and the smoke from the filth of the sacrifices covered the city.
A dark cloud of fumes from the burning filth rose from the middle of the city and covered its surrounding walls.
During that dismal pagan festival assembled there, the believers were in great mourning. Their heads were bowed, and they remained covered and sighed.
They covered their faces with a veil for fear of persecution. Suddenly, on the third day, the emperor ordered the Christians to be arrested.
The pagans and Jews accompanied the soldiers, dragging the believers out of gardens and hiding places.
With great brutality they brought them to the place where the crowds had gathered with the king for the sacrifices.
Those who feared the tortures and the shadows of death slipped and fell away from the truth and from the triumphant height of life in the faith.
They turned aside and readily offered sacrifices before everyone. When the believers heard these things, they groaned over the destruction of the souls of the fearful.
But those who were strong and stood firm against the sufferings of the time for Christ’s sake stood courageously on the unshakable rock of truth.
The burning arrows of the Evil One were lodged in their bodies as in a shield. They endured tortures and afflictions.
The beauty of their bodies was destroyed and cast like dung upon the ground, and the limbs of their bodies were cut off.
They were hung on the towers and upper parts of the wall. Their heads, too, were fastened to wooden stakes all around the city gate.
Ravens and other birds, together with kites and crows, flew over the city, carrying away and eating scraps from the bodies of the saints.
Great mourning spread over the limbs of the believers, and bitter sorrow was fixed in the minds of the zealous.
Terror and fear gripped everyone. This was a battle that inspired astonishment. This was a contest that filled its spectators with terror.
This was an astonishing struggle, at which those above and those below were amazed. The foundations of the buildings groaned over the agony taking place within them.
The roofs of the buildings also wailed, compelled to bite themselves because of the cries of suffering that grew intense beneath them.
The streets of the city were in pain. From the dragging of the Christians, the streets of the city were in pain.
Because of the dragging of the Christians who were dragged over them. Tears welled up in eyes
over the corpses of their loved ones, which they saw with birds of every kind settling upon them.
The city walls trembled as though about to fall, while the bodies of the saints lay heaped upon them. What suffering could have been harsher than this?
The believers informed against one another to escape from merciless men. Fathers disowned their sons.
Sons would not acknowledge their fathers. Friends distanced themselves from their friends because of the affliction that surrounded them.
But faith in Christ was being built up through affliction, and the victorious were tested in truth and by the proving of their endurance.
Now Maximilian, Iamblichus, Martellus, Dionysius, John, Serapion, Exacustodianus, and Antoninus were firmly established in faith in the Son of God,
and bore the suffering of his cross in their bodies. As they saw these things every day, they sighed, and their faces were gloomy with sorrow.
The radiance of their faces grew dim and disfigured. They remained at the gate in vigil, fasting, and prayer, uttering supplications.
For they were soldiers and members of the king’s palace, leaders and prominent men of the city itself.
At the time of the sacrifices, [?] the king and the crowds were taking part, these believers would steal some time and go into the archive building.
They lay face down on the ground, lowering their bellies to the earth. With tears and prayers they groaned before God, and they put dust on their heads. But he waited for a time, the sons of [?]
and their appearance. At the time of the sacrifices, when everyone was seen in the temple of the idols, he went in [?] and found the blessed men alone in the house.
Their bodies were bowed down upon the dust, their faces were laid on the ground, and their bodies were covered with dust and with the tears and weeping of their eyes.
The enemies of the truth came forward and accused them before the wicked king, saying, “Augustus, king forever,
through the peace of your reign you bring even those far away to the sacrifices of the gods. Yet look: those nearby rebel against your authority and despise your commands.
They act deceitfully in your service and profess the Christian religion in a secret conspiracy within the household of your kingdom.
Their leader is Maximilian, and his seven companions are sons of prefects,
prominent and well-known men of this city.” Then the king became agitated and sent men to seize them and bring them before him.
There were tears in their eyes, and the hair of their heads was covered with the dust of the ground on which they had been bowing down in supplication before God.
The king said to them, “Why did you not remain with us at the peace offerings to the gods of the whole world, to whom we were making offerings?
Why did you not join the leaders and the executioner of the people of your city? Now come forward and joyfully perform the sacrifice,
as everyone is obliged to do for the gods.” Then Maximilian, together with his blessed companions, answered and said,
“We have a mighty God, who fills heaven and earth. To him we offer the hidden and pure sacrifices of our thanksgiving.
We offer the incense of the praise of our tongues to the [?] of his being, with integrity of mind, and through the utterance of our supplication we continually appear before him. We,
therefore, do not offer the incense of filthy smoke before idols. Nor can we [?] our souls and the purity of our bodies with the impure [?] before demons.”
Then the king spoke with all of them through a succession of questions, and this was the confession they professed.
The king gave orders, and the belts of eight of them were cut off. He said to them, “Since you now dispute the sovereignty of our gods,
you are hereby excluded from the high rank of service in our kingdom, until I have an opportunity and you are examined rationally before me through questions about your statements.
Now I am giving you an opportunity to think and live.” He gave orders to remove the iron chains from their shoulders and had them taken out of his presence.
Decius himself went out to visit other cities, intending afterward to return to Ephesus.
Then Maximilian and his companions had an opportunity to carry out deeds of [?] in accordance with their faith. They took gold and silver from their fathers’ houses,
and they gave alms to the poor, both secretly and openly. They consulted one another and said, “Let us leave the inhabited part of this city
and go to the great cave on Mount Anchilus. There let us continually appear before God in supplication, without the disturbance of the world
and without the turmoil caused by human hands, until the king returns and we appear before him. Let us not cease praising God,
and let him carry out his will toward us.” This whole beautiful crown of believers agreed to this plan.
There were eight of them in all. They put [?] silver in a bag, took it with them, and went up
to the cave on Mount Anchilus. They stayed there for many days, lying facedown before God in prayer and supplication,
for the preservation of their lives. They appointed their companion Iamblichus, a wise and nimble young man, to run their errands.
He would change his clothes to look like a beggar, take money with him, and go down to the city.
He would learn what was happening in the king’s palace and give alms to the poor from the money he carried.
He would buy a supply of bread and go back up to his companions, informing them about what was happening in the city.
One day King Decius came to the city of Ephesus. At that time he ordered the palace guards to offer sacrifices, together with Maximilian’s group and his companions,
whom he knew and had in mind. Fear fell upon all the believers in the city, and they began to flee from him.
Iamblichus too became alarmed and left the city, taking only a little food with him. He went up the mountain to the cave, to his companions.
Alarmed and bewildered by distress, he told his companions about the tyrant king’s arrival in the city,

and that orders had been issued and they had been summoned, along with the palace guards, to come in and offer sacrifices before him. When they heard this, they trembled and became alarmed, and offered supplication before God.
With their faces pressed to the dust of the ground, with earnest pleading and bitter anguish, they entrusted their lives to God.
Iamblichus got up, prepared the little food he had bought, and set it before them. He had them sit down to eat, regain their strength, and prepare for the struggle against the tyrant.
They lifted their faces and sat together in the middle of the cave. With tears in their eyes and sorrow in their hearts, they ate that food.
It was sunset. As they sat grieving and talking with one another, they began to doze,
because their eyes were heavy from the sorrow in their hearts. But the merciful God, who always cares for the workers in his vineyard,
ordained for them a peaceful and pleasant death, in preparation for the wonder that was to be revealed.
Without being aware of their passing or the departure of their spirits, they lay down together on the ground, like people settling down to sleep,
and gave up their spirits, with a confession of faith on their lips and their money lying beside them, as they lay stretched out together on the ground.
The next morning the king called for them and sought them among the palace guards, throughout the city, and in every quarter, but he did not find them.
The king said, “I am deeply distressed by the departure of these young men, the sons of prominent men,
since they supposed that our royal majesty was angry with them because of the offense of their earlier transgression.
But the mercy of our royal majesty does not hold offenses against those who transgress and then return to the merciful gods.”
The prominent men of the city answered and said before the king, “As for the young men, [?], let your royal majesty not be distressed.
For wherever they are, they are still persisting in their insolence, as we have heard.”
And they had an opportunity to carry out their evil intention during these [?] in which Your Majesty had given them an opportunity to repent.
They distributed their silver and gold in the city’s streets. As for them, [?], and from that time onward they have not been seen. And if
Your Majesty wishes them to appear before you, let their fathers be arrested and put under pressure. Then they themselves will bring them before us.
The king heard these things and became furious. He sent men who seized their fathers and brought them before him.
The king questioned them, saying, “Where are those rebels who rebelled against the service of our kingdom,
despised our fearsome commands, [?] against the service of our kingdom, and also despised the worship of the honored gods?
Now I command that you die in their place because of their insolence.” Their fathers answered, saying,
“We appeal to your dread majesty, my lord, for we have not despised Your Majesty’s command, nor have we abandoned the worship of the honored gods.
Why do we deserve death in place of rebels who plundered our silver and gold and distributed it? They are now hiding in the cave on Mount Anchilus,
a place a considerable distance from the town. We are in danger, whether they are alive or dead, throughout all this time in which they have not appeared to us.”
Then the king released their fathers, and they left his presence. But the king considered what he should do to the confessors.
Without his intending it, God put it into his mind to block the cave’s entrance with stones, as a burial place for their pure and holy bodies.
He was not allowed to disturb the bodies of the sleepers, who were being preserved for God in his foreknowledge,
so that through their awakening they would proclaim the resurrection when they were revealed to those who doubted. The king said, “This is my command concerning those rebels:
because they rejected my kindly and gracious commands and rebelled against the worship of the gods,
let them be excluded from the glory of my kingdom, and let them never again appear before the gods. Henceforth, as for that cave to which they fled, let
its entrance be blocked with solid stones. Let their lives be tormented, and let them die in misery, imprisoned forever.”
The king and the whole city supposed that the confessors were alive in their confinement. But Antodorus and Arbus, the king’s trusted servants,
who were believers and Christians but concealed themselves out of fear of the king, took counsel together and said,

“Let us write the confession of those confessors on lead tablets. Let them be placed in a bronze chest, and let us seal it with a seal. Secretly, with the help of those who are piling stones at the cave’s entrance, let them be placed inside. Perhaps God will intervene,

and before his coming the cave will be opened by some means, and the pure bodies of the saints who were [?] in it will be honored because of the account of their confession in the document deposited at the cave’s entrance.”
These two faithful men carried out what they had planned. The document was sealed and securely deposited, in a secret shared by the two of them.
When all these things had been done, completed, and sealed through God’s working, King Decius and that entire generation died.
Many kings reigned in the royal succession, down to the time of Theodosius son of Arcadius, the faithful king.
If you wish, discerning reader, to take delight in this account of the blessed men, proceed to the time of Theodosius son of Arcadius.
For it was in that year that they revived and their resurrection was revealed. As for King Decius, when God shortened the span of his life,
and handed him over to those who sought his life, he was killed at Brutus. He received the torment reserved for the devil and his servants.
Gallus and Volusianus reigned for two years and four months. The year 2,269.
