Saint Cornelius was bishop of Rome for two years. After him, Saint Lucius held office for eight months.
After him, Stephen held office for three years. At this time the river that flows through Alexandria the Great changed and became blood. Shortly afterward it dried up, and its bed became dry.
When it had remained like this for many days, and people began to suffer and be distressed by the lack of water, then the merciful God made it flow,
and as it had done before. The year 2,270. Novatus divided the church and established the heresy of Novatus.
This Novatus said that anyone who had participated in any way in idol worship or sacrifices during the persecution carried out by Decius could not be received by the church.
He cited the saying of the apostle: “If anyone sins after receiving baptism,
a sin leading to death, there is no longer a sacrifice to be offered for his sin.” Because of this, a council of sixty bishops assembled in Rome.
They anathematized him and expelled him from the church, because he was unwilling to turn away from the position he maintained.
At this time, again, there was a devastating plague throughout the whole land, especially in Alexandria and Egypt.
It was so fierce and severe that people could scarcely manage to bury one another. It struck the pagans particularly hard, more than all other peoples,
because, whenever one of them fell sick, his relatives would abandon him and flee. They died, and there was [?] no one to carry out and bury any one
of them, so that the houses, streets, roads, and porticoes were filled with them. They lay rotting and putrefying, with no one to bury them.
The Christians, however, carried out and buried as many of them as they could, through the compassion of zealous people among them.
They buried as many of them as they could, paying gold, digging large pits, and piling them into them.
This greatly endeared the Christians to the pagans, since the pagans, according to their custom, did not approach the dead.
At this time a council assembled in the city of Laodicea. In this same year, Saint Demetrius received the episcopal throne of Antioch.
The year 2,271. Gallus and Volusianus were killed in the street of Flavinius.
Valerian and Gallienus reigned for fifteen years. The year 2,272. Valerian launched a persecution against the church.
In that same year, Shapur, king of the Persians, advanced against Syria, taking captives and plunder. Valerian went down to fight him with a large army.
When they met and fought one another, Valerian was defeated. His entire army was destroyed, and he himself was taken prisoner and carried off to Persia. There he served as a slave until his death.
The Persians devastated Cappadocia, and it was never inhabited again. They also took captives from the West and Mesopotamia, and devastated Cilicia and Antioch.
After Valerian was carried off into captivity, Gallienus gave the Christians relief. The year 2,273.
Saint Cyril became bishop of Antioch; and Eutychian became bishop of Rome for eight months.
After him, Gaius served for fifteen years. In Alexandria, Saint Theonas took office for fifteen years.
In Alexandria, Saint Theonas took office for nineteen years. At this time the Manichaean heresies, destructive to humanity,
entered the world. This Mani was an Arab by birth and a barbarian. He entered the land of Egypt and spread corruption, causing harm through his demonic heresy, foolish talk.
He lost his reason and went mad. He gave himself over to those who were like him, and wanted to take on the likeness of our Lord.
He proclaimed that he himself was the Spirit, the Paraclete, and exalted himself in his madness. He chose twelve disciples for himself, in imitation of Christ.
In the year two thousand two hundred (and seventy) and six, Paul of Samosata became bishop of Antioch.
In the year 2,280, Maximus became bishop of Alexandria for nine years.
In the church of Rome, Saint Dionysius took office. In Jerusalem, Hymenaeus took office.
In the year 2,272, a synod assembled at Carthage in Africa, in the days of the venerable and holy Cyprian of Carthage,
and Mar Stephen of Rome, Demetrius of Antioch, and Dionysius of Alexandria. In the year 2,284,
Paul of Samosata rejected the true teaching and revived the heresy of Artemon. A synod assembled against him at Antioch, excommunicated him, and deposed him,
because he would not turn away from the position he maintained. Domnus became bishop of Antioch in his place.
At this time New Antioch was built by Saturninus the general, who later also became emperor and was killed at Apamea.
In the year 2,280, Gallienus was killed at Milan. After him, Claudius reigned for one year and ten months.
At that time the following were well-known shepherds in the church: Saint Cyprian of Carthage; Stephen of Rome;
Firmilian of Caesarea; Gregory and Athenodorus, brothers and bishops of Pontus; Helenus of Tarsus; Nicomas of Iconium;
Hymenaeus of Jerusalem; Maximus of Alexandria; Theotecnus of Palestine; Maximus of Bostra; Eusebius of Laodicea;
and also Anatolius of Laodicea, renowned for his knowledge of the learning of the philosophers. In the year 2,287, Claudius died.
Aurelian reigned for five years and six months. In this same year, Saint Timothy became bishop of the church of Antioch.
In the year 2,291, when Aurelian was preparing to launch a persecution against us,
lightning from heaven stopped him. He was also killed by the new guard. Tacitus reigned for six months and was killed in Pontus.
Florian reigned for three months and was killed at Tarsus. Probus reigned for six years and four months.
In the year 2,292, Felix became bishop of the church of Rome for five years.
In the year 2,298, Saint Cyril became bishop of Antioch.
In the church of Rome, Eutychian held office for eight months, and after him Gaius for fifteen years.
In the church of Alexandria, Saint Theonas held office for nineteen years. In the year 2299, Probus was killed at Sirmium.
Carus reigned with his sons Carinus and Numerian for two years. Carus died in Mesopotamia.
Numerian was killed by him in Thrace. Carinus likewise was killed in the battle against Caranax [?]. After them there reigned—[?] 33.
Diocletian, for twenty years. In the third year of his reign, he made Maximian his partner in the imperial rule,
Herculius. In the year 2310, Constantius, the father of Constantine the Great, began to reign in the country of Arantia [?], for twelve years.
In the year 2313, Marcellinus became bishop of the church of Rome. In this same year, the land of Egypt rebelled.
A large Roman army came, surrounded the city, and afflicted it with famine. Now one faction was helping the Roman army,
and Eusebius was with them, and they were not shut up in the city. He enjoyed freedom of speech and a distinguished reputation with the Roman commander.
When Anatolius, the bishop of the city, saw that the people of the city were dying of famine, he informed Eusebius about this.
Eusebius asked the Roman commander to spare those who came out to him. When he agreed to this,
he informed Anatolius of it. When Anatolius tried to persuade the people of the city but did not succeed, he said to them again,
“Perhaps you will not oppose me in this: let the old men and old women, the children and the weak be allowed to leave the city,
so that bread may be available for those who remain.” Thus they dressed men in women's clothing, and they went out at night.
In this way he saved everyone who wished to escape death. In the end, the Alexandrians were defeated by the Romans, and those who had caused the rebellion were killed.
In the year 2316, Zabdas became bishop of Jerusalem, for three years. After him came Hermon. In the church of Antioch, Tyrannus became bishop.
In Alexandria, Peter became bishop. He later suffered glorious martyrdom in the ninth year of the persecution. In the year two
thousand three hundred seventeen, Veturius, the commander, briefly persecuted the Christians serving in the army.
From then on, the persecution intensified against all the faithful. In the year 2319, there was a violent earthquake.
Much of Tyre and Sidon collapsed in it, and many people perished in it. In the year 2320, the destruction of the churches took place.
In the nineteenth year of this reign, in the month of Adar, at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, Emperor Diocletian issued a decree, and it was published in all the cities.
In it he commanded that the churches be demolished to the ground and the books burned with fire, and that those who held positions of honor be disgraced.
Those who had been slaves and had been freed were to be deprived of their freedom if they persisted and did not deny their faith.
The leaders who presided over the churches everywhere were to be handed over to imprisonment and then compelled to offer sacrifices.
Some of the shepherds lost heart from fear. Others each underwent tortures: some were beaten, and others were torn with combs.
Others were put in frying pans. Others were thrown to wild beasts. Others were thrown into the depths of the sea. Others received their crowns through ice and cold.
At Nicomedia, Dorotheus, Peter, and Gorgonius suffered martyrdom. Together with countless others, they were killed by the sword.
Through [?] and [?]. Anthimus, bishop of Nicomedia, also suffered martyrdom, as did Lucian and Tyrannion, bishop of Tyre.
Silvanus, bishop of Gaza, together with thirty-nine others whose heads were cut off and who were burned in the fire. Pamphilus, bishop
of Caesarea. Peter, bishop of Alexandria, together with others: Potus, Dios, Ammonius, Phileas, and Hesychius,
and Theodore, bishop of the churches in Egypt, together with well-known men. In the lake of Sebaste, forty men received their crowns together.
These were leading and well-known men, and also nobles of that country. And in the ice they [?] in the fire. Saints Sergius and Bacchus:
The duke made them run on sharp iron [?]. After subjecting them to every kind of torture, he then cut off their heads at Resafa.
In the year 2321, Diocletian and Maximian withdrew from imperial rule.
And he appointed Maximian and Severus emperors in their place. There is a certain custom among the Roman rulers [?]:
whenever, for any reason—whether from fear of enemies or for any other reason—
one of them withdraws from government, he is to shave his head and go home, no longer having any involvement in the administration of the empire.
And under the law, if he keeps to himself, no one is to harm him in any way. These men did so and gave up the imperial crown.
In the year 2322, Constantius departed this world with great honor.
His son Constantine reigned after him for thirty-one years and ten months. Here I wish to pause my account briefly
and show what wonders God performed through his faithful servants, and what evils Satan brought about through those who served him.
This Constantius the Elder and his wife Helena were believers who feared God. Throughout their reign he persecuted no one. Instead,
they showed themselves gentle and kind toward everyone. Thus the honored Constantius completed his life and departed this world, while everyone acknowledged his kindness.
But his son Constantine did not follow his father's faith. Instead, he constantly showed himself a persecutor of the faith of Christ.
Even though he had a terrible affliction in his body, he would not relent and cease the evil of his persecution.
In his zeal for idol worship, he imitated Saul the persecutor. Thus he was full of threats and murderous intent toward all Christians.
As he imprisoned, killed, crucified, and stoned them, the affliction in his body grew still more severe. His whole body was full of leprosy.
And there was a foul smell, like a tomb full of corpses whose stench spreads in every direction. So it was with this man:
the stench of decay spread from him in every direction. Because of this, he was full of murderous threats against everyone who did not worship the gods,
on the grounds, he claimed, that they would give healing to his body. Every day he saw his body wasting away and decaying through the leprosy that afflicted him.
He sent and gathered to himself all the magicians, sorcerers, Chaldeans, and wise men, both those under his authority and those outside his authority. From the account of Constantine the Great.
For his whole body was covered with leprosy. The wise men whom he had gathered advised him to bring three hundred [?] young children,
slaughter them, and bathe in their blood. Then Constantine quickly sent out orders in accordance with their wicked advice
and gathered many children. He set out with his retinue through the city to go to the place where they were to be slaughtered, to bathe in their blood.
As he went, he heard the sound of loud wailing and lamentation, so great that the whole city shook. And when
the king heard it, he said, “What is this noise?” They told him, “It is the mothers of these children, mourning for their beloved sons.” Then the king turned back and stood weeping.
He returned to his palace, reproaching the wicked, merciless advisers, and said, “The lives of these innocent and pure children are dearer to me
than the health of my body. Besides, I am not even certain that if I bathe in their blood, I will be cleansed of my leprosy.”
The king ordered that money be given to their mothers and that they return to their own regions with great honor.
But the good and merciful God of the Christians, when he saw that he had done this, turned him toward himself.
While he was sleeping at night on his bed, he sent two of his disciples to him, namely Peter and Paul.
They appeared to him in a dream and said to him, “Because God has seen your compassion, that you spared the children, he has had mercy on you too.
He has sent us to show you a spring of water in which you can bathe and be cleansed of your leprosy. But send and have Bishop Sylvester brought to you.
He has fled to the mountain out of fear of you and hidden in a cave. He will come and show you the spring of water. When you go down into it, you will be cleansed of your leprosy.”
When the king awoke, he sent men to the place the apostles had told him about, and they brought Sylvester. The king rose to meet him and welcomed him with great honor.
He questioned him, saying, “Do you have gods called Peter and Paul?” Sylvester said, “Peter and Paul are not gods,
but servants of God.” The king said, “Do you have their images? Bring them to me so I can see them.”
When they brought them to him, he said, “Nothing could be more accurate than these images. For they appeared to me in this very likeness and spoke with me, telling me to send
for you and bring you here, so that you could show me a spring of water.” Sylvester said,
“They spoke to you about the water of baptism. If you believe in our God and go down into this water in his name, you will shed the leprosy [?] of your body along with the leprosy of your sins.”
The king said, “If I had not believed, I would not have sent for you.” Sylvester said to him, “Fast this week
and implore God to forgive you for what you have done to his servants. Order the church to be opened and the temples of the deaf and blind idols to be closed.
Order the Christians whom you have imprisoned to be released. Order that the taxes of those who have nothing be remitted, and give alms to the weak.”
The king did all these things just as he had been instructed. And when that holy day of Sunday came,
Sylvester brought the king to the baptismal font, saying to him:
These waters, O emperor, forgive sins and give heavenly grace to anyone who believes with all his heart, and they prepare eternal life for him.
When Sylvester brought him down into the baptismal font, because of the emperor’s great faith the whole font flashed like a torch of fire, and its sound was heard like a frying pan crackling.
All the emperor’s leprosy came off him, and it was seen floating on the water like fish scales. His whole body became like a [?].
Because of the change he saw in his body, he became convinced and believed in the forgiveness of sins and in the life of the new world.
Then, after baptism, [?] forever, the emperor began to say, “This is indeed the true God.
For if he were not the God who created me, he could not renew me again. Let him alone be worshiped, and let the error that has continued until today come to an end.” And when
he spoke at length about the fear of God, the worship of the one God, and the abolition of the worship of man-made gods,
his officials and the whole city praised him. He ordered that a large and spacious church be built quickly in Constantinople.
These things happened in the eighth year of Emperor Constantine, son of Constantius.
In the year 2324, Maximian, emperor of Rome, died, and his son Maxentius reigned for six years.
In the year 2325, Severus died, and Constantine took over his kingdom. In that same year he also defeated Maximian, emperor of the West.
Emperor Constantine himself took over his kingdom. He made Licinius, his brother-in-law, the husband of his sister Constantina, his partner in the empire.
Now Maximian, ruler of Syria, persecuted the Christians harshly and mercilessly. And while the Christians were being so mercilessly oppressed by him,
Now Maximian, ruler of Syria, persecuted the Christians harshly and mercilessly.
And while the Christians were being so mercilessly oppressed by him, he killed their shepherds and sent them into exile, and threw the priests and all the people into prison.

He demolished, uprooted, and tore down all the churches, altars, and sanctuaries to their foundations, and their possessions were plundered. And while he was thus tormenting the children of the church,
God brought an affliction of torment upon him, and it penetrated to his very life. For suddenly an abscess developed in the hidden parts of his body,
and afterward a deep sore, that is, a fistula. An incurable, gangrenous ulcer developed in his bowels,
from which countless worms continually streamed. Then, as he decayed, his appearance became an indescribable horror to those who approached him.
Then the physicians who could not bear his foul smell
were mercilessly put to death. While he lay amid all these afflictions, he realized that he was suffering these things because of what he had done to God’s servants.
He ordered those close to him to stop the persecution of the Christians immediately, and, by the emperor’s command, their churches were to be rebuilt quickly at the expense of the imperial treasury.
Everything taken from any one of them was to be restored to them, and their bishops and priests were to return to them.
Thus action swiftly followed the command, and they were adorned with greater beauty and [?] than before.
So when the Jews, the pagans, and all the nations saw their splendor, they all converted and became Christians.
They acknowledged that there was no other god besides this one. Maximian himself died while acknowledging God before everyone, and Constantine took over his kingdom.
For this same Maximian, the third, when war broke out between him and Constantine because of the persecution of the Christians,
and when the armies stood facing one another—that is, the tyrant’s army and Constantine’s army—
the tyrant himself was living in luxury at home. He received punishment from God as he deserved, and suddenly his whole body was wracked with pain.
He was tormented by severe pain, and he lay prostrate, wasting away from hunger. His entire body was being melted by an invisible fire.
His appearance was disfigured. Only his brain remained alive [?]. His eyes burst out of their sockets, and he was left blind.
While acknowledging that these things had happened to him because of what they had done to God’s servants, he breathed his last. Inner Armenia, unable to endure his persecution,
rebelled against him. He sent a large army against it, and the whole army was destroyed there. All the troops who remained pledged peace to Constantine without a battle.
God took vengeance on those who had sided with the tyrant, as they deserved.
For in the days of these tyrants there had been neither famine nor pestilence nor war, but suddenly all these occurred: famine, pestilence, and many wars.
The entire army perished in Armenia. Those in the villages [?] perished from famine, and those who had provisions perished from pestilence.
The famine became so severe that a measure of wheat sold for two thousand five hundred zuz.
Maxentius, the one remaining among these wicked men, who ruled in Rome, surpassed all his predecessors in wickedness.
When Constantine heard about him, he took pity on those who were being oppressed in Rome and called on God for help.
He advanced swiftly to fight him. Thus, when they engaged one, then two, then three of the tyrant’s divisions,
he defeated them with God’s help. When he reached Rome, they were distressed, fearing that because of the tyrant he might be forced to fight the Romans themselves.
But God dragged the tyrant out of the city as though in iron chains. When he fought and was defeated, he turned his back and fled.
He and those with him began to cross the bridge that had been laid across the river.
When they went onto it and it was full, the bridge’s fastenings came loose, and the boats sank into the great depths, full of men.
Thus this wicked man perished like lead in mighty waters. After his death, the people of Rome received Constantine with great honor.
Constantine granted freedom to all Christians in the eighth year
of his reign. At this same time, Queen Helena went down to Jerusalem to rebuild it and to investigate the discovery of Christ’s cross.
For a revelation about this had been given to her in a dream. When she went down to Jerusalem, she found that the original Jerusalem lay in ruins,
as was said in the prophet. There she diligently searched for Christ’s tomb, from which he rose after being buried.
Although it was difficult, she found it by God’s grace. I will briefly explain what caused the difficulty.
All those who believed in Christ held that [?] in honor after the Passion.
But their opponents covered the place over and even built a temple to Aphrodite there as an act of opposition. And he erected her statue over the tomb.
Seeking to erase the memory, [?] her statue over the tomb. Seeking to erase the memory of the place itself.
This, it is said, had been done long before and had remained in place. But it then became known to the emperor’s mother, and she took down that unclean statue.
She dug and uncovered that holy place. When she had cleared it and opened the tomb, she found three crosses in it.
One belonged to our Lord, and two belonged to those two robbers. She also found the board that proclaimed Christ as King of the Jews in different scripts.
But the emperor’s mother was greatly distressed because she did not know which was the honored cross. Now a woman from the district
had been afflicted with an illness for a long time and was already close to death. Macarius, the bishop of the city,
ordered that the crosses be taken and laid on her one by one. After those two crosses of the robbers had been brought to her, she gained no benefit,
but was still struggling, as before, about to breathe her last. Then the third cross, which belonged to Christ, was brought near. And immediately
that woman was restored from death to life and became well. In this way the saving cross was identified.
Then the emperor’s mother built a great church over the tomb. She built a new Jerusalem opposite the old one.
She divided the saving cross itself and honored a portion of it by placing it in a silver casket. She left it there for those who afterward wished to see it.
She took another portion and sent it to the emperor. The emperor also received the nails that had been driven into his hands.
The empress had also found these in the tomb and sent them to him. He made from them a helmet for his head and a bridle for his horse. And in time of battle
he used them. The emperor himself sent a great deal of gold to Macarius for the churches being built by his mother.
He urged him to advance their construction. She built a new Jerusalem. In Bethlehem she built a church at the place of the birth.
In Bethlehem she built a church at the place of the birth, and also on the mountain where the ascension took place. She was so humble in her own estimation
that she would even join the other women in the assembled congregation to offer prayer. Likewise, also for the virgins who [?] the congregation, she would offer prayer.
Likewise, when she invited the virgins enrolled in the order of the church to enjoy a meal, she served them with her own hands.
She placed cooked dishes on the table before them. She also gave much of her own property to the churches and to the poor.
After conducting her life in complete reverence for God, she departed from this world at the age of eighty.
They carried her body to Rome, the imperial city, and buried it there in the burial place of the emperors.
Here ends the historical account that we took from Eusebius, together with [?] that we gathered from many sources, as provisions
for the road along which we travel. Again, we draw from Socrates the historian. In the year six hundred and fourteen of Alexander, Edessa was overwhelmed by floodwaters.
Its eastern walls were breached, and it fell, and [?], and it swept out everyone in it.
This flood caused great destruction there among people and livestock, and throughout the plain of Edessa and Harran.
At this same time Constantine built the city of Drepanum and named it Helenopolis after his mother Helena. He also built Constantia.
He named it after his sister Constantia. In the year 2335, Licinius persecuted the Christians in the palace.
In this same year there was a great earthquake, which caused great destruction in many places. In the year 2342:
Licinius was killed, and Constantine alone held imperial power. In the year 2346:
There was an earthquake, and many places in [?] collapsed in it. The total number of years from Abraham to the twenty-eighth year of Constantine is 2,350 years.
From the Flood to Abraham: 942 years. From Adam to the Flood: 2,200 years.
From Adam to the Flood: 2,242 years. All the years together:
5,526. In the era of Alexander, this year is the year 657.
Again, the history of Socrates. Another account, arranged by chapters. In the year 610 of Alexander the Macedonian, king of the Greeks:
Arius divided the church, saying that God has not always been Father,
but that there was a time when God was not Father. Nor has the Word always been God; rather, he came into being from nothing.
For God, who exists, made the one who did not exist from what did not exist. For this reason there was also a time when he did not exist.
For the Son is a creature and a work. Moreover, he is not even like the Father in essence, nor is he the Father's true and natural Word,
nor his wisdom, as Solomon said. Rather, he is one of the works and things that came into being. He was made Word and [?] in a figurative sense.
He himself also [?] the Word in the strict sense and the wisdom of God, through which God made everything, including him. For this reason he too is changeable and mutable by nature,
as are all rational beings. The Word is alien, distant, and foreign to the Father's essence.
The Father is hidden from the Son. For the Word does not know the Father completely and truly,
nor can he see him precisely. For the Son does not even know the essence of his own being as it is. For he was made for our sake,
so that God might create us through him as through an instrument. He would not have existed beforehand if God had not wished
to create us. Someone asked them whether God the Word could change, just as Satan changed.
They did not hesitate to say that he could. His nature is changeable because he is something made. He further added and said, “If the Father begot the Son,
then the one who was begotten has a beginning to his existence. From this it is clear that there was a time when the Son did not exist.
It therefore follows necessarily that he has his existence from nothing.” The proponents of this heresy are the following.
Arius and Achillas, and Aithilius and Carpones, and another Arius, and many others with Eusebius of Nicomedia,
and Theognis of Nicaea. The first to fight against it was Saint Peter [?], bishop of Alexandria.
After him came Achillas, also of Alexandria, and then Alexander, in whose days the Council of Nicaea assembled.
In the year 615, the emperor ordered the temples of idols to be uprooted and the carved images to be broken. In the year 617,
Emperor Constantine arranged for notable churches to be built. One of them is at the place called the Oak of Mamre,
under which Abraham received the angels. The emperor learned that a pagan altar [?] had been set up at that place,
and pagan sacrifices were being offered. He ordered another church to be built in Baalbek, for the following reason.
The inhabitants of that city—I cannot say who originally became their lawgiver [?]—had this custom:
their wives were to be held in common. Because of this, there was disagreement among them about whose son a newborn child was.
For there was no way at all to distinguish fathers and sons. They would give their virgin daughters to strangers passing through, for them to have illicit sex with them.
The emperor worked to abolish this custom, which had prevailed among them from the beginning. By a fitting law, he raised them and their daughters out of degradation
and enabled them to know their family lineage. He built a church and ordered that a bishop and a body of priests be appointed there.
By such a means he did much to unsettle the evil practices of Baalbek. At this same time,
when he demolished the temple of Aphrodite at Aphaca in Lebanon, he put an end to the foul tables of bread that were held there,
which were called the Hilaria. In the year 618, the Indian people were made disciples.
We again recount how, in the days of this emperor, Christianity increased in every region.
For at that time the peoples of Inner India and of Iberia also truly came to Christianity.
I will explain briefly why I added the word “Inner” to my account.
When the apostles apportioned their journeys among the nations by lot, Thomas received the mission to the Parthians.
Matthew was sent to the land of Cush. India, which borders Cush, fell to Bartholomew. Inner India, then, India—
which borders Cush. Inner India, then, is the country adjoining it, inhabited by barbarian peoples
who use different languages. Before the days of Constantine,
the message of Christianity had not shone upon this country by any means. I will also explain the cause that now brought them too to Christianity.
There was a philosopher named Meropius, a native of Tyre. He had taken it upon himself to see this India [?] and give an account of it,
since he too was emulating the philosopher Metrodorus, who had done this before him. He took with him two boys who were his relatives.
who were themselves also trained in Greek rhetoric. He went with them to India. After he had traveled throughout the whole country and seen it all,
as he wished, he steered his ship toward a place with a harbor because they needed provisions.
For it happened that the peace treaty between the Romans and the Indians had been broken a short time before.
The Indians seized that philosopher and those traveling with him on the ship, and killed them all except these two young men.
But they kept the young men alive, taking pity on them because of their appearance, and presented them as a gift to the king of India.
The king, pleased with the young men’s appearance and recognizing their knowledge, took one of them, whose name was Aedesius,
and made him cupbearer at his table. He appointed the other, whose name was Frumentius, keeper of the keys of the royal palace.
A little later, when that king was approaching [?], he left a young son and his wife to manage the affairs of the kingdom.
The king’s wife asked them to take care of her son, who was still a small child,
until he reached manhood. When the young men agreed to her request, they immediately took responsibility for administering the king’s affairs
upon themselves. It was Frumentius who managed everything. They also took care to inquire about the merchants who came to that country,
so that, whenever they found someone who was a Christian, they could meet him. When they found such people and he learned from them about what had happened among them,
they then gave them permission to live in quiet places, so that they could perform Christian prayers there.
After a short time, they also built a church and made disciples of some of the Indians.
He arranged for them to gather with them for prayers. After that young man, the king’s son, had reached full maturity,
Frumentius and his companion handed over to him the affairs they had managed well. They asked him to let them return to their own country at once.
The king and his mother urged them to stay. But when they would not agree, he let them have their wish.
Then, out of love for their homeland, they departed from there. Aedesius, eager to see his parents and relatives, made his journey to Tyre.
Frumentius, however, went into Alexandria and informed the bishop there about everything that had happened to them.
He also told him about their journey to India and the hope that the Indians would accept Christianity.
He asked him to send a bishop and clergy there, and not to neglect people who were willing and able to receive life.
The bishop, considering what would be helpful, had Frumentius himself accept the office of bishop there, saying, “They cannot find
anyone more than you to whom this has happened.” Frumentius, having been deemed worthy of the rank of bishop,
returned to the land of India and became a preacher of Christianity there. He also built many churches.
He was granted divine grace, so that he also performed many signs and healed the bodies of many people as well as their souls.
At this time Antony the hermit and Paul, the first monk, were well known. They were well known. In Rome Julius the patriarch was well known.
In Antioch, Eustathius was patriarch; in Constantinople, Estanclus [?] was patriarch. In Jerusalem, Maximus was well known.
Also well known were Hosius, bishop of Corduba, a city in Italy, and Paphnutius, bishop of one of the cities of the Thebaid.
In the year 619, the holy Estrabilus [?], patriarch of Constantinople, died.
The holy Patrophilus succeeded him. In the year 621, there was a great earthquake.
It caused great destruction in many regions. And in the year 624,
war broke out between Licinius and the forces of Constantine. Licinius, who ruled jointly with him, held to pagan beliefs
and hated the Christians. But he shrank from stirring up an open persecution against them because he feared Emperor Constantine.
In secret, however, he plotted against many of them. After a short time, he even dared to harm them openly.
Already he was preparing for war in various places. And because it had by no means escaped
Emperor Constantine that he was doing these very things and other things like a tyrant,
Constantine was moved by this cause to great distress and hostility toward him. From then on they were fighting every day,
once the love that had clothed them in a mere outward show was cut off from between them. After a short time, they were moved to wage war against one another.
After they had fought many engagements at sea and on land, finally, near Chrysopolis in Bithynia,
which is one of the ports of Chalcedon, the tyrant Licinius was defeated and surrendered. When Constantine captured him alive, he spared him
and did not put him to death. Instead, he ordered him to live quietly in Thessalonica. And in the year 622, this tyrant
gathered barbarian men around him and devised ways to turn his defeat into victory. When the emperor learned of this, he became intent on bringing him down.
He gave orders concerning him, and he was killed. At this time Mani the heretic was well known. We shall tell where he came from.
But weeds also commonly spring up among good wheat, for envy loves to lie in wait against good things.
Shortly before the time of Constantine, a paganizing Christianity sprang from true Christianity,
just as other, false prophets followed the prophets, and false apostles followed the apostles.
For at that time the religion of Proclus, who was renowned among the Greeks as a philosopher, was presenting itself as Christianity
through Mani [?] of the seventh [?] of his history, in this [?] to us. Since his history is not complete, for this reason it seems
to me necessary to supply what was left out above. For it becomes known who Mani was and where he came from.
A certain Arab named Scythianus had a wife who was a captive from Upper Thebes. And because of this woman,
He lived in Egypt and was educated in Egyptian learning. He introduced the religion of Proclus [?] Pythagoras into Christianity.
He spoke of two natures, good and evil, as in the teaching of Proclus. He calls the evil one Strife and the good one Love.
This Scythianus had a disciple, Buddas, who had previously been called Terebinthus.
He handed over the books that had been composed [?] to those whom he was misleading through them. By name, however, they are called “Teachers” [?].
In religion, however, they belong to paganism. Mani urges the worship of many gods, since he himself was without God.
He teaches that the sun should be worshiped. He introduces fate and speaks of the transmigration of bodies. He openly followed the religion of Proclus and Pythagoras and the rest of the Egyptians.
He does not accept that Christ came in a body, but says that he appeared as a phantom. He rejects the Law and the Prophets.
He calls himself the Paraclete. He brings all these things that are foreign to the orthodox church. He even dared to call himself an apostle.
But for this falsehood and wickedness of his, he received the punishment he deserved, on an occasion such as this.
The son of the king of the Persians had fallen ill [?], and his father was, so to speak, moving every stone so that his son might recover from
that illness. He learned about Mani, and, supposing that the things he was boasting about himself were true,
he sent for him and had him brought as though he were an apostle, thinking that his son would recover through his hands. Mani went, clothed in that stolen guise he had assumed.
The king’s son was immediately entrusted to him. When the king saw that his son had now died in his hands,
he imprisoned him and was preparing to repay him with punishment. But Mani escaped from there by some means or other
and reached safety in Mesopotamia. But even so, the king tracked him down [?] from Mesopotamia.
He flayed him, filled his skin with straw, and hung it up before the city gate for passersby to see, for [?] and for an evil hour.
From the place where a person works, from there he receives his wages. In the year 636, the Council of Nicaea assembled.
These were the leaders of this council: Hosius, bishop of Cordoba, and Alexander, patriarch of Alexandria;
Julius of Rome, through his representatives, the priests Vito and Vincentius; Paphnutius of Thebes; and Spyridon of Cyprus.
More than anyone else, Athanasius, the deacon of Alexandria, distinguished himself there as a champion. The council cut off and expelled from the church Arius
and all who agreed with his views: Eusebius of Nicomedia, Theognis of Nicaea, Maris of Chalcedon,
and many others with them. In the year 637, Saint Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, died.
Athanasius, the deacon there, succeeded him. In the year 639, Patrophilus, bishop of Constantinople, died.
Saint Alexander succeeded him. At this time Eustathius of Antioch and Maximus, bishop of Jerusalem, were also prominent.
In the year 640, a council assembled in Antioch and deposed Eustathius of Antioch.
There was a great earthquake in that city, so that the whole city narrowly escaped being overturned and destroyed.
Because of the bishops’ dispute, the see of Antioch remained without a bishop for eight years. Then one of those who agreed with Arius’s views was appointed.
Euphronius. In the year 641, there was an earthquake that [?] destroyed many places.
In the year 643, Aitallaha became bishop in Edessa. He built a cemetery and the eastern side of the church.
In the year 642, Constantine made his sons Caesars. He placed Constantine, his eldest son, over the eastern territories.
He built Tella-Mauzalat in Mesopotamia and named it Constantinople after himself.
He also built Amida, the city in Mesopotamia. He made the second son king over the western territories; his name was
Constantius. The third, whose name was Constans, he placed in Rome.
In the year 640 [?], unjustly [?] to him [?]. And because it is not right that [?] in silence [?], I will tell you a little about him, with a hint and a brief digression.
[?] this [?] Satan, who always made these people his instruments, [?] for their destruction, these [?] in them [?] and his deeds.
At that time there arose in the Church Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, and Theognis, bishop of Nicaea. These men should not be called bishops,
but slanderers—that is, the Antichrist himself—because of the divisions, disputes, disturbances, and many evils he caused in the holy Church and among God’s people.
Because these men had embraced Arius’s views, they inflicted many evils on Saint Athanasius of Alexandria and Paul of Constantinople, because they had not accepted the wicked Arius.
They plotted against him and presented an accusation to the emperor: he had seized what the emperor had allotted for the [?] of the poor of Alexandria.
They plotted against him again and presented an accusation to the emperor, saying that he was unwilling to supply [?] the wheat sent from Alexandria to the public treasury. After this they also said
that he wanted to plot against the imperial government. They also brought a dead man’s hand and said that he kept it and practiced divination with it.
In the year 645, the emperor ordered a council of bishops to assemble in Tarsus.
He also ordered them to assemble from there in New Jerusalem, and there, there to investigate Athanasius’s case thoroughly. But Saint Athanasius was found innocent on every count.
For the appearance of Arsenius demonstrated this and bore witness to it. He also showed both his hands, which had not been cut off from his body.
For they had been saying that the hand was his. But God brought Arsenius himself to the council, even against his will,
because he wanted him to see with his own eyes the plot he had devised. In the year 644,
New Jerusalem was built by Empress Helena, the wife of Constantius and the mother of Constantine the Great.
In the year 646, Saint Athanasius was sent into exile, not on account of the faith,
but through the plot the bishops devised against him because he had not accepted Arius. All the years are counted together from the fifteenth year
of Tiberius and the manifestation of our Savior up to the twenty-eighth year of Emperor Constantine.
646 years. And from the second year of Darius, in which the temple in Jerusalem was restored:
855 years. From Solomon and the first building of the temple in Jerusalem: 1,367 years.
From Moses and Cecrops, the first king of the Athenians: 1,845 years.
From Abraham and the reign of Ninus and Semiramis: 2,350 years. From the Flood until Abraham:
942 years. From Adam until the Flood: 2,242 years.
The entire span of these years amounts to 5,034. The year 646.
Arius was admitted into the church. The emperor ordered Alexander of Constantinople to receive him into communion.
That wicked man Eusebius of Nicomedia also threatened him, saying that if he did not receive Arius, he would have him deposed.
But the holy man ran to the holy altar and stretched himself out on his face beneath the holy table.
He said this in his prayer: if the faith of Arius was going to be established, then, as for himself and that day appointed for the petition—
may he neither reach it nor see it. But if the faith that he himself held was the true one,
may Arius quickly pay the penalty for his wickedness, since he was the cause of all the evil.
Arius, however, wanted to deceive the church and the emperor as well. He wrote on a sheet as though he were a believer, and this very sheet he was carrying beneath his armpit
when he swore an oath to the emperor, saying, “I truly believe this, just as it is written,”
while he handed the emperor the statement of faith written on another sheet. It was Saturday, and the emperor ordered that he be received into communion.
For when he went out to go to Alexander [?] to Eusebius, with the honor of [?], he was escorted [?] of the city.
When he approached the square called the Forum of Constantine, where the column called the Purple Column stands,
Arius was suddenly seized by a certain fear arising from his conscience. Along with the fear came weakness and looseness of the bowels.
He asked about a latrine and learned where one was located. Immediately he went behind the forum to relieve his bowels.
At once severe distress seized him, and much blood came out along with his excrement.
After this, a discharge of pieces of his intestines also came out. Along with these, his spleen and liver also came loose. And so he died immediately.
That latrine still existed up to the present in Constantinople, in the portico called the Butchers’ Portico. Everyone who comes to it points a finger at it,
as they tremble at the memory of his death—the man to whom Alexander’s prayer did such things. The year 649.
Constantine the Great died, and his sons inherited his kingdom. He lived for sixty-five years, and of these he reigned for thirty-three
years. In this same year, the holy Mar Jacob, bishop of Nisibis, also departed from this world.
In the year 650, Eusebius of Nicomedia stirred up unrest in the church over the faith of Arius.
In this same year, Saint Athanasius returned to Alexandria. In the year 651, Eusebius of Caesarea died.
Acacius succeeded him. In the year 652, Saint Alexander of Constantinople died.
Those who followed the teaching of Arius appointed Macedonius in his place, while those who adhered to the expression “of one substance” appointed Paul.
In the year 653, Paul was expelled from Constantinople, and the emperor brought Eusebius of Nicomedia there.
In the year 654, Eusebius of Nicomedia assembled a council at Antioch and established a creed other than that of Nicaea.
He expelled Athanasius from Alexandria and appointed Gregory in his place. He supported Gregory through the Romans.
In the year 655, this Eusebius died, and all the people seated Paul on the episcopal throne. The Arians seated Macedonius.
In the year 660, the cities of Amid and Tella were built [?] Constantine the Younger. In the year 661,
war broke out between Constantine the Younger and his brother Constantius. Constantine was killed, and Constantius and Constans inherited his empire. In the year six hundred
and sixty-two, Ar[?] was sent by the emperor to remove Paul from the church. The people of Constantinople killed him.
In the year [?] and sixty-three, the Arians removed Gregory from Alexandria and appointed George in his place.
In the year 664, Paul left Constantinople, and the emperor installed Macedonius in his place.
While they were bringing him in, 3,150 men from among the city's people were killed.
In the year 667, the council at Sardica assembled.
It confirmed Paul's and Athanasius's right to their episcopal thrones. In the year 668, Athanasius went down to Alexandria.
As he was going down, Maximus of Jerusalem assembled a council, and they united with one another. At this time Ephrem the teacher also became known.
In the year 670, Vetranio and Magnentius rebelled in Rome and killed Emperor Constans. In this same year,
Paul and Athanasius were removed from their episcopal thrones. As Paul was being taken away, those escorting him strangled him at night in the city of Cucusus.
Athanasius fled and escaped. Lucius of Adrianople also died in prison, bound in heavy iron chains.
When Macedonius took control of the church, he committed great evils and many murders among those who professed “of one substance,”
such as not even the idol-worshiping tyrants had committed. But the wickedness of George of Alexandria grew greater than that of Macedonius.
For after the seven days of the Feast of Unleavened Bread, virgins were being led to
prison. Bishops were being brought in chains by the Romans. The homes of orphans and widows were being plundered,
and many murders were taking place everywhere. At this time Bishop Photinus arose and split the church.
He renewed the faith of Sabellius and Paul of Samosata. For this reason the emperor ordered a synod to assemble at Sirmium.
He introduced another faith, but even on this they did not agree with one another. For this reason the emperor ordered all the bishops of the West to assemble at Ariminum.
The Eastern bishops assembled at Nicomedia. A great earthquake struck it, and it collapsed and buried its inhabitants.
For this reason they assembled at Seleucia in Isauria, but these too did not agree with one another. Year 671.
There was a battle near Mursa between the usurper Magnentius and Emperor Constantius. Magnentius was defeated.
His army was destroyed, and he fled. In the year 672, Aetius the heretic arose and threw the church into turmoil.
The emperor gave an order, and a synod assembled at Milan. More than three hundred bishops gathered there.
When Paulinus, bishop of Tiberias in Galilee, Eusebius of Arcalon, and Dionysius of Alba realized
that they wanted to depose Athanasius, they stood up forcefully and prevented the assembly from doing this. In this same year,
Abraham, bishop of Edessa, died. Barses came from Harran to Edessa by order of the emperor. Year 673.
Macedonius was expelled, and Saint Meletius took his place. He was the one who, a little
later, received the see of Antioch. In this same year Emperor Constantius died, and Julian succeeded him.
He lived forty-five years, and reigned for thirty-eight of them. Again, at this same time,
Apollinaris arose and divided the church, making his heresy known. At first he said that God the Word did not assume a soul in becoming human.
And afterward, like those who [?] this through a change of mind, God [?]; it had no mind, however. Rather, God the Word himself was [?] (in place of a mind) in the human being who was assumed.
Those who are called by this name say that they differ from us only on this point. They say, however, that the Trinity is of one substance.
Macedonius also divided the church. He dared to say that he was unwilling to include the Holy Spirit in theological discussion of the Trinity.
Eustathius of Sebaste also said, “I do not even dare to call the Holy Spirit God.”
For this reason, those who confess the doctrine of one substance call them “fighters against the Holy Spirit.”
Year 674. A severe persecution came upon the church at the hands of the wicked Julian, and many people were martyred.
Because the persecution was chaotic, many perished in it. Eusebius, bishop of Rome, and all its leading men stood
firmly in their struggles. He endured many tortures at the hands of the tyrant, but he did not die.
Maximus, the son of the prefect of Constantinople, Theodore the confessor, and Elpidius the military commander were martyred.
In the land of the Samaritans, a large number of monks who were going to prayer were martyred, because Samaritans and Jews attacked them and killed them all with clubs.
Emperor Julian compelled the Jews to offer sacrifices, and they did so. They asked the emperor to have their temple in Jerusalem rebuilt.
And he ordered them to build it and to have their expenses paid from the public treasury. Because of this, they quickly prepared everything.
Stones and timber, fired bricks, lime instead of clay, and the other things needed for the building.
But when Saint Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, saw these things, he prophesied and said that it was time for the saying of our Savior to be fulfilled:
“No stone will be left here upon another.” Saint Cyril foretold these things. During the night there was a great earthquake,
so that the stones of the temple’s ancient foundations came up, and all of them were scattered by the violence of the earthquake.
Even the houses near the site were uprooted, and news of that destruction spread throughout the land.
Then, on the following day, fire came down from heaven and destroyed all the work of the architects and builders, together with the tools of the other trades.
Then one could see sledgehammers, tongs, axes, and pickaxes burning in the flames of the fire,
and, in short, everything they had prepared for the building. All day long the fire burned among the tools.
The Jews were greatly afraid. Although unwilling, they acknowledged that Christ is God, but they did not do his will. Nor did the
third miracle that happened among them bring them to faith. On another night, impressions of crosses appeared stamped on their clothes in the form of rays of light.
When daylight came and they saw this sign, they tried every means of scraping it off and rubbing it away, but they could not. Now Julian, the uncle of the tyrant emperor,
went to Jerusalem and entered the holy temple. He even touched the sacred vessels of the church there. The Lord struck him, and he became infested with worms and died.
At this time the following shepherds were prominent in the church: Gregory the Elder of Nazianzus, together with his sons; Basil of Caesarea;
Maris of Chalcedon, who heaped great insults on the tyrant. Because he was blind, the tyrant said to him, “The Galilean will not heal you.”
Athanasius of Alexandria. Eusebius of Rome was also prominent, as were Cyril of Jerusalem and Metes [?] of Constantinople;
and Paulinus of Antioch; and Lucifer, bishop of the city of Pharhelion [?]. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, was also prominent.
Like a mighty pillar, he upheld and strengthened all the regions of the West through the teaching that the Son is of the same essence.
Vologeses of Nisibis was also prominent, along with Eusebius, bishop of Samosata; another Athanasius, of Ancyra; and Uranius of Qinnasrin.
At this time Saint Julian the Elder was also prominent. Year 674.
Emperor Julian went down into Persia and devastated the whole land from Nisibis as far as Ctesiphon in the land of
the Arameans. He deported many people from there and settled them on Mount Sanso [?]. In that same year he died in Persia from an arrow that flew through the air.
Jovian, the commander of his army, became emperor in his place. He made peace between the kingdoms and gave Nisibis to the Persians.
Through the peace he made, he also brought the persecution in Persia to an end, and all the churches were opened. The entire population of Nisibis went into exile at Amida in Mesopotamia.
He built walls for them to the west of the city. Year 675. A synod assembled in Antioch.
And it upheld the faith of Nicaea. In the same year an assembly was held at Gangra, and they deposed Macedonius and Eustathius of Sebaste.
In the same year Emperor Jovian died, and Valentinian succeeded him as emperor in Rome, and his brother Valens in Constantinople.
Valentinian belonged to the faith of those who believe that the Son is of the same substance as the Father. Valens, however, was an Arian, and he also began a persecution against the church.
He went down to Antioch and harshly persecuted all those who professed the teaching that the Son is of the same substance as the Father. In this same year Procopius rebelled in Constantinople.
In the same year there was again [?] a great earthquake, which devastated many cities. The year 676.
The sea crossed its boundary and caused such extensive flooding that ships sailed over places that had formerly been dry land, trodden by people.
But from other regions [?] it receded so far that dry land became visible.
The year 677. The usurper Procopius was killed. The emperor gave orders and tore down the wall
of Chalcedon, because the city had welcomed the usurper and insulted the emperor. The year 678.
Valens sent into exile all the bishops who professed the teaching that the Son is of the same substance as the Father, except Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus.
At this time Valens brought water into Constantinople. He intensified the persecution against those who professed that the Son is of the same substance as the Father.
The year 679. There was a severe earthquake in Bithynia, and the city of Nicaea was overthrown by it on October 11.
At this same time there was another earthquake in the Hellespont, and many cities collapsed in it. In this same year,
the holy Julian the Elder died. Also in this same year, the holy [?] Eusebius, bishop and martyr of Rome, died, and Liberius succeeded him.
Also prominent were Evagrius, bishop of Constantinople, Meletius and Eustathius of Antioch, Cyril of Jerusalem,
and Athanasius of Alexandria. At this time Eunomius divided the church, saying that God knows nothing more about his own nature than we do.
It is not better known to him and less known to us; rather, he knows about himself what we know about him.
And whatever he possesses, he in turn finds that very same thing in us, without any difference. Eunomius said these things and many others.
At that time the persecution by the Arians against those who professed that the Son is of the same substance as the Father became severe.
They insulted them, persecuted them, beat them, threw them into prison, and deprived them of their [?].
When they could no longer endure these things, they came to the emperor to ask him for peace, hoping to gain even a little relief from the oppression. But when
they thought this, their hopes were bitterly disappointed, for they imagined that they would find justice with an unjust man.
Eighty upright men were therefore chosen from among the priests of the church. Their leaders were these:
Urbanus, Theodore, and Menedemus. They came to Nicomedia [?] and presented a petition to the emperor, informing him of the oppression and abuses they were suffering.
The emperor became angry [?] with them and secretly ordered Modestus, the prefect, to kill the men.
When this man had received the order, he put them in a ship and lit a fire in it. In this way he burned them in [?].
At this same time there was a great famine throughout all the regions of Phrygia. Because of the severe distress, the whole population left the land and went to Constan[?].
In the year 680, Saint Athanasius of Alexandria died, and Saint Peter succeeded him.
Athanasius had administered the church for forty-six years with great care. The year 681.
Peter of Alexandria was persecuted, along with all the monasteries in the desert and all the monks there, by Euzoius of Antioch
and Lucius of Alexandria, the Arians. At this time the following monks were well known: Anthony, Ammonius, Pior,
Isidore, Pambo, Peter, Macarius the Egyptian, and Macarius of Alexandria. These last two were banished to an island
where there were many barbarian inhabitants. Through divine grace, they turned all the inhabitants of that island to God.
In this same year the baptistery of Edessa was built. After Liberius
of Rome, Damasus received the throne. After Cyril of Jerusalem, John succeeded him. The year 683.
Valentinian, emperor of the Romans, died. And [?] his son [?] Valentinian reigned again. The year 684.
The holy teacher Mar Ephrem died on June 19. The year 686. The Goths devastated the land of the Romans.
The year 687. War broke out between the Arabs and the Romans. At this time Mavia was ruling over the Arabs.
This Mavia said that unless she was given Moses as bishop, a man who was himself of Arab descent, there was no way for the war to end.
This Moses was renowned for his faith and asceticism, and he excelled in a chaste life and in miraculous signs.
For he had been brought up among the monks in the desert. Mavia asked for this man to become bishop of her people,
and on this condition the war would end. When the Roman military commanders heard this, they agreed to make peace on this condition.
They ordered that this be done quickly. Moses was taken and brought to Alexandria to receive ordination there from Lucius.
Moses [?], saying, “I am not worthy of the priesthood. But if this helps the public welfare, let Lucius not lay his hand on me, because
his right hand is full of much blood.” Lucius said that he should not insult him, but should first learn from him the character of his faith.
Moses replied to him, “Words are not needed. Rather, the things you have done to the faithful condemn you, showing that your religion is not Christian.
For a Christian does not strike, insult, or fight. It is not right for a servant of God to fight.
Your own deeds cry out through those who were sent into exile, thrown to wild beasts, and subjected to various kinds of death.
The evidence of things seen with the eyes is greater than that of things heard with the ears.”
When Moses had said these things and many others to Lucius, his relatives took him to the mountain to receive ordination from those who were in exile.
And so, through the episcopate of Saint Moses, the war between the Arabs and the Romans ceased, and peace reigned between the kingdoms.
In the year 688, Lucius was expelled from Alexandria, and Saint Peter returned from exile and occupied his see.
He died shortly afterward, and Saint Timothy succeeded him. In the year 689, the barbarians devastated the land of Thrace.
They reached Constantinople itself. Valens went out against them, and while fighting them he was killed by them.
Gratian took over his empire and took Theodosius the Great as his partner in imperial rule.
In that same year, all the bishops returned from exile and took possession of their churches. The Orthodox took possession of the church in Edessa, and Eulogius became their bishop.
He built the church of Saint Daniel, which was called the church of Saint Dometius. In the year 690, the barbarians attacked Constantinople.
Empress Dominica gave the Romans gold and weapons from the treasury. They went out against them at night, defeated them, and pursued them.
Mavia gave the Romans a large force of Arabs to help them, and it joined them.
In the year 692, there was again war between the Romans and the barbarians, and the barbarians were defeated by Emperor Theodosius.
In the year 693 of Alexander, a council of 150 assembled in Constantinople.
Its leaders were these: Timothy of Alexandria, Meletius of Antioch, Damasus of Rome,
[?] of Constantinople, and John of Jerusalem. These bishops were also prominent at it: Gregory of Nazianzus,
Gregory of Nyssa, Eulogius of Edessa, Helladius of Caesarea, Pelagius of Laodicea, Diodore of Tarsus, Otreius of Melitene,
and Amphilochius of Iconium. It laid hands on [?], confirmed the faith of Nicaea, and divided the provinces and patriarchates,
giving Damasus of Rome authority over Italy, with all the western regions and the upper regions of Gaul and Spain to be subject
to him. After him, it gave authority to Nectarius of Constantinople, with all the regions of Asia and the Greek East to be subject to him.
After him, it gave authority to Timothy of Alexandria, with Egypt and Aegyptus and all the interior regions to be subject to him.
After him, it gave authority to Meletius of Antioch, with Palestine, Mesopotamia, and all the eastern and lower regions in Persian territory to be subject to him.
In the year 694, Saint Meletius died in Constantinople, and they brought his body down to Antioch.
Paulinus succeeded him. In that same year, the emperor brought the bones of Paul the apostle up to Constantinople.
In the year 695, Emperor Theodosius built Reshaina in Mesopotamia. In the year 696,
Arcadius, the son of Theodosius, became emperor alongside his father. In the year 697, Saint Timothy of Alexandria died.
Theophilus took his place. In that same year, the usurper Maximus rebelled and killed Emperor Gratian.
In the year 698, Emperor Theodosius fought against the usurper Maximus and killed him.
And his army was destroyed. In this same year, the holy Eulogius, bishop of Edessa, died, and Cyrus succeeded him.
He brought the coffin of Thomas the apostle to Edessa. The year 699.
All the temples of idols in Alexandria were uprooted by the emperor’s command and through the diligence of Theophilus, the patriarch there.
In this same year, Evagrius became patriarch in Antioch alongside Flavian. And in the year 700,
the churches of the Novatians were taken over for the orthodox, and the priest who had been appointed
to oversee repentance was removed, and everyone was allowed to approach the divine mysteries according to his conscience. The year 701.
There was unrest in the church over Easter. In the year 702, Honorius became emperor. The year 703.
The usurper Eugenius rebelled. In the year 704, the usurper Eugenius killed Emperor Valentinian on his bed.
The year 705. [?] Eugenius in Gaul. But the emperor [?] great [?] called upon God for help.
But God, who does not neglect the prayer of those who fear him, did not neglect the righteous emperor’s prayer on this occasion either.
Rather, when he drew up his battle lines, a fierce wind began to blow, turning the arrows of Eugenius’s men back upon them.
It also carried the arrows of Theodosius’s men against them with great force. And the usurper himself was killed,
and his entire army perished in battle. The year 706. Emperor Theodosius died, and his sons took over his rule.
In this same year, the Huns entered Roman territory and devastated all the regions of Syria at the foot of the arid mountain,
namely Arzan, Martyropolis, Amida, Hanzit, and Samosata. When they crossed the Euphrates, the bridge collapsed beneath them.
The Roman armies gathered against them from all sides and destroyed them, and not one of them escaped. At this time, the people were shut up in the fortress of Zita.
When this scourge—the army of the Huns—reached the territory of Amida, all the people of the region fled and entered the fortresses
on the River Tigris and [?] the Daba, which are called the fortress of Great Zita, the fortress of Little Zita, and the fortress of Egil, that of Sennacherib, king of Assyria.
This great fortress of Zita stood between the Tigris and the Daba. The Daba flowed west of the wall, and the Tigris east of it.
They join one another south of the wall. The fortress is very difficult to attack and cannot be conquered, because it stands at a great height and has only one gate.
But the Huns seized the gate in the wall. They also stationed themselves at the water channels leading down to the Tigris and the Daba and seized them,
until the people inside were dying of thirst. Those who remained finally surrendered the fortress.
But the Huns, being merciless, slaughtered all the people with the sword, took the rest captive, and burned the fortress down.
That fortress was never inhabited again. Rufinus, the emperor’s prefect, was killed by the Romans while he was sitting at the emperor’s feet,
because, they said, his tyranny had been the cause of the Huns’ coming. The year 707. Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople, died.
Saint John succeeded him. This John was originally from Antioch in Syria.
He was the son of Secundus, [?] a leading citizen, and was a pupil of Libanius the sophist.
He was trained in strenuous disciplines by Saint Evagrius and Basil of Caesarea. Year 708.
Theodore became bishop of Mopsuestia, and Maximus of Seleucia. At this time Absamya became known
as a teacher. He was the son of Mar Ephrem’s sister [?] and composed hymns on the coming of the Huns.
Year 709. The people of Alexandria were thrown into turmoil by those entrusted with the priesthood.
These priests did not stop stirring up trouble among them; they rose against one another and trained themselves in wickedness.
The trouble had its origin in Egypt, over a question like this: whether God has a body and is in human form,
or is without a body and free of any human form. Over this question, many disputes and disturbances were stirred up by many people.
Some of them agreed with this assertion, while others maintained the opposite position.
This was especially so among the monks. Year 710. Severian of Gabala became known, and Antiochus of Acre.
Year 711. Epiphanius of Cyprus became known. Theodore of Mopsuestia, the interpreter of the Scriptures, also became known.
In the year 717, John of Constantinople was removed from his see, though not on account of the faith,
but because of his public rebuke of the empress. The empress herself died four days after John’s exile.
Everyone said that it was because of the injustice she had committed in deposing John (that this had happened). Again, in that same year,
there was a great hailstorm, the like of which had never been seen. Cyrinus, bishop of Chalcedon, used to call John wicked.
While the synod was assembled, Marutha accidentally stepped on Cyrinus’s foot. As a result, gangrene developed, so that because of this affliction the foot
had to be amputated repeatedly. The other foot also had to be amputated, because the disease spread throughout his body.
Because of this, many people were saying, “Cyrinus was punished, hail fell, and the empress died.” There was also a division in the church,
not because of the faith, but because of the injustice done to John. Arsacius succeeded him. He was the brother of Nectarius,
who had preceded John. Year 718. This Arsacius, bishop of Constantinople, died.
Year 720. Emperor Arcadius died. His son Theodosius the Younger succeeded him. Arcadius had reigned with his father Theodosius
for thirteen years, and after his father for fourteen years. His entire life was thirty-one years.
Year 721. Saint Theophilus, patriarch of Alexandria, died. Saint Cyril, his brother’s son, succeeded him.
Year 722. Diogenes became bishop in Edessa and built the church of Barlaha. In this same year,
Macedonius joined the church and accepted the faith that the Son is of the same substance. Theodosius was removed from his throne, and Agrippa took his place.
In the year 723, Diogenes died, and the holy Rabbula took his place. He built the church of Saint Stephen,
which had been a Jewish synagogue. In the year 724, in the month of Nisan, there were great floods
and severe ones in the Daisan, which passes through the middle of Edessa, during the night. The river's outlets became blocked, and the waters were held back.
It overflowed into all the streets. All the houses of brick [?] and mud became soaked and fell on their owners, suffocating them inside.
Apart from the houses reinforced with stone and mortar, nothing remained undamaged by the flood, except a few situated at the foot of the mountain.
Even in those mortar-built houses, many people suffocated in their lower rooms. When the wall was breached by the force of the flood,
it swept away houses, timber, reeds, people, and all the things needed for human life.
It caused even greater disasters throughout the plain of Edessa and Harran and along its entire downstream course, until it joined the Euphrates, than those it had caused in the city. At this time,
a great many pagans believed and were baptized because of the following event. There was a paralyzed Jew who had been lying on a bed for many years.
The whole art of medicine had been tried on him, and he had performed all the Jewish prayers. When none of these had helped him,
he sought refuge in the holy baptism of the Christians and believed that through this alone he would be healed. When this became known to the patriarch Atticus,
he instructed him and told him the good news about baptism in Christ. He ordered that he be carried on his bed and taken to the baptistery.
That paralyzed Jew received baptism with genuine faith. When he came up from the water, he was seen to be free
of all his ailments, and he leaped about with those who were healthy. This sign appeared at this time, and because of it many pagans believed and were baptized.
Again, at this time, the priest Sabbatius of Constantinople caused many disturbances in the church over Easter.
When Bishop Marcian saw the many disturbances he had caused, he said, “If only I had laid my hands on thorns rather than on Sabbatius!”
In the year 725, the holy Marutha, bishop of Martyropolis, was prominent.
He was sent by Emperor Theodosius to Yazdegerd, king of Persia, and made peace between them.
At this same time, the Persian synod assembled and confirmed the faith of Nicaea. Its leaders were Marutha of Martyropolis
and Yahballaha, catholicos of Ctesiphon. It assembled in Ctesiphon itself. After Paulinus of Antioch, Porphyrius succeeded him,
and after him, Alexander. In Rome, after Damasus, Siricius became patriarch there, and after him, Anastasius,
and after him, Innocent, and after him, Zosimus, and then Boniface. After him, the holy Celestine succeeded.
At this time, Rabbula of Edessa, Acacius, bishop of Amida, and Acacius, ruler of Samosata, were prominent.
In the year 728, Alaric the barbarian devastated Rome and took its inhabitants into captivity. In the year seven hundred and twenty
And nine. Theodosius killed Alaric the barbarian, and his entire army also perished in battle.
At this time the teacher Mar Isaac, from Amida, a city in Mesopotamia, became known. He wrote discourses about the destruction of great Rome.
In the year seven hundred and thirty, the Jews laid an ambush for the Christians in Alexandria and killed many of them.
The emperor issued orders against them, and they were all destroyed. Those who remained he expelled from the city. The year seven hundred and thirty-one.
Eutyches the heretic arose and divided the church. In the year seven hundred and thirty-two, a harsh, violent, and merciless persecution arose
against the Christians in the land of the Persians. In the year seven hundred and thirty-four, Saint James the Dismembered was martyred,
from Beth Lapat, a city of the Huzites. In the year seven hundred and thirty-five, Arzun was taken captive by the Romans.
For in this year a large Roman army came down, took Persian Arzun captive, and brought its people to Amida.
Saint Acacius, bishop of Amida, went out, took gold from the church of Amida itself, and ransomed ten thousand households from captivity.
He also ransomed the remaining nobles and sent them to their own country with ample provisions.
In that same year Ardaburius, the commander of the Roman army, fought a battle against Narses of the Persians. Narses and his army were defeated, and he fled.
In the year seven hundred and thirty-six, the Roman army came down again and attacked Nisibis. They reckoned it [?], after they had put the city under pressure.
He built movable wooden siege towers against it and advanced beside the wall. And many of those who were fighting on the wall
he killed. Narses, for his part, also prepared a large Persian army to fight the Romans. Narses sent word to Ardaburius
that they should fight by agreement and designate a place and a day for the battle. But the commander of the Roman army said to the messengers,
“Say this to Narses: ‘The Roman emperors do not wage war whenever you want.’”
While these things were being said, the Roman emperor sent a large army, wishing to defeat the Persians.
He also entrusted the entire war to God's hands and confidently took courage in this. Because the emperor believed in God, he quickly received help from him.
For while everyone in Constantinople was in anguish and great anxiety about what had happened in the war,
angels of God appeared near Bithynia to people who were traveling to Constantinople on their own business.
They instructed them to tell the emperor and the people to take courage, pray, and believe in God, for the Romans would be victorious.
They said that they had been sent by God to give the Romans victory in battle. But Bahram, king of the Persians,

when he saw that his army had been destroyed, that the region of Arzun had been taken captive, that Nisibis too had been subjected to the distress of a siege, and that war was upon them from every side,
prepared to come to battle in person. Since they were afraid of the Roman army, he hired Mundhir, king of the Arabs, and his army to come to his aid.
When Mundhir arrived with many tens of thousands of Arabs, he encouraged the king of the Persians.
while promising him that he would soon subject the Romans to him [and hand over to him Antioch] in Syria. However,
his promise was not fulfilled. For God [cast] fear upon the Arabs, and they thought that the Roman army was coming against them.
When they became panic-stricken and had nowhere to flee, they threw themselves, fully armed, into the Euphrates River.
About a hundred thousand of them drowned, together with their livestock. Ardabur also killed seven commanders of the Arab armies by treachery.
The others who remained were easily destroyed with God's help. An excerpt from the account of these eight young men of Ephesus.
Namely, Maximilian, Iamblichus, Martellus, Dionysius, John, Serapion, Exacustodianus, and Antoninus, martyrs and sons of the leading men of Ephesus.
At this time, a heresy of error and confusion brought forth falsehood and disturbed and troubled the church.
It sought to obscure the promise of [?], and they wanted to abolish the promise of the resurrection of those who sleep in the dust, which our Lord gave to his church.
Disturbing reports reached the ears of the faithful emperor. Even the idol worshipers who were in his palace
openly displayed false writings before him. And bishops who loved impurity, who were prominent and praised at that time,
placed great obstacles in the church. The leader of the disturbance was Theodore, bishop of the city of Aegae,
together with the rest of those whose names ought not to be mentioned in this account of the confessors.
For they disturbed God's church and troubled the purity of the faith through the perverse arguments of their words.
Then the mind of Emperor Theodosius himself was troubled every day amid weeping, and he fell into many anxieties,
as he saw the faith of the church being torn this way and that. For some of the heretics were saying that there is no resurrection of the dead.
Others, in turn, were saying that bodies that had decayed, decomposed, and been scattered would not rise again.
Rather, they said, only the soul receives the promise of life. These speakers of falsehood went astray,
and they did not understand that no infant has ever been born from the womb without a body, nor has a body come forth from the womb without a soul, the breath of life.
Their understanding became deaf, and they did not listen to the promise spoken by our Lord: “The dead who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and live.”
Again it is said, “Those who sleep in the dust will awake and sing praise.” Again it is said, “Those who sleep in the dust will awake and sing praise.”
Again it is said, “Look, I am opening their graves and bringing you out of their graves.” But the heretics, devoid of life,
had turned the sweetness of life into bitterness for themselves, and they troubled and obstructed the pure minds of the faithful.
Emperor Theodosius's mind grew weak; he became feeble and ill. He fell upon sackcloth and ashes in his bedchamber.
Then the merciful God himself, who does not wish anyone to perish away from the path of truth, wished to bring healing to sick minds
and to reveal the promise of life through the resurrection of the sleepers, who had been preserved in his knowledge for that time, and easily to cast out the sickness-causing poison from
