The peace of the church, and that he might shore up its structure against the turbulent waves and the weeds that had sprung up within it.
And that light and comfort might shine upon Emperor Theodosius, and that, together with his fathers, he might be crowned with the crown of victory.
Then suddenly God put it into the mind of Arlis, the owner of the land containing the cave in which the confessors lay,
to build a shelter there for his livestock without delay. Servants and laborers worked there for a day or two.
They rolled stones away from the entrances of other tombs, and they also brought stones for the building from the entrance of that cave.
On the night of the second day, when the entrance of the cave had been opened, the command of God, the giver of life, decreed life for the dead who lay within it.
And he who gives the breath of life to the infant enclosed in its mother’s womb, and that will which assembled and revived the scattered, dry bones in the valley,
and that power which called to the buried Lazarus and brought him out of the tomb (alive)—he himself, by the utterance of his mouth,
gave the spirit of life also to those confessors who had lain in the cave. They stirred and sat up joyfully, their faces radiant.
They greeted one another as they did every morning, and no sign of death could be seen in them.
For the clothes they had been wearing when they fell asleep were still just as they had been upon their bodies.
Their bodies and flesh were entirely intact, and they thought they had merely slept from morning until evening and then awakened.
The concern and anxiety of the evening still remained with them. They were thinking about what Decius was planning against them. And while

they were downcast and mourning, with tears in their eyes, they turned toward Iamblichus, who attended to their needs, and questioned him, learning from him what had been said in the city that evening.
He said to them, “It is as I told you: this evening we were ordered to sacrifice to idols.” Then Maximilian answered and said to them, “My brothers,
we are destined to stand before the fearful judgment seat of Christ. But let us not be afraid before the judgment seat of human beings,
and let us not deny the life we have through faith in the Son of God.” He said to Iamblichus, “Now it is time to buy provisions.
Take money, then, and go to the city. Find out what orders Emperor Decius is issuing, and come back.
That is, add to the provisions you brought us this evening, and come back, for they were hastily prepared, and now we are hungry.”
They thought they had slept only a single night’s sleep. Iamblichus got up in the morning, as he did every day,
and took some of the money in the purse, including coins of sixty-two and of forty-four from that period,
which had been minted in the days of the emperor shortly before the time of the confessors,
that is, three hundred and seventy-two years before that day on which the confessors awakened. At daybreak, when it grew light,
Iamblichus came out of the cave. When he saw the stones lying there, he was astonished, but he did not give any thought to what had happened.
He came down from the mountain and made his way toward the city, keeping off the road, because he was afraid someone might recognize him.
and bring him before King Decius. He did not know that the bones of that impure man had crumbled and lay in Sheol. And when Iamblichus
approached the city gate, he raised his eyes and saw the sign of the cross above the city gate,
which had been fixed high above it. When he saw it, he was astonished. He stole glances at it, looking this way and that in alarm.
He went back and forth, pondering and wondering in his thoughts. He went around to another gate, and there too he saw it and was astonished.
He went around the whole city, to all its gates, and saw that the sign of the cross had been fixed above every gate.
Even the city looked different to him. There were other buildings that he had never seen. He walked along in astonishment,
like someone seized by dizzy spells. He came and stood at the gate he had been familiar with before, and he marveled.
He said to himself privately, “What can this mean? In the evening this sign of the cross was kept inside the rooms,
and now, in the morning, it is placed above the city gate!” As he walked around, he gathered his thoughts and steadied his body, saying, “Perhaps it is a dream.”
Afterward he took courage. Covering his head with his cloak, he went into the city. As he entered the marketplace,
he heard many people talking to one another and swearing by the name of Christ, and he became still more afraid.
His thoughts grew confused. He stopped and said to himself, “What can this mean? I do not know.
Last evening there was no one who spoke openly in the name of Christ, and now, this morning, everyone's tongue is occupied with it.” He said to himself, “Perhaps this is not the city of Ephesus,
for its buildings are different, and the speech on its people's tongues has changed. Yet I know of no other city near ours,
nor have I seen one.” He stood there, wondering privately to himself. A young man met him, and he questioned him, saying,
“Tell me, young man, what is the name of this city?” The young man said to him, “Its name is Ephesus.”
Iamblichus, still astonished, said to himself, “Perhaps something has happened to me and I have lost my mind.
I must get out of this city quickly, lest I lose my way and perish, for dizzy spells have seized me.”
Iamblichus himself recounted all these things to us after he went up to his companions in the cave, when their resurrection became known and was recorded in a book.
Then Iamblichus, eager to leave the city, approached the bread sellers looking like a beggar.
He took money out of his purse and gave it to the bread sellers. They looked at the money and were astonished at the sight of the coin, how large [?].
They passed it from one to another, whispering and looking at the man. They said, “This man has found a treasure,
and it comes from ages and years long past.” Iamblichus watched them whispering about him and looking at him, and he became alarmed.
His whole body trembled with fear. He thought that they had indeed recognized him and were planning to take him to King Decius.
Others came up in front of him and stared. As he stood there, filled with fear, he said to them, “I beg you,
“Here is the money; I give it to you, and I do not want to take any bread.” But they laid hands on him and seized him.
They said to him, “Where are you from? You have found a treasure belonging to the kings of old. Show us, so that we can share it with you and keep your secret.
“Otherwise, you will be handed over to be sentenced to death.” He was astonished within himself. “You will be handed over to be sentenced to death.”
He was astonished within himself and said, “Look, the very thing I was not afraid of—even this
has been added to my terror.” Those men said to him, “A treasure cannot remain hidden, young man, as you imagine.”
But Iamblichus did not know what to say to them about this. They saw that he was silent and was not speaking.
They lifted his cloak and put it around his neck. While they stood in the middle of the main street and put pressure on him, word spread throughout the city.
The report said, “Someone who has found treasure has been discovered.” Crowds rushed out and gathered around him. They looked at him and said,
“This young man is a stranger, and he has never seen us before.” Although Iamblichus wanted to speak and convince them that he had not found any treasure,
because everyone was saying, “I do not know him,” he was bewildered and unable to finish speaking. For he had been confident within himself
and thought that he had parents in the city and a large, well-known family in the city of Ephesus. He knew and was certain
that in the evening he had known everyone, yet in the morning not a single person recognized him. Like a madman, he looked around to see any of his brothers or acquaintances, but there was no one.
While the [?] held him and he stood among the crowds, the city was thrown into an uproar, and word spread to the church.
It reached the holy Maris, the bishop of the city. At that time Augustus, the proconsul, was also being received by the bishop.
For God's will had brought them together, so that through their hands the treasure of the resurrection of the dead might be revealed to all peoples.
Both ordered that the young man be kept under careful guard and brought to them with the money in his hand. So they dragged Iamblichus away to take him to the church.
He thought that they were taking him to the emperor Decius. He looked this way and that
while the crowds laughed at him as though he were mad. And so, amid a great commotion, they brought him to the church.
The proconsul and Maris took the money from his hand and marveled at it. The proconsul said to Iamblichus, “Where is the treasure you have found,
seeing that you are even holding some of its money in your hand?” Iamblichus said, “I have never found any treasure, as you claim I have.
“But I know that the money in my hands comes from my parents' money and is part of the currency of this city.
“For I do not know what these things are that have happened to me.” The proconsul said, “Where are you from?”
Iamblichus said, “As far as I know, I am from this city.” He said to him, “Whose son are you? Whoever knows you should come and testify on your behalf.”
He told them his parents' names, but no one knew them. Nor did anyone recognize either him or his parents.
The proconsul said, “You are [?], and there is no truth in you.” But he stood with his head bowed, silent and bewildered.
And we were saying, “Perhaps he is mad.” But others said, “No, he is pretending to be mad so that he can escape this predicament.”
The proconsul looked at him angrily and said, “How can we consider you mad? Or how can we believe you when you say that the money is from your ancestors’ purse?
For look: judging by its inscriptions, the coin’s stamp is more than two hundred and seventy years old, dating to a little before Emperor Decius.
It has not been mixed with other coinage, and it does not resemble this currency that people use for buying and selling.
Did your ancestors live many generations and years ago? Look, you are a young man, and you want to deceive the elders and wise men of the city of Ephesus.
Now I order that you be handed over for imprisonment and flogging until you confess where the treasure you found is.”
Then, when Iamblichus heard these things, he fell on his face before him and said to them, “I beg you, my lords,
answer one thing that I ask you, and I will reveal to you everything in my heart. Where is Emperor Decius, who was in this city?”
Then Maris said, “My son, there is no emperor on earth today named Decius, except for one who died many generations ago.”
Then Iamblichus answered, with his face to the ground before them,
and said, “Now, my lord, anguish has seized me, and no one will believe what I say. Come with me, and I will show you my companions in the cave on Mount Anchilus.
You will learn from them. I myself know that we have been there for these past few days, hiding from Emperor Decius.
Just last evening I saw Emperor Decius enter the city of Ephesus. Whether this city is Ephesus, I do not know.”
Then Bishop Maris was astonished at this and said, “This is some revelation that God has shown through this young man. Let us go and see it.”
Maris rose, and the proconsul with him, and they mounted their riding animals. The nobles and officials of the town and the crowds from the city went with them.
They went up the mountain. When they reached the cave, Iamblichus went in ahead of them to the confessors, and Bishop Maris entered after him.
As he entered the doorway of the cave, he found a bronze box in the corner to the right of the entrance.
Two silver seals had been placed on it. He took it and stood outside the entrance, and called the nobles and officials of the town.
In the proconsul’s presence he removed these seals, opened the box, and found two lead tablets. He read them, and this was what was written
on them: “The confessors Maximilian, Iamblichus, [?], Dionysius, John, Serapion, Exacustodian, and Antoninus fled [?] from Emperor Decius.
By the emperor’s command, this cave was walled up with stones, shutting them inside. Their confession is written below.”
When they read these inscriptions, they were amazed and praised God for the wonders and extraordinary things he shows to human beings.
They all cried out in praise, and went inside and found these confessors sitting in radiance.
Their faces were like fresh roses. Maris and the proconsul fell down and bowed before them to the ground,
they and the officials and all the crowds, praising Christ their Lord because they had been found worthy to see this astonishing sight.
And they also testify to what he said about them, and to everything that he made known to Maris, the proconsul, and the city’s leading men concerning the days of Emperor Decius.
Immediately, mounted messengers were sent to Emperor Theodosius with a letter. He said to him, “Let Your Majesty come quickly and see the wonders that God has shown in the world during your reign.
For the light of the promise of life has shone upon us from the dust, and the resurrection of the departed has dawned from the tombs in radiant bodies that have been renewed.”
When Emperor Theodosius heard this, he immediately rose from the sackcloth and ashes in which he had humbled himself. His victorious spirit was strengthened, and he became radiant.
He stretched out his hands toward God and said, “I thank you, Christ the Son, King of heaven and earth,
because light has dawned upon us from the Sun of Righteousness, and the lamp of my confession has not gone out from among the torches of my ancestors.
Nor has the seal of my faith grown dim or fallen from the victorious crown of Emperor Constantine,
the believer.” And [?] the bishops and the emperor’s leading men with him. And swiftly, on horses and in carriages and chariots,
they came from Constantinople to the city of Ephesus. The whole city went out to meet the emperor, together with the bishops and the city’s leading men.
They went up to the confessors in the cave on Mount Anchilus. The confessors hurried to meet the emperor, and at the sight of him their faces shone.
He embraced them and wept upon their necks. He sat before them on the dust of the ground and gazed at them.
He praised God, while his heart thundered with thanksgiving, and said, “When I see you, it is as though I were looking at Christ the King
when he called Lazarus and he came out of the tomb. It is as though I already hear his voice at his coming in glory,
when the dead come out of their tombs to meet him without delay.” Maximilian said to the emperor, “From now on, remain in peace, in the fullness of your faith.
May Jesus Christ, the Son of God, protect your reign from the schemes of the evil one. Be assured that it was for your sake that our Lord awakened us before the great day of resurrection.
For we were like an infant who, as long as he remains in his mother’s womb, is unaware of honor or dishonor, pride or lowliness.
Although alive, he is unaware of death and life. So we too were quiet and at rest, like sleepers without a care.”
When they had said these things, while the emperor, the nobles, and the bishops were looking at them, they grew drowsy and fell asleep.
They laid their heads upon the dust and gave up their spirits at God’s command.
The emperor stood over them, weeping, and spread his royal robes over their bodies.
The emperor [?] that eight golden coffins should be made for their bodies. That very night they appeared to the emperor in a dream.
They said to him, “Our bodies were raised from dust, not from gold and silver. So now leave us in our own place, upon the dust in the cave.”
Then the emperor immediately gave orders, and golden coffers were prepared beneath them. He left them in their places,
where they remain to this day. With a great gathering of bishops, a great feast was held in commemoration of the confessors.
The emperor gave generous alms to all the poor of the region and released the bishops who were being held in exile.
And in the joy of his faith he returned, and the bishops also came with him to Constantinople, praising God, the Lord of the dead and the living.
May we too, together with them, praise and glorify the glorious Trinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, now and always, and forever and ever.
Amen. Let us return to the sequence of our narrative. Here ends the section of the account of the youths of the city of Ephesus...
Again. In the year 737, Helion went down to Mesopotamia to make peace with the Persians.
When Helion came to Mesopotamia and went down below Dara, he camped in the trench that the Romans had recently made there for their protection. He had sent as an envoy concerning
peace Maximus, a wise man. When he went to the king of the Persians, the king was readily willing to receive the embassy, because much of [?] had been consumed by famine.
But those known among the Persians as the Immortals did not allow him to do this. They numbered about ten thousand mighty warriors.
They said, “We will not accept peace until we go and fall upon them suddenly, while they are unprepared.”
He imprisoned that envoy and kept him under guard. He sent the Immortals to attack Helion and those with him in battle.
When they arrived, they divided into two groups, and one wing of the Romans was hemmed in between them. [?] One division of the Persians was drawn up against them.
For the other division of the Persians was lying in ambush behind them and was not visible to them.
For they fell upon them suddenly, and when battle was about to begin, the Romans were trapped in the middle.
They were close to being destroyed when suddenly a Roman force of about twenty thousand appeared from a hill.
They became aware of what was happening ahead of them—events brought about by divine providence. They were under the command of Procopius.
When he saw that his fellow Romans were close to being destroyed, he came up behind the Persians, and now the Persians were trapped in the middle.
He killed them all in a short time. They also turned against the other division that had been lying in ambush and slaughtered them all.
Thus those known among the Persians as the Immortals proved to be mortal.
Christ exacted vengeance from the Persians because they had killed many of his Christian servants.
When the king of the Persians learned of this disgrace that had befallen him, he pretended not to know what had happened.
He received the envoy and said to him, “It is not for the Romans’ sake that I am making peace; rather, I am granting you a favor.”
Thus the war with Persia was brought to an end for the sake of the Christians there. The Persians’ persecution of the Christians in their land also ceased.
In the year 739, Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, died, and Sisinnius succeeded him.
In the year 741, this Sisinnius died, and Nestorius took his place.
Again, in the year 743, Nestorius divided the church and the true faith, and said:
“It is not right for Mary to be called the Mother of God.” He also said, “I do not call someone who was one or two months old God.”
On how Nestorius stumbled and fell into an illness of this kind.
Let no one suppose that the troublesome Nestorius had any share in this [?] before this incident.
Otherwise, he would not even have been advanced to the patriarchate of Constantinople. Rather, what Scripture says happened to him: “There is a modesty that produces sins.”
When he wanted to honor his friend, he himself was dishonored. When he sought to lift him out of the mire, he himself sank into the abyss of destruction.
For he was a man untrained in reading the divine Scriptures. He happened to stumble in the following way.
He had with him a priest from Antioch named Anastasius. He held this man in great honor and consulted him on various matters.
One day, while this Anastasius was preaching in church, he said, “As for calling Mary the Mother of God—
let no one call her that. For Mary is a human being, and God cannot be born of a human being.”
When this was heard, it disturbed the priests and all the people. For from the beginning the people had accepted that Christ is God.
They had also accepted that his humanity should not be separated from his divinity in the incarnation. When such a disturbance arose in the church, Nestorius himself made every effort
to rescue his friend from such a blunder through one verbal pretext after another. Because of his friendship with him, he did not want to rebuke him as a blasphemer.
For this reason he wanted to confirm Anastasius’s statement. He delivered a sermon about this in church and began using it to uphold Anastasius’s statement.
Everywhere he rejected the expression “Mother of God.” Because of this, many divisions arose in the church.
Concerning the sermon Nestorius delivered in the church of Constantinople, the holy Peter the Iberian, who was an eyewitness to this event, says
what he testified before us. This Peter the Iberian was the son of the king of the Iberians.
Theodosius, emperor of the Romans, took him from his father as a hostage, so that his father would not plot against him. Emperor Theodosius raised him as a son,
together with Pulcheria, the emperor’s sister. When he grew up, he came to love the chaste practices of monastic life and left the royal palace. Later he became bishop of Apamea.
He testified as follows: “While I was still in Constantinople, before I renounced the world, when Nestorius was still alive
and held the episcopate, the commemoration of the forty holy martyrs was being celebrated in the church called the Church of the Mother of God.
He stood up to preach before all the people, close to where I was. He had a womanish but clear voice.
About halfway through his sermon, he began to blaspheme, saying, ‘Do not boast, Mary, as though you had given birth to God.
For you did not give birth to God, excellent woman, but to a human being, an instrument of God.’ As soon as he said this,
a demon came upon him up on the platform, so that his face and his right hand were twisted backward.
As he was sinking down and about to fall, the attendants and deacons caught him, carried him away, and took him into the sacristy.
From then on, most of the people withdrew from communion with him, especially those in the palace. I too withdrew before all the others, although he loved me very much.”
So this man stumbled and fell from heaven like the morning star. He did not turn away from his evil intention, because Satan had entered him.
In the year 744, the first council assembled at Ephesus. It anathematized and cast out the wicked
Nestorius, because he would not turn away from the position he maintained. The leaders of the council were these: Saint Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria;
Memnon of Ephesus; Juvenal of Jerusalem; John of Antioch. Also prominent were Rabbula of Edessa, Acacius of Amida,
and another Acacius, of Samosata. In the year 746, Saint Mar Rabbula [?] of Edessa died, and Ibas succeeded him.
He built the new church, which today is called the Church of the Apostles. At this time Saint Mar Barsuma of the region of Samosata was prominent,
as was Saint Simeon the Stylite. Also at this time, a great calamity and bitter destruction befell the Jewish people
because of a deception, as a result of which many of them became Christians. What happened to them was as follows.
A Jewish deceiver appeared in Crete and pretended to be Moses.
He told them that he had been sent from heaven to lead out the Jews who lived on that island and take them across the sea.
For he said that he was the one who had formerly led the Israelites across the Red Sea. For a year he traveled around the villages and towns of that island,
persuading the Jews who lived there to accept his words. He advised them to abandon their possessions.
He promised them that he would lead them through the sea to the Promised Land as though on dry ground. They were carried away by the hope these words offered,
and from then on they believed with all their strength. They even scorned their possessions, allowing anyone at all to take
whatever he wished. When the day that the Jewish deceiver had appointed for them arrived, he went ahead,
and they all followed him, with their wives and children of every age.
He brought them to a cliff on a mountain overlooking the sea and ordered them to throw themselves into the sea.
Those who went first to that headland did so and immediately died, some being battered and others drowning in the water.
Indeed, nearly all of them would have perished if some Christians, seemingly through God's providence,
fishermen and merchants who happened to be there, had not reached them and rescued those who were drowning. Then they became aware of their madness
as they lay in distress. Those who happened to be there stopped the others who were coming to throw themselves into the sea,
telling them about the destruction of those who had thrown themselves in first. When they recognized the deception, they reproached themselves for their hasty belief.
They also wanted to kill the false Moses, but they could not seize him, for he was nowhere to be seen.
Many came to believe that he was a demon clothed in human form, who had appeared to bring destruction upon their people.
For this reason, many Jews abandoned Judaism and took refuge in Christianity.
In the year 747, Maximus, bishop of Constantinople, died, and Saint Proclus succeeded him on his throne.
This Proclus brought the bones of Saint John from exile to Constantinople, and united
those who had been divided over him. At this time, John wanted to devastate the territory of great Rome with many barbarians.
As they were gathering and intending to devastate Rome together with all the western territories of Italy, the emperor heard about this.
As was his custom, he cast all his anxiety upon God and entrusted the entire management of the affair to him, persevering diligently in prayer.
He did not have to wait long to receive what he was asking for. For lightning fell from heaven, struck their leader, and burned him up, along with many of the barbarians who were with him.
The rest were destroyed by severe diarrhea and wasting disease. Finally, fire again came down from heaven and destroyed most of those who remained.
This caused great terror among the barbarians, who saw that the Romans were being helped by God, while they themselves were perishing without a battle.
And they withdrew from their land. In the year 755, Saint Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, died.
In the year 756, Dioscorus became patriarch of Alexandria. And in the year 757,
the second council assembled at Ephesus. The leaders of this council were these: Saint Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria;
Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem; and Julius, bishop of Cos, who represented Leo of Rome,
because Leo had not yet turned aside from the true faith of Nicaea; and also Stephen, bishop of Hierapolis. At this council, anathema was pronounced against
Paulinus, patriarch of Constantinople; Eusebius of Dorylaeum; Domnus, patriarch of Antioch; and Theodoret
of Cyrrhus; Ibas of Edessa; Daniel of Harran; and Sophronius of Tella. In this year, Pelagius, a priest of Edessa, prophesied.
He had been expelled by Ibas because he rebuked him for the wickedness of his faith. He said that Abba Peter the Iberian himself used to tell us
about the blessed Pelagius of Edessa, that he led a virtuous life.
He was a monk and a prophet. When, he said, he heard the blasphemies of Ibas, bishop of Edessa, he rebuked him openly and suffered greatly at his hands.
When he was persecuted by him, he came to the regions of Palestine and lived in solitude, while Juvenal was still alive,
before the council and the violation of the faith. Grace dwelt in him so fully that he was filled with the spirit of prophecy and frequently saw visions.
He used to visit Abba Peter, who was then living in solitude in the monastic settlement at Maiuma of Gaza,
because of the great love they had for one another. One day, while he was walking with the abba and discussing
thoughts and godly virtues, and in the powerful place [?] of the Council of Chalcedon, seven years [?],
the violation that was to be committed at Chalcedon by the bishops. He even named the wicked Marcian, in whose days and through whose agency it was to take place,
and the remaining things, one by one. He also said to Peter, “For me and you, Father, he has…”
For that time which is to come upon us, when we are persecuted together with all the saints, those who do not submit to consenting to the violation of the faith.
And so it will be fulfilled during the persecution itself. This indeed happened and was finally fulfilled, just as he had said.
Again he prophesied about Pulcheria, the sister of Theodosius and the woman who brought up Abba Peter the Iberian,
and about her war against the saints and her union with Marcian—this same Abba Pelagius the prophet.
As Abba Peter used to tell us, when he was with other saints in the elder’s presence,
he spoke again of another vision before the council. He began to say, weeping, “Woe to Pulcheria! Woe to Pulcheria! Woe to Pulcheria!”
When we had pleaded with him at length to reveal to us what he meant by these words, he said, “Pulcheria, who pledged her virginity to God
and cast down Nestorius, to whom all the saints everywhere used to write as to a holy woman and a virgin,
who stood at the forefront of the orthodox, will transgress against the faith and against her virginity, and will marry a man named Marcian.
And she will crush the saints.” This indeed happened, and his word was fulfilled. She violated her vows and the chastity she had pledged to Christ,
and married Marcian. She became an heir to his kingdom, his wickedness, and the torments reserved for him. He said, “After six years they will both die,
leaving no heir.” Again, this same Pelagius the elder spoke about Juvenal of Jerusalem,
as Pamphilius, a deacon of the church of Jerusalem, told us. He
was his friend and went in with him once to pray at the holy place of Golgotha, while it was still night.
For this was his custom. As he stood praying, he was caught up in a vision. Overcome by weeping and tears, he began to say, “Juvenal!
Juvenal!” Finally, when the weeping and the vision had ceased, the deacon Pamphilius questioned him, falling down before him in private,
asking what these things in the vision about Juvenal meant, and why he had kept crying out “Juvenal!” without ceasing, while weeping.
He said, “Just as you now see Juvenal escorted with honor by monks and clergy, so, if you are still alive here,
you will see him being led away by Romans and demons.” Elidius of the Cells also prophesied and spoke about the persecution and Emperor Marcian
before it happened. He also revealed concerning Dioscorus of Alexandria that he would not obey him and would be persecuted by him. John, a priest of Alexandria, told us,
the one known as being of the house of Tatian, a well-known and distinguished man: “When I was a boy, I had a desire to renounce the world.
And when I had [?] to visit Abba Elidius, the prophet of the Cells, I hurried to him to reveal my desire to him
and learn from him whether the Lord would bring my desire and zeal to fulfillment, and to ask him to pray for me. But he said, ‘Wait for now.
For I do not see tranquility at present. But go and live quietly, taking care to make progress in virtuous conduct.
For after a certain time, persecution will come upon the church. Then, as you flee,
“You will come here and become a monk.” And I said to him, to Abba Elidius, “What persecution?
Is paganism going to flare up?” He said to me, “No, but a wicked emperor named Marcian will arise
and make the bishops declare in writing that the one who was crucified was not God. And when all these submit to him and obey,
the bishop of Alexandria alone—I mean Dioscorus—will not obey him. Because of this he will be handed over and driven into exile,
and there he will die.” And I said to him, “Will the people of Alexandria let him go into exile?” He said to me, “He will be forced,
and another man, a denier of the faith, will take his place.” And when I was distressed by what had been said, he said,
“But God will raise up for himself in those days a priest who does his will,” indicating the blessed Timothy.
“The one who preceded him as a tyrant will be killed,” he said, referring to the wicked Proterius. “But the faithful one,
after remaining in the episcopate for a few days, will be cast into exile.” When the old man had said these things and fallen silent,
I was in great distress and said, “My lord, Father, will the bishop [?] remain in exile? Will the city and all Egypt perish, and wickedness prevail?”
But he remained silent. When I persisted in pleading with him, he said to me, “If there is time, he will return. And after remaining a short time,
he will die in the orthodox faith.” When he had said these things, he fell silent. And I fell down before him, wanting to learn from him what would happen afterward.
But he said to me, “What you have heard so far is enough for you. For after these things the time of the Antichrist will arrive.” Abba Zeno also spoke
about the council and the persecution of the saints. Now [?] Abba Zeno, the wanderer and prophet, was from Kefar Searta,
a village in Palestine. He spoke to Abba Stephen, the deacon of Jerusalem, and prophesied before the Council of Chalcedon.
For Stephen wanted to go and live as a stranger for God's sake, and to be found worthy of the honor of those who live as strangers.
For this reason he came to Abba Zeno and asked him whether the Lord would prosper his undertaking. But he said to him, “Go for now.
For persecution and an uprising of heretics are about to come upon the church because of the orthodox faith.
Then, even against your will, you will go out to live as a stranger, if you persevere in orthodoxy and are perfected in it,

because of the council that will take place in Chalcedon.”

About a holy man who lived in solitude, and about Satan's encounter with him,

and how he revealed to him concerning the council that it was being convened by him.

Abba Innocent of Pamphylia used to tell us,
a chaste man and leader of the brothers, saying, “There is a large, deep ravine in Pamphylia where one of the holy ascetics lives.
Before the council, he saw the devil, who came to him and said to him, ‘Fall down and worship me.’ But the holy man blew at him and rebuked him.
And that filthy demon departed, saying to him, ‘Why have you refused to worship me? Look, I am gathering all the bishops to Chalcedon for a council,

and I am holding a council. There all the bishops will worship me.’”

Again, Abba Paul [?] said that from
After twenty years, there is to be a transgression on the part of the bishops. This was the falling away from God that the apostle had foretold.
This would happen through a wicked man who would become emperor, whose name was Marcian. That emperor died after six years and a little more.
After him, for a short time, there was a false peace, in part [?], in the church, and it was quiet. Thus events continue to unfold until the coming of the Antichrist.
Again, Abba Andrew: While he was in a vision, he saw a great gathering of bishops who appeared to be heating a furnace.
They were throwing into it a beautiful baby who looked like light. They were plastering the furnace shut on every side, so that not even smoke could be seen coming from it,
nor could air enter it. After three days, he saw the baby coming out of the furnace unharmed, and he knew that he was the Lord.
As someone who [was accustomed to speaking with him], he said to him, “Lord, who are these people who did this to you and threw you into the furnace?”
He said to him, “The bishops have crucified me again, and they have planned to take my glory.” And he spoke rightly:
The Nestorians suffer from the disease of the Jews. They say that the one who was crucified was an ordinary human being, not God who became flesh.
Again, when the elder looked, he saw an elder standing at a distance, who did not agree with those other bishops
and did not take part with them, either when they were heating the furnace or when they threw the child into it and plastered it shut. The elder said
to the child, “Who is this elder?” He answered, “He is Dioscorus, the archbishop of Alexandria,
who alone did not take part in their schemes.” The elder, as someone who had been granted freedom to speak, took courage and said to the Lord, “How does this come about,
that all the bishops of Alexandria fight for the truth even to death?” He answered, “Ever since Simon of Cyrene carried my cross.
Now Cyrene is part of Egypt. From that time it was made known beforehand through prophecy that Egypt—of which Cyrene is a part,
situated in Libya—would carry my cross to the end, follow me, and show zeal for me even to death.”
Anatolius became patriarch in Constantinople in place of Paulinus, and Maximus in Antioch in place of Domnus.
In Edessa, Nonnus succeeded Ibas. The second council of Ephesus confirmed the entire constitution of Nicaea
and also upheld the first council of Ephesus, without leaving anything out. The year seven hundred and fifty-eight.
A great quantity of dust fell from heaven upon Jerusalem and all the villages around it, along with tokens of every sort.
For when the unlawful council was about to take place, the sky suddenly became gloomy, with darkness and thick cloud.
Tokens rained down in the holy city, in all the villages around it, and in many places in Palestine.
They were alike in shape in every respect and resembled those made by human beings. They bore various grotesque stamped designs.
Many people therefore gathered some of them. Some people who used them unknowingly were blinded.
They said that Hesychius, the monk of Jerusalem, gathered a large quantity of them and also showed them to Empress Eudocia.
He also sent to Constantinople a depiction of that sign, which indicated the blindness that was taking hold of the world through the bishops’ denial of the faith.

Much dust could also be seen beneath the brooms in the sign that came down from heaven.

The year 759.
For the honored cross that had shone and flashed for many years in the Church of the Holy Ascension was suddenly burned by fire and turned to dust.
It was a large cross, which Queen Helena had set up in the sanctuary in Jerusalem. When this happened, it shook the hearts of all who feared God.
Consequently, the God-fearing Empress Eudocia made a bronze one in its place to comfort and reassure the people. It can still be seen shining today.

It contains six thousand pounds of bronze.

The year 762. The blessed Theodosius the Younger died.
On the day of his death, a voice came from heaven, saying, “Look, the righteous man has perished from the earth, and no one takes it to heart.”
This voice was heard by everyone in the imperial city. [Emperor Theodosius lived] fifty years.
He reigned for forty-two of them, [because] he became emperor when he was eight years old, with Anthemius the prefect as his guardian.

On the reign of Marcian and the darkness that gathered on the day he put on the crown, foretelling the stumbling block that came upon the Church and the world.

Now the throne was taken
after him by Marcian. On the very day when the wicked Marcian was raised to imperial power and put on the crown, darkness suddenly covered the whole earth, together with gloom and falling sand.
The darkness was like the darkness that had overtaken Egypt; so completely did it darken the air.
As a result, all the inhabitants of the imperial city were in great fear and turmoil. They wailed loudly and mourned,
as though the end were rapidly approaching. This was a prophecy of the suffering that was destined to come upon the whole earth
at the hands of the tyrant himself, and of blindness and darkness concerning the fear of God. It was as though the whole creation, one might say,
was mourning beyond words and giving advance warning of the denial of God that would take place, and of the suppression of the orthodox faith
by the wicked emperor himself and by the great assembly of bishops from the inhabited world. The darkness continued like this until evening.
When the tyrant himself saw the turmoil and mourning among the soldiers and throughout the city, and that everyone regarded it as an omen concerning his reign,
as though it was destined to convulse the whole world with great evils, he became afraid and deeply disturbed.
He first posted public proclamations, trying to outwit the wrath coming from God and imagining that he could deceive the peoples. For he said the opposite,
as the document itself teaches those who read it: “The whole world ought to expect an abundance of great blessings from my reign,
for the suffering caused by the emperor before me is being driven away as the world welcomes the light of my good government.”
This was the beginning and the first of his decrees. This document, when it was posted throughout the whole
inhabited world, was, for those who have ears (to hear), eyes to see, and a heart to understand, a sure rebuke and written proof
of the falling away and estrangement from God that came about immediately and without delay through the tyrant’s zeal.
which was held by the bishops at Chalcedon. Marcian married Pulcheria, the sister of Emperor Theodosius the Younger,
after she had preserved her virginity for fifty years. She herself had also cast out Nestorius.
She broke her vows to Christ and also abandoned her faith. To avoid leaving the palace, she became Marcian’s wife.
The prophecy that the priest Pelagius of Edessa had uttered about her long beforehand was fulfilled in her:
that Pulcheria would break her vows of virginity and faith, join herself to Marcian, and that through their hands the faith would be corrupted,
as is written above. On how and from where evils began to spring up in conduct and in faith during this same year.
It will not be unwelcome to discerning ears to hear, in this account that lies before us, where the evils that sprang up in the church began,
and who planted and who watered this bitter root, which produced branches and fruit and defiled the whole creation.
It was Theodoret, who had been deposed by Dioscorus because of his corrupt faith, together with Ibas of Edessa and Daniel of Harran,
and Flavian of Constantinople, along with their companions who had been expelled with them. When he found a suitable opportunity for their impiety, he gathered gold
in great quantities, and they went up to Leo, patriarch of Rome, and informed him about everything.
Through that bribe, which blinds the eyes of the soul, they subjected him to their impiety, and he abandoned his faith.
He composed a document for them according to their wishes, the one called the Tome, ostensibly against the teaching of Eutyches.
Leo himself wrote and urged on Emperor Marcian and his wife Pulcheria, the sister of Theodosius.
This is what gold did to Leo the patriarch and to the faith. Pulcheria, because Leo spoke harshly against her brother Theodosius,
accepted [his Tome]. She also subjected Marcian [to the wishes] of Leo. Yet in the days of Theodosius, Leo had been orthodox.
With the great quantity of gold presented to him by Theodoret, Flavian, and Ibas, he now became corrupt in his soul and in his faith.
Through his intervention he corrupted the whole church. In the year seven hundred and sixty-four, Emperor Marcian gave orders,
and the council at Chalcedon was convened. Five hundred and sixty-seven bishops assembled there.
When they had assembled and Leo’s Tome was read, they all stood up together and bound themselves under a curse thirty-six times not to accept the Tome
or assent to it. When Emperor Marcian arrived, he ordered that anyone who would not accept the Tome should rise from his seat and sit on the ground.
Because they loved their seats and their positions of authority, they violated their own curses and the faith as well, and remained quietly seated in their places.
Only Dioscorus of Alexandria did not rise. He was banished to Gangra, and the emperor appointed his syncellus Proterius in his place.
The leaders of this council were these: Anatolius of Constantinople, Juvenal of Jerusalem, and Theodoret,
who had been deposed by Dioscorus, together with the representatives of Leo of Rome. On the vision that appeared at Chalcedon itself.
Nor is this unworthy of being included in this account. A few days before the emperor ordered that the council assemble at Chalcedon,
there appeared someone in the form of a small Indian man, very dark in complexion and [?] and in appearance.
He was playing and dancing throughout the streets of Chalcedon at midday. In this way he appeared to all the inhabitants of that city.
No one could seize him. When this happened among them, it plunged the city's inhabitants into mourning.
They said that Satan had a division to cast into the world, with God's permission. And this did indeed happen.
At this time the following were known among the orthodox: Dioscorus of Alexandria, Peter the Iberian, and Romanus the abbot;
and Basil, whom the people of Jerusalem appointed in place of Juvenal; Marcian the monk; Barsauma of Samosata, the monk; and Simeon of the pillar.
Also known were Simeon the monk of [?] and his seventy disciples, Paul of Surta, and Jacob of Kfar Rehima. Until this time,
all those who loved the discipline of standing spent their lives in trees. With Simeon, pillar-dwellers began to appear in the world.
For after the events at the Council of Chalcedon, disputes arose and multiplied, and disturbances were stirred up throughout the whole church everywhere.
Divisions arose everywhere. The faithful peoples fell upon one another, and the shepherds, with murderous resentment toward one another
and that pestilential hatred, were entangling themselves with one another in insults, persecutions, evil deeds, and spiteful attacks,
so that, as it is written, the whole body of Christians became a reproach to its neighbors
and an object of mockery and ridicule to those around them. Thus the foolish and unwise people of the crucifiers,
as they mocked and ridiculed the Christians, reached such a pitch of insolence that they wrote a document

which was posted at the entrance to the public baths in the imperial capital, as follows:
Letter composed by the Jews to Emperor Marcian after the dissolution of the Council of Chalcedon.
To the merciful Emperor Marcian, from the Hebrew people. All this time we have been regarded as people whose fathers crucified God and not a human being.
But since this holy council assembled at Chalcedon and demonstrated that they crucified a human being and not God,
we therefore ask that this offense be forgiven us and that our synagogues be returned to us.
The people who forgot the God who made them and reviled the Mighty One who redeemed them were able to reach this degree of insolence.
In the year seven hundred and sixty-six, there was a great and terrible earthquake. Many cities and places collapsed in it,
so that Tripoli in Phoenicia was entirely overthrown. And in the year seven hundred and sixty-nine,
Nonnus, bishop of Edessa, built the church of John the Baptist and a hospice for the poor outside the Beth-Shemesh Gate [?].
Within the hospice he also built a shrine for Saint Cosmas and Saint
Damian. In the year seven hundred and seventy, there was a severe earthquake, and Antioch in Syria collapsed in it—its fourth overthrow.
[?] at dawn on Sunday, September 13. Emperor Leo sent a great deal of gold and rebuilt its ruined buildings. The year 771.
The holy Mar Simeon the Stylite died while Ardabur was commander of the East. All the people of Antioch assembled,
crying out and pressing him to send troops to seize the blessed man's body for them and bring it to their city.
Then Ardabur himself sent a large force of Goths. After a great battle, they managed to seize the blessed man's body and bring it to Antioch.
After it had been received by the people of Antioch with a great procession, he immediately built a large martyrs' shrine for him, and he was laid there in a coffin.
The year 776. Emperor Leo issued a decree that no one should dare to work on Sunday.
Nor should anyone dare to use a lyre, a pipe, a [?], or any musical instrument on the holy day of Sunday. Instead, all activity was to cease,
and everyone was to attend to the church, and everyone was to rest. The year 777. Emperor Leo built Callinicum in Mesopotamia.
The year 782. Nonnus, bishop of Edessa, died, and Cyrus succeeded him.
The year 783. Emperor Leo launched a harsh persecution against the Arians throughout all the territories of his dominion,
expelling and oppressing them and taking away their churches. He ordered that they should not assemble at all. The year 784. There fell
ashes from heaven like rain. They accumulated on the ground and on the roof tiles to a depth of one span. The whole city and the entire palace were in great fear.
Great fear and trembling came over everyone, and they persisted in prayer, sorrow, and tears night and day.
Everyone was saying this: “These ashes that fell from heaven were fire that God was raining down upon the earth in anger.
But in his mercy the living God spared the world and extinguished it, and it became ashes, so that it would not burn up and destroy [?] the entire human race.
Now let us repent of our evil deeds, so that we do not perish utterly in our sins.” The year 785.
There was a great fire in the imperial city, the like of which in severity had never occurred before. The fire took hold of it [?] and burned from sea to sea.
And not [?] how it had no end [?]. When Emperor Leo saw it, he went up and fled across to Saint Mamas, and in his distress he stayed there for six months.
There he built a large harbor called Neon Embolon. The year 786.
Leo the Elder made Leo, his daughter's son, the son of Zeno, emperor alongside himself. The year 788.
Leo the Elder died, and Leo the Younger assumed imperial power when he was seven years old. The year 789.
Leo the Younger's mother deceived him as one would a little child. She said to him, “When your father bows before you with the officials, take the crown on your head and put it
(on his head).” Leo the Younger, who was a little child seven years old, did so. He took the imperial crown from his head
and placed it on his father's head. Then Zeno was henceforth seen to hold imperial power. He was an Isaurian by birth. His son Leo made him consul.
The year 790. Basiliscus, the brother of Verina, the wife of Leo the Great, rebelled against Zeno to seize imperial power.
But Zeno escaped to Isauria and stayed there. In the year 791, there was a severe earthquake.
Gabala, a city of Syria, collapsed in it. Basiliscus sent fifty pounds of gold and rebuilt it.
In the year 792, Zeno returned to Constantinople with a large army and was received by the entire senate.
Basiliscus fled to the Great Church and entered the baptistery. Zeno sent men and stripped him of the imperial insignia, and his wife and children as well.
Because he had given them his word that they would not be killed by him [?], he instead sent them to the fortress of Limnae in Cappadocia.
They were imprisoned in one of its towers, and he sealed the doorway in front of them. He died there. They were buried while still alive.
In the year 794, Zeno sent Peter, the patriarch of Antioch, into exile.
This was not on account of matters of faith, but because he had plotted against him and made an agreement with Basiliscus. He appointed Stephen in his place.
After holding office for a short time, Stephen was found to be a Nestorian. When he went outside the city to celebrate the commemoration of the Forty Martyrs, there gathered
his clergy. They sharpened reeds and stabbed him, and he died. They threw his body into the River Orontes. When Zeno heard this,
he exacted punishment from these men. After him he appointed Calendion, who was also found to be a Nestorian, and they sent him into exile.
Then a great outcry arose from the people of Antioch for the return of Peter, who had been deposed. The emperor ordered that he be brought back.
He held his throne throughout his life and died there in Antioch.
In the year 796, Emperor Zeno produced this document, called the Henotikon, and united the church during his reign.
For when Zeno had assumed imperial power, he found the holy church everywhere troubled and disturbed,
with divisions also arising from the innovations contrary to church order that had occurred at the council assembled in the city of Chalcedon, and from the rest of the confusion within it.
After trying many ways to quiet the disturbances everywhere, he considered the matter and produced a short document of union. This was the Henotikon, of which I have spoken:
until then, many peoples had been divided from one another, even though these were confirmed heretics.
The opposing party drew itself up against the document [?]. But, as it is written, they devised a plan but could not carry it out.
But the holy church received the document he had produced, issued in the Spirit [?]. From that time it came to [?].
There was peace and quiet between the parties, and the many evils and disputes everywhere ceased.
It seemed right to me also to include this document in this account, although it is very well known everywhere. It reads as follows.
Copy of the document called the Henotikon, which Emperor Zeno produced for the unity of the church. It reads as follows: Emperor Caesar
Zeno, faithful, victorious, triumphant, great and honored, ever Augustus, to the bishops and peoples in Egypt, Alexandria, Libya, and Pentapolis.
We know that the stability, foundation, strength, and invincible armor of our empire is the faith that alone is orthodox and true.
That which the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea established under divine protection.
The one hundred and fifty holy fathers who assembled at Constantinople also reaffirmed it [in the same place].
As night and day we continually devote ourselves to prayer, care, and laws, so that through this the holy, catholic, and apostolic Church everywhere may benefit.
She is the incorruptible and indissoluble mother of the scepter of our empire, while the faithful peoples remain in peace and harmony with God.
They offered acceptable prayers on behalf of our empire, together with the reverend bishops, the God-fearing clergy, the heads of monasteries, and the monks.
For [?] our great God and giver of life, Jesus Christ, who became incarnate and was born of the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God,
honors confession and worship offered in wholehearted devotion, and graciously accepts them. For the races of enemies are crushed and wiped out,
and all people bow their necks to our dominion, which is under God.
Peace and the good things that come from it, a favorable climate, abundant crops, and everything beneficial to humanity are generously bestowed. Thus, since the blameless faith
preserves us and the affairs of the Romans, petitions were presented to us by the God-loving heads and superiors of monasteries and other monks.
With tears they pleaded that the holy churches might be united and that the members might be joined to one another.
Those who hate what is good have long hastened to divide them, knowing that when they fight against the whole body of the Church, they are defeated.
For this has caused countless generations, whom time has carried away during all these years of life,
some of them to depart deprived of the washing of rebirth,
and others, without having shared in divine communion, to be led to that departure from human life from which there is no release.
They have been subjected to tens of thousands of killings, and not only the earth but now even the whole air has been defiled by an abundance of blood.
These things [?] we wish to change for the better.
For this reason, then, we are concerned that you should know that we, the orthodox churches throughout the entire dominion of our empire, and the God-loving priests who govern them
have received one statement and one definition of faith: that of the previously mentioned three hundred and eighteen
holy fathers, which the aforementioned one hundred and fifty fathers defined.
And again, two hundred and twenty [?]. We have not had it, nor do we have it, nor do we know that anyone has it.
If anyone holds anything apart from this definition of the three hundred and eighteen holy fathers who assembled in the Holy Spirit,
we consider him an outsider. This, as we say, we trust to preserve our empire and all the peoples who are deemed worthy of life-giving baptism.
They receive this when they are baptized. To it all the two hundred and twenty holy fathers who assembled at Ephesus adhered,
and they also deposed the wicked Nestorius and those who subsequently held his views.
For we too anathematize this Nestorius and Eutyches, as having held views contrary to what has been said.
We also accept the twelve chapters stated by Cyril of blessed memory, the lover of God who was archbishop of Alexandria.
We confess the only-begotten Son of God, who truly became human, our Lord Jesus Christ.
He is of the same nature as the Father in his divinity, and the very same one is of the same nature as us in his humanity.
He came down and became incarnate from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary, the Mother of God. He is one Son, not two.
For we say that both the miracles [?] and the sufferings that he willingly endured in the flesh belong to the one only-begotten Son of God.
But we utterly reject those who divide or confuse, or introduce a mere appearance.
For his true and sinless incarnation from the Mother of God did not add another Son.
The Trinity remained the Trinity [?], even when one of the Trinity, God the Word, became incarnate. Therefore, knowing that neither
the holy churches of the orthodox everywhere, nor the God-loving priests who govern them,
nor our imperial majesty have accepted or accept any other statement or definition of faith apart from what was stated by the holy fathers,
come and live in divine peace, without being divided. For we have written these things not to introduce a new faith, but to reassure you.
We anathematize anyone who has held, now holds, or at any time holds any other view, whether at Chalcedon or at any other council.
Especially the things stated by the Nestorians and the Eutychians, and those who hold their views.
Join, then, the one spiritual mother, the holy and apostolic Church, enjoying with us in her the divine communion, according to the definition of faith,
which is one alone: the previously stated definition of the holy fathers.
Our mother, the Church, holy in every respect, waits to embrace you as beloved children and longs to hear your voice.
Therefore [?] yourselves. For when you do this, you will also win for yourselves the favor of Christ our Savior and God.
And you will be praised by our imperial majesty. Pray for us, chosen ones of God. All these things are sufficient for your godly love. Pray for us. The end. [Chronicle of Pseudo-Joshua the Stylite]
Again, a historical account of the times of distress that occurred in Edessa and Amida and throughout Mesopotamia.
I received the letters of your God-loving holiness, O most excellent of men, Sergius, priest and abbot, in which you instructed me to write, as a memorial,
when the locusts came, when the sun was darkened, and when the earthquake, famine, plague, and war between the Romans and Persians occurred.
Along with these things, they also contained great praises of me, which put me greatly at odds with myself,
since not one of them is actually found in me. I, however, wished to write about the qualities in you, but the eye of my mind was unable
to contemplate and see as it truly is the wondrous robe that your diligent purpose has woven for you and clothed you in.
For you have clearly shown that you are fervent in love, which fulfills the law. You have cared not only for the brothers who are under your authority at this time,
but also for all lovers of learning who will enter your blessed monastery.
And in your diligence you wish to leave written records of the chastisements which
have taken place at various times because of our sins, so that when they read and see what happened to us, they may guard against our sins and escape our punishments.
Yet I cannot adequately marvel at the fullness of your love, which overflows toward everyone without diminishing or running short. Nor can I describe it as it truly is.

Since I have not come close to putting it into practice, I do not even know how to speak about it. From the encounter you once had with me, you became bound to me in love, like Jonathan, that faithful friend.
Indeed, the attachment of Jonathan’s soul to David’s soul was not as great as this, when he saw that the mighty warrior had been killed by David’s hands and the army had been delivered.
For he loved him because of his good deeds. But you, though you saw nothing good in me, loved me more than yourself.
Even Jonathan’s rescue of David from death at Saul’s hands is not worthy of wonder compared with what you have done. For he was merely repaying what he owed him.
For David had first rescued him from death and given life to him and his father’s entire household, so that they would not die at the hands of the Philistine.
Although I have done nothing like this for you, you constantly entreat God on my behalf, that I may be rescued from Satan and that he may not kill me through sins.
Rather, this is what should be said: you have loved me as David loved Saul. And you are so intoxicated by the abundance of your affection
that, in the fervor of your love, you do not even recognize my true measure, but think things of me that are beyond me.
For in the time before this, you supplied my need through the instruction in your letters. You cared for me like fathers who, although they have received no benefit from
their children, take care of everything they need.
But today, in your discernment, you have humbled yourself and asked me to write to you about things beyond my ability, so that through this very act you may become still greater.
Although you know these things better than I do myself, you wish to learn them from me. Nor do I begrudge you this and shrink from what you have commanded. But know this:
I too, when I saw these signs taking place and the chastisements that followed them, thought that they deserved to be written down and preserved in memory,
and not left to oblivion. But because I considered the weakness of my understanding and my own lack of learning,
I shrank from this task. Now, however, that you have commanded me to do this very thing, I am as afraid as someone who does not know how to swim well
and is ordered to go down into deep water. And because I rely on your prayers to lift me up, which you continually send to God on my behalf,
I believe that I will be drawn up, safe from drowning, out of the sea into which you have cast me. I swim in its shallows as best I can, for its depth cannot be fathomed.
For who is capable of giving a fitting account of the things God does in his wisdom to put an end to sins and to chastise wrongdoing?
For the precise workings of God’s providence are hidden even from the angels. You can learn this
from the parable of the weeds in the Gospel. For when the householder’s servants said to him, ‘Do you want us to go and gather them?’
He who knew the circumstances as they really were said to them, “No, lest, while you gather the weeds, you uproot with them also
the wheat.” We say this according to our understanding: because of the multitude of our sins, our punishments have been [?].
If God’s protection had not held the world together to keep it from falling apart, the lives of all human beings would already have come to an end.
For in what other times have afflictions like these happened in succession, except in these times in which we now live?
And because their cause has not ceased, they themselves have not yet ceased either. Besides this, we have seen something with our own eyes and heard it with our own ears,
and we are living through it. Reports from far and near have also terrified me, as have the calamities that happened in various places: terrible earthquakes,
the destruction of cities, famines and plagues, wars and disturbances, the captivity and exile of populations, and the uprooting and burning of churches.
Astonished yourself at how numerous these things were, you wrote to me asking me to record them in sorrowful and mournful words that would astonish readers and listeners.
I know that this was your concern, and that you said it with good intentions: that those who hear these things should also feel remorse and turn to repentance.
But know that writing mournfully is one thing, and writing truthfully is another. For anyone endowed with the natural power of speech, if he wishes,
can write sorrowful and mournful accounts. But I am unskilled in my speech, and in this book I record only those things
that all the people in our country testify are true.
It is for those who read or hear them to examine them and, if they wish, turn to repentance.
But perhaps someone will say, “What benefit do these things bring their readers if no words of admonition are interwoven with them?” I,
however, being unable to do this, say that these punishments that have come upon us are sufficient to correct us and those who come after us.
By remembering and reading about them, we also learn that they were sent upon us because of our sins. But if they did not teach us this, they would be of no benefit to us.
But this cannot be said, for punishments serve us in place of instruction. And that they are sent upon us because of our sins
is attested by all the faithful under heaven, who agree with the words of the blessed Paul: “When we are judged by our Lord, we are disciplined, so that we may not be condemned with the world.”
For all the discipline that human beings receive in this world is intended to make them stop sinning, so that the judgment of the world to come may be less severe for them.
And those who are disciplined because of wrongdoers, although they themselves have not sinned, receive a double reward.
But the mercy that is always shown even to the unworthy comes from God’s kindness, grace, and patience,
for he wishes this world to endure until the time determined in his knowledge, which does not err.
That these things are so is clear from the testimony of the Holy Scriptures and from the events that have happened among us, which we have undertaken to record.
For the afflictions of famine and plague pressed upon us at the time of the locusts, until we were close to being abandoned to destruction.
And God had mercy on us, although we were unworthy, and gave us a little relief from the afflictions that were coming upon us one after another. And this, as I said, was because of
his goodness. But after we had enjoyed some respite, he also changed the scourges he used against us, striking us through the Assyrian, who is called the rod of wrath.
I am not, then, denying the Persians’ freedom of choice when I say that God struck us through their hands.
Nor am I bringing against God the blame for their insolence. Rather, because I consider that he did not exact punishment from them because of our sins,
I have stated that he himself struck us through their hands. For the intention of that wicked people is especially evident in this: they showed no mercy to those who were handed over to them.
For they had always been accustomed to show their disposition in mistreating people. The prophet also reproaches them for this very thing when, prophesying about the destruction of Babylon, he says,
as though from the Lord’s own mouth: “I was angry with my people, who defiled my inheritance, and I handed them over to you, but you showed them no mercy.”
So they also harmed us in this way, with their merciless disposition, as was their custom. For although the rod of their blows did not reach our own bodies,
and they were unable to gain control of our city—because Christ’s promise, which he made to the faithful King Abgar, could not be annulled,
when he said, “Your city shall be blessed, and no enemy shall ever rule over it”—
yet through the believers who were plundered, taken captive, killed, and ruined in the other cities that were conquered, and who became like mud in the streets,
all those who had learned to suffer with those who suffer tasted no small suffering. Those, in turn, who were far removed from this were, through fear for
their own lives, tormented in their unbelief, because they thought that the enemy would also gain control of Edessa, as he had of the other cities,
about which we are going to write to you. But since, according to the saying of wise Solomon,
“War is brought about by provocation,” and you wish to learn precisely this—what causes provoked it—
I wish to explain to you briefly where its causes originated, even though it may seem that I am speaking about matters whose time has passed.
Then, a little later, I will also explain to you when it gained strength from these causes. For although it took its occasion from overt events,
which I wish to recount to you so that you may have a clear understanding of this matter,
you should not be led into joining foolish people in blaming the reigning ruler, the faithful Emperor Anastasius. For he was not the origin of the war.
Rather, it had been brewing for a long time, as you can understand from what I am writing to you.
In the year 609, the Romans built the city of Nisibis, and it remained under their rule for sixty-five years.
After Julian’s death in Persia, which took place in the year 674, Jovian, who succeeded him as emperor of the Romans,
valued peace above everything else. For this reason, he allowed the Persians to rule over Nisibis for a period of one hundred and twenty years,
after which they were to return it to its owners. These years came to an end in the reign of Zeno, emperor of the Romans, but the Persians were unwilling to return the city.
This matter stirred up a dispute. There was also a treaty between the Romans and the Persians,
that if either needed the other when they were at war with one of the nations, they would help one another.
When they provide three hundred fighting men with their weapons and horses, or three hundred staters in place of thirty men.
That is, according to what the side in need wants. With the help of God, the Lord of all, the Romans therefore had no need of help from the Persians.
For believing kings have reigned from that time until now, and their rule has been strengthened by help from heaven.
The Persian kings, however, used to send envoys and receive gold because of their need. They were not receiving it as tribute,
as many people supposed. For in our own days, Peroz, king of the Persians, because of his wars with the Chionites, who are the Huns,
received gold from the Romans many times, not by demanding tribute, but by appealing to them on the grounds
that he was fighting his battles on their behalf: “So that they do not cross into your country,” he said.
What made this claim credible was the slaughter and captivity inflicted by the Huns in Roman territory in the year seven hundred and seven,
in the days of the emperors Honorius and Arcadius, the sons of Theodosius the Great. All Syria had been delivered into their hands
through the treachery of Rufinus the prefect and the negligence of Addaeus the commander. With the help of the gold he had received from the Romans,
Peroz subdued the Huns, took many places in their country, and added them to his kingdom.
Eventually, however, he was taken captive by them. When Zeno, emperor of the Romans, heard about it, he sent gold of his own, ransomed him, and made peace between him and them.
Peroz made a treaty with the Huns, promising that he would never again cross the border of their country to wage war against them.
But he went back on his word and broke his treaty, like Zedekiah, and went to war. Like him, they were delivered into the hands of his enemies, and his whole army was destroyed and scattered.
He himself was captured alive, and in his arrogance he promised to give thirty mules loaded with silver coins as a ransom for his life.
He sent to the country he ruled and barely managed to gather twenty loads, for he had exhausted the entire treasury of the king before him in his earlier wars.
In place of the other ten loads, he left his son Kavadh with them as a pledge and hostage until he could send them.
He made a treaty with them for a second time, promising not to wage war again. When he returned to his kingdom, he imposed a poll tax throughout his land.
He sent ten loads of silver coins and ransomed his son. Then he gathered an army again and went to war.
And the words of the prophet who said, “I saw the wicked man rising high like the trees of the forest. When I passed by,

he was no more; I looked for him and could not find him,” were fulfilled in him there in actual events. For when battle broke out and the armies clashed with one another, his entire army was destroyed.
He himself was sought but could not be found. To this day, it is not known what became of him:
whether he was buried beneath the bodies of the slain, whether he threw himself into the sea, or whether he hid in a cleft in the earth and died of hunger,
or whether he hid in the forest and was eaten by wild animals. In the days of this same Peroz, the Roman Empire was also thrown into turmoil.
For the members of the palace harbored hatred toward Emperor Zeno because he was of Isaurian origin.
Basiliscus rebelled against him and became emperor in his place. Afterward Zeno gained the upper hand and secured his rule. And because he had experienced the hatred that many bore toward him,
he prepared an impregnable fortress for himself in his own country, so that, if anything bad happened to him, it would serve as a refuge.
His confidant in this matter was the military commander of Antioch, whose name was Illus. He too was an Isaurian.
For he had given all his countrymen positions of honor and authority. Because of this, he was hated even more by the Romans.
When the fortress had been equipped with everything it needed, and Illus had deposited an incalculable amount of gold in it, he came to the imperial capital,
to inform Zeno that his wishes had been fulfilled. But Zeno, knowing that he was deceitful and desired the throne,
ordered one of the soldiers to kill him. For many days, the man who had received this order sought
an opportunity [?] to carry out his deed in secret, but found none. He encountered Illus inside the palace, drew his sword, and raised it to strike him.
Immediately, one of the soldiers accompanying Illus struck him in the arm with a knife. The sword fell from his hand and cut off Illus's ear.
Zeno, to keep his plot against Illus from being exposed, immediately ordered that the soldier be beheaded without questioning.
But this very action made Illus suspect all the more that Zeno had given the order. He set out from there and went down to Antioch, having resolved
to take revenge whenever he had the opportunity. But Zeno feared Illus, because he knew his wickedness,
and sent men to reassure him, saying that the plot had not originated with him and that he himself had not wanted to kill him.
But he could not soften Illus's stubborn attitude. For Illus despised him and refused to obey his command and come to him.
Finally, Zeno sent another military commander against him, whose name was Leontius, together with the army under his command.
He ordered him to bring Illus to him by force and, if he resisted, to kill him as well. But when this man came to Antioch, he was bribed with gold by Illus.
He disclosed to him the order he had received to kill him. When Illus saw that he had concealed nothing from him,
he in turn showed him the great amount of gold in his possession, on account of which Zeno wanted to kill him.
He persuaded Leontius to join him and rebel with him, also pointing out to him the Romans' hatred of Zeno.
Once Leontius had been persuaded, Illus was able to reveal his intention. For on his own he could not
rebel, nor could he himself become emperor, because the Romans hated him too, on account of his ancestry and his harsh disposition.
Leontius became emperor in Antioch in name, while Illus himself directed affairs.
As some people say [?], he was even planning to kill Leontius if they defeated Zeno.
They were accompanied by a man who was a sorcerer and a deceiver, named Pamprepius. Through his deception, he threw all their affairs into confusion and reversed their fortunes.
To secure their rule, they sent envoys to the Persians with a great amount of gold, so that they would establish a treaty of friendship with them.
Or, if they needed a force to help them, they should send one to them. Now when Zeno heard about what had happened in Antioch,
he sent one of the generals, named John, there with a large army. But the followers of Illus and Leontius,
when they heard about the large army coming against them, lost heart. The people of Antioch, too, were afraid, because they could not endure a siege.
They pressed them to leave the city and, if they could, engage in battle.
This alarmed the followers of Illus even more, and they planned to leave Antioch and cross the Euphrates eastward.
They sent one of their men, whose name was Matronianus, with five hundred cavalrymen to prepare a royal residence for them in Edessa.
But the people of Edessa opposed him, shut the city gates, and guarded the wall as in wartime. They did not allow him to enter. And when
the followers of Illus heard this, they were compelled to meet John in battle. They could not withstand this, because John attacked them fiercely.
He destroyed most of the army with them, and the others scattered, each to his own city. Since they themselves could not withstand his onslaught,
they took those who remained with them and escaped to that fortress which I mentioned above as being impregnable
and also supplied with everything. John pursued them but did not catch them. He encamped [?] around the fortress and kept watch over them.
But because they trusted in the fortress’s impregnability, they allowed the troops with them to go down,
keeping only the picked and valiant men with them. John vented his anger on those who came down from the fortress.
But he could not inflict any harm on the followers of Illus. Besides the natural inaccessibility of the site [?], it had also been made remarkably impregnable by human workmanship.
There was only one road leading up to it, and this was so narrow that two people could not go up it side by side.
After a long time, when John had exhausted his stratagems, a plot was made against the followers of Illus by some of those with them, and they were captured while asleep.
At Zeno’s command, both of them were killed, together with those who had betrayed them. The hands of all those with them were cut off.
Such was the turmoil among the Romans in the days of Peroz. After he had been searched for and could not be found, as I said above,
his brother Balash became king over the Persians in his place. He was a gentle man who loved peace, and he found nothing in the Persian treasury.
