His land had been devastated by the Huns’ plundering. For your wisdom is well aware of the great losses and expenses that kings incur in wars,
even when they win, let alone when they are defeated. Nor did he receive any assistance from the Romans, as his brother had.
For he sent envoys to Zeno asking him to send him gold. But because Zeno was preoccupied with the war against the followers of Illus and Leontius,
and because he also remembered the gold that had been sent by them at the beginning of their rebellion and was still there among the Persians [?],
he was unwilling to send him anything. Instead, he sent him this message: “The revenues of Nisibis that you receive are enough for you,
for they have rightfully belonged to the Romans for many years.” But Balash, because he had no gold with which to support his armies,
He became despised in their eyes. The Magi also hated him because he was abolishing their laws.
He wanted to build bathhouses in the cities for bathing. When they saw that he was not respected by his troops, they seized him and blinded him.
They installed in his place Kavadh, the son of his brother Peroz, whose name we mentioned above and who had been held as a hostage among the Huns.
It was he who stirred up war with the Romans because gold was not given to him. For he sent an envoy and one large elephant as a gift to honor the emperor, so that he would send him gold.
When the envoy reached Antioch in Syria, Zeno died, and Anastasius became emperor after him. When the Persian envoy informed his master Kavadh
of the change that had taken place in the Roman Empire, he sent instructions to him to go up promptly and ask for the customary gold,
or to tell the emperor to prepare for war. Instead of speaking words of peace and reconciliation, as he should have done, and rejoicing with him at the beginning
of the rule newly given to him by God, he embittered the faithful emperor Anastasius with threatening words.
But when he heard his arrogant words and learned of his evil ways, and that he had revived the abominable heresy of the Magian religion called Zaradushtakan,

which teaches that women should be held in common and that everyone may have intercourse with whomever he wishes, and that he had mistreated the Armenians under his authority because they would not worship fire,
he despised him and did not send him gold. Instead, he sent him this message: “Just as Zeno, who reigned before me, did not send any, neither will I send any until you return Nisibis to me.
For the wars I have with the barbarians called the Germans and with those called the Blemmyes
and with many others are no small matter. I will not neglect the Roman armies and support yours.”
When the Armenians under Kavadh’s rule heard that he had received no peaceful response from the Romans, they took courage and grew strong.
They tore down the fire temples that had been built for the Persians in their country and killed the Magi among them.
Kavadh sent a marzban against them with an army to punish them and force them back to worshiping fire.
They fought against him and destroyed both him and his army. They sent envoys to the emperor, offering to submit to him, but he was unwilling to accept them,
so that he would not be thought to be provoking war with the Persians. Therefore, those who blame him for not giving gold
should blame the man who demanded what was not his, as though by force. For if he had asked peacefully and persuasively, it would have been sent to him.
But he hardened his mind like Pharaoh and threatened war. We trust in God’s justice that he will also
bring upon him a punishment greater than Pharaoh’s because of his impure laws, since he wished to corrupt the law of nature
and abolish the way of reverence for God. Moreover, all the Cadiseni under his rule also rebelled against him and sought to enter Nisibis
and install a king of their own there. He fought against it for no short time.
The Tamurites, too, who lived in Persian territory, rebelled against him when they saw that he was giving them nothing.
They relied on the high mountains where they lived, and they would come down, plunder, and raid the villages around them.
and to merchants, foreigners, and local people, and those going up [?]. Even the nobles of his kingdom hated him because he allowed their wives to commit adultery.
The Arabs under his authority, too, when they saw the disorder in his kingdom, also carried out raids throughout Persian territory as far as their strength allowed.
At this time another disturbance also arose among the Romans. For after Zeno’s death, the Isaurians rebelled against Emperor Anastasius.
They wanted to appoint as emperor someone of their own choosing. When Kavadh heard this, he thought that an opportunity had presented itself.
He sent envoys to Roman territory, expecting that they would be afraid and send him gold because the Isaurians were rebelling against them.
Emperor Anastasius sent him this reply: “If you are asking for a loan, I will send it to you. But if it is a matter of the customary payment,
I will not let the Roman armies grow weak in the war against the Isaurians while I help the Persians.”
This humbled Kavadh’s pride, because his scheme had not succeeded. The Isaurians were defeated.
They were devastated and killed, and all their cities were demolished and burned. But the nobles
of Persia had secretly planned to kill Kavadh because of his impure conduct and his perverse laws. When he learned of this,
he abandoned his kingdom and fled to the land of the Huns, to the king with whom he had been brought up while he was a hostage.
His brother Jamasp became king over the Persians in his place. Kavadh himself married a woman in the land of the Huns who was his sister’s daughter.
His sister had been taken captive there in the battle in which his father was killed. Because she was a king’s daughter, she became the wife of the king of the Huns.
She bore him a daughter, and when Kavadh fled there, she gave her to him in marriage. Emboldened by having become the king’s son-in-law,
he wept before him every day, asking him to give him an army to help him, so that he could go and kill the nobles and establish himself over his kingdom.
His father-in-law gave him a substantial army, as he had requested. When he reached Persian territory,
his brother heard about it and withdrew before him. Kavadh accomplished his purpose and killed the nobles. He also sent a message to the Tamuraye, threatening them
that if they did not submit to him willingly, they would be defeated in battle. But if they became his soldiers,
they would enter Roman territory with him, and from the plunder taken there he would give them a share to make up for everything they had been deprived of.
They were afraid of the army of the Huns and surrendered to him. When the Qadishaye, who were encamped around Nisibis, heard these things, they too submitted.
When the Arabs learned that he was preparing to wage war against the Romans, they gathered around him with great enthusiasm. But the Armenians, because they feared that he might take revenge
on them for the fire temples they had previously demolished, were unwilling to obey him. He gathered an army and fought against them.
When he gained the upper hand over them, he did not devastate them. Instead, he promised them that he would not even compel them to worship fire,
provided they helped him in the war against the Romans. Out of fear, they agreed, though they were unwilling.
As for what Kavadh did after entering Roman territory, I will tell you about it in its proper place.
Now, since you also instructed me to write about the signs and chastisements that occurred in their times, and about the locusts, the plague, and the fire—and these were earlier in time—
I turn my account back to them. So that the narrative will not be confused, I am setting down the years one by one, clearly distinguished.
For each year separately I will write what happened in it, with God as my helper through the assistance of your prayers, chosen one.
The year 806 of Alexander. I have now informed you sufficiently about the cause of the war and how it was stirred up,
as I believe, our father, although I have written these accounts briefly, because I avoided a lengthy discussion.
Some of these things I found in old books, and some I learned through meeting people who had served as envoys to both kings,
and others from people who had themselves been involved in these events. But now I want

to tell you about the things that happened among us, because the severe chastisements and the signs that occurred in our days began in this year. At this time, good health prevailed throughout our entire region.
But the pains and diseases of our souls were many. God, however, who desires sinners to turn from their sins and live,
made our body into a mirror and filled our entire flesh with sores, so that through our outward condition he might show us what our inward condition was like,
and through the blemishes of our bodies we might learn how ugly the blemishes of our souls were. Just as everyone had sinned, everyone was struck by this affliction.
For swellings and eruptions appeared on all the inhabitants of our city. Many people's faces became swollen and filled with pus, making a terrifying sight.
There were others whose entire bodies became covered with sores or pustules, even on the palms of their hands and the soles of their feet.
There were others who developed large open sores on one or another of their limbs. But through the grace of God, which sheltered them,
the illness did not remain with anyone for long, nor did any deformity or damage develop in the body.
Rather, although the scars of the sores remained visible after recovery, the limbs were left intact, able to perform their necessary functions in the body.
At this time in Edessa, thirty measures of wheat were being sold for a denarius, and barley [?]. The year 807.
On the seventeenth day of the month of Adar in this year, while good things were being sent abundantly from heaven to all humanity, and the crops
were plentiful through blessing, and rain was falling, and the fruits of the earth were growing in their season,
most of the city's inhabitants had cut off their hope of life by openly doing evil. While they were reveling in pride,
they offered no thanksgiving for God's gifts. Instead, they were neglectful of [?] thanksgiving,
and were being corrupted by the diseases of sin. As though the secret and public sins in which they were engaged were not enough for them,
they made preparations on this specified day, which was Friday, the eve of the Sabbath, when the dancer performs; it is called the Trimerin.
They lit innumerable lamps in honor of this festival, although this custom had not previously existed in the city.
From the gate of the theater to the Gate of the Rocks, the lamps were arranged on the ground beside the river.
He placed burning lamps along its rim. They were also hung in the porticoes, in the Antiphorus, in the upper market, and in many other places.
Because of this wickedness, however, a miraculous sign from God occurred to rebuke them.
For the cross held in the hand of the statue of the blessed Emperor Constantine moved about one cubit away from the statue’s hand.
It remained like this on Friday and Saturday, until evening. But on Sunday the cross moved of its own accord and approached its place.
The statue held it in its hand, just as it had held it before. Through this sign, discerning people understood that the deed that had been performed
was far from God’s will. The year eight hundred and eight. But this sign from above was not enough for us to stop our wickedness.
Instead, we hurried all the more toward sins and readily approached them. The lowly slandered their neighbors.
The powerful were full of favoritism. Envy and deceit gained control over us all, and adultery and sexual immorality increased.
The disease of swellings grew more severe among people, and the eyes of many were damaged, both in the city and in the villages.
Bishop Mar Cyrus was moved by a worthy zeal. He urged the inhabitants of the city to make a silver litter to honor the vessels of the mysteries,
so that they could be placed in it when people went to celebrate with them at the commemoration of one of the martyrs. Everyone gave whatever he could afford.
Eutychianus, the husband of Auriana, was the first to show goodwill, giving one hundred dinars from his own resources.
The governor Anastasius was relieved of office, and Alexander came in his place at the end of this year.
He cleared the city’s streets of rubbish and removed the benches that had been built for the craftsmen in the porticoes and streets.
He placed a chest in front of his headquarters and made a hole in its lid. Above it he wrote that anyone who wished to report something
and could not easily do so openly should write it down and throw it inside without fear. In this way he learned about many matters, since
many people wrote and put their reports into it. Every Friday he regularly sat in the martyrs’ shrine of Saint John the Baptist and Saint Addai the Apostle.
He settled lawsuits without partiality. The oppressed were emboldened against their oppressors, and those who had been robbed against their robbers.
They brought their cases to him, and he judged them. Even cases that were more than fifty years old and had not been pursued
were brought before him and settled. He built the parapet near the Gate of the Rocks, and he also began building a public bath,
which had been planned for construction years earlier near the grain storehouse. He ordered the craftsmen to hang above their shops, on the eves of Sundays,
crosses with five lamps burning on them. The year eight hundred and nine. While these things were taking place,
the time came again for the festival at which pagan stories were sung. The city’s inhabitants devoted even more attention to it than before.
For seven days beforehand, they would come up together from the theater in the evening, wearing linen tunics,
covered with [?], with their loins ungirded. Lamps shone before them, and they burned incense. They stayed awake all night and went around the city.
They applauded the dancer until morning, with singing, shouting, and [?]. On these pretexts they even neglected to go to prayer.
No one gave any thought to his duty. Instead, they boldly mocked the modesty of their ancestors,
saying, “They did not know how to do these things as we do.” And they said, “They were ignorant and uneducated—
the inhabitants of the city in former times.” In this way they acted wickedly.
There was no one to correct, rebuke, or admonish them. Although Xenaias, bishop of Mabbug, had been received as a guest in Edessa,
and was considered more than others to have undertaken the work of teaching, he did not speak to them about this matter for more than one day.
But God, in his mercy, clearly showed them his care for them, so that they would turn away from their wrongdoing.
For two basilicas and the warm room of the summer baths collapsed. By God's grace, no one was injured there,
although many people were there, working inside and outside. None of them died,
except two men who became wedged in the doorway of the bathhouse as they fled from the sound of the collapse.
As they clung to its two sides, one on either side, because of its narrowness, they delayed while arguing about which of them should go out first.
Stones fell on them, and they died. All discerning people thanked God for sparing the city the mourning of many people.
For those baths were due to open for bathing within a few days.
The building collapsed so completely that even its lowest stones, laid at ground level, were uprooted from their places.
In this same year an order came from Emperor Anastasius that the gold payment made by craftsmen once every four years should be abolished, and that they should be freed from the tax.
This order came not only to Edessa, but to all the cities of the dominion
of the Romans. The people of Edessa had been paying 140 pounds of gold once every four years. The whole city rejoiced.
Everyone, from the greatest to the least, dressed in white. They carried lighted candles and censers giving off fragrant smoke.
With psalms and hymns, thanking God and praising the emperor, they went out to the martyrs' shrine of Saint Sergius and Saint Simeon.
They celebrated the Eucharist there, then returned to the city and held a festival of joy and merriment throughout the week.
They resolved to celebrate this festival every year. All the craftsmen reclined at feasts and enjoyed themselves,
and bathed [?] and reclined at meals in the courtyard of the church and in all the city's colonnades. In this same year, on the fifth day of June,
Bishop Cyrus departed from this world, and Peter [?] succeeded him. He added the festival of Hosannas to the annual festivals.
He established the custom of consecrating water on the night before the feast of Epiphany. And concerning the oil of anointing on Thursdays [?] before all the people,
along with the rest of the other festivals [?]. Alexander the governor was removed from office, and Demosthenes succeeded him. By his order, all the colonnades of our city were whitewashed.
But those who had experience of such matters were greatly troubled by this. For they said that it was a sign [?] of battles that would take place in the city.
The year 810. At this time a demonstration of God's justice was revealed to us, to put an end to our evil conduct.
In the month of May of this year, around the day on which that evil pagan festival was to be celebrated, locusts [?] came into our region from the south.
That year they did no damage or harm among us, but only laid their eggs in our region in no small quantity.
While the eggs they had laid lay embedded in the ground, terrible earthquakes were taking place. And this is clear:
They were taking place to awaken humanity from its immersion in sin, so that it would not be chastised by famine and pestilence.
In August of this same year, an order came from Emperor Anastasius that wild-beast shows were to be abolished in the cities of the Roman Empire.
In September there was a violent earthquake, and a loud sound from heaven was heard on earth.
The earth was shaken from its foundations by that sound, and all the villages and cities felt that sound and the earthquake.
Persistent rumors and bad news reached us from every direction. And according to what some people said,
a remarkable sign appeared in the River Euphrates and at the hot spring of Abrana: the flow of their sources ceased that very day. I do not think this report is false,
because the earth is often split open by earthquakes, and it happens that even the waters flowing through these places, where the cracks appear, are stopped in their course.
Sometimes they are even diverted in another direction. So too, blessed David, when recounting in the eighteenth psalm the punishments
that came from God upon his enemies through the shaking of the earth, the upheaval of the mountains, and other things like these, makes known
that this also happened. For he said, "The sources of the waters were uncovered, and the foundations of the world were revealed at your rebuke, Lord."
A letter also arrived in this same month and was read before the whole congregation of the church, saying that the city of Nicopolis had suddenly collapsed
at midnight, engulfing within it all its inhabitants, as well as the strangers who were there.
Some brothers from our schools had been traveling there; those who were found inside it were buried there.
Their companions who returned told us about it. For the entire circuit of the city wall, and everything within it, was overturned that night.
None of them remained alive except the city's bishop and two other men who were sleeping behind the sanctuary of the church.
When the roof of the building in which they were sleeping fell, one end of its beams rested against the wall of the sanctuary itself, and it did not bury them.
One truth-loving brother told me this: "On the evening of the night when it collapsed, a companion and I were eating supper inside it.
He became restless and said to me, 'Get up! Let us go out and spend the night outside the city, in that hollow where we usually stay.
For I cannot spend the night here. The air is oppressive to me, and I cannot get to sleep.' So he and I got up
and went outside the city. We spent the night in that hollow as usual. And when dawn was drawing near,
I woke the brother who was with me and said to him, “Get up, for it is daylight.
Let us go into the city and attend to our business.” So he and I got up, went into the city, and found it with
all its buildings overturned. People and livestock, oxen and camels, were buried there, and the sound of their groaning came from beneath the ground.
Those who had gathered there brought the bishop out from beneath the church timbers under which he had been sheltered.
He asked for bread and wine so that they could celebrate the sacrament with them, because the whole city had been overturned and nothing in it remained standing.
Then a blessed traveler happened to come along and gave him a few small loaves. He offered the Eucharist and prayed.
He gave those who were there communion in the sacrament of life. At that moment, I think, he resembled righteous Lot when he escaped from Sodom.
Let what has been said so far suffice. Now, in that same northern region there was a shrine of the martyrs called the shrine of Arsamosata.
It had been solidly built and beautifully adorned. On the appointed day when the saint’s commemoration was held,
which they observed there every year, many people gathered there from every direction, some for prayer and others for trade.
For the gathering held there provided people with a substantial livelihood. While a great crowd was there—men, women, and children,
of every stature and size—there were powerful flashes of lightning, violent thunderclaps, and terrifying sounds. Everyone fled to that shrine of the martyrs to seek
refuge with the bones of the blessed ones. While they were greatly afraid and were standing in prayer and worship at midnight,
the shrine of the martyrs collapsed and crushed beneath it most of the people who were inside. This happened on the very day when Nicopolis had collapsed,
in the year eight hundred and eleven. Yet despite all these earthquakes and calamities, not one of us stopped doing evil.
Our land and our city were left without relief, since we had been reserved to be disciplined last. Because reports from far away did not frighten us, we suffered a blow for which there is no cure.
Let us therefore acknowledge God’s justice and say, “The Lord is righteous, and his judgments are entirely just.” For even now, in his patience,
he wishes through signs and wonders to restrain us from our evil deeds. In October of this year, on the twenty-third, a Saturday,
at sunrise the sun’s light was taken away from it, and its luminous disk became like silver.
It had no visible rays, and our eyes could look at it easily, without hindrance.
For it had no brilliance, flashes, or rays to prevent our eyes from looking at it. Rather, just as we can easily look at the moon,
so we could look at it as well. It remained like this until about the eighth hour.
The earth, on which the little remaining light rested, looked pale, as though ashes or sulfur had been scattered over it.
On this day another frightening and terrifying sign appeared on the city wall. This city, because of the faith of its king
and the righteousness of its inhabitants in former times, had been found worthy to receive a blessing from our Lord. It now came close to wiping out its present inhabitants.
Because of their many sins. For a breach opened in the wall south of the Great Gate, and some of the stones from that spot were scattered a considerable distance away.
At the command of our father Mar Peter the bishop, supplications were held, and everyone sought mercy from God.
For he led out all his clergy, all the male and female ascetics, and all the members of the holy church, rich and poor alike,
men together with women and children. Carrying crosses, they went around through all the streets of the city,
with psalms and hymns, wearing black clothes as a sign of humility. All the monasteries in our region also maintained their services with great diligence.
Through the prayers of all the holy ones, the sunlight was restored to its [?], and we received a little encouragement.
In November we saw three signs in the sky at midday. One of them was in the middle of the sky, toward the south,
resembling in color the rainbow that appears in the clouds. Its hollow faced upward—that is, its convex side was downward and its ends upward.
One was in the east, and another in the west. Then again, in January, we saw another sign toward the west and south,
of the same color, resembling a spear. Some people said about it that it was a broom of destruction,
while others said that it was a spear of war. Up to this point we had been admonished through reports and signs. From this point
onward, however, who can describe the distress that surrounded our region on every side? In March of this year, locusts emerged from the ground against us.
Because they were so numerous, we thought that not only had the brood in the ground come out against us, but that the air itself was spewing them out upon us,
and that they were also coming down upon us from heaven. While they were still crawling, they devoured and consumed the whole of Arab, the entire district of Reshaina, and the district of Tella,
and the district of Edessa. Once they took flight, their columns could be seen from the border of Assyria as far as the western sea.
To the north they went as far as the border of the territory of the Urtaye. They devastated and ruined these regions, consuming everything in them,
so that, even before the war began, we could see with our own eyes what was said about the Babylonian:
“Before him the land is like the garden of Eden, and behind him a desolate wilderness.” Had the Lord's command not restrained them,
they would have devoured people and livestock, as we heard they had done in one of the villages.
Some people placed a small infant in a field while they were working. While they went from one end of the field to the other, the locusts swarmed over the child and bit it to death.
Immediately, in April, grain and everything else began to become expensive, and four modii of wheat were being sold for a dinar.
In June and July, the inhabitants of these regions made efforts to [?] and sow millet to provide for their needs,
but it did not suffice for them, because it did not succeed. As the year drew to its close, misery from hunger surrounded the people, and they sold
their possessions for half their value: livestock, cattle, sheep, and pigs. For the locusts had eaten the entire harvest,
and there was nothing for the livestock. Many abandoned their own regions and moved to other regions in the north and west.
And the weak people who were in the villages—the elderly and the young, women and children, and those who were suffering from hunger—
who could not walk and travel to distant places, went into the cities to beg and stay alive.
Many villages and estates were emptied of their inhabitants. Yet even those who went to distant places did not escape punishment.
Instead, as it is written about the people of Israel, wherever they went out, the hand of the Lord was against them for harm.
The same thing happened to them too. For plague struck them in the places to which they had gone. Those who entered Edessa were likewise overtaken by plague.
I will speak about it shortly, as well as I can. But I think there is no one capable of describing it as it actually happened.
Now I will write to you about the high prices you asked me about. I had not wanted to record anything about this, but I am forcing myself so that you will not think
that I disregarded your instruction. At this time wheat was being sold at four modii of wheat for a dinar, and barley at six.
Chickpeas cost five hundred nummi a qab; a qab of vetch cost four hundred nummi, and a qab of lentils three hundred and sixty nummi.
Meat, however, had not yet become expensive. But as time went on, prices rose, and the distress
of famine grew more severe among the people. Everything that could not be eaten became cheap:
clothing, utensils, and household possessions. These things were being sold for half or a third of their value,
yet they were not enough to feed their owners because bread was so expensive.
At this time our father Mar Peter traveled to the emperor to appeal to him to remit the tax.
But the governor seized the village landowners, put them under severe pressure, and demanded payment from them. While the bishop was still pleading with the emperor,
gold was sent by the governor to the imperial capital. When the emperor saw that the gold had reached him, he was unwilling to remit the tax.
But so as not to send our father away empty-handed, he remitted two folles for the villagers, along with the payments they used to make.
He also freed the townspeople from having to draw water for the Romans. Then the governor himself traveled to the emperor, with his sword strapped on.
He left Eusebius to take his place and plunder the city. When this Eusebius saw that the bakers could not keep up with making bread for the market,
because of the great number of villagers who filled the city, and because of the poor who had no bread in their homes,
he ordered that anyone who wished could make bread and sell it in the market. Jewish women came, and he gave them wheat from the storehouse.
They made bread for the market. But even so, the poor were in distress because they had no money with which to buy bread.
They wandered through the markets, porticoes, and courtyards, begging for a piece
of bread, but no one had bread to spare in his house.
When one of them begged some coins but could not buy bread with them, he used them to buy turnips, cabbage, or mallows.
and ate it raw. For this reason, vegetables became expensive, and there was a shortage of everything in the city and the villages.
Thus people went into the holy places and, because of their hunger, ate the consecrated bread like ordinary bread.
Others cut pieces from the carcasses of animals that are not eaten, cooked them, and ate them. You yourself are a trustworthy witness to these things.
The year 812. In this year, after the grape harvest, wine was sold at six measures for a dinar.
And a measure of vetches sold for three hundred nummi. The famine grew severe in the villages and the city.
Those who remained in the villages were eating bitter vetches. Others took [?] to fill themselves.
Those in the city wandered through the streets, picking up vegetable roots and leaves, rummaging in the refuse and eating them.
They slept in the porticoes along the streets and howled night and day from the agony of hunger. Their bodies wasted away.
They became shrunken and looked like [?] because their bodies were so thin. The whole city was full of them.
They began dying in the porticoes and the streets. When Demosthenes the governor went up to the emperor,
he told him about this distress. The emperor gave him a considerable amount of gold to distribute to the poor. When he returned from the emperor
to Edessa, he marked many of them with lead seals around their necks and gave each of them a pound of bread a day.
Yet they could not survive, because they were suffering from the agony of the hunger that had wasted them away.
The mortality grew severe at this time, in the month of November, and again in December, when frost and ice began to form.
Because they spent the night in the porticoes and the streets, the sleep of death overtook them as they slept.
Children and infants cried out in all our streets. Some of their mothers had died, while others would abandon them
and run away when they wanted something to eat, because they had nothing to give them. Corpses lay exposed in all our streets.
The city's inhabitants could not keep up with burying them. For while they were taking out those who had died first, as soon as they returned,
they would find others. Through the diligent efforts of Mar Nonnus, the keeper of the hospice, the brothers would then go around and gather these corpses.
The whole city gathered at the gate of the hospice, and they went out and buried them from one morning to the next. The church stewards also,
Mar Tutael the priest and Mar Stratonicus, who some time later was deemed worthy of becoming bishop in the city of Harran,
prepared a shelter in the church building at Edessa. Those who were suffering would enter and lie down there.
Many corpses were found in the shelter, and they buried them together with those from the hospice.
The governor took down the doors of the basilica beside the winter bath and put straw and mats inside it. They slept there, but it did not have enough room
for them. When the leading men of the city saw this, they too prepared shelters, and many people entered and took refuge in them.
The Romans also prepared places where the sick could lie down, and they took care of their expenses.
They were dying swift and agonizing deaths. Although many of them were buried every day, their numbers kept growing.
For word had spread through the countryside around the city that the people of Edessa cared for those in need.
For this reason, countless people entered the city. The bathhouse below the Church of the Apostles,
near the Great Gate, was also full of sick people. Many bodies were carried out of it every day.
The whole city was eager to join together in accompanying those who were carried out of the hospice,
with psalms, praises, and hymns, and with voices full of hope in the resurrection. The women also joined in with sorrowful weeping and loud cries.
The zealous shepherd, Mar Peter, walked at their head. The judge was also with them, along with all the city's freeborn citizens.
When these had been buried, everyone would return and accompany those from their own neighborhood. When the graves belonging to the hospice and the church were full, the governor went out
and opened the old tombs beside the Church of Mar Quna, which had been built for earlier generations through hard labor. They filled these, and then opened others, but they were not enough for them.
Finally, they opened and filled every [?] where there was an old tomb. For more than a hundred bodies were carried out of the hospice every day,
and on many days a hundred and twenty, or even a hundred and thirty, from the beginning of November until the end
of March. At that time, throughout all the city's streets, nothing could be heard except weeping for the dead
or the cries of those in agony. Many also died in the church courtyards, in the city's courtyards, and in the inns.
They also died on the roads as they came to enter the city. In February, prices rose still higher, and the plague grew worse.
Wheat was selling at thirteen qabs for a dinar, and barley at eighteen qabs.
A pound of meat cost a hundred nummi, a pound of chicken three hundred nummi, and an egg forty nummi.
In short, everything edible was expensive. Prayers of supplication were held in March so that the plague among the strangers would be stopped.
As the city's inhabitants pleaded on their behalf, they resembled the blessed David when he said to the angel who was destroying his people, “If I have sinned and done wrong,
what sin have these innocent sheep committed? Let your hand fall on me and on my father's household.” But in April the plague began among the city's inhabitants.
Many biers were carried out in a single day, and no one could keep count of them. This devastation by plague did not occur in Edessa alone.
Rather, from Antioch to Nisibis, people were being destroyed in this way and tormented by famine and plague.
Many rich people who had not been going hungry died. Many of the city's leading men also died that year.
In June and July, after the harvest, we hoped that we would at last find relief from the high prices.
But our expectations were not fulfilled as we had hoped. Instead, wheat from the new harvest was selling for as little as five modii for a dinar.
The year 813. After these afflictions of locusts, famine, and pestilence, about which I wrote to you
above, we had a little relief through God's mercy, so that we could endure what was still to come,
as we learned from the events themselves. For the grape harvest was abundant, and wine was sold straight from the winepress at twenty-five measures for a dinar.
The poor were supported by the vineyards through the raisin harvest. For the farmers and laborers used to say that the raisin harvest was greater
than the wheat harvest. For a hot wind blew when the grapes were beginning to ripen, and most of them dried up. Discerning people therefore said
that this had happened through the providence of God, the Lord of all, and that this event was a mingling of [?] with punishment,
so that the villagers could sustain themselves with these raisins and would not perish from hunger as they had the previous year.
For even at this time wheat was selling at only four modii for a dinar, and barley at six.
Such, then, was the sign of mercy [?] during the months of Tishrin. The whole winter of this year was also exceedingly rainy.
The seed that had been sown grew taller than a man in various places, even before Nisan had arrived.
Even the fallow land yielded only a little less than the land that had been sown. The roofs of houses likewise produced abundant fodder,
which some people harvested and sold as field [?] fodder. Because it had ears and was fully grown, its buyers did not recognize it.
We were expecting and hoping that this year too grain would become very cheap, as in former years. But this expectation was not fulfilled.
For in the month of Iyyar a scorching wind blew for three days and scorched all the grain in our region, except in a few small places.
In this same month, when the day arrived on which that wicked festival of Greek myths was celebrated, the one mentioned above,
an order came from Emperor Anastasius that the dancers were no longer to perform in any city within his imperial dominions.
Anyone who considers how these events turned out will therefore not blame us for saying that, because of the wickedness practiced by the inhabitants of
the city at that festival, the punishments of famine and pestilence came upon us one after another. For within thirty days after it was abolished,
wheat that had been selling at four modii for a dinar sold at twelve, and barley that had been selling at six modii sold at twenty-two.
It became plainly evident to everyone that God's will can bless even a small harvest
and give abundance to those who repent of their sins. For although all the grain had been scorched, as I said,
all this relief came within thirty days from the little that remained. But perhaps someone will still say
that my judgment was mistaken, since this repentance was not voluntary, so as to bring mercy on its account.
For the emperor abolished that festival by force, ordering that the dancers should not perform at all.
But we say that God, because of his abundant goodness, was seeking an opportunity to show mercy even to those who were unworthy. And there is
We have proof of this in the mercy shown to Ahab when he drew back at Elijah’s rebuke: he did not bring upon him in his lifetime the disaster that had already been decreed against his household.
But I am not saying that this was the only sin practiced in our city.
For many sins are committed both secretly and openly. And because the authorities also share in them,
I did not want to name the sins openly, lest I give those who like to make accusations an opportunity to say of us that I am speaking against the rulers.
Yet, so that I do not leave the matter entirely concealed, since I also promised above to tell you what caused war to be stirred up against us,
and so that I say nothing further about the authorities, I will set down the prophet’s words, from which you can understand.
When he saw the [?] of his people engaging in deeds like those committed today in our city, and especially among you and throughout the surrounding region,
he said to them, as though from the Lord’s own mouth: “Woe to anyone who says to a father, ‘What are you begetting?’ and to a woman, ‘What are you conceiving?’” As for the remaining matters,
it is better to remain silent, for it is right to obey the words of Scripture, which say: “Whoever understands will remain silent at that time, because it is a time of evil.”
But if our Lord grants that we see you in good health, we will speak with you about these things as far as we can.
Now, however, hear about the disasters that occurred in this year and about the sign that appeared on the very day when they occurred.
For this too is something you asked of us. On the twenty-second day of the month of August in this year, as Friday was dawning, a great fire appeared
to us, spreading across the [?] quarter of the sky all night long. We thought that it was about to sweep away the whole earth that night in a flood of fire.
But the mercy of our Lord kept us unharmed. A letter was sent to us by acquaintances who were traveling to Jerusalem,
which said this: on that night when the great blazing fire appeared,
the city of Ptolemais, which is Acre, was overthrown, and nothing was left standing in it. Then again, some days later,
people from Tyre and Sidon came to us and told us that on the day when the fire appeared and Ptolemais was overthrown,
on that very day half of each of their cities fell—that is, half of Tyre and half of Sidon.
In Beirut too, only the Jewish synagogue collapsed, on the very day when Acre was overthrown.
The inhabitants of Nicomedia were handed over to Satan to be disciplined, and many of them were tormented by demons,
until they remembered our Lord’s words, devoted themselves to fasting and prayer, and received healing. Also, Kavad, son of Peroz, king of the Persians,
on the very day when that fire appeared, assembled the entire Persian army, came up toward the north,
and entered Roman territory with the army of Huns that he had with him. He laid siege to Theodosiopolis in Armenia
and captured it within a few days. For the governor of that region, whose name was Constantine, rebelled against the Romans
and surrendered it to him because of some hostility he had toward the emperor. So Kavad plundered the city, devastated it, and burned it.
He devastated all the villages in the northern region, and they led away into captivity the survivors who remained.
He made Constantine chief of the nobles. He left a garrison in Theodosiopolis and departed from there. The year 814.
Great troubles also overtook the land of Mesopotamia, where we live, in this year.
Thus the things that Christ our Lord decreed against Jerusalem in his [?] and fulfilled in deed, and also the things spoken about the end of this world,
may also apply to what happened to us at this time. For after earthquakes occurred in various places, as I wrote to you,
and after there were famines and plagues, there were terrors and alarms, and great signs appeared from heaven.
Nation rose against nation and kingdom against kingdom. We fell by the sword and were taken captive to every land, and our country was trampled by foreign nations.
So, had it not been for the words of our Lord, who said, “When you hear of wars and upheavals, do not be afraid,
for these things must happen first, but the end has not yet come,” we would have dared to say that the end of the world had arrived.
Indeed, many thought and said this. But we considered that this war was not taking place throughout the whole world.
Along with this, we also remembered the words of the blessed Paul, with which he warned the Thessalonians about the coming of our Lord, saying
that they should not be alarmed by a message, a spirit, or a misleading letter supposedly from
him, claiming that the day of the Lord had arrived. He showed that the end cannot come until the false Messiah is revealed.

From these words of our Lord and his apostle, therefore, we understood that these things had not happened to us because it was the last age. Rather, they happened to discipline us, because our sins had grown great...
For Kavadh, king of the Persians, came from the north on the fifth day of October, a Saturday.
He and his entire army encamped against the city of Amida, which is here in our region of Mesopotamia.
When Anastasius, emperor of the Romans, heard that Kavadh had assembled his army, he did not wish to confront him in battle, so that blood would not be shed on either side.
Instead, he sent him gold through Rufinus and instructed him that, if Kavadh was at [?] and had not yet crossed into Roman territory, he should give him the gold and send him away.
But when Rufinus reached Caesarea in Cappadocia, he heard that Kavadh had devastated Ingila, Sophene, Armenia, and Arabia.
He left the gold in Caesarea and went to him. He told him to withdraw beyond the frontier and receive the gold, but he refused.
Instead, he seized Rufinus and ordered that he be kept under guard. He and his entire army attacked Amida with every method of warfare, by day and by night.
He built a siege mound against it, while the people of Amida built up and increased the height of the wall. When the siege mound had been raised, the Persians brought up a battering ram.
As they repeatedly struck the wall, the new construction loosened and fell, because it had not yet settled.
But the people of Amida cut an opening through the wall beneath the siege mound. They secretly dragged into the city the earth that had been heaped into it, while supporting
the structure with posts. The siege mound was undermined and collapsed. And when Kavadh could not overcome the strength of the city,
He sent Nu'man, king of the Arabs, with his entire army, to go south into the territory of Harran. Some of the Persian army also advanced ahead of them.
As far as the city of Constantina, which is Tella. They plundered, seized property, and devastated the whole region.
On the nineteenth day of the month of November, Olympius, duke of Tella, and Eugenius, duke of Melitene, who had come down at that time, went out,
They and their army, and destroyed the Persians they found in the villages around Tella. When they turned to return to the city,
Someone informed them that there were five hundred men in a single force not very far from them. They prepared to go against them.
But the Roman troops with them had scattered to strip the dead. Since it was night, Olympius ordered them to light a fire on top of a hill
And sound the horns, so that those who had scattered would gather around them. But the Persian commanders who were encamped in the village of Tell Beshmai,
When they saw the glow of the fire and heard the sound of the horns, armed their entire force and came against them.
When the Roman cavalry saw that the Persians outnumbered them, they turned back. The infantry, however, could not escape,
But were forced to fight. They gathered and drew themselves up for battle, forming what is called the chelone, that is, the tortoise.
They fought for a long time. When the Persian force grew too strong for them, and Huns and Arabs also joined the attack against them,
Their ranks were broken, and they were thrown into confusion among one another and became entangled among the cavalry.
Many of the Romans were trampled, crushed, and killed beneath the hooves of the Arabs' horses, and the rest were taken captive.
On the twenty-sixth day of this same month, Nu'man also came from the south and entered the territory of Harran, devastating and plundering it.
He carried off the people, livestock, and possessions of the whole territory of Harran, and came as far as Edessa,
Devastating, plundering, and taking captives from all the villages. The number of people he carried off into captivity was eighteen thousand five hundred,
Besides those who were killed, and besides the livestock, possessions, and plunder of every kind. The reason all these people were found in the villages
Was that it was the grape harvest. Not only were the villagers going out for the harvest, but many people from Harran and Edessa had also gone out and were taken captive.
Because of these events, Edessa was shut up and kept under guard. Trenches were dug, the wall was repaired, and the city gates were reinforced with plates,
Because they were worn out. They wanted to renew them and make barriers for the river's sluices, lest anyone enter through them.
There was not enough iron available for the work, so an order was issued that every household in Edessa should provide ten pounds of iron.
When this had been done, the work was completed. But when Eugenius saw that he could not defeat all the Persians,
He took the troops he had left and went against the garrison they had in Theodosiopolis. He destroyed those who were in it and captured the city. Kavadh, meanwhile, was still fighting against Amida,
Striving and toiling to raise the siege mound that had collapsed. He ordered the Persians to fill it with stones
And timber, and to bring articles made of haircloth, wool, and linen, and make them into something like panniers or sacks.
and fill them with earth, and build above the siege mound he had made, so that it could easily rise level with the wall.
Then the people of Amida assembled a machine that the Persians themselves nicknamed “the Butcher,” because it obstructed all their work and inflicted destruction on them.
For with that machine the people of Amida hurled enormous stones, each weighing more than three hundred pounds.
In this way the covering of wool felt under which the Persians sheltered was torn apart, and those standing beneath it were slaughtered.
The head of the battering ram was also broken by the continuous barrage of stones hurled without end.
For the people of Amida could not inflict as much damage on the Persians with anything else as they could with these enormous stones.
For that covering of wool felt had been laid in many layers over the siege mound, and the Persians kept pouring water over it.
It could not be damaged by arrows because of its thickness, or by fire because of its wetness.
But these enormous stones hurled from the Butcher destroyed the covering, the men, and the military equipment.
Thus the Persians were defeated and abandoned their work on that siege mound. They decided to return to their own country.
For during the three months they had besieged the city, fifty thousand of them had been killed in the battles fought every day, night and day.
But the people of Amida became confident in their victory and grew careless. They no longer guarded the wall as diligently as before.
On the tenth day of January, a great deal of wine was drunk
by the guards on the wall because of the cold. When night came, they lay down and sank into a deep sleep.
Others abandoned their posts because rain was falling, and went down to shelter in their houses.
Whether, then, it was through this negligence, as we believe, or through treacherous betrayal, as some have said, or through punishment from God,
the Persians gained control of Amida’s wall by means of ladders, although neither the gates had been opened nor the wall breached.
They devastated the city, plundered its possessions, trampled on its holy things, dishonored its worship, stripped its churches, and carried its inhabitants into captivity,
except for the elderly, the infirm, and those who had hidden themselves. They left a garrison of three thousand men there, and all the rest went down to Mount Sinjar.
So that the Persians who remained would not be troubled by the smell of the bodies of the people of Amida, they carried them out and piled them in two heaps outside the northern gate.
The number of those carried out through the northern gate was more than eighty thousand, apart from those they brought out alive
and stoned outside the city, and apart from those piled up on top of the siege mound they had built,
and apart from those they threw into the Tigris, and those who died in all the various ways whose deaths we cannot recount.
Then Kavadh released Rufinus to go and report to the emperor what had happened. He, for his part, recounted these atrocities everywhere.
At this news the cities east of the Euphrates were alarmed and prepared to flee westward. But the honored Jacob, the church visitor, who
For he had composed many discourses on passages of Scripture, and had written hymns and songs about that time of the locusts.
Even at this time he did not neglect what was fitting for him to do, but wrote letters of encouragement to all the cities.
He urged them to trust in God's deliverance and encouraged them not to flee.
When Emperor Anastasius heard, he too sent a large Roman army to spend the winter in those cities and guard them.
But all the plunder that Kavadh had taken and all the captives he had captured were not enough for him, nor was he satisfied with the great amount of blood they had shed.
Instead, he sent envoys to the emperor, saying, “Send me gold, or prepare for war.” This happened in the month of Nisan.
The emperor, however, sent no gold, but prepared to take revenge and avenge those who had perished.
In the month of Iyar he sent three generals against him: Areobindus, Patricius, and Hypatius, with many commanders accompanying them.
Areobindus went down and camped on the frontier near Dara and Ammudin, opposite the city of Nisibis. He had twelve thousand men with him.
Patricius and Hypatius camped before Amida to drive the Persian garrison out of it. They had forty thousand men with them.
At this time Apion the prefect also came down and stayed in Edessa to arrange provisions for the Roman army that was with them.
Because the bakers could not keep up with making bread, he ordered wheat to be given to every household in Edessa, and ordered them to make army biscuits at their own expense.
The people of Edessa supplied six hundred and thirty thousand measures on the first occasion. But when Kavadh saw
that the men under Areobindus were few, he sent against them the force he had at Singara: twenty thousand Persians.
Areobindus pursued them once and then a second time, until they were driven back to the gate of Nisibis, suffering losses. Many of the fugitives were suffocated at the gate
as they crowded together to get inside. In the month of Tammuz, Huns and Arabs also gathered with the Persians to attack him,
with Constantine at their head. When he learned this from scouts, he sent Calliopius of Aleppo to Patricius and Hypatius, saying,
“Come to me and help me, because a large army is about to attack us.” But they did not listen.
Instead, they remained in their positions near Amida. When the Persians attacked the men under Areobindus,
he could not fight them. Instead, he abandoned their camp and escaped to Tella and Edessa. All their equipment was plundered and carried off.
Meanwhile, the men under Patricius and Hypatius were assembling three wooden towers to bring up against the wall of Amida.

When the construction of the towers had been completed at great expense, and they had been reinforced with iron so that nothing could damage them, news reached them of what had happened on the frontier.
They burned the towers, withdrew from there, and went after the Persians, but did not catch up with them.
One of the commanders, named Pharasmanes, and another named Theodore cunningly sent a flock of sheep to pass near Amida.
They and their troops lay in ambush. When the Persians inside Amida saw the sheep, about four hundred picked men came out to seize them.
He attacked the Romans who were lying in ambush, defeated them, and captured their commander alive.
He promised them that he would hand Amida over to them. For this reason Patricius and Hypatius returned there.
When that marzban could not fulfill his promise, because those inside the city would not obey him, the general ordered him to be crucified.
The Arabs allied with the Persians came to the Khabur, and Timostratus, the duke of Callinicum, marched out against them [and defeated them].
The Arabs in Roman territory, who are called the people of Tha'laba, also went to Nu'man's camp and found a caravan going up to him,
with camels carrying clothing [?] up to him. They fell upon them, slaughtered them, and carried off the camels. But they did not succeed in taking the camp itself,
because it had moved into the depths of the desert. Then, in the month of August, the entire Persian army assembled again,
along with the Huns, Qadishites, and Armenians, and they came as far as Opadana. Patricius and his men heard about this, and he set out to march against them.
While the Romans were still on the road and had not drawn up for battle, the Persians encountered their advance troops and struck them.
When those who had been struck turned back, the rest of the Roman army saw the advance troops who had been struck.
Fear fell upon them, and they did not stay to fight. Instead, Patricius turned back first, and the whole army followed him.
They crossed the Euphrates River and escaped to the city of Samosata. Nu'man, king of the Arabs allied with the Persians, was also wounded in this battle.
One of the Roman commanders, named Peter, fled to the fortress of Ashpiran. When the Persians surrounded the fortress,
the inhabitants of the fortress became afraid of them and handed him over to them. The Persians led him away in chains, and the Romans who were with him
they killed. But they did no harm to the inhabitants of the fortress. Now Kavadh, king of the Persians, was planning to march against Areobindus at Edessa.
Nu'man, king of the Arabs, was also urging him on because of what had happened to his caravan. But a troop commander from Nu'man's camp, who was a Christian,
spoke up and said, “Your Majesty should not trouble yourself to march against Edessa to fight, because there is an unbreakable promise from Christ, whom they worship,
concerning it: no enemy will ever gain power over it.” When Nu'man heard this, he threatened to do worse things in Edessa than had been done in Amida.
He also spoke blasphemous words. Christ indeed displayed a clear sign in him: at the very moment when he blasphemed, the wound he had received in his head became inflamed,
and his whole skull swelled up. He got up and went to his tent, remained in this distress for two days, and died.
But even this sign did not restrain Kavadh's insolence or turn him from his evil purpose. Instead, he appointed a king in Nu'man's place and set out to wage war.
When he reached Tella, he encamped against it. The Jews who were there plotted to hand the city over to him.
They made an opening in the tower adjoining their synagogue, which had also been entrusted to them to guard.
They informed the Persians about it so that they could break through it and enter by it. But this became known to Count Peter, who was in captivity,
and he persuaded those guarding him to bring him close to the wall, saying that he had clothing and various belongings stored in the city.
He sought to persuade the people of Tella to give him something for their own sake. The guards agreed to his request and brought him forward. He then told the soldiers who were standing on
the wall to summon Count Leontius, who was guarding the city at that time.
They summoned him and the commanders. Petra spoke with them in Latin and revealed to them the Jews’ plot.
To keep the matter from becoming known to the Persians, he asked them to give him a set of clothes.
At first they acted as though they were mocking him. Then they threw him a set of clothes from the wall.
For he truly needed clothes to wear. Then he came down from the wall.
And, pretending that they were unaware of the Jews’ plot and did not know where the place was,
they went around examining the foundations of the entire wall, as though they wanted to see whether there was a hole or a tunnel.
He did this for Petra’s sake, lest the Persians discover that he had disclosed the matter and subject him to further torments.
Finally they came to the place where the Jews were keeping watch, and he found that they had dug and prepared a substantial excavation inside the tower, just as they had been told.
When the Romans saw what was there, they went out against them in great anger and went throughout the city.
He slaughtered every Jew he found—men and women, old people and children. They continued doing this for days.
Only with difficulty did they stop their destruction, at the command of Count Leontius and through the entreaties of the blessed Bishop Bar-Hadad.
They guarded the city carefully, night and day, while the holy Bar-Hadad went around visiting them, praying over them and blessing them.
He praised their diligence and encouraged them, sprinkling baptismal water on them and on the city wall. He also carried
the Eucharist around with him, to give them communion in the sacrament at their posts, so that none of them would leave his watch and come down from the wall for this reason.
He also went out confidently to the king of the Persians, spoke with him, and reproached him. When Kavadh saw the man’s dignity and also became aware of the Romans’ vigilance,
he did not consider it advantageous to remain near Tella with the whole army he had with him. For one thing, provisions were unavailable to him in the devastated countryside.
For another, he feared that the Roman commanders might assemble together and attack him jointly.
For these reasons he quickly set out toward Edessa and camped for about twenty days on the river Gallab, which is called the river of the Medes.
The marauders among his forces roamed the countryside and devastated it. On the sixth day of the month of September,
the people of Edessa demolished all the monasteries and inns near the wall, and he burned the village of Kfar-Selem, which is Neghbath.
They demolished all the fences of the surrounding gardens and orchards and cut down the trees within them.
They brought up the bones of all the martyrs who lay around the city. He brought weapons up onto the wall and fastened screens of haircloth above the [?].
On the ninth day of this same month, Kavadh sent word to Areobindus that he must either admit his marzban into the city.
Or he should go out to meet him on the plain, as though he wished to conclude a treaty of peace with him.
But he secretly ordered his army that, if Areobindus allowed them to enter the city, they should turn and seize the wall and its entrances,
until he himself arrived and entered after them. But if he came outside to meet them, they should lie in wait
for him, capture him alive, and bring him to him. Areobindus, however, because he was afraid to let them enter the city,
went outside to meet them. He did not go far from the city, but only as far as the church of Saint Sergius.
Bawi, who was the astabid—a title meaning “master of the Persians”—came to him and said to Areobindus,
“If you want us to make peace, give us ten thousand pounds of gold, and make a binding agreement with us that we will receive the customary gold payment every year.”
Areobindus offered to give as much as seven thousand pounds, but they would not accept it.
They continued arguing with him from morning until the ninth hour. And because he found no opportunity for their treachery,
because of the Romans guarding him, and because they were also afraid to attack Edessa on account of what had happened to Naaman, they left Areobindus in Edessa, and he went to attack Harran.
He sent all the Arabs to Serugh. But Rephius, who was in Harran, went secretly out of the city and attacked them.
He killed sixty of their men and captured the leader of the Huns alive. Because he was a well-known man
and was highly valued by the king of the Persians, he promised the people of Harran that, if they handed him over alive, he would not attack them.
They were afraid of war and handed over that Hun, sending with him, as a mark of honor, fifteen hundred rams
along with other things. Meanwhile, the Persian Arabs who had been sent to Serugh went as far as the Euphrates River,
laying waste, taking captives, and plundering everything they found. Patriciolus, one of the Roman commanders, and his son Vitalian
had only just arrived from the west at this time to go into battle. He was bold and fearless, since he had not been present at the earlier events.
When he crossed the river, he encountered one of the Persian commanders and fought [?] with him. He destroyed all the Persians who were with him.
He set out toward Edessa, but heard from a fugitive that Kawad had surrounded the city. He turned back, crossed the river, and remained at Samosata.
On the seventeenth day of this month, a Wednesday, we saw the words of Christ and his promises to Abgar
being fulfilled in practice. For Kawad gathered his entire army, set out from the Euphrates River, and came and encamped against Edessa.
His camp extended from the martyrs’ shrine of Saint Cosmas and Saint Damian, with troops encamped throughout all the gardens, at the church of Saint Sergius, and at the village of Bekin,
as far as the shrine of the confessors. Its width extended as far as Shahurta of Sarrin. This whole countless army surrounded Edessa that day,
besides the guard posts he had stationed in the mountains and on the heights. The entire plain was filled with them. All the city’s gates were open,
yet the Persians could not enter it because of Christ’s blessing. Instead, fear fell upon them.
They remained in their positions, with no one engaging them in battle, from morning until about the ninth hour.
Then a few men went out from the city and fought against them. They killed many Persians, while not one of their own men fell.
The women carried water and brought it outside the wall for those fighting to drink.
Young boys were throwing stones with slings. Thus the few men who had come out from the city drove them away
and pushed them back from the wall, for they had not been far from it, but only about a bowshot away.
They went and camped beside the village of Qubbe. Later in the day, Areobindus again went out through the Great Gate.
As he stood facing the Persian army, he sent word to Kavadh: “Now you have learned by experience that the city does not belong to you,
nor to Anastasius. Rather, it is the city of Christ, who blessed it and stood against your armies
so that they would not gain control of it.” Kavadh sent word to him: “Give me hostages to guarantee that you will not come out after me when I leave,
and send me the men you captured yesterday, along with the gold you promised, and I will withdraw from the city.”
Areobindus handed over Count Basil to him, along with the men captured from his army, who numbered fourteen.
He made an agreement with him to give him two thousand pounds of gold within ten days. Kavadh departed and went to camp at Dhabana.
But he did not wait until the deadline. Instead, the following day he sent one of his men, named Hormizd, and ordered him to bring three hundred pounds of gold.
Areobindus gathered the leading men of the city to discuss how that gold could be collected. When they saw that Hormizd had arrived so quickly,
they drew strength from their trust in Christ, took courage, and said to Areobindus: “We will not send gold to a liar.
For just as he has gone back on his word and has not waited until the day you appointed for him, so he will go back on his word and lie once he has received the gold.
We believe that if he fights against us again, he will be put to shame, because Christ stands in defense of his city.” Then
Areobindus too took courage and sent word to Kavadh: “Now we know that you are not a king, for no king gives his word and then goes back on it and lies.
If he lies, he is no king. Now that you have shown yourself to be false, send Count Basil back to me, and do whatever is in your power to do.”
Then Kavadh became furious. He armed the elephants he had with him, set out with his entire army, and came again to fight against Edessa,
on the twenty-fourth day of the month of September, a Wednesday. He surrounded the city on every side,
more closely than before, while all its gates stood open. Areobindus, however, had ordered the Romans not to fight against him,
so that no breach of faith would be seen on his own part. But a few of the villagers who were in the city went out against him with slings.
They brought down many of the armored men with him, while not one of their own men fell. His troops nevertheless pressed boldly forward to enter the city.
But whenever they approached its gates, they sank down like a steep heap of sand, faltered, and turned back.
But because of the speed at which their horses galloped, the slingers mingled among them.
Although the Persians were shooting arrows, the Huns were swinging axes, and the Arabs were leveling spears against them, they could not wound a single one of them.
Rather, they were like those Philistines who came up against Samson: although they were very numerous and armed,
they could not kill him, while he, though without weapons, killed a thousand of them with a donkey’s jawbone. So too
the Persians, Huns, and Arabs, although they and their horses were falling from the stones the slingers were throwing, could not kill even one of them.
When they saw that they could neither enter the city nor injure the unarmed men mingling among them,
they set fire to the Church of Saint Sergius, the Church of the Confessors, all the monasteries that remained, and the church of Negbath, for the townspeople had left this one standing.
Now Areobindus, the commander, saw the zeal of the villagers, that they had not been disgraced, and the help that had accompanied them.
In the afternoon he gathered all the villagers who were in Edessa into the church and gave them gifts of three hundred denarii.
Kavadh left Edessa and went and camped beside the Euphrates River. From there he sent messengers to the emperor to inform him of his coming.
The Arabs who were with him crossed the river at the crossing, plundered, devastated, took captives, and burned everything they found.
A few of the Persian cavalry went to Batnae. Because its wall had been breached, its inhabitants could not resist them.
Instead, they received them without a battle and surrendered the city to them. The year 815. When the emperor of the Romans learned what had happened,
he sent Celer, his master of offices, with a large army. When Kavadh heard this, he made his marches along the Euphrates River,
intending to return and stay in his own territory, called Beth Aramaye. When he reached the vicinity of Callinicum, he sent a marzban there
to fight against them. Timostratus, the duke, marched out against him, destroyed his entire army, and captured him alive. When Kavadh reached the city,
he drew up his entire army against it, threatening to destroy it and carry off all its inhabitants by the sword and into captivity
unless they handed the man over to him. The duke was afraid of the size of the Persian army and handed him over.
When Celer, the master of offices, reached Mabbug on the Euphrates River and saw that Kavadh had withdrawn before him,
and that winter had already arrived and he could not pursue him, he summoned the commanders of the Roman armies
and dismissed them because they had not obeyed one another. He assigned cities to them in which to spend the winter until the time for battle came.
On the twenty-fifth of December, an order came from the emperor that the tax should be remitted throughout Mesopotamia.
When the Persians who were in Amida saw that the Roman army had moved far away from them, they opened the gates of the city of Amida.
They went out and came in wherever they wished. They sold merchants copper, lead, iron, [?] utensils, and everything that could be found in the city.
They also placed [?] in it. When Patricius heard this, he left Melitene, where he was spending the winter, and came and camped outside Amida.
He killed all the merchants he found bringing grain and oil down there, as well as those buying goods from there.
He also found the Persians who had been sent by Kavadh to bring weapons, grain, and livestock there. He slaughtered them and took everything they had with them.
When Kavadh learned of this, he sent a marzban against him to take revenge on him. When they approached one another to fight, the Romans, because of
their fear arising from their earlier defeat, advised Patricius to flee. He accepted this advice.
In their haste, not knowing where they were going, they came upon a river called Callath. Because it was winter,
and the river was in full flood, they could not cross it. Every one of them who hurried to cross the river drowned with his horse.
When Patricius saw this, he encouraged the Romans, saying, “Roman soldiers,
let us not disgrace our ancestry and our military service by fleeing from our enemies. Instead, let us turn against them. Perhaps we can overcome their strength.
But if they prove stronger than we are, it is better to die by the sword with a good reputation for courage
than to perish like cowards, drowned in the water.” Then the Romans accepted his advice because of the predicament the river had put them in.
They turned furiously against the Persians and slaughtered them. Amida. Patricius sent and gathered craftsmen to him from other cities,
and many villagers. He ordered them to dig into the ground and make a tunnel beneath the wall so that it would give way and fall.
In the month of March, while the rest of the Romans were assembling to march down with the magister, a certain sign from God was given to them to encourage them and give them confidence in victory.
We learned of it in writing from members of the church of Zeugma. So that you will not think I am saying something of my own invention,
or that I have been persuaded to affirm a false report, I am setting down the very words of the letter that came to us.
They are as follows: “Hear, then, of a marvel and a glorious joy unlike any that has ever occurred. For this belongs to us
and to you and to all the Romans. It is a wondrous event, difficult for the minds of mortal human beings to believe.
But we have seen it with our own eyes, held it, and kissed it with our lips. You should believe it without any hesitation.
On the nineteenth of March, on Friday, the day of our Savior’s death,
a goose laid an egg in Agra, a village in the district of Zeugma. On it are beautiful, legible inscriptions in Greek.
They are of the same substance as the egg itself and are raised, both to sight and to touch, like the inscriptions that monks put on blessed loaves.
Even blind people can feel their shape. They are as follows: a cross is marked on the side of the egg.
From it, going all the way around the egg until it reaches the cross again, is written ‘The Romans.’ Then another cross is marked,
and from it, all the way around until it reaches the cross again, is written ‘are victorious.’ The crosses are marked one above the other, and the words are written one above the other.
There is no Christian or Jew who sees this marvel and keeps his mouth silent from praise.”

But we do not dare to imitate the inscriptions that the right hand of God wrote within the womb, because they are exceedingly beautiful. Therefore, explain this without hesitation to everyone who hears.
These are the [?] of that letter from the people of Zeugma. The egg itself was given by those in whose village it had been laid
to Areobindus. The Romans assembled a large army, went down, and encamped near the city of Reshaina.
About ten thousand men were also sent from Qawad's forces to attack Patricius. They went up and encamped at Nisibis to rest there.
They sent their livestock to graze on Mount Sinjar. When the magister [?] heard this, he sent Timostratus, the duke of Callinicum,
with six thousand cavalry. They went, fell upon those who were tending the horses, and slaughtered them.
He took away horses, sheep, and much plunder from there, and returned to the Roman army at Reshaina. Then they all set out together
and went and encamped outside the city of Amida, alongside Patricius. In the month of May, Calliopius of Aleppo became prefect. He came and took up residence in Edessa.
He gave wheat to the Edessenes to make army biscuits at their own expense. At this time they baked eight hundred and fifty thousand measures of wheat.
Apion went to Alexandria, so that he could also have army biscuits made there and send bread.
When Patricius had advanced through the tunnel he had dug beneath the wall of Amida, he supported it with timbers and set them on fire.
The outer face of the wall gave way and fell, but the inner face remained standing. He decided to dig through that same tunnel and enter the city.
When he had broken through the excavation and the Romans began climbing up, a woman of Amida saw them. In her joy she suddenly shouted, “Look! The Romans are entering the city!”
The Persians heard her and ran at the first man who had climbed up, and stabbed him. After him a Goth named Aldes climbed up.
He had been appointed tribune at Harran. He stabbed three of those Persians. No other Romans climbed up after him, because
the Persians had become aware of them. When Aldes saw that no one was climbing up, he became afraid and turned back.
He decided to take down with him the body of the Roman who had fallen, so that the Persians would not mock it.
As he dragged the body and descended into the mouth of the excavation, the Persians struck him too and wounded him.
He directed water there from a large spring nearby. And they drowned there [?] a large spring that was nearby.
They drowned four heavily armed Roman soldiers there who were ready to climb up. The rest fled and got out of there.
The Persians gathered stones from inside the city and blocked the excavation with them. They piled a great deal of earth over it and carefully guarded the whole area around it,
lest it be broken through somewhere else. They dug trenches inside, along the entire circuit of the wall, and filled them with water,
so that if the Romans made another tunnel, water would flow into it and it would be discovered. When Patricius learned this from a deserter who came down to him,
he gave up tunneling. One day, while the whole Roman army was encamped and at ease, an occasion for battle arose in this way.
A boy was tending camels and donkeys. As one donkey grazed, it wandered off and went up close to the wall.
The boy was afraid to go in and bring it out. When one of the Persians saw him, he climbed down from the wall on a rope.
He wanted to cut it up and haul it up for them to eat, for there was no meat at all inside the city.
But one of the Roman soldiers, a Galilean by birth, drew his sword, took his shield in his left hand, and ran at the Persian to kill him.
Because he had reached the wall, those standing on top of it threw down a large stone and crushed that Galilean.
The Persian began climbing back up the rope to his position. When he reached halfway up the wall,
one of the Roman commanders approached, with two shield-bearers walking in front of him.
And he shot, while two shield-bearers were walking in front of him. He shot an arrow between them and struck that Persian.
He knocked him down beside that Galilean. A shout went up from both sides, and because of this they were stirred up and rose to fight.
All the Roman forces were gathered around the city, surrounding it on every side.
