Forty of them fell, and a hundred and fifty were wounded. Of the Persians on the wall, only nine were seen to have died.
[?] were wounded. For it was difficult to fight them while they were high up on the wall.
They had also built small shelters for themselves along the whole wall. They stood inside them and fought, remaining invisible to those outside.
But the master of soldiers and the commanders decided that they should not fight them, because killing them [?] would not bring victory to the Romans,
since they still faced a war against all the Persians. If Kavadh were defeated, these men would surrender or perish in their confinement.
For this reason he ordered that no one should fight them, so that the main body of the army would not be needlessly alarmed by the Romans who were killed or wounded.
In the month of June, Constantine, who had gone over to the Persians,
saw that their cause had not succeeded and fled from them, together with two prominent women from Amida
who had been given to him by the king of the Persians. For fourteen days he traveled night and day through an uninhabited desert, with the few people accompanying him. When he reached safety,
he made himself known to the Arabs allied with the Romans. They took him and brought him to the fortress called Sura. From there they sent him to Edessa.
When the emperor heard of his arrival, he sent for him. When he arrived to appear before him, the emperor ordered one of the bishops
to lay his hand on him and ordain him a priest. He was to go and live in the city of Nicaea, never appear before the emperor, and take no part in public affairs.
Now Kavadh, when he captured Amida, had also entered its public baths and experienced the benefit of bathing.
So, immediately upon returning to his own country, he had ordered bathhouses to be built in all the towns of Persian territory.
Adid, an Arab under Persian authority, surrendered with his entire force and submitted to the Romans. Then, in the month of July,
the Romans again fought the Persians in Amida, and Gainas, the military governor of Arabia, struck many of them with arrows.
When the day grew hot, his armor became burning hot on him. He loosened the fastening of his breastplate a little, and they shot a ballista bolt from Amida, struck him, and he died.
When the master of the troops saw that his siege of Amida was bringing him losses, he took his army and went down into Persian territory.
He left Patricius near Amida. Areobindus also took his army, and they entered Persian Armenia.
He slaughtered ten thousand Armenian and Persian men, and they took thirty thousand women and children captive.
They plundered and burned many villages. When they turned back to return to Amida, he drove off sheep, cattle, and other livestock—
one hundred and twenty thousand. As they were passing beside the city of Nisibis, the Romans lay in ambush.
They were bringing the captives past with only a few men accompanying them. When a marzban who was there saw that they were few, he armed his troops and went out
to take the captives away from them. They pretended to flee, and the Persians took courage and pursued them. When he had gone far away from his own people,
the Romans rose from their ambush and slaughtered them. Not one of them escaped. There were about seven thousand men.
Mushegh the Armenian, who was under Persian authority, also surrendered with his entire army and submitted to the Romans. The year eight hundred and sixteen.
The survivors among the inhabitants of Amida who had escaped the sword and remained there were suffering great distress and torment from hunger.
For the Persians were afraid that they might hand the city over to the Romans.
They bound all the men who were there and threw them into the arena. Thus they perished from hunger, remaining in their fetters forever.
But they gave the women some of their food, because they were having illicit sex with them, and also because they needed them to grind grain and bake for them.
When their provisions ran short, they despised the women and left them without food.
For during that year each of them received only a handful of barley a day.
They had absolutely no meat, wine, or any other food. And because they were very afraid of the Romans,
they never left their guard posts at all. Instead, they made themselves small ovens on the wall
and brought up hand mills for themselves. At their posts they would grind that handful of barley, bake it, and eat it.
They also brought up large kneading troughs and placed them between the [?]. They filled them with earth and sowed vegetables in them.
They ate whatever grew in them. To tell what the women there were doing may seem unbelievable to those who come after us. Today there is no one
among those eager to learn about events who has not heard everything that happened, even if he lives very far away from us.
Many women therefore gathered together and made a secret pact among themselves. They would go out stealthily into the city streets in the evening or the morning.
Anyone they found whom they could overpower, whether a woman, a child, or an old man, they would drag into a house, kill, and eat,
either boiled or roasted. When they were exposed by the smell of roasting meat, and the matter became known to the marzban who was there, he tortured many of them and killed them.
Those who remained were threatened so that they would not do this again and kill anyone. But they were permitted to eat those who died, and they did this openly.
They ate the dead flesh of human beings, while the rest of them gathered shoes, worn-out scraps, and discarded things from the streets and courtyards and ate them.
The Roman troops, however, lacked nothing. Everything was supplied to them at the proper time, being sent down with great care by the emperor’s command.
Goods for sale were more plentiful in their camps than in the cities: food, drink, footwear, and clothing.
All the cities had biscuit baked by their bakers and sent it to them, especially the people of Edessa.
For in this year too, by order of Calliopius the governor, the city’s inhabitants baked six hundred and thirty thousand measures in their courtyards,
besides what the villagers throughout the whole district baked, along with the foreign and local bakers. Again, in this year there went up
Mar Peter, the bishop, to the emperor, to persuade him to remit the tax. The emperor answered him harshly
and rebuked him for abandoning the care of the poor at such a time and coming up to him. For he said
that God himself would have put it into his heart, if it were appropriate, to do good to the blessed city without anyone’s petition.
While the bishop was still there, the emperor sent a remission to all Mesopotamia through someone else, without his knowing it.
For the district of Hierapolis too, he remitted one-third of the tax. Now the Roman commanders who were encamped outside Amida
would go down in raiding parties into Persian territory, plundering, taking captives, and laying waste. The Persians fled before them
and crossed the River Tigris. There they found Persian cavalry gathering to attack the Romans.
They took courage against them and remained beyond the Tigris. The Romans crossed after them and destroyed all the Persian cavalry,
who numbered about ten thousand men. They plundered the possessions of all those who had fled, burned many villages, and killed every male in them
aged twelve and above. They took the women and children captive. For the master of the army had given all the commanders this order:
if any Roman was found sparing a male aged twelve or above, he himself was to be killed in his place.
In every village they entered, they were not to leave even a single house standing.
For this purpose he selected strong men from among the Romans, and many villagers who accompanied them as they went down.
After the roofs had burned and the fire had died out, they uprooted even the foundations. They also cut down

and destroyed vineyards, olive trees, and all the other trees. The Arabs allied with the Romans also crossed the Tigris ahead of them, plundered, [?], and destroyed everything they found in Persian territory.
Knowing that you examine everything carefully, I ask your Holiness to consider this as well:
this war became a source of great profit for the Arabs on both sides, and fulfilled their wishes in both kingdoms.
When Kavad saw that the Romans were laying waste to his country and that no one was standing against them, he [wanted] to come out to meet them.
For this reason he sent Astabid to the magister to negotiate peace. He had a force of about twenty thousand with him.
He sent all the prominent men whom he had taken captive from Amida, Qatra, whom he had taken from Ashparin, and Basil, whom he had taken from Edessa as a hostage.
He also sent back the body of Duke Olympius, who had gone down to him on an embassy and died there, in a sealed coffin.
This was to show that he had died a natural death and nothing else. His servants and those who had gone down with him bore witness to this.
The magister received them and sent them to Edessa, except for the judge of Amida and Count Peter. For he was angry and furious,
and wanted to put them to death. He said that the places they had been guarding had been surrendered through their negligence.
The Persians themselves testified to this, saying that Amida’s wall could not be taken by force. Astabid, however, was pleading with him and begging him
to give him the Persians who were shut up in Amida in exchange for those whom he had brought. For although they were holding out against their attackers,
they were suffering terribly from hunger. But the magister said, “Do not mention these men’s case to me, because they are confined in a city
of ours and are our slaves.” Astabid said to him, “Then let me send them provisions, for it is not fitting for you
to let your slaves perish from hunger. Whenever you wish, it is easy for you to kill them.” He said to him, “Send them.” Astabid said,
“Swear to me, you and all the leaders and military commanders who are with you, that no one will kill those whom I send [?].”
They all swore to him, except Duke Nonnus, who was not with them at Apharsana. The magister had left him behind for this very reason,
so that, if any oath were sworn, he would not be bound by it. Astabid therefore sent three hundred camels loaded with sacks of bread, with arrows placed inside them.
Nonnus attacked them and seized these from them, and killed those who were accompanying them. When Astabid complained about this
and demanded an answer from the magister: “I cannot find out who did this, because of the great size of the army with me. But if you know who it was,
and you have the strength to take revenge on him, I will not stop you.” Astabid was frightened by this and continued to plead for peace.
After many days [?] had passed while he was pleading, severe cold set in, with much snow and ice. The Romans left their camps one by one,
and each man took his share of the plunder and went off to carry it home. Those who remained and did not return to their own regions
went into Tella, Reshaina, and Edessa to shelter from the cold. When Astabid saw that the Romans had weakened and could not endure remaining in
the open, he sent word to the magister: “Either make peace and let the Persians leave Amida, or prepare for battle.”
The magister ordered Count Justin to assemble the army, but he could not.
When he saw that most of the Romans had scattered away from him, he made peace and allowed the Persians to leave Amida on this condition:
if both kings approved and ratified what he had done, it would stand; otherwise, the war between them would continue.
When the Roman emperor learned what had happened, he ordered that a [?] be established in all the cities, especially in Amida.
As though seeking to end the hostility and secure peace, he sent honors and gifts to Kavadh through a man named Leo.
And all the vessels used at his table were made of gold. No one knows how severely the people of Edessa who were transporting grain to Amida suffered,
except those who were themselves involved in the undertaking. For many of them died on the road, along with their pack animals.
The worthy John, bishop of Amida, had died before the Persians laid siege to it.
The members of its clergy had gone up to the holy, God-loving man, adorned with every divine virtue,
the zealous and illustrious Mar Paulinus, patriarch of Antioch, so that he might appoint a bishop for them.
They were held in the citadel throughout their time there. Afterward, when they were released from captivity,
the clergy petitioned the patriarch for the worthy Nonnus, a priest and steward of the church of Amida. He made him their
bishop. When the worthy Nonnus received the office of chief priest, he sent Thomas, his rural bishop, to Constantinople,
to take charge of the people of Amida who were there and to ask the emperor for a gift.
Those who were there reached an agreement with him and petitioned the emperor that this Thomas should be their bishop.
The emperor granted their petition and wrote to the patriarch not to oppose them. The emperor also gave them the judge whom he requested.
The emperor and the patriarch gave gifts to the church of Amida, and a large amount of gold for him to distribute to the poor.
Because of this, all those who had been wandering in other regions gathered there.
They carried the bodies of the dead out of Amida every day, and then received whatever had been allotted to them.
Urbicius, the emperor’s eunuch, who had performed great acts of charity in the land of Jerusalem and in other regions,
also went down there and distributed a dinar to each person there. From there he came to Edessa and gave a tremissis to every woman who wished to receive one,
and one silver coin to every child. Almost all the women received it, both those in need and those who were not. In this same year,
after the war had ended, wild beasts turned on us. Because of the great number of corpses that had fallen in those battles,
they had acquired a taste for eating human bodies. When the corpses of the slain had rotted away and were gone,
the beasts entered the villages, snatched children, and ate them. They also attacked men traveling alone on the roads and mangled them.
People were so frightened that at threshing time there was no one in the whole district who would spend the night at his threshing floor without
a raised shelter, for fear of the ravenous beasts. But with the help of our Lord, who always cares for us
and in his mercy rescues us from all our trials, some of them fell into the hands of the villagers, who stabbed them
and sent their dead bodies to Edessa. Hunters also caught some of them, bound them, and brought them in alive. Everyone saw them and praised God.
He who said, “I will put the fear and dread of you upon every animal on earth.” For although locusts, famine, plague, and captivity were sent upon us because of our sins,
along with dangerous animals and other punishments, both those recorded in writing and those not recorded, nevertheless, in his grace he delivered us from them all.
In his mercy, through your prayer, he also strengthened me, insignificant as I am, to write, as far as I could, about the things that happened,
as a memorial for those who endured them and for the instruction of those who come after us, so that, if they wish, they may learn wisdom from these few things I have written.
For the things I have left out are more numerous than those I have written down. Indeed, I said at the beginning that I was not capable of recounting them all.
For if the hardships that each individual suffered had been recorded, they would have made lengthy histories, which even a large book would not have been enough to contain.
You can also learn from what others record. Even those who came to our aid under the name of saviors, as they traveled down and back up,
plundered us almost like enemies. They made many poor people get out of their beds and slept in them themselves, while their owners lay on the ground in cold weather.
They drove others out of their houses and went in and lodged there. Other people's livestock they forcibly drove away as though taking captives,
and they stripped the clothes from other people's bodies and took them. They treated others to severe beatings over any matter whatsoever.
They picked quarrels with others in the marketplaces and caused them losses over some trivial pretext.
They openly plundered everyone's scant food and the supplies that particular people had in the villages and towns.
Along the roads they attacked many people. And because the city's courtyards and inns were not sufficient to accommodate them,
they lodged with craftsmen in their shops. In full view of everyone, they abused women in the streets and houses. From elderly women, widows, and poor women,
they took oil, firewood, salt, and other things for their own needs. By making these women serve them, they kept them from their spinning.
In short, they oppressed everyone, great and small. No one was left untouched by their wickedness.
Even the local officials who had been appointed to organize and billet them held out their hands for bribes.
Although they took payments from everyone, they protected no one. Instead, to those from whom they had initially removed the soldiers,
they sent others after a few days. They even lodged with priests and deacons,
although these had an imperial decree forbidding soldiers to be quartered with them. Why should I tire myself by listing so many things
that perhaps even those more capable than I could not recount? Now, after he crossed the Euphrates River westward, and the magister went to the emperor,
Areobindus to Antioch, Patricius to Melitene, Pharesmanes to Apamea, Theodore to Damascus, and Cleopas to Mabbug, there was a little relief
in Edessa. The small number of men remaining there made things easier for the city. Eulogius, the governor, concerned himself with rebuilding it.
The emperor gave him [?] pounds for the building expenses. He rebuilt and restored the entire outer wall surrounding the city.
He also restored and repaired the two aqueducts that enter from the village of Telzema and from Maudad. He also rebuilt and completed the public bath that had collapsed.
He also renovated his own headquarters and carried out much building throughout the city. The emperor also gave the bishop twenty pounds for expenses and for repairing the wall.
And Urbicius the eunuch gave ten pounds to build a martyr shrine for the blessed Mary.
As for the oil [?] that used to be given to the martyrs' shrines and monasteries from Christ's treasury,
which amounted to six thousand eight hundred sextarii, the governor himself took it away from them.
He ordered that it be used for lighting the city's colonnades. The custodians pleaded earnestly with him about it, but he would not be persuaded.
So that he would not be thought to despise the sanctuaries built for God, he gave each martyr shrine two hundred sextarii from his own resources.
Until this year, four modii of wheat were sold for a dinar, and six of barley.
Wine sold at two measures for a dinar. After the new harvest, six modii of wheat were sold for a dinar, and ten of barley.
The Arabs belonging to the Persians did not cease or remain quiet, but crossed into Roman territory independently of the Persians.
They took two villages captive. When the Persian marzban stationed in Nisibis learned of this, he seized their leaders and killed them.
The Arabs in Roman territory also crossed into Persian territory without orders.
They took an estate captive. When news of this affair reached the master of offices—for he had gone down at the end of this
year to Apamea—he sent word to Timostratus, the duke of Callinicum. He seized five of their leaders and put two of them to death by the sword.
He crucified the other three on wooden stakes. Pharasmanes left Apamea after the master of offices had gone down there, and came and stayed in Edessa.
He received authority from the emperor to be commander of the army in place of Hypatius. As for the wall of Batnae, the fortress in Serugh,
which had fallen and was breached throughout, it was rebuilt and restored through the efforts of Eulogius, the governor of Edessa.
The worthy priest Hades covered the doors of the men's section of the church of Edessa with bronze. The year eight hundred and seventeen.
The commanders of the Roman army informed the emperor that the troops were suffering great harm because they had no city situated on the frontier.
For whenever the Romans went out from Tella or Amida to patrol the region of Arab because of raiding bands, they were in danger
wherever they camped, because of enemy ambushes. And if they happened to encounter forces more numerous than their own,
and decided to retreat, they endured great hardship because there was no city nearby in which they could take shelter.
For this reason the emperor ordered a wall to be built around Dara, a village situated on the frontier. Stonemasons were recruited from all over Syria.
They went down there and began building it. But the Persians used to come out from Nisibis and hinder
them. Because of this, Pharasmanes left Edessa and went down to stay in Amida. He would go out to the builders and help them.
He also conducted a great hunt of wild animals, especially the wild boars that had multiplied there since the country had been devastated.
He used to hunt more than forty of them in a single day. As proof of his skill in hunting, he also sent some of them to Edessa, both alive and dead.
The virtuous Sergius, bishop of Biretha Castra, which lies near us on the River Euphrates, also began building a wall for his city.
The emperor gave him a substantial amount of gold for his expenses. For Europus too, which lies west of the river in the province of Mabbug,
the magister ordered a wall to be built, and the local inhabitants worked on it as much as they could.
After Pharasmanes went down to Amida, Romanus the duke came in his place. He and his army took up quarters in Edessa.
He performed many acts of charity for the poor. The emperor, in addition to all his good deeds, did still more in this year:
he sent a remission of the tax to all Mesopotamia. And they all rejoiced. [?] good deeds, he did still more in this year:
he sent a remission of the tax to all Mesopotamia. All the estate owners rejoiced and praised the emperor.
But the common people grumbled, crying out and saying, “The Goths should not be quartered on us, but on the estate owners,
since they are the ones who benefited from this remission.” The prefect ordered that their request be granted. When this began
to be carried out, all the leading men of the city gathered before Romanus the duke.
They appealed to him, saying, “Let Your Excellency prescribe what each of the Goths should receive every month,
so that when they enter the houses of wealthy people, they do not plunder them as they used to plunder the common people.”
He accepted their appeal and ordered that they receive one aspada of oil each month, two hundred pounds of firewood, and a bed and bedding for every two of them.
When the Goths heard this order, they rushed at Romanus the duke in the residence of the house of Barsa to kill him.
As they were climbing the stairs to his quarters, he heard the noise of their uproar and commotion and realized what they intended to do.
He quickly put on his armor, took up his weapons, drew his sword, and stood at the upper doorway of the place where they were staying.
He did not kill a single Goth, but waved his sword and prevented those coming up first from entering to attack him.
Those below, in their fury, were forcing those above them to go up and enter to attack them.
The stairs of that residence were wooden, as Your Holiness knows. So when those who had gone up first could not enter for fear of the sword,
and the others were pressing against them, a beam broke and fell on them. A few of them died, and many suffered injuries
to their limbs, became disabled, and never recovered. When this collapse gave Romanus an opportunity,
he escaped across the roof from one residence to the next and got away. He said nothing further to them.
For this reason they remained where they had been quartered, behaving just as they pleased, with no one to discipline them,
restrain them, or admonish them. Our bishop, Mar Peter, suffered from a severe and distressing illness throughout this entire year.
In the month of Nisan, the distress afflicting our city grew still worse. For the magister gathered the entire army.
He set out to go down to Persian territory to establish and renew a peace treaty with them.
When he entered Edessa, Persian envoys came to him and informed him that the Astabid who was coming to meet him to establish a treaty with him had died.
They appealed to him, saying that, if he had come down for peace, he ought
not to go beyond Edessa until another Astabid was sent by the king of the Persians. He accepted their request.
He stayed in Edessa for five months. Because the city could not accommodate the Goths who were with him, they also quartered themselves in the villages
and in all the monasteries, large and small, around the city. Thus even those who lived in solitude
were not allowed to remain in the quiet they loved, because the soldiers also quartered themselves with them in their dwellings. They indulged so excessively in food and drink,
since they were not eating at their own expense, that on the very first day they arrived, some of them, after feasting in upper rooms, went out
at night, staggering from the great quantity of wine. They stepped into empty space, fell down into the depths, and departed this life with a miserable end.
Others, as they sat drinking, were overcome by sleep, fell from the upper rooms, and died on the spot.
Others burned up on their beds from excessive eating. Others, for their part, [?] because of minor offenses.
Others entered a garden to take vegetables. When the gardener stood up to stop them from taking them, they dealt him death with an arrow, and no one was called to account for his blood.
Others, meanwhile, grew increasingly wicked, with no one to restrain their wickedness. Those with whom they were quartered [?] dealt with them very cautiously
and did everything according to their wishes. Since they gave them no opportunity to harm them, the soldiers were overcome by their own rage and killed one another.
But you are well aware that there were also others among them who lived in an orderly way.
For it is impossible that an army as large as that should not also contain such men. The wickedness of the bad men became so violently destructive
that even the bolder people among the Edessenes were stirred to do something improper.
They wrote complaints against the magister on sheets of paper and secretly posted them in prominent places in the city.
When he heard about this, however, he did not become angry, as he might have done, nor did he investigate who had done it.
Because of his kindness, he did not even consider doing any harm to the city. Instead, he took great pains to leave Edessa quickly and without delay.
The year 818. The magister therefore took his entire army and went down to the frontier.
The Persian envoy came to him at the city of Dara, bringing with him hostages who had been sent by the Astabid.
They again urged him that, if he wished to make peace, he too ought to send hostages in exchange for those he had received. Afterward, the two sides could approach one another on friendly terms
and meet face to face, each accompanied by five hundred unarmed horsemen. Then they could sit in a pavilion and do what was necessary.
He accepted their request and sent hostages. On the day appointed for him, he went unarmed to meet Astabid.
But because he feared that the Persians might be plotting some trick against him, he stationed the entire Roman army opposite them, fully armed.
He gave them a signal and ordered them to come to him quickly if they saw that signal.
When Astabid also came to meet him and sat down in the [?], the Romans and all the commanders with them—
one of the Roman soldiers took notice and saw that everyone who had come with Astabid was wearing armor underneath.
They reported this to Pharesmanes, the commander of the army, and to Duke Timostratus. These men showed the signal to the troops.
Immediately they raised a battle cry and reached them, surrounding Astabid and those with him and hemming them in.
When the troops in the Persian camp learned that Astabid and those with him had been surrounded, they fled in fear.
They entered Nisibis. The Romans wanted to kill Astabid together with those who were with him.
But the master of the army urged them not to become a cause of war and obstruct peace. Only with difficulty did they agree.
They obeyed him and allowed Astabid and those with him to leave their midst without doing them any harm.
For even in victory the Roman commanders are peaceable. But when Astabid returned to his camp,
and saw that the Persians had entered Nisibis, he was afraid to remain alone and also went in to join them.
He kept pressing them to leave the city with him, but they were afraid and unwilling to leave.
So that their fear would not become known to the Romans, Astabid sent for his daughter and brought her to Nisibis. In accordance with Persian custom, he married her.
When the master of the army sent him a message assuring him with oaths, “No one will harm you, even if you come out alone,”
he sent back this reply: “It is not out of fear that I am not coming out, but so that the days of the wedding feast may be completed.”
Although the master of the army was fully aware of the whole affair, he disregarded it as though he did not know.
Some days later, when Astabid came out to him, all the claims that had been laid down for me to press against the Persians—
he set them aside out of love for peace. He established a treaty with them and made peace. They drew up documents between them and specified in them a fixed period
during which they were not to wage war against one another. All the troops were happy and rejoiced at the peace that had been made.
While they were still there on the frontier, Celer, the master of the army, and Calliopius received letters from Emperor Anastasius,
which, with concern and compassion for the whole region of Mesopotamia,
were filled. He wrote to them as follows: if they judged that the tax ought to be remitted,
they were to have authority to remit it without hindrance. They decided that the entire tax should be remitted for the people of Amida.
And half of it for the people of Edessa. They sent word of this to Edessa, and shortly afterward they also sent other letters.
These announced the peace that had been established. On the twenty-eighth day of November, he took the whole army and withdrew from the frontier regions.
When he reached Edessa, the magister intended not to enter it because of their grumbling against him. But the blessed Bar-Hadad, bishop of Tella, persuaded him
not to give anger an opportunity to take control of him, and not to leave behind him any cause for grievance or anxiety for anyone. He readily accepted his appeal.
All the people of Edessa, from the greatest to the least, also went out to meet him with great joy, carrying candles.
All the clergy, the members of the covenant, and the monks also went out with them. They entered the city with great joy.
He dismissed the whole army to continue its journey that same day. He himself stayed three days and gave the governor two hundred dinars to distribute as gifts.

The citizens rejoiced at the peace that had been established, delighted in the relief they would now have from the distress they were enduring, and exulted in the hope of the good things they expected to come.
They thanked God, who in his grace and mercy had extended his peace over both kingdoms. As he departed, they escorted him with praises fitting for him and for the one who had sent him.
If this emperor appeared different at the end of his life, let no one take offense at the praises given to him.
Instead, let him remember what Solomon did toward the end of his life. These few things out of many I have written for you, beloved, as well as I could,
both unwillingly and willingly: unwillingly, so that I would not weary a wise and knowledgeable man
who knows more about these matters than I do; but willingly, out of obedience to your command.
And now I ask that you too fulfill the promise in your letter: that you will continually offer prayer to God for my sinfulness.
For now that I know your wish, I will take care to record whatever happens in the times to come that is worthy of remembrance, and send it to you, Father,
if I remain alive. But let us pray, we from here and you, Father, from there,
and all people everywhere, that the subject of the history may be the great change that has taken place in the world.
And just as we could not recount the events of the evil times as they truly were, because their afflictions were so many,
may we likewise be unable to relate the events to come because their blessings are so many.
Instead, may our account fall short of telling of the good conduct of the people of our city, and of the peace and harmony reigning in the world,

and of the great plenty that comes about, and the abundant harvest produced by the blessing of God, who said, “The former troubles will be forgotten and hidden from my sight.” To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.
A chronicle from the creation of the world to the year 1087 of Alexander. Part Two.
The year 800. The school of the Persians was uprooted from Edessa. The chief bishops who became known one after another.
In Rome: Hilary. He took office after Leo. And in Alexandria, after the wicked Proterius had been killed,
the holy Timothy [?], the disciple of Dioscorus, took office. After him came another Timothy, who was called Salophakiolos [?].
Of Constantinople: Anatolius, and after him Gennadius, and then Acacius. In Ephesus: John, and after him Paul,
who was deposed because he did not accept the Council of Chalcedon. In Antioch: Domnus, and after him Maximus,
and after him Martyrius, who was expelled; Peter, who returned from exile. In Jerusalem: Anastasius, who succeeded Juvenal,
and after him Martyrius, and after him Sallustius. He is known at this time. In Antioch: Sallustius. He is known at this time.
Again, in Antioch, after Peter the believer there were Calendion, who was deposed; after him came Palladius, and after him Flavian.
In Constantinople, after Acacius came Fravitta [?], and after him came Euphemius, who was deposed in the days of Anastasius. In Alexandria:
after Timothy, John, who was expelled; after him Peter, and after him Athanasius. In Rome, after Hilary, Simplicius,
and after him Felix, who is known at this time. The succession of all these chief bishops continued until the death of Emperor Zeno.
Again, at this time, the faction of the Greens set a fire and burned down the synagogue of the Jews. They dug up and brought out
all the bones of their dead that were around their synagogue, and burned them in the fire. When Emperor Zeno learned of this,
he became angry with the Greens, saying, “Why did they not burn all the living Jews along with their dead?”
Thus this affair came to an end, and no one was called to account. In the year 808, Emperor Zeno died,
and Anastasius reigned after him. He was originally from Dyrrachium, a Christian and a believer. In the year 809,
Euphemius of Constantinople went into exile because he was found to be a Nestorian. Macedonius took his place.
In the year 810, a great swarm of locusts came upon the land and destroyed everything. This is as we have already recorded above concerning it.
In that same year there was a severe and violent earthquake. Nicopolis was overturned by it and buried all its inhabitants,
except for the church and the bishop’s residence. In that very same year, a sign resembling darkness appeared in the sky.
Again, on the very day of the sign and the earthquake, the hot spring at Abarne stopped flowing for three days. Then it returned to its place, as it had customarily done before.
The river Euphrates also stopped flowing on that very day. Also, the great church of Arsamosata collapsed in the earthquake on the day of its assembly,
and killed many people inside it. In the year 811, in the month of October, on the twenty-third, a Saturday, the sun grew dark
for eight hours. Dust lay over the earth, as though ashes or sulfur had been scattered over it.
On this same day another sign appeared in the wall of Edessa. A breach opened in the wall south of the Great Gate.
The stones of that section were scattered a considerable distance away from it. Again, in the same year, in November,
three signs appeared in the sky at midday, resembling the rainbow seen in the clouds, with their curves below and their ends above.
One of them was on the southern side, in the middle of the sky; another was to its east, and another to its west.
And so they were turned toward the sky. Again, in that same year, in the month of Kanun, another sign appeared in the sky, resembling a spear.
It was in the southwestern quarter. Some people called it the broom of destruction, while others called it the spear of war.
But we have already recorded their story above. The year 812. There was famine, locusts, and a great plague.
The year 813. There was a great earthquake, and Ptolemais, Tyre, and Sidon were overthrown. The Jewish synagogue was also uprooted and collapsed.
On that same night of the earthquake, which occurred on the twenty-second of the month of August, on the eve of Friday, a sign appeared in the northern quarter, resembling blazing fire.
The year 814. Kavadh captured Amida and Theodosiopolis, killing their inhabitants and taking them captive.
At Amida, the slain brought out through the northern gate numbered eighty-five thousand,
besides those brought out through the other gates, those thrown into pits and sewers, and those buried within the city.
In the school called the School of the Urtaye, while all the monks of the monastery of John of the Urtaye were standing at worship there, two executioners came in upon them.
They killed ninety of them and took the rest captive. In that same year, the Romans and Persians fought a battle at Tell Bashmi.
The Romans were defeated. They also attacked Tella and Edessa and took captive the people of the Harran district, as we have recorded above.
In this year there was another sign in the sky, resembling darkness. At this time the following shepherds were known in the church:
Jacob, bishop and teacher of Batnan of Serugh; Philoxenus of Mabbug; Peter of Edessa; Antoninus of Aleppo;
Constantine of Laodicea; Peter of Apamea; Thomas of Amida; John of Tella; John [of] Hierapolis;
Paul, patriarch of Alexandria; John of Harran; Nonnus of Circesium; Paul of Callinicum; Peter of Reshaina;
Theosebius of Ephesus; Aaron of Arshamshat; Aetherichus of Anazarbus; Felix of Rome; Sallustius of Jerusalem.
The year 815. There was a great earthquake, and the island of Rhodes collapsed in it. This was its third destruction.
Because it happened at night, it killed many people, and few survived. The compassionate emperor sent a great deal of gold to those
who were found alive there. They began uncovering and bringing out the bodies of those who, in the great wrath, had been crushed there as in a winepress of destruction.
The year 816. The Romans ravaged the whole land of the Persians, killing, destroying, taking captives, and plundering,
from Nisibis to the border of Beth Aramaye. They killed every male aged twelve and above,
and carried off the rest into captivity. They also ravaged Persian Armenia, taking captives and plunder, and carried off everyone in it into captivity.
In this same year, the holy Nonnus was bishop of Amida. When he sent Thomas, his archdeacon, to the imperial city
on various matters, this Thomas plotted against him with the people of Amida [also those who held priestly office [?]]. Thus Thomas became bishop of Amida [in place of Nonnus].
[The year 817.] A wall was built for Dara in Mesopotamia by order of Emperor Anastasius.
In this same year, Celer, the master of offices, came down and made peace between the Romans and the Persians.
The year 818. There was fighting and a great uprising against Anastasius.
For he wanted, in accordance with the custom prevailing in the East, also to say, “You who were crucified for us, have mercy on us.”
For this reason, great disturbances, many killings, and the plundering of many people took place in the imperial capital.
Emperor Anastasius himself, because he loved God, wanted to add to the words “Holy God, Holy Mighty One,
Holy Immortal One” the words “You who were crucified for us, have mercy on us,” as was the practice in these numerous eastern regions.
When he ordered this, because the entire family of the noble Juliana, together with Juliana herself,
and most of the city were Nestorians, along with the monks of the Acoemetae and the other monks, all Constantinople rose in revolt against the emperor.
They assembled amid turmoil and threats, in many bands, alleging that he wanted to introduce an innovation, something foreign, into the Christian faith: the words “You who were crucified for us.”
They further claimed that the robber who was crucified with our Lord was named Dumax, and that it was to him that they cried, “You who were crucified for us, have mercy on us.”
They said other such foolish things as well. Then they ran and surrounded the palace, shouting, “Another emperor for the Romans!”
As a result, the prefect of the city, whose name was Plato, fled and hid from the people's anger.
They ran to the house of Marinus, the Syrian former prefect—that is, the administrator of the empire—to kill him. When he learned of this, he [?] to escape from them.
They set fire to his house and burned it down, and seized everything he owned. For they said that he, being a Syrian, had misled the emperor
into introducing the words “You who were crucified for us.” They publicly chopped up and smashed his silver with axes.
A poor Syrian monk was found in his house. They killed him, cut off his head, and fixed it on a spear. They carried it about like this,
running through the city and shouting, “Look! Here is the conspirator!” That is, the enemy of the Trinity.
When they came to the house of Juliana, the great patrician, they shouted for her husband Areobindus to become emperor of the Romans.
But Areobindus fled to the opposite shore. At the horse races ordered by the emperor, he went up to his seat in ordinary clothing, without a crown.
When the people of the city saw the emperor's humility, and also found that he soothed them with kind words,
their fury subsided. They began to praise him and urge him to put on his imperial crown. He, in turn, urged them not to attack one another.
They listened to him and remained peaceful and quiet toward him and toward one another for a few days. In the end, however, they again became agitated and rose in unrest for other reasons.
He ordered punishment against them and asserted his power forcefully as emperor. He brought retribution for their earlier hostility down upon their own heads.
Many perished under torture, and many others were thrown into the sea. Thus great fear fell upon all the peoples.
They were kept quiet by force, not only in the imperial capital but also in all the cities of the Romans.
On the removal and exile decreed against Macedonius, patriarch of Constantinople.
Now, after many evil deeds had been committed by Macedonius the heretic, God wished his wickedness to leave the church of the faithful
and go to the congregation of the Jews, who shared his wishes. Then the emperor gave the command, and his exile was decreed. And when he wanted

to put to shame his friend and like-minded associate, his magister, he said to him something that deeply crushed and distressed him, namely: “Hurry to carry out the command you have been given.” And when the magister went,
Macedonius was found to have fled and hidden in the church, with his head bowed and resting between his knees. He said to him, “The ruler of the world has decreed your exile.”
He said to him, “Where to?” He answered him, “Where your companion, the former one, went: to Euchaita.”
The church stewards pleaded with him, saying, “Our lord, we beg Your Greatness to have compassion on his old age and not take him out during the day.
Otherwise, the city will be set on fire. Instead, order that he remain until evening, and then let him leave secretly, in the darkness.”
A Gospel book was also brought, and they swore that they would guard him until evening and that he would not be taken away,
leaving men to guard him. And in the year eight hundred and twenty, in the month of Tammuz, on its seventh day,
at evening the magister came with a large force. They brought Macedonius out of the church of God, and he handed him over to those who had been ordered to take him into exile.
This happened to him as he deserved, and great fear came upon the whole church of the orthodox. And so there was quiet and rest in [?].
After him another man, a monk named Timothy, arose to occupy the throne of the imperial city, in the year eight hundred and twenty-one.
The holy Simeon, bishop of Beth Arsham, was known as Simeon the Persian Disputant. This man once took some prominent

and well-known men, three in number, from among the Magi, made them disciples, and baptized them. When their associates heard that they had turned away from the religion of the Magi and become Christians,
they informed the king about them and received an order that, if they had truly converted and would not renounce Christianity, they should die.
But these men, who were worthy of the crown of life, when they saw the king’s threats and sword,
were neither afraid nor shaken. The blessed man himself was also arming them with zeal for martyrdom for the sake of eternal life.
They stood firm against the decree and the sword issued against them, saying, “Far be it from us to deny the living God, who made heaven and earth,
and his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who called us and brought us near to himself by his grace—to deny him and worship his creation in his place.”
Then, ten days after their spiritual birth, the blessed men departed to God with a good testimony, through a swift death by the sword.
At this time Satan stirred up a delusion in the region of Pharan: that there were people who neither ate bread nor drank water.
Some of the brothers, whose monasteries were unknown, and others from among the heads of the monasteries there put forward an empty claim.
They falsely proclaimed about themselves that they did not eat bread or drink water, and they described themselves as abstaining from wine.
But they were impiously satisfying the constant need of their hunger and thirst from the holy mysteries.
Most of their nourishment also came from the consecrated offerings. For this reason, they also leavened the loaf they made with soot.
With great effort they pounded it so that it would serve them as food, and not as the sacrament of the body

of Christ, which is represented by unleavened bread. Moreover, whenever they reclined to eat, they offered ordinary bread through one another's hands and ate it. And, it is said, whenever they traveled on the road, or went on a long journey,
two or three times in a single day they satisfied their natural hunger and thirst with it—with the very body and blood of Christ our Lord.
When they reached their destination, they would, it is said, offer the Eucharist again in the evening and receive it as though they had been fasting.
Even during the holy days of the forty-day fast, they dared to act this way, without fear of God or shame before other people.
For it was said of them that, when they had prepared the consecrated offering in a basket and freely eaten as much of it as they wanted,
each of them would dilute the cup of the living blood with hot water and drink as much as he wanted. Then he would fill it again and give it to his companion.
But Saint Rabbula of Edessa and Saint Gamalinus, bishop of Perrha, opposed this error.
In the year 822, Vitalian rebelled against Anastasius. In the year 823,
a synod assembled at Sidon in Phoenicia. The leaders of this synod were the following: Symmachus, patriarch
of Rome; Timothy, patriarch of the imperial city; Flavian, patriarch of Antioch; John, patriarch of Alexandria;
Elijah of Jerusalem; John of Tella; and Philoxenus of Mabbug. Flavian was found to be a heretic, and for this reason Emperor Anastasius ordered
that it assemble again at Antioch to appoint a patriarch there in place of Flavian. When it assembled, they appointed there a monk named Severus,
from the monastery of Theodore. He was the grandson of Severus, bishop of Sozopolis in Pisidia,
one of the 220 who, together with the great Cyril, deposed Nestorius. If you find that it assembled at Sidon,
and then find it written that it assembled at Tsidon, do not be confused: the two are one and the same, even though their forms differ.
When that holy man went to the raised platform and ascended the throne of Saint Ignatius, all the people of Antioch, with their wives and children, cried out,
shouting these words together: “For a long time we have wanted to share in the holy mysteries.
Free our city from false belief! We want to baptize our children! Anathematize the Council of Chalcedon!
Anathematize now the council that overturned the world! Anathematize now the council of those who acted unjustly! Anathema to the Council of Chalcedon!
Anathema to Leo's Tome! Let all the bishops anathematize it now! Whoever does not anathematize it is a wolf, not a shepherd!”
If there was anyone suspected of sharing Flavian's views, he would hear himself addressed by name: “So-and-so, anathematize the council!”
And this indeed happened, as the council was anathematized by everyone. While they were shouting these and similar words and offering praise,
the great Severus, for his part, rejoiced all the more greatly at these things.
He composed a discourse full of teaching marked by complete theological precision. At the same time, in it he put Nestorius’s worship of a human being to shame.
And he exposed the dreamlike fantasy of Eutyches. He also opposed the Council of Chalcedon and the Tome of Leo.
He delivered many arguments against them, warning against turning aside toward either of the two cliffs, which were equally impious.
Rather, let us walk on the royal road and confess one incarnate nature of God the Word, from two.
After saying a few things about correcting conduct, as time allowed, to the people who were growing weary,
he dismissed them to rest their bodies. Such a glorious day had come about through the arrival of that glorious man.
When he immediately went up to his episcopal residence, he found the food preparers and cooks of the episcopal household, and all the equipment they had provided,
and removed them from there. He also demolished the bathhouse that was there, just as the God-loving kings Josiah and Hezekiah had demolished the pillars of Baal.
He lived according to the strict monastic practices that had formerly been his custom: a table on the ground, no bathing, and prolonged services of psalmody.
He ate vegetables, like the young men in Babylon. Bread of a very cheap and inferior sort was brought to him from the market. And in the year 826,
a council assembled in Tyre by order of Emperor Anastasius. All the eastern bishops gathered there, along with those of Apamea,
Euphratesia, Osrhoene, Mesopotamia, Arabia, and Phoenicia of Lebanon. The leaders of this council were:
Severus, patriarch of Antioch; Timothy of the imperial city, through his representatives; Elijah of Jerusalem,
through his representatives; John, patriarch of Alexandria; Symmachus, patriarch of Rome; Philoxenus of Mabbug; John of Tella;
and Paul of Edessa. John bar Aphtonia was also prominent, as was Quma from the monastery of Mar Aqiba. Severus brought the truth to light
and explained the document called the Henotikon, which Emperor Zeno had issued. He showed that it was intended to nullify what had been done at Chalcedon.
They openly anathematized that council there, along with the addition that had been made to the faith. The bishops who had assembled with Severus and Philoxenus proclaimed the whole truth.
In the year 827, Ailmarcius [?] rebelled against Emperor Anastasius in Rome and seized all the western territories.
He took possession of the imperial power in Rome, for he was a fierce man. In the year 828,
a great crowd gathered from Egypt, Alexandria, and the region beyond the Jordan, together with Edomites and Arabs.
They came to the feast of the Dedication and the raising of the cross in Jerusalem, which took place on the fourteenth of September.
Then demons possessed many people, and they barked at the cross like dogs. Then they became quiet, and the demons came out of them.
This caused discerning people much concern and distress. Yet they did not understand the reason precisely until the event itself
revealed the outcome. God had given advance notice of the subsequent turning away from the faith and the stumbling that would occur later.
Which chief bishops were prominent in the days of Emperor Anastasius. In Rome there was Felix, and after him Symmachus.
And after him, Hormisdas. In Alexandria: the faithful Athanasius and John, and John and Dioscorus. Of Antioch:
Flavian, who was deposed, and Severus the faithful. Of Constantinople: Euphemius and Macedonius, the heretics, and Timothy the faithful,
and John, who accepted the Council of Chalcedon at the beginning of Justin’s reign and soon died. Epiphanius succeeded him.
In Jerusalem: Sallustius and Elijah, who was expelled; John, who accepted the council in the days of Justin the Elder,
and after him Peter. The chief bishops who lived in the days of Justin the Elder and introduced the Council of Chalcedon:
In Rome, Hormisdas. In Alexandria, Timothy. In Jerusalem, Peter. Of Antioch, Paul the Jew,
and Euphrasius, who burned in a vat of pitch during the destruction of Antioch, and Ephraim of Amida. Of Constantinople, Epiphanius.
These were in the days of Justin the Elder, who reigned after Anastasius. In the year eight hundred and twenty-nine,
Emperor Anastasius died, and Justin the Elder reigned after him. This man was trained in warfare and the military exercises of the Romans,
but was entirely without instruction in the words of the holy prophets and the teachers inspired by the Holy Spirit. At the beginning of his reign, he was led astray by those who confess two
natures in Christ after the union. And because he was a simple man
and unversed in divine doctrines, he was persuaded by their words to introduce the Council of Chalcedon into the church,
which had enjoyed a little peace since the time of the Henotikon, issued by Emperor Zeno [?] for the annulment of the council.
And the faithful peoples were living peacefully, without disturbance, throughout the Roman dominion.
Then he ordered that the council be entered in writing and proclaimed in the church, and that anyone who did not accept the council be sent into exile.
From that time, many divisions and disputes arose in the church. Those who were urging him to do this cunningly advised
that these three true councils should also be entered in writing and proclaimed along with that of Chalcedon,
so that by this means they might be able to lead astray the faithful who opposed this council of Chalcedon
and divert their thoughts by having these true councils counted together with it, so that they would not recoil and turn back.
The emperor himself was soon drawn into this as well, and ordered that it be done. But the bishop of the city, whose name was John,
seeing the evils that were destined to arise in the church, hesitated to enter the councils in writing in the church.
When a feast day came, on which the emperors would customarily go to church,
Justin’s wife, whose name was Lupicina, who was herself zealous about this and urged others on,
sent word to the bishop: “Unless you enter the councils in the church’s diptychs, I will not enter the church,
nor will I receive communion from your hands.” Thus he was compelled to enter them in writing, and he proclaimed them.
To all four councils at the feast itself. And there was uproar, turmoil, and disturbance among all the faithful.
Amantius the chief chamberlain and Andrew the chamberlain also opposed this. Because of these things, they were beheaded.
After these things, with the introduction of the Council of Chalcedon, great turmoil and disturbance immediately arose in the imperial city.
The people were agitated, the churches were thrown into confusion, and the monasteries of men and women were disturbed. Many divisions arose among the Christians.
They became two factions, two divisions, and two opposing sides. While these things were happening in this way, persecution spread through the eastern regions.
Then the holy patriarch Severus withdrew from his see and his city. And when he learned of the violence of the persecution,
he reached Alexandria. From that time onward, all the orthodox bishops were persecuted and left their sees.
The names of the holy bishops who were persecuted and left their sees. From Cilicia, these: Eutychius of Anazarbus;
Julius of Aegae; John of Mopsuestia; Paul of Epiphania; John of Irenopolis; Paul of Alexandria Minor.
From Cappadocia: Proclus of Colonia; Musonius of Therma; Nicephorus of Sebaste. From Syria:
The holy Severus, patriarch of Antioch; Constantine of Laodicea; Antoninus of Aleppo; Philoxenus of Mabbug;
Peter of Apamea; Nonnus of Seleucia, who died in Amida; Isidore of Qinnasrin; Mara of Amida—both of these died in Alexandria;
Thomas of Damascus, who died in Constantinople; Alexander of Abila, who died in exile; Thomas of Yabrud, who died
in exile; John of Palmyra, who died in exile; John of Durin, who died in exile; Sergius of Cyrrhus, who died in exile;
Thomas of Germanicia, who died in Samosata; Paul of Edessa, who accepted the council and entered his city; John of Harran, who died in Antioch;
John of Himeria, who died in exile; Eustathius of Perrhe, who died in exile; Eustathius of Perrhe, who died in exile;
Peter of Reshaina, who died in exile; Nonnus of Circesium, who died in exile; Paul of Callinicum, who died in exile;
Marion of Sura, who died in exile; John of Tella, who was martyred in Antioch by Ephraim of Amida; Thomas of Dara,
who died in exile; Aaron of Arsamosata, who died in exile. From Asia, Caria, and Aphrodisias: Euphemius,
archbishop of Aphrodisias, who died during the persecution; Menophinus of Antioch on the river Maeander; Zeuxis of Alabanda,
who died in exile; Peter of Alinda, who died in exile; Julian of Halicarnassus, who became a Phantasiast;
Theosebius of Ephesus. He was summoned to go up to the imperial city to accept the council. He went in and threw himself down before the altar,
and on the third day he died. Elirianus of Neocaesarea; Elpidius of Castrania; Theodore of Olba; Luke of Amorium;
Eusebinus of Hadrianus; Peter of Mallus; Victor of Philadelphia; Peter of Myndus; Agathodorus of Iasus;
Pelagius of Celenderis; Photinus of Arsinoe; Alexander of Conana. The bishops numbered fifty-four in all.
In the year 831, Paul the Jew became patriarch of Antioch.
After the departure of Saint Severus, Antioch remained without a bishop for one year. Then a vessel of destruction was chosen and sent there:
Paul, who was called Eutyches—that is, if it is right to say so, also a Jew.
He had been superintendent of the hospice of Eubulus in the imperial city.
He was in keeping with the words of our Lord, who said in the Gospel, “Stumbling blocks are bound to come, but woe to the man through whom they come!”
This applies very well to this man, who inherited that woe of which it is written. Through him came turmoil, divisions, stumbling blocks, and disputes
upon the church of God throughout all the regions of the East. For it was he who introduced and inscribed the despised Council of Chalcedon,
first in the church of Antioch. Because of this there were harsh persecutions, afflictions, and the expulsion of all these bishops who have been mentioned,
and of all the other monastic communities, because they would not accept or submit to the wickedness of Paul the Jew.
The year 836. Before these events, at the beginning of the reign of Emperor Justin, a star appeared
in the east, resembling a great spear, with the spearhead pointing downward.
It turned about fearfully, and everyone could see long rays issuing from it.
It was called a comet, as the Greeks say. Fear seized everyone at the sight of it.
For as it rose and appeared, it flashed fearfully, turned about, and displayed threatening changes,
so that many people said and thought many things: that punishment, the sword, and destruction awaited them, because of the terrifying appearance of that star.
These things were not long delayed, for many calamities soon struck, together with the sword, and much blood was shed.
And what was harsher and more bitter than all the rest was the turmoil in the church: the divisions, disputes, persecutions, killings, and afflictions that soon overtook it.
This, then, was the appearance of the star. In the year 837, a fire suddenly broke out throughout Antioch.
Much of the city suddenly began to burn, as though through wrath from God, giving advance warning of the overthrow and destruction that threatened it.
In this way, fire would suddenly break out everywhere, in every part of the city, for as long as six months.
Many people in it perished, along with the rest of its buildings, while people could not discover where the fire was starting.
For the fire would consume the upper stories, five and six floors up, and thus destroy all the people around it.
Concerning the persecution that Paul the Jew carried out against all the churches and monasteries, and the rest of the Christians throughout the East.
Along with these were also the large and small monasteries of the chaste monks throughout all the territories of Antioch,
Seleucia, Qinnasrin, Aleppo, Apamea, and Mabbug, throughout all Arabia and Palestine, and in all the cities of the south and the north.
and in the desert of the hermits, as far as the Persian frontier, and also in the remaining cities and regions throughout the East.
They were persecuted and driven out, plundered and [?], and fell by the sword. They were confined in prisons and in various courts and places of torture.
Many were also mercilessly handed over to death by torture, and their possessions were seized. And against the rest,
armed troops of the barbarous Romans were deployed, along with rural bishops, visiting clergy, and the other persecutors who pursued them everywhere
and mercilessly drove them from place to place, also striking them with clubs and swords, barbarously and savagely,
without the restraint of the fear of God. They repeatedly treated them mercilessly, as though they were pagans.
Moreover, the other believers who welcomed the persecuted and allowed them to enter their villages or their houses—
they plundered them, flogged them, and abused them. By then, a single violent storm of persecution,
harsh and oppressive, hung darkly and threateningly over all the regions, cities, and villages alike.
And a single thread of evils, over all the churches, monasteries, cities, and villages, and even as far as the desert of the hermits who inhabited the wilderness,
was stretched out. The greedy and barbarous seizure of property continued constantly in every city and village, and among the peoples and throughout the regions.
It fell not only upon churchmen, monks, and nuns, but also upon young men and women with infants. People of every age [?] were persecuted, driven out, and displaced,
and cast into different places under various sentences of exile. They endured every kind of torture and every kind of evil,
and bore every affliction for the truth of the upright and unblemished faith.
Even if these things were written down briefly, their accounts would exceed the bounds of narration, though they were recorded in many books.
No one can encompass them, because they are beyond telling—especially what the great and small monastic communities throughout Syria,
in the monasteries of men and women, both western and eastern, suffered and endured in the time of Paul the Jew, and afterward in the times of Euphrasius [?] and Ephraim.
They continually endured and bore every persecution, every affliction, and every torture, together with the hardship of hunger and thirst, exposure and nakedness.
Some of them would settle in a place one day and be driven from it the next. Sometimes this happened that very evening, when they were not even treated like
travelers or allowed to spend the night, wherever any one of the monastic communities happened to settle.
Consequently, most of them would spend the night out in the open, like animals, in fields and mountains beneath the sky.
Sometimes this happened even during the harsh days of winter, in rain, snow, and ice, amid severe exposure and the violence of the harsh winter.
In the winds, they huddled together and sat on stones, spending the whole night with nothing beneath them.
None of them could even turn onto his side and lie on the ground. Sometimes, even in this condition, they were still persecuted and driven from their dwellings.
They came down from their pillars and out of their places of confinement; they were also dragged from the places where they stood, and suffered other things of this kind.
It often happened in many monasteries that, when they had finished the prescribed order of their service and sat down in the evening,
to taste whatever God had sent them, persecutors would suddenly arrive and fall upon them with clubs,
while their tables were set and their pitchers poured out. In this way they would drive them out and themselves sit down at the tables
and eat the food that had been prepared for them. The others would go out hungry and exhausted, their souls distressed,
although among them were many elderly and infirm men and women advanced in years, as well as those who had come down from pillars
and those who had come out of places of confinement after a long time. Thus, amid these torments, afflictions, and bitter assaults,
the entire monastic order, both men and women, suffered and endured exceedingly throughout all the days of Paul, and in the remaining
regions, one after another, as far as the Persian border. By then a single wave of persecution was sweeping over all the orders that had not entered into Chalcedonian communion.
When Paul had completed one year, the emperor saw that, because of his tyranny, the people were breaking away from the church, and learned of the many evils he had committed.
He removed him and cast him out of the church. He also departed from this life and went to give an account of these things before the justice of God and to receive the reward of his labor,

and to receive in his own person what his error deserved, as it is written.

An account of Paul of Edessa and of the evils that took place because of his removal.
Now, while the thick smoke of turmoil and persecution was rising ever more intensely throughout all the regions of the East, it reached even the city of Edessa,
where Paul was bishop. It was suspected that his faith was not sound,
but that he was afflicted with the evil disease of the two natures. Yet he did not reveal the falseness of his thinking,
because he feared the fierce zeal of the people of Edessa. For when he had been summoned once, twice, and three times and had not gone,
a man named Patricius went after him with a large force of Roman soldiers. When he entered Edessa and sought to seize Paul,
Paul fled and went down into the baptismal font, to show that, as he claimed, he did not wish to go.

Then the city's inhabitants and the entire monastic community around the city, burning with fierce zeal for the truth, gathered together, took up stones, and ran to the palace where Patricius was staying. They began pelting him with stones
and everyone with him, intending to drive him out of the city so that he could not take Paul away. When he saw the great crowd that had gathered against him
and the fierce pelting with stones from every side, he ordered the sword to be used against them. Then the force of Goths came out with bows and arrows, and many were struck and died.
They fled before them, and the soldiers began cutting them down with swords, especially those wearing the monastic habit. Everyone they found they killed with the sword.
Many died by the sword—all who could not flee and escape or hide somewhere. Those who hid escaped the sword.
There was great mourning and grief throughout the whole church. Thus they took Paul and departed. When this Paul appeared before Paul the Jew of Antioch,
many thought that he shared his views and secretly agreed with him, and that, in order to conceal this from the people of Edessa,
so that they would not reject Paul and refuse to accept his administration, the affair was carried out [?]. Thus Paul was released and returned to his city.
They were pleading as though he had not agreed with him. The people of Edessa went out to meet him, and the orthodox welcomed him, as though, they said, he had fought and won.
A short time later, the bishop of Harran died, and Paul wanted to appoint there a priest of the church of Edessa named Asclepius.
This man had a brother in the imperial capital who had been appointed prefect of the praetorium.
But after raising his hopes, he broke faith with him and appointed someone else in his place. Eventually Asclepius went up to his brother and told him about Paul,
saying that he did not accept the Council of Chalcedon. When this became known to the emperor, he sent word to Pharasmanes, who was
the military commander, to expel Paul from Edessa. Thus Paul was expelled, and Asclepius took his place.
Now Paul the Jew died after one year, and Euphrasius took his place. It was he who appointed Asclepius in Edessa,
urging him to persecute and plunder. This he carried out and accomplished throughout his episcopate, many times exceeding what he had been ordered to do.
Before these events, before Paul's expulsion, he had sent for the blessed Mar Jacob, bishop and teacher of Batnae in Serugh,
so that he would come to him. But Jacob kept declining to come, since he saw that Paul was not sound in his faith.
While Paul himself was pressing the blessed man to come, Jacob went in and threw himself down before the altar.
He prayed with anguish and many tears, saying, “Lord God, you who know what is in everyone's heart
and examine the innermost thoughts and the heart, if you know that the falsehood of two natures is in Paul's heart, do not let me see his face.”
When Paul pressed him strongly to come, he left the city of Batnae and traveled as far as a monastery called the Monastery of the Persians,
which is six miles from Edessa. He entered that monastery and spent the night there. During the night, his departure was revealed to him, and he was commanded to return to his city.
So he got up during the night and urged those with him to saddle the pack animal quickly and return to the city,
saying, “In two days I will depart from this world.” While all those with him were astonished and amazed,
he returned and reached his city. He gave instructions concerning his church and all his teaching, and after two days he departed from this world.
The power of this holy man's prayer, together with all his teaching, became known throughout the whole church of God and throughout Syria, while everyone marveled
and gave thanks to God. When Paul learned of these things, he appointed in his place a man named Moses.
On the persecution of the great Monastery of the Easterners at Edessa, together with the rest of the monasteries throughout the East and the West.
As for this great and renowned Monastery of the Easterners at Edessa, already in Paul's time, when they saw that he was unsound in his fidelity to the truth,
they had broken away and separated from him. They discontinued their custom of receiving the Eucharist from the church of Edessa.
Thus they decided to celebrate the Eucharist in their own monastery, and they no longer received the Eucharist from the church. The rest of the people of Edessa and Amida also did this.
They demanded that everyone, from the greatest to the least, anathematize the Council of Chalcedon and the Tome of Leo and put this in writing in his own hand.
And everyone who says or acknowledges that there are two natures in Christ after the union. This is what they all wrote and decreed.
These very same words were also to be written on the outside of the gates of all the monasteries.
All the monasteries throughout Syria did this. But the monks [of the monastery] of the Easterners
were being driven out at a harsh time by Pharasmanes, the military commander, at the instigation of the wicked Asclepius. They kept pressing them and forcing them to leave.
But they said, “How can you demand that we leave in this harsh winter?
Even merciless barbarians would not do this, when we have among us old people and sick people,
many lying in beds, unable to set a foot on the ground.” Then Pharasmanes ordered Asclepius
to give them pack animals and camels to carry their belongings. So they packed up and left two days before Christmas,
carrying the sick and the old people on beds. When the whole city learned of their departure,
people came running from every part of it—men and women, old people and children, young men and infants—to see them and receive their blessing.
When they saw them being harassed and driven out, and leaving, they wailed and raised their voices in bitter weeping,
especially when they saw the old and sick people being carried on beds.
They wailed loudly, weeping and saying, “Woe to us! Christianity has perished in our days! Woe to us! What has happened in our days?
Woe to us! What are we seeing with our own eyes? The destruction of the Christian faith has taken place in our own generation. Why should we go on living now,
after this dreadful spectacle of paganism, the destruction of the faith, and once again the persecution and flight of God’s servants?”
So men and women ran along, weeping and lamenting. They grasped the feet of the blessed men and pressed them to their eyes,
wailing and weeping bitterly, and lamenting their own plight. So they all went out, carrying their crosses.
A great crowd followed them for two or three days, while other monastic communities came out and joined them.
These were the following: the monks of the monastery of Saint Zacchaeus, the monks of the monastery of Saint Conon, the monks of the Exedrae, and the monks
of the Souls; the monks of the monastery of Saint Samuel; the monastery of Hindibana; the monastery of Eusebius of Abna; the monastery of Saint Julian the Elder, of the River of the Medes;
along with the rest of the other monasteries. This whole great and beloved assembly reached the monastery of Saint Solomon of Maqlitha at the feast of Christmas.
Then the blessed men, stirred by fierce zeal, said to the whole gathering of monks and young men, “Since each of us has drawn up a document in his own name,
and we anathematize the Council of Chalcedon and Leo’s wicked Tome, and we are preparing to celebrate the Eucharist and receive communion at this feast,
be aware that we will not give communion to anyone who has not done as we have done and does not anathematize as we do.”
The whole gathering agreed and willingly pronounced the anathema. So they received communion, giving thanks to our Lord. Afterward, they dismissed the laypeople and the whole crowd.
The community of monks alone went out and reached Tella of Mawzalt. And when the whole city had gone out to meet them,
it welcomed them with choice perfumes, with sorrow and great weeping. They stayed there for one day in the monastery called Beth Arabaye.
From there they headed for Tell-Beshmay[?] and lodged in the shrine of the martyrs called Mar Sari.
When they had been there a few days, Bar Kili, of evil memory, who was in Amida, sent orders and drove them away from there.
They went down to the southern region, to Mardin, and stayed in the monastery called Ain Hilaf. When they had completed about six and a half years,
through the efforts of Empress Theodora, an order was issued to Belisarius, and he brought them back into their monastery. When they had been there a short time, about eight
years, a dispute arose among them through Satan's influence. About seventy men broke away and left them.
Although many efforts at mediation had been made, and many people urged them to receive these men and make peace with them, they would not be persuaded.
When these things had been cunningly contrived by Satan, one of them, whose name was Elisha, went out in his madness[?], with others accompanying them.
He went up to Ephraim, the patriarch of Antioch, in opposition to the whole monastery, and they submitted to him. He prepared letters for them and sent them to the emperor.
After changing their appearance and dressing them in the clothes of imperial agents, for fear of the empress, he sent them to the emperor.
They went up, informed the emperor, and delivered the letters. They received harsh orders, came down, and drove the monks out again, for a second time.
Elisha himself, with his entire company, entered and seized the monastery. They ravaged its possessions and took everything that belonged to it.
Then they turned on the blessed men, stripped them, and abused them. Because of this, persecution was stirred up again throughout the East.
An account of Mara, bishop of Amida, of the course of the persecution there, and of the other monasteries of Amida.
Now when the blessed bishop of Seleucia in Syria had been persecuted by Paul the Jew and had left his episcopal seat in Seleucia,
after the departure of the blessed Severus[?]—for this blessed Nonnus was from the city of Amida—
he went down and lived quietly in his own city. Then it happened that the blessed Thomas, bishop of Amida, a great and spiritual man, an ascetic, holy, and compassionate monk,
departed from this world. Before the persecution, he prayed to God and said, “Lord God Almighty, who sits upon the cherubim, while the seraphim [?] in the chariot of his glory,
if persecution is going to reach this region, take my soul from me, and do not let my eyes see the turmoil of your holy church,
which you purchased and redeemed with the precious blood of your only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.”
And so, one day after the prayer of this great man of God, Thomas, he departed from this life, entered into rest, and was buried in peace.
Everyone marveled and gave thanks to God for the power of Saint Thomas's prayer.
For after his death, they seized the blessed Nonnus, bishop of Seleucia, who was living quietly in the city,
and forcibly seated him on the episcopal throne of the church of Amida, against his will. Before he had completed three months as bishop of Amida, he departed from this world.
After him came the blessed Mara, one of the prominent and well-known men, who was known as belonging to the house of Constantina.
He had distinguished himself greatly in the episcopate, and when he had completed [?] years, persecution reached the regions of Mesopotamia.
