The blessed Mara himself was also arrested. He was required either to submit to, accept, and proclaim the Council of Chalcedon,
or to be expelled and leave his see. But the blessed Mara chose to be persecuted with the faithful and to leave his see,
rather than, through love of his see, fall away from the truth of the orthodox and blameless faith. Thus he accepted exile for the truth
of Christ. He was banished to the city of Petra, in the desert of Arabia in Palestine, with his two sisters, virgins of Christ
and deaconesses, whose names were Shmuni and Nona, together with the blessed Isidore, bishop of Qinnasrin.
When they had been in exile there for about seven years, and the victorious Justinian died, through the efforts of his faithful wife Theodora,
he was persuaded and ordered that the blessed Isidore and Mara should leave that harsh and bitter exile in the city of Petra
and enter Alexandria the Great. This happened, and they went there and had a little relief from the affliction of their former exile.
Later they ended their lives there in Alexandria. Only the bones of Saint Mara were brought down to Amida by his blessed sisters

and laid in the church of Beth Sharla, which he himself had built.

On Abraham bar Kaili, and on the crucifixions and the other killings and evils he committed.

And on the holy martyr Cyrus, priest of the village of Ligin.

Now there was a bishop in Amida whose name was Abraham,
a cleric of that same church, a native of Tella by birth, who was called bar Kaili. When he became bishop and came down there from Antioch,
Satan took complete possession of him, and he threw himself into harsh and merciless persecution, plunder, and destruction
of human lives, beyond all his predecessors, both earlier and more recent.
This wretched man went so far as to employ killings, crucifixions, and burnings of the faithful, barbarously, wickedly, and without mercy,
while in every way he shamelessly devised hideous destruction for people, along with tortures and bitter floggings,
and deadly confinement in prison, in the courthouse, and in the underground pit that served as a prison for murderers
and others condemned to death. They were thrown into it and put to death inside, and their corpses were brought out and secretly cast
into ruined tombs, like those of dumb animals. For this deceiver, faced with the fierce zeal of the people of Amida for the true faith,
used to present himself to them as someone who did not proclaim the Council. But on one occasion, to Thomas the duke, a Goth who was duke at that time,
he sent word, had four men brought, and crucified them, one at each gate. They remained hanging on their crosses until evening.
When the day was dawning for the commemoration of the blessed Mother of God outside the northern gate of Amida, the wicked bishop mounted and went out to conduct the commemoration.

When he saw their corpses hanging on the crosses, he ordered that they should not be taken down, until people were distressed by the stench of decay. Only then did he allow them to be taken down and buried.
It was also the [?] of the Resurrection, and they were shouting in front of them, saying, “Look! Here are new martyrs who have come from among the Christians!”
Why, then, are Christians criticized by these pagans for doing this? For they too, in just the same way,
did it. He tortured men and women because they resisted him when he demanded that they accept the Council of Chalcedon.
All these things happened close to us, while we watched with our own eyes. This man first drove out and expelled all the holy monastic communities around the city.
Then he [?] its entire district, also registering the neighborhoods, courtyards, and houses of the city,
the men and women, and everyone [?] by name. He demanded that they come in under the lash and receive communion,
even down to the babies—not only those already born, but also those not yet born.
He required the women to register so that, when they gave birth, they would bring their children for baptism. Thus, if a baby happened to die,
or there was a miscarriage—or even if not—the clergy would come and inspect her. The household of a woman whose baby had died without her bringing it for baptism was in danger.
These evils, plundering, and destruction were taking place not only in the city itself, but throughout the district and territory of Amida.
Concerning the martyr Cyrus the priest. And another deed, more dreadful, cruel, and bitter than all the others.
A priest named Cyrus, from the village of Ligin, was arrested and ordered to receive communion.
When he would not agree, they brought him up to the city, to the bishop. The bishop shouted at him harshly and angrily, saying, “Why do you not receive communion?”
He replied, “You yourselves teach me to take offense at your communion and not receive any of it. For communion that is administered by force—
that is not communion.” Then the bishop swore, “You will not leave here, and you will receive communion!” But he in turn swore,
“I will never receive forced communion from you.” The bishop gave orders, and communion was brought. He ordered them to seize that priest
and fill a spoon and put it into his mouth. But he clamped his mouth shut, and they could not put the spoon into it. So he ordered a whip to be brought
and its handle forced into his mouth, so that they could put the spoon into his mouth. They were wrenching his teeth so hard that they were nearly torn out.
When they pushed the handle into his mouth, he spoke to them indistinctly, since he could not move his tongue and speak properly. He swore, saying, “By the truth of Christ,
if you put communion into my mouth, I will spit it in your faces!” And so, with bitter fury and deadly rage, they pushed a spoon in beside the whip and emptied it into his mouth.
But he blew the communion out of his mouth and flung it away—that which properly deserved to be called what it was: filth.
When Bar Kaili saw what that priest had done, he seized upon it as a pretext for putting him to death, something he had already intended,
so that he might destroy him too, like the others who had perished at his hands. Drunk with the accursedness and bitterness of Satan, who has been a murderer from the beginning, he hurriedly ordered
that wood and fire be brought to the city’s four-way arch and that the priest be burned. It was Wednesday in Holy Week during the fast.
So he had the priest stand at the four-way arch. They piled wood all around him [at the four-way arch], set it alight, and burned him.
While the city looked on, swaying and dancing at that appalling and heartbreaking sight, they watched a human being burn and his smoke rise like that of dumb animals without speech.
It would have been shameful and inhuman even to treat dumb animals with all this ruthlessness, cruelty, and hardness of heart.
When the whole city was disturbed and thrown into turmoil over this evil—the unjust and wicked burning of Bara the priest—
they planned to do the same to Bar Kili himself, following the example he had shown, and burn him just as he had burned that priest.
Some of the city's leading men, however, intervened and, out of fear of the king, restrained them from doing this. Many nevertheless separated themselves from him.
They regarded him as a murderer and a Jew, and stopped receiving his communion. But when they feared that this might become known to the king,
and that he would sentence him to be burned just as he had burned another, he acted first and wrote a report stating, supposedly, that an elderly man had trampled the Eucharistic offering underfoot,
and had been burned for this reason. In this way he managed to mislead people and cover up the murder. That in what we have recorded we have neither departed from the truth nor treated him unjustly,
the Lord is our witness, as are all the contemporaries of this wicked and ruthless deed. This evil also became known throughout the East and the West,
while everyone lamented the things done by those who wore the outward appearance of the priesthood but were far from
its power. As for the rest of this man's evil deeds, which we saw with our own eyes, touched with our own hands, and also heard with our own ears, if we undertook to record them,
we would need many books: how this man devised unnatural schemes and kept planning further plots, as it is written,
and every day issued various malicious sentences against those who would not commit themselves to the heresy of the two natures.
He himself did not even adhere to it willingly, but only to curry favor. Sometimes he would take those disfigured people who are called Tulqaye [?] there,
and send them to be quartered in the houses of believers who would not agree with him. They committed acts that even barbarians knew nothing about.
At other times he used troops of the barbarians themselves, who were stationed as a regiment in that very city.
At other times, when the opportunity suited him, he would order the complete destruction of anyone who opposed him.
He would bring a band of lepers from the monastery of the Arians outside the city, which is called Saint Romanus's—as many as could be found there—
and send them to be quartered in a believer's house. The man would be compelled to abandon his house and flee from their hideous and terrifying appearance,
when he saw their disfigured faces and their entire bodies, diseased and oozing, streaming with loathsome decay,
with diseased hands dripping blood and pus, more hideous than the dead lying in their graves. Besides all this, their souls were bitter and deceitful, and their thoughts were bent on the destruction
of the Christians: how they might spread their [?], their disease, and their putrefaction over their fine, clean utensils,
and roll about in their beds, filling them with putrid discharge and making them repulsive.
They would also put on their fine clothes, and plunder and take anything they liked. There was no one to restrain or stop them.
And when they had eaten and fouled everything in the house to which they had been sent, if they happened to learn that orders had been given for them to leave it,
They would go in and open whatever was there, whether a jar of wine, a flask of oil [?], or a vessel of honey or anything else.
They would gather together and all dip their filthy hands into all these vessels.
They would contaminate and foul them until people could no longer taste their contents, but would afterward throw them away
and destroy them, so that complete ruin would come upon any household to which the Arians were sent. They would have preferred that people who did not know God should be sent against them,
rather than Arians. But Bar Kaili, intent on harming and destroying people, would send these men against them all the more,

along with the rest of the other things that cannot be told or written down.
On Ephraim’s journey down to the East, the great persecution he carried out, and the assembled community of the monasteries of Amid.
For when Ephraim himself, the son of Appianus, a native of Amid who had been made patriarch in Antioch, went down to the East, he persecuted, disturbed, and threw into turmoil the whole East,
the church of God, and all Syria. He traveled around every region and city, evicting large and small monasteries, bringing people down from

their pillars and demolishing these too, and bringing recluses out of their cells. He forced people to receive communion by sword and club and the force of barbarians. So too, against the monasteries of Amid,
not only those around the city but those throughout the whole district, he would send men to drive them out through Abraham Bar Kaili,
whom we mentioned in the preceding account. This was what he used to do to us. When they had been persecuted and had left, a great crowd gathered together,
and they took up their crosses and traveled on, reaching an old monastery that had once been large and strong,
called the Monastery of the Hill of Mulberry Trees. After they had rested there for a few days and had begun to care for it and put it in order,
troops from the Roman regiments were sent, together with a rural bishop and an ecclesiastical visitor, to drive them out of there.
When the Roman force entered and saw the extended ranks standing one behind another at worship,
God cast fear upon them, and the monks appeared like giants in their eyes. They withdrew and began saying to one another,
“Let us keep away from a fight with these men. If one of them picks up a club, he will smash twenty of us.”
So they withdrew and left the monks alone. They went and quartered themselves in the surrounding villages and began oppressing the villagers.
They plundered them, slaughtered their livestock, and ate them, saying, “Until you go and raise an outcry,
men and women together, against that community of monks, and they leave, we will stay in your houses and eat and plunder everything you have.”
So all these villages gathered together, weeping and lamenting and begging the monks to have mercy
on them and leave. Thus they yielded and left. Otherwise, they had been ready to fight them,
saying, “If, as you say, the emperor ordered you to drive us out of our monasteries, look, we have left.
But you have not been ordered to drive us out of another place. Unless you bring an order, even if there are five thousand of you,
you will not drive us out without our either conquering or being conquered.” But when they saw the distress and outcry of the whole region,
They left of their own accord and went to a place called Madbaha. They settled in a monastery called Hawrintha, a thousand men or more.
They pitched shelters in the wilderness in rows, so that their camp, persecuted for Christ’s sake, now looked like a city.
All the surrounding villages came running, not only to weep, but also to see this marvel.
This was especially so when they stood in rows at worship or sat at the tables.
This monastery lies between three jurisdictions: those of Edessa, Amida, and Samosata.
When Patriarch Ephraim arrived in Edessa, he sent them his brother John, who was himself one of the provincial governors.
He came with rural bishops and many clerics, ostensibly to persuade them. Ephraim sent them this message: “Do you not
know me—that I am your son and a fellow citizen of yours? I was brought up under your care and in your monasteries, and I am concerned for your peace and your honor.
As for this stumbling block over which you are stumbling in matters of faith, let two or three men from each monastery come to me.
I will provide you with a way out and relief. Or I will come to you, and you must receive me willingly.”
When these things and many others had been spoken in the hearing [?] of that entire assembly,
the elders who led that assembly answered: “If, as he says, he is our son and our fellow citizen, let him stop waging war against us.
For, as he and the man in Amida saw fit, they have driven me out of our monasteries. Here we are, living in these rugged, harsh mountains. What business does he have with us?
Let him know for certain that none of us will go to him, and that even if he comes here, we will receive him only as a persecutor and an enemy.
Whatever he does against us, we are ready to endure.” When these things had been said firmly and decisively to [?] his brother John,
he said, “I am deeply distressed about you and about what you are going to suffer.”
So they departed and went away, and reported to him everything that had been said. When he heard these things,
this son and fellow citizen, as he called himself, blazed with anger like the furnace of the Babylonians. He wrote to Amida,
ordering all the military units stationed there to march against them, armed as for battle, and to seize and bind
them, and thus bring them all to him. When Bar Kaili received this order,
he sent a strong armed force against that community, accompanied by many clerics. When they had assembled and set out to come,
a message was written to the heads of the monasteries: “An armed cavalry force is coming against you. Consider what you will do.”
It was winter. Then all the heads of the monasteries gathered and took counsel: “We have no scriptural command to fight.”
They agreed among themselves that each abbot should divide the brothers of his monastery among his clergy, and that each cleric, whether priest or deacon,
should take his group and go to whatever district he wished, where he had acquaintances. The elders themselves were to gather together.
And they were to cross the Euphrates and all remain until they saw the outcome of his action. This they did, and each priest took his company and left.
For we ourselves, unworthy as we are, had already received ordination to the priesthood while we were still young. And so the monastery was left full of everything:
the provisions for that entire community, besides the vessels used in worship and the books, the bronze ware and utensils, and the rest of the things of this kind,
which everyone had taken care to remove from his dwelling and put beyond their reach. The large building of the infirmary also remained,
where there were people suffering from various illnesses, some of them close to death, who had entrusted themselves to God. Because of the severity of the winter
and the seriousness of their illnesses, they could not flee from the persecutor.
The rest were forced to cross difficult rivers that were swollen and reached up to their necks, while snow fell and winds blew, and there was severe frost.
Orders had already been written to all the authorities that anyone, in whatever village, who received one of them or let him enter his house
would have his house confiscated for the treasury and would himself be sentenced to death. Thus many were forced
to go into inaccessible rocky clefts and caves along the great river Euphrates and hide like wild animals.
A great many of them were there, and we ourselves, unworthy as we are, were among them. When news of this was heard in the surrounding villages,
all those whose hearts God had moved made secret arrangements with one another, for fear of the persecutors.
In the middle of the night they would load up bread, wine, flour, and the other things needed for their nourishment, and bring them to them secretly.
When they saw the distress they were in and the cramped places where they were living, like wild animals on rocky ledges,
they would weep and lament, crying out in sorrow for themselves and for Christianity, because of what had happened to it. They would hand over their gifts and return in great mourning.
Others climbed up to the bare heights, which are inaccessible mountains covered with snow, and in the pens of goats and sheep
they hid out of necessity. Thus everyone, everywhere, suffered from the severity of the exposure and the frost, and from the cramped conditions of the place.
As for their other needs, God, who is good and rich in mercy toward everyone who calls on him, saw their persecution for his name's sake
and did not leave them to suffer. And because, as before, just as
we explained above, at the very time when these things happened, one after another, during our youth,
we had recorded some of them in brief notes, while speaking of their full extent—things that would have required many books to record—
we have refrained from recounting a second time everything that the church of God suffered in these times,
things that we endured for many years with that spiritual community. And so that we do not stray from the history we have undertaken, we return to it.
In the year 833, the holy Mar Jacob, the teacher and bishop of Batnae in Serugh, died.
Moses succeeded him. In the year 836, floodwaters entered Edessa.
It seemed right to us not to conceal in silence the calamity and great disaster that overtook Edessa, the metropolis of Osrhoene, in our days.
This happened in the year eight hundred and thirty-six, when, as it is written, the decree of the Most High had now come upon many, and floods of water occurred in various places.
At about the third hour of the night, while many were asleep, many others were bathing in the public bathhouse,
and still others were at supper, suddenly powerful torrents arose in the river Daisan itself.
And they entered [?] This river Daisan passed through the middle of the city. Suddenly, in the darkness of the night, the wall was breached upstream, and it blocked and held back
the mass of water behind it. The water overflowed in full force and rose into all the streets and all the courtyards of the city surrounding the river.
Within one hour, or at most two, the city filled with water and was flooded, so that water suddenly entered through all the doors of the public bathhouse,
and everyone who was inside drowned there. When they looked toward the doors to go out and escape, they found the flood pouring in through the doors
and covering everyone who was on the lower floors. They all drowned and perished together. As for those on the upper floors,
if any were there and became aware of what was happening, and ran to go downstairs and escape, the flood met them, and they sank and drowned.
There were also others who, while they were [?], sunk in sleep and unaware, had their houses swept away because they were not firmly built.
They went down and sank in the flood itself. Only those whose lives the merciful God wished to preserve escaped,
because their houses stood firm and did not fall, especially those built of stone and lime,
throughout the area that sloped downward toward the river. The places that were high up and situated on the mountain slopes were also spared.
How the wall was breached, the water went out, and the city was drained; and the damage it did throughout the plain of Edessa and Harran.
When the city [had filled up] for the most part and was flooded, apart from the places already mentioned, and the waters were held back,
the city became like a lake. Then the city wall, which had first been breached upstream, was also breached downstream.
Unable to withstand the force of the mass of water, it suddenly broke open in three places. The towers were overturned and [?],
and were swept away by the force of the mass of water, which swept up and carried away corpses floating like cork.
Not only this: it also swept away houses, courtyards, palaces, the public bathhouse, and all the other different kinds of things that people owned,
even the stones and timbers of many [?]. The land outside the city was flooded.
The damage and destruction outside were not much less than what had happened inside.
Even as far as the Euphrates, as the river Daisan flowed through other rivers,
the force of the flood swept things away and carried them afloat: human corpses, livestock carcasses, possessions, and animals.
Thus, when God caused his mercy to shine forth and the flood subsided, and the city and the land outside it were drained, for many days—
Those who survived it were digging, clearing away debris, and bringing out bodies.
And the remaining events, with great sorrow and bitter anguish of spirit, concerning the blessed men whom the wicked Asclepius arrested one day before the flood.
On the day before that wrathful flood, the wicked Asclepius, who was the bishop of the city,
had arrested monks from all quarters, about ten blessed men, mournful and chaste, and tormented them
to make them enter into communion with him. When they would not yield to him, he imprisoned them, threatening to torture them the next day and force them into submission.
That very night the flood occurred, so that everyone thought that God had become angry with the bishop and the city because of the oppression of these blessed men.
After the water had drained out of the city, all the survivors took stones and ran to the bishop’s house to stone him,
Asclepius. But he managed to hide, escape from them, and flee to Antioch, to Euphrasius, who shared his views.
When Euphrasius received him, he brought him up into the pulpit with him and addressed the city about him, saying, “Come, see a second Noah,
who, as though in an ark, was himself saved from a second flood.” But Asclepius died there and never returned to Edessa.
There was relief for all the faithful. Those whom he had imprisoned also came out after his flight, and each went back to his monastery.
At this time the following were prominent: Abraham, bishop of Hanzit, and Mar Maron, the stylite of the monastery of Hasika,
and Mar Simeon the Recluse, and Mar Sergius, his disciple at Qalash. Also prominent was Mar Mara, abbot of the monastery of Surta on the Tigris,
and Mar Addai, the visitor from the Monastery of Paradise, and Mar John, and Zaqnaya [?]. The persecuted patriarchs: Theodosius of Alexandria,
Severus of Antioch, and Anthimus of Constantinople. These were the heretics: Euphrasius of Antioch; Epiphanius of Constantinople;
Hormisdas of Rome; Peter of Jerusalem; Timothy of Alexandria. The year eight hundred and thirty-seven.
Antioch was overthrown. In the seventh year of Justin’s reign, which was the year eight hundred and thirty-seven,
Antioch the Great was also overthrown—its fifth overthrow—at the seventh hour of the day. It was a terrible and bitter overthrow,
which no one can describe. For such harsh and bitter wrath came from heaven that those who had escaped
the terrible onslaught of wrath in the earthquake and overthrow were seized by fire and burned.
Flying sparks flew about and burned everything on which they settled. The earth itself was crackling from below, from within the soil,
boiling and burning everything that was there. Likewise, even the foundations, together with all the buildings upon them,
were being heaved up, leaping, rising and falling, splitting apart, being overturned, collapsing, and burning in the fire.
Those who escaped and tried to flee were met by fire, which caught them and burned them, so that they burned like wood.
Tongues of flame blazed terribly and bitterly through the force of fierce wrath. And again, from heaven, like rain,
Flames were raining down. The whole city was now ablaze like a blazing furnace, until it was completely overturned and fell.
It was overturned and burned with fire. Only a few houses remained at the foot of the mountain above it.
Even these were cracked and leaning toward collapse. Day after day they too were falling down and setting fire to those that remained.
For not a house, a church, or a building of any kind remained—even the garden walls were split, broken through, overturned, and brought down.
The rest burned and smoldered and became like dispersed vapor. For wet sand was erupting and rising from beneath the earth.
Even the foul smell of the sea and something like watery dampness could be detected in it. Sprays of seawater also rose amid the boiling sand.
On the burning of the great church of Antioch for seven days. Now the great church built by Constantine the Victorious,
which was said to have no equal throughout the Roman Empire, had remained standing, though cracked.
On the seventh day, fire suddenly caught hold of it too, from top to bottom. It fell and smoldered on the ground.
Likewise, the other churches that had escaped collapse in the earthquake were finally, through a sudden fire,
burned in great wrath and overturned down to their foundations. Lives were lost and destroyed in the city of Antioch,
which became like a winepress of wrath for all its inhabitants. As John of Antioch, who wrote these things about it, recorded:
As far as the survivors were able to count those who had died and whose bodies were being uncovered and found, two hundred and fifty thousand were counted.
For it was a festival, and for this reason many people had gathered in the great city, renowned for its buildings and its possessions.
It had been hospitable to strangers; suddenly it became a grave for strangers together with its inhabitants. We cannot write the full number of those who perished.
We have only recorded a little out of much about the terrible wrath [?] that suddenly overtook the great city of Antioch.
On the cross that appeared in the sky after the collapse of Antioch. On the third day after its collapse,
which was Sunday, a cross of light appeared in the western part of the sky.
All those who had survived saw it and were shaken. They kept crying, “Lord, have mercy,” while looking at it for about an hour.
Then it was hidden by clouds, while everyone was filled with wonder. After this, God's mercy and grace were revealed,
as people were found alive after thirty and forty days—men, women, children, and infants—amid all that fiercely blazing fire.
Thus all people might marvel and give thanks for God's abundant mercy, for he does not withhold his grace from his creation.
The earthquake continued throughout all these days and nights, for a year and a half, constantly and at every hour.
On the horrible death of Euphrasius, patriarch of Antioch. For while those who had survived and escaped the wrath were digging,
together with those who had gathered in the city of Antioch from other places and the surrounding cities, they were bringing up the bodies buried during the wrath.
The body of Euphrasius was found in a cauldron [?] belonging to a woman who sold wineskins, beneath his episcopal residence.
When the episcopal residence overturned and collapsed, he was caught in the collapse and fell into the vat. His whole body sank into the vat, and he was boiled in the pitch.
His head was found hanging over the outside edge of the vat. In this way he was recognized by his face, while his bones were found stripped of pitch. And some people,
heretics who shared his views and were in Antioch, were misleading people and saying that he had been taken up to heaven.
But God, to expose their error, had preserved his face uncorrupted, as though he were alive.
Fear and trembling seized everyone who saw it, and the faithful were greatly astonished as they recalled the insolence of his wickedness and his cruel schemes,
and the persecution and plundering he had carried out, and the sufferings he had inflicted on people. He did not do these things alone,
but also urged all the bishops under his authority to carry them out—to persecute, plunder, and torture people.
Having received a pretext and power from him, they all threw themselves into these evil deeds,
competing with one another and striving to outdo their companions in persecution and wickedness in every region and city.
Many books would not be enough to record these things—the afflictions, persecutions, and evil deeds in every region and city.
Many books would not be enough to record these things—the afflictions and persecutions, and also the tortures, bonds, and imprisonments
that were being inflicted in every region and city by bishops, clergy, and visiting church officials,
and by rural bishops and [?], at the command and instigation of Euphrasius and his predecessor, throughout their lives.
On the destruction of Seleucia and Daphne and their surroundings by terrible earthquakes [?]. Seleucia in Syria and Daphne, which lies above Antioch,
over an area twenty miles long and wide, were also overthrown and ruined, becoming a terrifying sight to those who saw them—not through fire, but through the earthquake alone.
When Emperor Justin learned of all this devastation and the complete destruction of Antioch, Seleucia, and Daphne, he took
off his crown in bitter grief, removed his purple robes, and sat in mourning.
He refused to hear or attend to anything at all, but sat sorrowfully weeping over Seleucia, Daphne, and Antioch.
For he knew them, loved them greatly, and used to praise them. Since it was the feast of Pentecost,
the emperor himself went out to church in this condition, mourning and weeping, without his imperial crown and dressed in mourning clothes
and in sorrow over their destruction. When his entire senate saw him mourning in this way, they too dressed in mourning clothes like him.
He sent five hundredweights, amounting to five hundred pounds, so that the city of Antioch might be cleared and rebuilt, along with Seleucia and Daphne,
and so that the bodies buried in them might be brought out—the many uncounted thousands of people who had perished in the terrible wrath. And this was done.
Antioch, Seleucia, and Daphne were rebuilt. In the year eight hundred and forty, there was a great earthquake, and Durkin was overthrown by it.
Concerning terrible punishments, those which come upon Dyrrachium [?]. Concerning terrible punishments.
Who can recount these things that human sins bring about at all times, and the destruction of cities?
Such a thing also happened to this city, Dyrrachium, the metropolis of the new province called [?], from which Emperor Anastasius came.
Suddenly it shook, tottered, and fell in a great earthquake. At this very time it collapsed and crushed its inhabitants.
In the year 841 there was a great earthquake. In it the city of Corinth, the metropolis of Hellas, also collapsed.
In the year 842, Anazarbus, the metropolis of Cilicia, was also overthrown. This was its fourth destruction.
After Euphrasius, Ephraim of Amida became patriarch in Antioch. By his wicked deeds he overshadowed all his predecessors.
And even [?], so that those of the house of Trajan and Diocletian ought to be disciples.
[?] In the year 842, Justinian the Elder made Justinian, his sister’s son, emperor alongside him.
In the year 843, Rufinus came down and made peace between the Romans and the Persians.
On that very day the stars were seen shining in the sky. In the year 844.
Agrippa, king of the Heruli, came to Justinian with his entire army, all his nobles, and twelve of his relatives.
He greeted him and asked him for permission to become a Christian. When Emperor Justinian himself heard this, he rejoiced.
For he had great concern and very great zeal to turn the nations that had gone astray to the faith.
He gave the order, and the king was baptized at the holy feast of Epiphany, together with his relatives, his nobles, and his army.
The victorious emperor himself received him from baptism, gave him many gifts, and sent him away. In the year 845.
Gordius, king of the Huns, came to the imperial city with a large army and asked to become a Christian.
They were instructed and baptized. Justinian himself received him from baptism, honored him, gave him many gifts, and allowed him
to return to his country. When he reached his country, he found his brother, whom he had appointed over his armies, and told him about his conversion to Christianity.
He also showed him the wealth and gifts from the Roman emperor, and his brother marveled. He then took the silver and gold idols that they worshiped.
Since he believed that there was only one true God, and that these idols were mute and were not gods, he broke them.
He sent them to the city of Bosporus to exchange them for money. When his brother and all his armies saw these things,
they were filled with anger against him, together with the priests of their idols. They devised a plot against him and killed him.
Because they feared the Roman emperor, they fled to another country. In the year 846, Justinian the Elder died.
His sister’s son Justinian became emperor. Concerning the kingdom of the Indians and how they became Christians because of a war.
At this time, then, war broke out between the kings of the Indians.
That is, between the king of the Indians, whose name was Axondan, and another king of Inner India, whose name was Andug, who was a pagan.
After they had stopped fighting one another, this king in turn went to war against the king of the Himyarites.
For they too were Indians. His name was Dimnon. This was the cause of the war between them:
Since the kingdom of the Ethiopians lay much farther inland than that of the Himyarites, which was outside India,
Roman merchants used to pass through the territories of the Himyarites and enter the inland territories of the Indians, which are called
Uzalis of India, and also the territories of the Indians and Ethiopians that lay still farther inland.
There are seven kingdoms of the Indians and Ethiopians: three of the Indians and four of the Ethiopians.
These lie far away and deep inland in the southern regions along the shore of the great sea. Now the Roman merchants,
those mentioned above, were passing through the territories of the Himyarites when he seized them, killed them, and plundered all their merchandise.
He said, “Because the Christians in Roman territories cruelly oppress the Jews who live in their territories and kill many of them, I am killing these men.”
In this way he killed many, until many people became afraid and stopped entering, and trade with the inland kingdoms of the Indians and Ethiopians ceased.
Concerning the message the king of the Ethiopians sent to the king of the Himyarites, and the war between them. Then the king of the Ethiopians sent this message to the king of the Himyarites:
“You have acted wickedly by killing the Christian Roman merchants, stopping trade, and cutting off supplies to my kingdom and the other kingdoms.
You have caused losses especially to my own kingdom.” For this reason they became bitter enemies and arranged to go to war against one another.
As they drew near to fight one another, Andug, king of the Ethiopians, said, “If I am granted victory over this torturer, the king of the Himyarites,
I will become a Christian, for I seek to avenge the blood of the Christians upon him.” Then they fought one another.
The king of the Ethiopians defeated the king of the Himyarites, captured him, killed him, and plundered his kingdom.
He conquered his territories and destroyed all his armies. Then, after his victory, he did not delay in fulfilling his vow.
Instead, he sent two of his nobles to Emperor Justinian, asking him to send him a bishop and clergy.
The emperor rejoiced greatly and ordered that they be given whichever bishop they requested. When those envoys made inquiries,
they found a man named John, a [?] at Saint John’s, who was a virgin, chaste, and zealous. They asked for him, and he was given to them.
They took him along with many clergy and returned joyfully to their own country. When they reached their king, Andug,
he too welcomed them [?] with great joy, along with the bishop and the priests who had come with them. He received instruction, was baptized, and became a Christian,
both he and all his nobles. They worked zealously for all the territories to become Christian and for churches to be established in them.
to the glory of the true God of the Christians. Through circumstances like these, God brought salvation to these misguided peoples.
Again, concerning that same kingdom of the Himyarites, and the evils and killings that the Jews committed there. After a time, however, the Jews among the Himyarites grew strong.
When the Christian king died—the one whom the king of the Ethiopians had installed there and made king over the Himyarite people from among them—and in bitter fury,
they killed and destroyed the entire Christian population there: men, women, children, and infants, young [?] old.
Thus the account of the martyrdom of the many martyrs there, through the zeal of the blessed Simeon the teacher,
was written down. It fills all who hear it with sorrow. We have also included it in this sequence.
It is as follows: The letter sent by the holy Simeon, bishop of Beth Arsham and leader of the faithful in the land of the Persians,
to Mar Simeon, abbot of Gabbula. It is also an account of the martyrdom among the Himyarites.
We inform you, whom we love, that on the twentieth of January in this year 835,
we left Hira of Naaman with the priest Abraham, son of Euphrasius, who had been sent by Emperor Justinian
to Mundhir, king of the Arabs, to make peace. We also wrote about him in our previous letter. We and all the faithful here are grateful to him
for helping our side. He confirms both what we wrote previously and what we are writing now.
For we traveled through the desert toward the south and east, a journey of ten days, and caught up with Mundhir
opposite the hills of sand [?], called Ramla in Arabic. As we were entering Mundhir’s camp,
pagan Arabs and Maaddites met us and said to us, “What can you do?
Look, your Christ has been driven out by the Romans, the Persians, and the Himyarites.” As we were being taunted by the Arabs,
we were distressed, and sorrow overtook us along with our distress. For an envoy sent by the king of the Himyarites to King Mundhir arrived near us
and gave him a letter full of boasting. It read as follows: “Know, my brother King Mundhir, that the king whom the Ethiopians installed in our country has died.
Winter arrived, and the Ethiopians could not come to our country and appoint a Christian king as they customarily do.
So I became king over the whole land of the Himyarites. First I seized all the Christians who professed Christ
and would not become Jews like us. I killed the 280 priests who were found, together with the Ethiopians
who were guarding the church. I turned their church into a synagogue of ours. Then, with an army of 120,000,
I went to Najran, the city of their kingdom. After besieging it for days without conquering it, I made promises to them under oath.
But I decided not to keep my word to the Christians, my enemies. I seized them to make them bring their gold, silver, and possessions. They brought them to me,
and I took them. I demanded Paul, their bishop. They told me that he had died, but I did not believe them until they showed me his tomb.
I brought up his bones and burned them, along with their church, their priests, and everyone I found taking refuge in it.
I tried to force the rest to renounce Christ and the cross, but they refused. Instead, they confessed that he is God and the Son of the Blessed One.
They chose to die for him. Their leader spoke at length against me and insulted me.
I ordered all their leading men to be killed. We brought their wives and told them to renounce their faith.
When they saw their husbands being killed, they were willing. But the daughters of the covenant were pressing to be killed first.
The wives of the leading men rebuked them, saying, “We ought to die after our husbands.” They were all killed at our command,
except Rumi, the wife of the man who was to become king there. We did not allow her to die, but kept urging her to renounce Christ and live,
to have pity on her daughters and retain everything she owned by becoming a Jew. We ordered her to go and consider it,
accompanied by guards from our army. She went out and walked around the streets and squares of the city with her head uncovered.
This was a woman whom no one had seen in public since she had grown up. She cried out, saying, “Women of [?], my companions,
Christian, Jewish, and pagan women, listen! My ancestry, my family, and whose daughter I am—a Christian woman—
you know, and you know that I have gold and silver, male and female slaves, many villages, and revenues. Now my husband has been killed for Christ.
If I wanted to marry a man, I have forty [?] dinars and much jewelry of gold and silver,
as well as pearls and beautiful, splendid clothes, besides my husband’s treasures. What I have said is no lie, and some of you know it.
A woman has no days of joy like the days of joy like the days of her wedding feast.
For from then on there are troubles and groans in bearing children, and again when she is bereaved of them and buries them.
But from this day onward I am spared all these things. On the first day of my wedding feast I was joyful,
and now, with gladness of heart, I have adorned my five virgin daughters for Christ. Look at me, my companions!
For here you see me twice: at my first wedding feast and at this second—you see me twice: at my first wedding feast and at this second.
With my face unveiled before all of you, I went in to my first bridegroom. Now, with my face unveiled, I am going to Christ, my Lord and my God, and the Lord and God of my daughters,
just as he stooped down in his love, came to us, and suffered for our sake. Follow my example, for I am no less beautiful than you.
Here I am, radiant in that beauty, going to Christ, with it unspoiled by the denial practiced by the Jews,
so that my beauty may be a witness for me before my Lord: it could not lead me astray into the sin of denial.
My gold, my silver, and everything I own—I have not loved them as I love my God. This rebellious king has given me permission to renounce my faith and live.
Far be it from me, my companions! Far be it from me to renounce Christ, the God in whom my daughters and I have believed. I was baptized in the name of the Trinity.
I worship his cross, and my daughters and I gladly die for him, just as he suffered in the flesh for us.
Look, everything desirable to the eyes and the body is left behind on earth and passes away. I am going to receive from my Lord something that does not pass away.
Blessed are you, my companions, if you listen to me, heed the truth, and love Christ our God. My daughters and I are dying for him.
From now on, may there be peace and harmony for God's people. May the blood of these brothers and sisters of mine who were killed for Christ become a wall protecting this city.
If you remain faithful to Christ my Lord. Look, with my face uncovered I am leaving this city, where I lived as in a temporary tent,
to go with my daughters to the everlasting city, where I have betrothed them. Pray for me, my companions,
that Christ my Lord may receive me and forgive me, for I have remained three days after my husband. And while we were hearing the sound of wailing from the city,
those who had been sent arrived, and when questioned, they told us things like those we have written above.
As she was being led around the city, Ruhm spoke to the women who were her companions, encouraging them, and there was wailing in the city.
We became so angry with the guards that we would have killed them, had we not been persuaded otherwise because they had allowed her to do these things.
Finally, she came out of the city with her daughters, like a madwoman, with her head uncovered, and stood before me without shame.
She was holding her daughters by the hand, and they were dressed as though for a wedding feast. She loosened the braids of her hair,
wrapped them around her hands, stretched out her neck, and bowed her head, crying out, "My daughters and I are Christians, and we are dying for Christ.
Cut off our heads so that we may go and join our brothers. [?] We are dying for Christ. Cut off our heads so that we may go and join our brothers and sisters,
and the father of my daughters." But after all this madness, I urged her to deny Christ and merely say that he was a human being.
She refused. One of her daughters insulted us for saying this. When I saw that there was no way to make her deny Christ,
I gave orders to terrify the remaining Christians. They threw her onto the ground, and her daughters were slaughtered, and their blood flowed into her mouth.
Afterward her head was cut off. I swear by the Lord that I was greatly distressed because of her beauty and that of her daughters. My chief priests and I decided
that children should not die because of their parents, according to the force of the law. I distributed the boys and girls among the troops,
so that they might raise them. When they grow up, if they become Jews, they shall live; but if they profess Christ, they shall die.
I have written these things and made them known to Your Majesty. I urge you not to leave any Christian among your people unless he renounces Christ and joins you.
But treat the Jews, my brothers who are under your authority, with affection, my brother. Write and send me a reply about this,
so that I may send you whomever you wish. All these things were written to Mundhir by the impure Jewish king.
When we arrived there, he assembled his army, and the letter was read before him. The envoy recounted how the Christians had been killed
and driven out of the land of the Himyarites. Mundhir said to the Christians in his army, "You have heard what happened. Now deny Christ."
“For I am no better than the kings who persecuted the Christians.” Then a Christian man from his army was stirred with zeal.
He boldly said to the king, “We did not become Christians during your reign, that we should now deny Christ.”
Mundhir became angry and said, “Do you dare to speak before me?” And he said, “Do you dare to speak before me?”
He said, “Because I fear God, I speak without fear, and no one can stop me. For my sword is no shorter than anyone else’s,
and I am not afraid to fight to the death.” Because of his family, and because he was an important and well-known man, brave in battle, Mundhir left him alone.
When we returned to al-Hira of Nu'man, in the first week of the fast, we found the envoy who had been sent by the king of the Himyarites before he died.
When this man heard about those who had been destroyed by this Jewish tyrant, he quickly hired a man from al-Hira of Nu'man and sent him to Najran to bring him a report,
after seeing and learning what had happened there. When he returned, he too recounted, in our presence, to the Christian envoy,
the things we have written above, and that three hundred and forty leading men who had gone out from the city to meet him had been killed.
He also spoke about Harith son of Ka'b, their leader, the husband of Ruhm, whom that Jew insulted, saying to him, “You relied on Christ
and rebelled against me. But have pity on your old age and deny him. Otherwise, you will die with your companions.”
He answered him, “Truly, I grieve for all my companions because they did not listen to me. I told them that you were deceitful,
and that we should not go out to you and accept your words, but should fight you. I trusted in Christ that I would defeat you and that the city would not be captured,
because it lacked nothing. You are not a king but a liar. I have seen many kings who have
integrity and do not deceive. I will not be false to Christ my God by becoming a Jew and an unbeliever like you.
Now you know that I have lived as I wished. I have lived a long time in this world. I have had sons and grandsons, and I have daughters, and my family is numerous.
I have distinguished myself in battles through Christ’s strength. I am certain that, like a vine that is pruned and bears abundant fruit,
so our Christian people will increase in this city, and the church that you burned will grow and be rebuilt.
It will exercise authority and give commands to kings. Christianity will reign, and Judaism will die out. Your kingdom will pass away, and your power will come to an end.
Do not boast that you have accomplished anything. When you are shaken, you will be swept away.” These things were spoken by the great Harith, the honored old man.
Immediately he turned around and said loudly to his believing companions in his company, “Have you heard, my brothers, what I said to this Jew?”
They said, “We heard everything you said, our father.” Again he said, “Are these things true or not?” They cried out, “They are true!” And he said,
“If anyone fears the sword and denies Christ, let him separate himself from us.” They cried out, “Far be it from us to be afraid, our father! We will all die with you for Christ,
and none of us will remain behind after you.” Then he cried out and said, “People surrounding me—Christians, Jews, and pagans—listen!
If anyone from my family, my relatives, or my clan denies Christ and gives his allegiance to this Jew, he has no fellowship with me and shall inherit nothing of mine.”
But whatever property of mine is found should go toward the expenses of rebuilding the church. If, however, any of my family does not deny Christ and survives me, let him inherit my furnishings.
Three villages from my estate, whichever the church chooses, should provide for its expenses.” When he had said this, he turned toward the king and said, “I renounce you
and whoever denies Christ. Here we stand before you.” His companions took courage and said, “Look, Abraham, the patriarch, is watching you, and us with you.
We renounce anyone who denies Christ and remains alive after you.” He ordered them to be brought to the valley called Wadia, to have their heads cut off,
and their bodies thrown into it. He stretched out his hands toward heaven and said, “Christ our God, come to our aid and give us strength.
Receive our souls. May the blood of your servants, shed for your sake, be pleasing to you. Make us worthy to see you, and acknowledge us before your Father, as you promised.
May the church be rebuilt, and may there be a bishop in this city in place of your servant Paul, whose bones they burned.” They greeted one another.
The old man Arethas made the sign of the cross over [?]. He bowed his head and received the sword. His companions ran and crowded together, and smeared themselves with some of his blood.
They were all martyred. There was a three-year-old child whose mother was going out to be killed, holding him by the hand.
When he saw the king sitting dressed in royal clothing, he left his mother, ran over, and kissed the king on his knees.
The king took hold of him and began caressing him. He said to him, “What would you like: to go and die with your mother, or to stay with me?”
The child said to him, “My lord, I want to die with my mother. That is why I am going with my mother, because she said to me,
‘Come, my son, let us go and die for Christ.’ But let me go to my mother, so that she does not die without my seeing her.
For she told me that the king of the Jews had ordered everyone who does not deny Christ to die. And I will not deny him.”
He said to him, “And how did you come to know Christ?” The child said to him, “I see him every day in church with my mother, whenever I come
to church.” He said to him, “Do you love me or your mother?” He said to him, “My lord, my mother.” Again he said to him,
“Do you love me or Christ?” He said to him, “I love Christ much more than you.” He said to him, “Then why did you come and kiss my knees?”
He said to him, “I thought you were the Christian king whom I used to see in church. I did not know that you were a Jew.”
He said to him, “I will give you walnuts, almonds, and figs.” The child said, “No, by Christ! I will not eat the Jews’ walnuts.
Just let me go to my mother.” He said to him, “Stay with me, and you will be my son.” The child said,
“No, by Christ! I will not stay with you, because your smell is foul and stinking, not sweet like my mother’s.” The king said to those nearby,
“Look at this evil root! From his infancy Christ has led him astray into loving him.” One of the officials said to the child,
“Come with me. I will take you to become the queen’s son.” The child said to him, “May your face be slapped! My mother is better for me than the queen,
because she takes me to church.” When he saw that they were holding him fast, he bit the king on his thigh and said, “Let me go, you wicked Jew, so I can go to my mother
and die with her.” He handed him over to one of the officials and said to him, “Keep watch over him until he grows up. If he denies Christ, he will live.”
Otherwise he would die. As that man's servant carried him, he kicked his feet and called to his mother.
"Mother, come and take me! I will go with you to church." Crying out to him, she said, "Go, my son. I have entrusted you to Christ.
Do not cry. Wait for me in the church with Christ until I come." When she had said this, they cut off her head.
These writings and the reports that were heard brought sorrow to all the Christians here. And so that these things might be made known
to the holy and faithful bishops—the things that happened in the land of the Himyarites—and so that they might commemorate these holy martyrs, we have written.
We appeal to your love to have these things quickly made known to the heads of the monasteries and the bishops, and especially to the chief priest of Alexandria,
so that a letter may be written to the king of the Ethiopians, urging him to prepare quickly and help the Himyarites. Let the chief priests of the Jews in Tiberias also be [?] and compelled
to send word to this Jewish king who has arisen, so that he may put an end to the ordeal and persecution in the land of the Himyarites.
Together with the remaining greetings contained in the letter of the chief priests of that time and of the faithful heads of the monasteries.
Again, concerning this little boy mentioned above in this account of the martyrs: it seemed right to us not to pass over him in silence.
Also concerning that little boy mentioned above in this account, who bit the king on his thigh while saying, "Let me go! I will go and die with my mother."

He held him while the boy struggled with him and would not be persuaded by him. He handed him over to one of his nobles to raise him, ordering that when he grew up, he should die unless he renounced Christ.
For when that Jew was killed by the Ethiopians, and all the Jews among the Himyarites were strangled,
that boy survived and grew up. When this became known to the Christian king who was there, he took the boy into his care.
As he continued to grow and reached full stature, the king held him in great honor as a martyr of Christ.
He made him chief of his patricians, and he became his confidant and counselor. His name is Baysar. This man, then,
he later sent on an embassy to Emperor Justinian. We also spent a long time in this man's company,
marveling at his goodwill, his gentleness and humility, and the nobility that shone upon his face,
and at his constant sorrow and the mourning that remained continually in his mind. From morning until evening he would go around the churches of the imperial city,
praying and giving alms out of what the emperor gave him, while regularly fasting until evening every day.
Eventually, while everyone who saw him marveled at these things and spoke about him with wonder, it finally became known about him
that he was that little boy who had defied that Jew and insulted him to his face, and finally bitten him on his thigh.
He himself did not want these things about him to become known. We have recorded these things concerning God's martyr.
Concerning the king of the Ethiopians, his expedition, and his killing of the tyrant and the Jews who were with him.
Afterward, when the king of the Ethiopians, who had killed the former king of the Himyarites and had become a Christian for this reason,
When he learned this, and about the destruction of the Christians and the tyranny of the Jews, he burned with zeal and led out his forces.
He marched against the tyrant, seized him and killed him, and destroyed his forces,
and completely wiped out all the Jews in the land of the Himyarites. He also appointed a zealous Christian man named Abraham as king there.
Thus all the Christians who had been scattered by persecution and fear of the Jews gathered there, and that land was established in Christianity.
He had sent to Alexandria and obtained a bishop for himself before the introduction of the Council of Chalcedon there. This bishop, after only a short
time in that land, died. When the king of the Himyarites learned that the Council of Chalcedon had been introduced into Alexandria,
and that Patriarch Theodosius had been persecuted and had left because of the faith, and because he would not accept the council,
he too took offense and would not accept a bishop from Alexandria. In the year 850, the Persians made war against Antioch.
It was captured, devastated, and burned. At that very time, in the fourteenth year of Ephraim, the powerful Persian forces gathered
and came with their king Khosrow. They captured the city of Antioch, burned it with fire, stripped it bare, and deported its inhabitants.
They even took the marble slabs that covered its walls and carried them down to their own country.
They also built a city in their own country in its likeness and named it Antioch. Ephraim himself fled from them,
so that afterward he would be covered with shame over his city and its destruction in his days. This indeed happened to him.
Thus, in this disgrace, after four years he departed from this earthly life. God knows what awaits him there. In the year 857,
the holy Timothy, patriarch of Alexandria, died. He entrusted his throne to a man named Theodosius, one of the members of the church there.
In the year 841, the great river Euphrates was blocked above the region of Claudia, opposite Cappadocia, beside the village of [?]sidin. For a mountain,
a large one, slipped and fell. Since the mountains there are very high and close together, it fell and blocked the passage from one mountain to the other.
This lasted three days and three nights. The river flowed backward toward Armenia, flooded the land, and submerged villages,
causing great damage. Downstream, however, it dried up in place after place, became depleted, and turned into dry ground.
Then people assembled from many villages with supplications, services, and many crosses. They went up in sorrow, with streaming tears and great trembling,
carrying their censers and burning incense. They offered the Eucharist on top of the mountain that blocked the middle of the river.
Then it began to give way little by little, opening a breach. Finally it suddenly broke apart, and the masses of water burst out and rushed downstream.
There was a great upheaval throughout the East, reaching even the regions of Persia, as villages and people were swept away,
along with many livestock and everything that lay in the path of the sudden mass of water. It devastated many places.
Some of the houses of the village situated above the mountain, however, survived, as did its vineyards.
remaining firmly on that other bank where they had come to rest, where they still stand to this day. Likewise, all the land upstream from the dam
it swept away and ruined as it came down. In the year 842, the sun grew dark and remained enveloped in darkness for a year and a half,
which is eighteen months. Even when its rays were visible for two or three hours,
they were feeble, so that even the fruit failed to reach full ripeness.
All the wine tasted as though it were made from unripe grapes. Then the Lord made his mercy shine upon
his handiwork and gave it light. Yet people again returned fearlessly to their hardness of heart, as before.
In the year 849, Saint Mar Severus, patriarch of Antioch, departed from this world on February 8.
On the sixth of the same month, Saint Mar John bar Qursos died. Others affirm that Mar John bar Aphtonia died on the fourth of that month.
In the year 850, Pompeiopolis was swallowed up. This Pompeiopolis, because of the great earthquake that occurred there,
was not overthrown like the other cities. Rather, a terrifying sign occurred there: the earth suddenly opened and split apart
from one side of the city to the other. Thus half of it descended and sank into that terrifying and deeply lamentable chasm, together with its inhabitants.
Thus it went down alive to Sheol, as it is written. As the people descended into that terrifying and dreadful chasm and sank into the depths of the earth,
the sound of all of them crying out together rose bitterly and pitifully from the earth to those who had survived, for many days.
Their souls were tormented by the sound of their cries from the depths of Sheol, but they could do nothing to help them.
Afterward, when the emperor learned of it, he sent a great deal of gold so that, if possible, those who had sunk into the earth might be helped.
But there was no way to help those who had sunk into the earth. There was no way for them to be helped or for even a single soul among them to be rescued.
That gold was given to the survivors for the upkeep of the rest of the city—to those who had escaped and been saved from the wrath of that terrifying calamity brought about by our sins.
In the year 851, Antioch was overthrown for the sixth time.
During the reign of Justinian, two years after the fifth overthrow of Antioch,
it was again overthrown for the sixth time, on November 29, a Wednesday, at the tenth hour,
in the seventh indiction, which, according to the reckoning of the people of Antioch, was the year 576.
On that very day there was a great earthquake lasting one hour. At the end of the earthquake, there came from heaven something like a great, powerful, prolonged peal of thunder.
From the earth rose the sound of a great, powerful, terrifying groan, like a bull bellowing. From the vibration of that groaning sound, the earth trembled and shook.
All the buildings that had been built in it after its collapse were overthrown and fell to the ground, along with the walls and gates of the city,
especially the Great Church, the other churches and martyrs’ shrines, and the remaining houses that had escaped the earlier earthquake, down to the smallest.
And so all the surrounding cities, on hearing of the calamity and destruction of the city of Antioch, sat in mourning, grief, and distress.
All the villages surrounding it, which had been built long before, were also overthrown, as far as ten miles away.
Seleucia and Daphne had fallen in the fifth upheaval, but in this sixth one they did not fall and were not [?].
For the city's inhabitants died or went into exile, apart from those who were injured; some suffered broken bones,
and some suffered various wounds. But God's mercy and grace were revealed and did not allow fire to spread and burn as it had in the first upheaval.
Most of those who were found alive fled to other cities, leaving Antioch deserted and ruined.
Others made shelters for themselves on the mountain beyond the city, using cloths, reeds, and woven mats.
And so they lived in these amid the hardships of winter. On the harsh winter that occurred, and on the supplications offered by those who remained in the city.
Immediately after the earthquake, when Antioch shook and fell, a harsh winter came, and snow fell to a depth of three cubits.
Those who had stayed in the city offered anguished supplications in great sorrow.
They even walked barefoot in the snow, carrying olive branches in their hands.
They went outside the city to the plain, as far as a mile away, while snow fell on them, and threw themselves down on the snow.
They cried out in anguished sorrow and bitter weeping, shouting, “Lord, have mercy!” To see them was a sight of sorrow and terror.
They shivered in the snow, their color changed, and they lay on their faces, crying out in great pain of body and soul.
Their faces were miserable and troubled with tears and sorrow, and with the severity of the winter cold. On the vision that appeared to a certain believer at that time.
And on the rebuilding of the city. At that time, then, while they were offering supplications, a vision appeared to a certain Christian
and believer, telling him to tell everyone who remained in Antioch to write on the gates of the courtyards, houses, and shops
that remained and had not fallen: “Christ is with you. Stand firm!” And so all those who had survived wrote this on the houses that had not fallen.
And so they took courage and went inside, and those that had remained standing stood firm, with Ephraim the patriarch among them.
He, together with the officials who had escaped, informed the emperor about all these things.
When he heard these things, he sat in mourning for many days over Antioch, as did the entire senate. He also sent a great deal of gold again,
ordering that the city be reduced in size and consolidated, that the outer wall be demolished, and that a wall be built through the middle of the city, leaving most of the extensive area outside.
This was indeed done. When the wall was built, it proved to be far from the Orontes River.
Most of the city remained outside, in ruins. The emperor ordered that a channel be dug outside the wall that had been built,

to provide a passage for the river, bringing the river close to it and allowing it to pass from one side to the other. And so the river was dammed and flowed through the channel alongside the wall that had been built.
This too was accomplished with very great effort and a vast amount of gold, through the care and diligence of Emperor Justinian.
In the year 852, on January 2, at the eighth hour, in the year
seven of the year seventy-six of its era [?], according to Laodicea’s reckoning, there was an earthquake. Laodicea was overturned from its foundations, from the Antioch Gate
as far as the Jewish quarter and as far as the sea. But the left side, where the church of the [?] Mother of God stood, did not collapse.
According to the count, seven and a half thousand people perished in it, including many Jews but few Christians.
Those found alive, though suffering severe injuries, were 274 Jews
and four Christians. But all the churches, with God’s help, neither collapsed nor were shaken.
Nor did fire take hold amid the collapse that occurred. The emperor also sent a great deal of gold for rebuilding Laodicea.
Thus it was rebuilt again, and its walls were restored. At that same time, Manichaeans were discovered in Constantinople and burned with fire.
At this same time, many people were discovered who adhered to the ruinous error of the Manichaeans.
They would gather in houses and perform the mysteries of the impurity and error of their teaching. When they were arrested, the emperor ordered that they be brought before him,
hoping that he could admonish them and turn them back from their ruinous error. When they came in, he discussed many matters with them,
admonishing them and showing them from the Scriptures that they were adhering to pagan error. They were not persuaded by him, however, but with arrogance inspired by Satan,
they shouted fearlessly before him, saying, “We are ready to be burned for Mani’s teaching and to endure every torture and affliction,
and we will not change it.” Then he ordered that their wish be fulfilled: they were to be put in a boat and burned with fire at sea,
and thus drowned in the sea. Their possessions were to be handed over to the treasury, because even prominent women,
high officials, and patricians were found among them. Thus, under this sentence of burning by fire, many Manichaeans perished,
and they would not be persuaded to turn back from their error. Further, concerning the pagans discovered in the imperial city in the days of Emperor Justinian.
In the nineteenth year of Emperor Justinian, through the efforts of our humble self, the affair of the pagans was investigated.
Prominent men and high officials were discovered in the imperial city, along with others who were grammarians, sophists, lawyers, and physicians.
When they were exposed and, under torture, informed against one another, they were arrested, flogged, and imprisoned. They were placed in churches to learn the Christian faith,
as was fitting for pagans—men who were patricians and high officials. One prominent and wealthy pagan among them,
whose name was Phocas and who was a patrician, saw the intensity of the investigation.
Moreover, those arrested had informed against him as a pagan, and he knew that a harsh sentence awaited him because of the fierceness of the emperor’s zeal. At night he took a poison
that caused death and forfeited his life in this world. When the emperor heard of this, he passed judgment very justly.
And he ordered that he be buried with a donkey’s burial, with no funeral procession of people for him and no prayer offered over him.
And so his household carried him away at night on a litter, went out, opened a grave, and threw him into it like the refuse of a corpse [?].
And so fear came upon all the pagans for a short time. The year 853.
There was a visitation of God’s grace in the regions of Asia, Caria, Lydia, and Phrygia, through the zeal of the victorious Justinian.
And it flowed abundantly from him through the mediation of our humble self—that is, John of Asia—so that, through the power of the Holy Spirit,
seventy thousand people might become disciples and turn from the error of paganism, the worship of idols, and the revelry of demons to the knowledge of the truth.
And they turned, were sealed, and were baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, renouncing the error of their ancestors.
And they were added to the ranks of the Christians, while the victorious emperor himself generously provided the expenses and baptismal garments and took care of them.
He also gave each of them a one-third gold coin. Thus, when God opened the minds of all these people
and enlightened their understanding with the truth, they themselves, with their own hands, joined us in tearing down their temples and demolishing the ranks of their idols.
They overturned the high places set up everywhere, and cast down their filthy altars, polluted with the foul blood of sacrifices to demons.
And they cut down the countless trees they worshiped, mocking all the error of their ancestors, so that
the sign of the cross of salvation was being set up everywhere among them, and churches of God were being marked out in every place.
And with great zeal and care, on high and rugged mountains, in valleys, and in the other places
from which paganism had been removed, they were being built and established, reaching a total of ninety-six.
And twelve monasteries were established in places from which paganism had been removed, where the name of Christianity had not been heard
from the foundation of the world until that time. Fifty-five churches were built from public funds, while forty-one
the new Christians themselves built at their own expense. Through our humble self, the victorious emperor supplied vessels of silver, linen furnishings,
books, and bronze generously from public funds, gladly and cheerfully. The year 854.
There was an earthquake, and the city of Cyzicus was overturned, and most of it fell. Most of the wall collapsed and fell, and breaches were also opened.
And the rest of it that had not fallen remained unstable, swaying and leaning as though about to fall. And because we happened to pass through it at that time,
we saw the columns of the public buildings leaning and standing on the edge [?] outside [?] beside them [?] people were passing [?].
And so most of the city itself, with cedar timbers,
was being supported and propped up. So too were many other cities. In this same year a great and terrifying star appeared, resembling a lance of fire,
in the evening, in the western sky. A great ray of fire extended upward from it, and it itself also shone brightly.
Small sparks of fire came out of it, so that terror seized everyone who saw it.
The Greeks called it a comet. It continued to rise and remain visible like this for about twenty days.
Afterward, while many were watching for what would happen after that sign, they saw many wars and dryness in the air,
and drought and a shortage of rain, and the sword's assault on the cities. The full extent of these calamities, and the account of them from every quarter,
we cannot record. In the year 855 of Alexander, a great and terrible plague broke out throughout the world,
in the days of Emperor Justinian. For the beginning of this account, then, the blessed prophet Jeremiah would have been very suitable for us,
since he was practiced in raising mournful songs of lamentation over the destruction and ruin of his people.
The account now being written—that is, lamented—would thus have suited him,
as a history of this dreadful and mighty scourge with which the whole world was being struck in our days.
For he would no longer have had to weep and lament over the destruction of just one city, Jerusalem, or over the Jewish people alone, but over cities
in great numbers, which wrath turned into winepresses, trampling and pressing all their inhabitants within them like fine grapes, without mercy.
Over the whole earth, against which the decree went out like a reaper against standing grain, cutting down and casting aside every height, every size, and every rank alike, without reckoning.
Over the corpses that burst open and rotted in the streets, with no one to bury them. Over houses, large and small, beautiful and desirable,
which suddenly became tombs for their inhabitants, where servants and masters suddenly fell together
and mingled their putrid fluids together inside their bedrooms. None of them survived to carry their corpses outside from the interior of the house.
Over others who perished and fell in the streets and became a dreadful, terrifying sight to those who saw them, with their bellies swollen,
their mouths open, disgorging putrid fluid like channels, their eyes [?], and their hands stretched upward,
[?] and rotting, lying in corners and streets, in the porticoes of courtyards, in churches and martyrs' shrines, and everywhere,
with no one to bury them. Over ships at sea, whose sailors wrath suddenly struck, so that they became tombs for those who sailed them
and remained adrift among the waves, carrying their owners' corpses.
Over other ships that reached harbors and were moored by their owners, and remained there, never again to be unmoored by them.
Over the [?] that wailed to one another. Over the bridal chambers of adorned brides,
who suddenly became dead and dreadful corpses within them. Over virgins who were kept in bedrooms, for whom no one could be found
to carry them from their bedrooms to the grave. Over the great roads that lay deserted. Over the paths on which travel ceased.
Over villages whose inhabitants all perished together. Over many other things like these, which surpass the speech and storytelling of all humankind.
Over these things the prophet now had reason to weep and say, “Woe to me!”—not over the ruin of the daughter of my people,
but over the destruction of the whole inhabited world, which was destroyed through its sins, and over the entire earth in its fullness, laid waste [?] and emptied of its inhabitants.
He could, I think, have used words from the prophecies of his fellow prophets
and brought them forward to say to the remnant left among humanity, “Dance in mourning and wail, you ministers of my God!”
Not merely because fine flour and the drink offering had ceased from the house of your God, but because wrath brought on by sins
had suddenly made God’s holy house like a tomb for dead bodies, and it stank with dead bodies instead of living worshipers.
He would also have repeated this saying: “Let the earth sit in mourning, and let all its inhabitants lament.” Nor would it have been far from the mark
to say, “Call the mourning women and the women who dance in mourning, so that together they may mourn”—not over a single corpse, or a single people, or an only child,
or a young husband snatched away by death, but over nations and kingdoms, over territories and regions,
and over fortified cities that were shut up, whose inhabitants groaned over the rotting corpses within them.
Now, when I, wretched as I am, wished to bring these things into the historical record, my thoughts were gripped by great confusion. And because of the many things and the horror,
one thing I considered was that all mouths and tongues were inadequate to recount it. And again, even if people could be found who would record a little out of the vast amount,
what benefit would there be in this, when the whole world has tottered and reached dissolution, and the span of the ages has been shortened?
And for whom would anyone write? Then I thought that it was right to make known a little out of the vast amount concerning our chastisement to those who come after us,
and to hand it down to them through our writings, even if they too are knocking with us at the door of the end. Perhaps they will fear and tremble—
