this remnant of the world that arises after us—at the terrible rod with which we were scourged because of our offenses.
Through the chastisement of us wretched people, they may gain wisdom and be delivered from wrath here and from the torment to come.
But for us, whom this time has overtaken, it is time to weep with the prophet and say, “Death has climbed through our windows, entered our gates, and laid waste our streets.”
Perhaps the eye of prophecy was looking at these present events when it prophesied these things about us, especially since this was seen in actual events:
“My sword will come out of its sheath and destroy the righteous along with the sinner.” This is indeed what happened: at a single command,
they became one winepress, and [?] were torn apart and eaten by dogs, exposed and trampled amid great panic.
And then, when the scourge had run its course, it began to cross the sea toward Palestine and the land of Jerusalem.
Moreover, certain terrifying apparitions were seen by people at sea as this pestilence passed from place to place.
Many people saw apparitions of bronze boats, with figures sitting in them in the likeness
of human beings whose heads had been cut off, holding poles that were also made of bronze. In this way they traveled over the sea and were seen going wherever they were headed.
Thus these apparitions appeared everywhere, especially at night, terrifyingly, like gleaming bronze.
They also appeared in the form of fire. They appeared as black men without heads, sitting in boats of [?].
They moved swiftly over the sea, so that the very sight of them almost killed those who saw them.
These, then, were seen sailing toward Gaza, Ashkelon, and Palestine. And along with their appearance, their [?] was there.
From then on, things far worse than those previously related about the city of Alexandria were happening throughout Palestine,
so that villages and cities were left entirely without inhabitants. There was also another sign of God's warning and righteous judgment.
For the wealth of many people was thus left unguarded: gold, silver, and other possessions, the pearls of this world.
The doors stood open, the treasuries were abandoned, and the houses were full of every possession and everything desirable in this world.
If anyone happened to covet these things and took and gathered something to possess for himself, thinking he would escape, judgment overtook him that very day.
For example, they used to tell of a certain city on the border of Egypt that had perished completely, with only seven men left in the whole city,
along with one little boy, ten years old. When these people gathered together, they went around the entire city and saw
that no one in it was alive except themselves, and that the remaining corpses were swollen and jumbled together.
When these people had remained alive for one day, then two, and finally five, they took counsel together, saying,
“Perhaps we will escape. But since it is easy for us now, come, let us enter the great houses and gather gold, silver, and whatever is in them for ourselves.
Let us fill one house. Perhaps we will live, and it will be ours.” These men, then—as people said, this truly happened—
dared to enter these houses, which had been wealthy but were now empty of inhabitants. They gathered things for three days and filled one large house with gold and silver alone.
On the third day they carried their loads inside, and wrath overtook them there, inside the house.
Suddenly they fell, and all of them perished in a single hour on top of what they had gathered, except for that little boy.
Thus that boy was left alone. When he saw that all these men had died,
and that there were no longer any living people in the entire city, he decided to leave and move outside the city.
When he came to the city gate, something in the form of a man seized him, turned him back, and set him down at the door of the house filled with what they had gathered.
It did this to him many times. Now a certain rich man, they said, had gone out to his estate some time before. When he heard that the city had been devastated,
he was afraid and remained outside, saying, “Perhaps God will have mercy on me and leave me alive.”
This man, they said, continued in prayer, repentance, and supplication. Although he had heard that the entire city had utterly perished,
after some days he could not refrain from sending someone to find out about his household and about the entire city.
He sent a steward with some of his other servants, saying, “Come now, go,
and find out the truth about what has happened to my household and to the whole city.” So these men
came to the city, entered it, and went around it. They found no one at all alive except that boy, who was sitting and weeping, nearly dying from weeping.
When they found him, they asked him, “Why are you sitting here? Why did you not flee?” Then he told them everything that had happened,
about those seven men, everything they had gathered, and what had happened to them. He also showed them their corpses
and what they had gathered. When that steward saw the great quantity of gold, his hour lured him too, and he said to the young men with him,
“Let us carry away some of this gold.” But they were afraid and said, “We will not touch it. Do as you please.”
But he went in and loaded as much of that gold as he could onto his pack animal. He also took that boy with him, and they set out to leave.
When he reached the city gate, someone in human form ran after him, seized him, and bound both him and that boy.
He made them double over. When the steward was seized, he thought, “These things are happening because of this gold.”
The others were shouting to him, “Go back and put it in its place! Perhaps you will be released.”
Then he and that boy returned to the house. When they entered, both of them perished. The rest fled and escaped in this way.
They also tell of another city in the territory of Palestine, where, at that same time, demons appeared to the inhabitants in the likeness of angels.
They deceived them, telling them to hurry to worship a certain bronze statue.
At that time it had been left standing like the other bronze statues found in cities. Formerly, however, it had been an idol of the pagans, and
it also had a name. Even then it was still secretly worshipped by the few who held to paganism.
The demons made the entire city, without exception, worship this statue, saying, “If you act promptly and worship such-and-such a statue,
death will not enter this city.” So those wretched people,
in whom the words spoken in the psalm were fulfilled—“They reeled and staggered like drunkards, and all their wisdom was lost”—
were likewise drunk, and their skills were lost and rendered useless by the onslaught of wrath. Through their error they were led to this,
supposing that they would escape death, not knowing the second death that would result from it. They all fell down and worshipped that statue.
But so that divine power might be revealed against their error, while they were gathered before that statue, suddenly—so that others too might not be cast into such error—
something like a whirlwind suddenly entered that statue and lifted it up about a thousand human heights, as far upward as the eye could see.
It hurled it down violently from that great height onto the ground. It was crushed and poured out like water over the ground, and could no longer be found.
The sword of death fell upon them. By evening, not a living soul was found in that city.
But as it is written in the prophet, “They all perished because they did not invoke the name of the Lord.”
This happened to these people too. An account of both, concerning the bitter suffering, and of the rest of the cities in all the regions.
As for the rest of the cities and regions of Palestine, and the whole north, the south, and the east, as far as the Red Sea,
we cannot recount these things. It was not only what had happened in Egypt and Alexandria, but many times as much.
In the region of the imperial city, these things were still being received as reports, while they were still far away.
Yet we ourselves were there at the time when the plague was still in Palestine.
We went down from Palestine to Mesopotamia at the height of its severity. Then we turned and went back up, since the punishment had reached there too.
And to the remaining regions of Cilicia, Mysia, Syria, Iconium, Bithynia, and Asia,
and [?] and Cappadocia: through these too we traveled from Syria, amid the same upheaval and severity of the plague, as far as the imperial city itself.
Day after day, we too, along with everyone else, were knocking at the door of the grave. When evening came, we thought that death would strike us during the night.
And if morning came again, our faces were turned toward the grave all day long.
In these regions we saw villages devastated and desolate, and corpses lying on the ground with no one to gather them.
Others, who survived as a small remnant, were carrying them away, throwing them down, and returning,
like stones that someone drags away and throws down, then comes back to carry more, throws them down again with difficulty, and returns to carry more, dragging them like this all day long.
Others stood joyfully digging graves for themselves. Others had completely disappeared, leaving their houses empty of inhabitants.
The stations along the roads were filled with darkness and desolation, and it was terrifying to enter or leave them. Livestock was abandoned and wandering,
with no one to gather it, scattered over the mountains: flocks of sheep and goats, and herds of cattle and pigs, which had become like the other
wild animals, forgetting peaceful life and the human voice that had guided them.
Lands were full and rich with every kind of fruit, which was dropping and falling with no one to gather it. Fields were abundant with grain,
standing throughout all the regions through which we traveled, from Syria to Thrace, white and standing ripe, with no one to reap and bring in the harvest.
The time for harvesting the vineyards had come and gone. The winter season was severe; their leaves had fallen, but their fruit remained,
hanging on their vines, with no one to gather and press it. As for that sight, so full of anguish, bitter to look upon and overwhelming in its mourning,
which met us day after day on our journey, how could anyone describe it, or what could we write, except that whoever saw it would say with the prophet,
“Let the earth sit in mourning, and let all its inhabitants lament”? And not only this, but also that other saying:
“The earth lamented and sat in mourning. The world lamented, sat, and mourned; the heights of the earth lamented,” and the rest.
At the sight of these things, we also had reason to remember what had been spoken long before through the blessed prophet.
He prophesied and said: “The earth will be utterly devastated; the earth will be utterly plundered; the earth will be shaken.
The earth will stagger violently; the earth will tremble violently and sway like a hut. Its wickedness will weigh heavily upon it, and it will again become fuel for the fire,
like a terebinth and like an oak that has fallen from its base.” All these things were completely fulfilled in our days, not over a long period,
but in a short time. For the earthquakes in the year before this year of the plague, and the
great tremors that occurred—these indescribable events happened five times, in the very city where we were. They were not slight tremors that came and passed in the blink of an eye,
but continued for a long time, until the hope of life was vanishing and being cut off from all flesh.
There seemed to be no possibility of survival after the onslaught of each of these earthquakes, and only then did they subside. This was the shaking of the earth written about in the prophecy.
In the third year before this year of the plague, and also in the fourth, and right up to this year, the whole land of the West was shaken.
Wars grew fiercer and more intense in the city of Rome and in [?], farther inland, and also in Carthage, in the land of Africa.
There were also countless powerful nations whom this empire opposed. Some of them, with God's help, were subdued by this empire,
namely Rome and Africa, with their territories and kingdoms. Their kings too were led away and brought to this city.
Until the end of their lives we saw them living in subjection, like the rest of the individual rulers, together with the captives from their countries.
But these barbarian nations, who, as it is written, rose up from the ends of the earth, grew strong and conquered, devastated, burned, and plundered.
They even came right up to the wall of the city while we were inside it, and took captives from its suburbs and from its inhabitants.
This happened not just for one year, but for three years in succession. Because of their strength, no one could stand against them.
They held this empire in such contempt that they sent messengers saying, “Prepare your palace for us,
for we are coming there.” Terror fell upon the emperor and the nobles, and from then on the palace gates were secured with iron and fortified,
as though the whole city had been conquered by them and they were concerned to fortify only the palace.
Such a calamity had neither occurred nor been heard of since this city was built.
So great was their fear of them that they ordered all the trees around the city to be destroyed for a distance of a hundred cubits.
Because it is the imperial city, all its affairs had until then been managed confidently, without apprehension.
Between the wall and the outer wall on the western side—for only there was there a stone wall, while the rest was sea—
they had cultivated large, sturdy cedar and cypress trees, and walnut trees—large, sturdy cedar and cypress trees, and walnut and fig trees—
as well as vineyards and gardens, which had been there for a hundred years. Now all of them were being destroyed and cut down.
When people could not move them from their places because of their bulk.

And so that destruction of the trees struck everyone with terror, as everyone was bewildered and said, “If they had not realized that it had caused harm, they would not have come to these things either.”
Again, these answer and press their case in this way, while those are confidently arrayed against them.
Then the spirit of the east was also stirred up—that is, the kingdom of Persia. It also grew strong and made preparations with all the mighty nations of the whole east.
All the kings of the eastern lands also mobilized. They headed toward this land of the Romans, conquered it, and passed through,
and brought it into subjection as far as the great city of Antioch [?]. They surrounded this city, and because it ventured to fight against him,
he defeated it, devastated it, conquered it, burned it, took its people captive, and uprooted it down to its very foundations.
He even took away the marble slabs that had covered the walls and doorways. They led its entire population into captivity, and likewise those of the other cities.
And he returned to his country, like someone who [?]. Why should I now recount these past events [?] what the course of the narrative is?
But so that we may understand the words of prophecy, which cry out in our ears every day like trumpets, though we are unwilling to listen:
how, one after another, they are all now showing us through actual events the force of their interpretations, and not at a distance.
But this calamity, which surpasses them all and is more grievous than them all—this one came and swallowed and overshadowed them all.
Nothing else could be recognized in it except itself alone, like those ugly cows that were shown to Pharaoh.
After they swallowed the good cows, only their ugliness was apparent. But this punishment did not swallow up only the good things;
it also overshadowed and swallowed up the evils that preceded it, and because of its own enormity,
it was as though the scourging before it had not even hurt those being scourged. Now, then, let us return to the narrative and to the sequence
of the afflictions that came upon us because of our sins. Leaving other things aside from now on, with sighs and bitter mourning
let us recount what happened to the city of kings. For these events deserve mourning more than anything else,
not only from us wretched people, but, if it were possible, heaven and earth should mourn over them.
Even these would still be far too small to provide the full measure of mourning they deserve. Who, then, my brothers, can recount that appalling and bitter spectacle?
Who could hear about the things that happened there without sobs bursting from his heart and melting all his limbs, as wax melts before fire?
Let alone those who looked with their own eyes upon that spectacle of misery, destruction, and sighs. Nothing else could be said of them
except the prophet’s words. Everyone who saw these things would ask as he asked, saying, “Who will give my head water and my eyes fountains of tears?
Then I would weep day and night without ceasing over the ruin and destruction of Babylon the Great,” which until now had roared in its royal power.
Now, look: its royal power is brought low and overthrown, and the angel of wrath alone has been made king and destroyer over all its inhabitants.
When, then, this chastisement overtook the city—a chastisement in which the riches of God’s kindness and goodness were truly visible, and which, although it was very terrifying, harsh, and fierce,
we ought not to call merely a sign of threat and wrath, but also a sign of mercy,
and also a call to repentance. Now the rod was being wielded with such patience and gentleness, until that very place
was reached. It was like a king preparing to go out to battle, who gives orders to the commanders of his armies, saying,
“Get yourselves ready, prepare your weapons, and see to your provisions, for you are marching with me to battle on such-and-such a day.”
And it was as though he were sending written messages to the cities in his territories: “Look, I am coming. Be ready, for once I arrive there will be no delay.”
In this way, this rod of God’s tender mercies, through its [?], like many messengers, was sending word from one region to [?],
and from city to city and to every place, saying, as it were, “Turn back, repent, and plead for forgiveness for your sins.
Prepare for yourselves provisions of righteousness from your possessions, for look, I am coming. I will make your [?] superfluous to you.”
God’s providential ordering makes this clear: it was as though these messages were being sent everywhere beforehand.
Only then would the rod reach that place, entering a city or a village.
It would fall upon it like a reaper, vigorously and swiftly, and upon the other settlements around it, a mile, two miles, or three miles away.
Until it had completed what it had been commanded to do in that place, it would not move on or enter the neighboring place. In this way it would seize and winnow,
slowly. This is what happened to this city: for a year or two it had been receiving the warning of what was happening through reports from everywhere.
Then it overtook the city itself. Here too, grace was actively at work on its behalf, urging it onward, and this was indeed being accomplished here in certain individuals.

It was like what happened in the days of Noah. When that blessed man, together with his household, heard the news of the threats and destruction, he was afraid and did not disregard it. Instead, he took care and built himself
an ark, which preserved his own life and everything he had—preserved his own life and everything he had. So, following the example of this blessed man,
many people in this time also managed, within a few days, to build themselves ships of charitable giving, to carry them across that flood of flame.
Others did so through sorrowful tears together with charitable giving, and also by distributing their possessions to the needy; others through mourning and humility,
through keeping vigil and practicing abstinence, and through cries of sorrow directed to God. In this way many who feared and trembled managed to purchase the kingdom for themselves.
Then the onslaught overtook them. But those who showed contempt and would not be persuaded to send their belongings ahead of them left them to others.
They themselves were snatched away from their possessions, while the possessions remained. Both these things happened to many people, especially in this city.
Chapter Four. A continuation of the account: how, when the pestilence reached the city of [?],
grace reached the poor first, to gather them in and bury them honorably, without the turmoil of wrath.
For when the rod approached this city, it first began vigorously among the ranks of the poor who lay in the streets.
On some days five thousand of them were carried out, on others seven thousand, on others twelve thousand, and as many as sixteen thousand in a day.
For it was still only the beginning. Men stood at the harbors, the crossings, and the gates, keeping count of them.
Thus they perished. With great diligence they were shrouded and buried, with everyone clothing them and accompanying their funerals, and [?]. And thus
they came to an end, with only a small number remaining. If anyone wanted to count just those who died in the streets,
although they were indeed counted, no fewer than three hundred thousand were carried out of the streets. Those who were counting,
when they reached two hundred and thirty thousand, saw that they were beyond counting and gave up. From then on they were carried out without being counted.
Once, then, the lowly had been released, those who had people to shroud and bury them in the great burial of the multitudes,
the destroyer stretched out his hand against the rulers of the world and those renowned for exercising earthly sovereignty,
those great in wealth and splendid in their authority. From this point onward, the common people together with the rulers
could be seen suddenly struck down and falling under one great and bitter blow, besides the lowly. And not only those who died,
but also those who escaped immediate death were struck in their groins, with that painful condition of swellings, as it is translated in our own Syriac language.
They, however, [?] called it “boubones.” It struck slaves and masters alike,
[rulers] and common people, without showing favoritism, as they lay opposite one another, groaning.
And it was ordained by God's decree of judgment that human beings should be astonished and remain in wonder
at his righteous judgments, which human beings can neither understand nor measure, as it is written: “Your judgments are like the great deep.”
We also saw that this great plague showed its power among the animals, not only the tame ones,
but also the wild ones, and even the creatures that crawl on the earth. For one could see livestock
and dogs and other animals, even mice, whose groins were swollen, lying dead.
Likewise, wild animals were found struck down by that same decree of judgment, lying dead.
This dreadful sign, then, suddenly overtook the people of this city after the release of the poor.
Another sign appeared as follows, persisting among those who were being snatched away and those who lingered, awaiting either death or life.
Three marks would appear in the middle of a person's palm, resembling black pustules, though they did not protrude outward,
but were deep within, like three drops of blood deep beneath the surface. Wherever these appeared, the end came with them.
The person had only an hour or two left, or perhaps as much as a day. These things happened to many.
Others, however, experienced neither this nor that: while looking at one another and talking, they would sway and fall.
Whether in the streets, in houses, in harbors, on ships, in churches, or anywhere else.
One person would be sitting at his trade, holding his tools in his hands and working, when it reached him and his life departed.
Others would enter the baths for their customary bath, but before they had time to take off their clothes, they fell down and died.
Another would go out to the marketplace to buy what he needed. While they stood talking or counting their small change,
death would suddenly strike down the buyer here and the seller there. The merchandise remained in the [?] together with its price, and there was neither
buyer nor seller to pick it up. In every way everything ceased and was ruined, and it all turned to mourning and lamentation.
In short, everything stopped, as everyone's hands grew slack, and buying and selling ceased.

The shops containing every kind of indescribable worldly wealth, and the great money-changing businesses, stopped operating. The whole city had already come to a standstill, as though it had perished,
so that its food supplies also ran out, and there was no one to get up and attend to his work,
until food disappeared from the marketplaces. There was great distress, especially among the people who lay prostrate under the burden of illness.
Thus, if a few people could be found who persevered and baked something for the marketplace, for something worth a single follis, if they wished,
they would charge a dinar. In this way everything stopped and came to an end. The one thing more pressing than anything else was this:
that everyone still alive should carry the corpses out of his house, while the remaining bodies were also cleared from the streets and taken out to the seashore.
The ships hurried along, dumping them everywhere, then returning to take others.
Anyone hearing these things ought to weep and sob for us rather than for those dead people, because of what our eyes were seeing.
Alas, my brothers, for that bitter sight! Alas for those terrible scenes of lamentation at that time, when someone stood on the seashore
and saw the biers colliding with one another! Those carrying them would return and throw two or three bodies onto the ground,
then go back again to bring more. Others carried bodies on planks and on poles, bringing them and piling them on top
of one another. Others, because the bodies had decayed and begun to putrefy, sewed them up in pieces of cloth and carried them on poles.
They came and threw them down, with putrid fluid flowing from them, then went back again to bring more. Others stood on the seashore,
dragging them and throwing them down into the ships, piling up heaps of two or three thousand, or five thousand,
and still more beyond counting, like the debris carried down great rivers, all along the seashore. Putrid fluid flowed down and poured into the sea.
With what tears could I weep at that time, my beloved, as I stood looking at those heaps, full of unspeakable horrors and terrors?
What sobs could have sufficed for me? What lamentations? What heartbreak? What mourning? What [?] and thoughts could have sufficed for the suffering of that time,
when human beings lay thrown into great heaps, bursting open on top of one another, their bellies rotting and their intestines flowing like streams down into the sea?
For how could the heart of someone who saw these things fail to melt within him at the sight of them, and the rest of his limbs dissolve along with it while he was still alive,
from grief, bitter weeping, and the shuddering of calamity, when he saw the white hair of old men who had spent all their days pursuing the vanity of the world,
who had toiled and amassed possessions, and had expected a splendid and honorable burial from their heirs, lying on the ground, their white hair shamefully befouled with their heirs’ filth?
And the beautiful young women and virgins who had looked forward to joyful bridal chambers
and garments with costly ornaments, who lay exposed and abandoned, befouled with the mire of other dead bodies,
and presented a miserable and bitter sight. It was not in a grave, but in [?] and in the harbors that
their corpses were rolled about like the carcasses of dogs. Beloved babies lay jumbled together and abandoned,
and those who packed them into boats would seize them and fling them away from a distance, trembling greatly.
Handsome, cheerful young men were heaped up and packed together, on the backs of their heads, beneath one another, and made into a pile.
Freeborn, chaste women, who had lived modestly and honorably and remained in their private chambers, lay swollen and exposed, with their mouths gaping,
heaped up in pitiful heaps. People of every age were packed together; people of every stature were bent over and thrown down in a single winepress of wrath.
People of every rank were crushed down upon one another like animals, not like human beings. And what could we say about these things,
except to cry out for mercy and say, “Your judgments are just, Lord, for you did not wish these things to happen to the creatures you formed.
Rather, the abundance of injustice and our straying from your commandments and your will have delivered us over to these things.” And let us repeat our cry and say with the prophet,
“Lord, in your wrath remember your mercy. For your name’s sake, Lord, have pity on your people, and do not neglect your inheritance.”
So, when those who carried the bodies had dwindled in number, the whole city—that city mighty through the ages, splendid in its dominion and abounding in wealth—
[suddenly became] a gloomy, stinking grave for its inhabitants, so that [there were no longer even graves available].
And this was harder than everything else: those [from the city, in distress,] were gathered up and piled into boats,
and [from this side to the opposite shore] they were thrown like dung upon the ground, with no one [to gather them up. Even the imperial court] sat
in mourning. As it is written, they had learned [that the hands of the people] who carried out the corpses had grown weak,
because they too had dwindled [and become exhausted. The city] stank with corpses, so that there were neither biers [nor people to dig graves].
Corpses lay in heaps in the streets. When [the merciful] emperor, [in whose days] these things happened, learned of this,
he stirred himself to zealous action and took the matter to heart. He gave orders, and six hundred biers were provided.
He appointed one of his referendaries, whose name was Theodore, a man who was himself zealous for good works,
and instructed him to take and distribute as much gold as was needed, to oversee these matters, and to encourage people with large gifts so that they would not neglect the work.
They were to dig large pits, pile the bodies into them, and fill them with corpses. This man went out energetically.
He crossed northward to the district called Sycae and went up a hill above the city.
He brought many men, gave them a great deal of gold, and had very large pits dug.
Seventy thousand were placed in each of them. He stationed men there to lower them, take turns, and pile them up.
They packed them in rows, one above another, as someone might pack grain into a stack. He also stationed men carrying gold beside the pits.
They encouraged the laborers and the ordinary people with gifts to carry the bodies up. He would give five or six denarii,
and even as much as seven or ten, for each load. He also went around the city, urging people on and bringing the bodies out.
He had received orders to fill every tomb he could find, whoever owned it. Thus, through this man's energetic efforts, the city was gradually
being cleared of corpses. Anyone who had many corpses would go and inform him, and he would have them brought out.
While this man was going around the city, a prominent man from among our people was also seen to be very active in these matters.
This man took notice of him and brought him along. From then on, he put him in charge of distributing gifts and providing care alongside him.
As they went around, they came upon a house that was completely shut up and stinking. People shuddered at its smell.
They went in and found about twenty people in it, dead and rotting, with worms crawling over them.
Overcome with anguish, they brought men and, by offering large gifts, had them gather the bodies with sickles and carry them in baskets.
They brought them out. Other households were found in which everyone was dead, though there were infants still alive and crying.
There were also other women who were dead, with [?] that had come out completely.
In other houses, it happened that one remained out of hundreds: a great man, each of whom used to be attended by a multitude of slaves,
who was left entirely alone; or perhaps he was left with a few; or perhaps neither he nor anyone belonging to him remained.
There were also those who had previously been attended by such a multitude of slaves, but now got up and attended to themselves
and to the sick in their houses. The palace was shut, and mourning hung over it, while these kings, with their tens of thousands and thousands
of those among them who held authority, and all the rest of the great senate, were being stripped and emptied every day.
They were suffering and had fallen into the same low condition as everyone else, and only a small number of people attended them.
This was in addition to the other things that people cannot possibly describe, as the sword fell and uprooted countless multitudes of people.
From then on, these things were happening many times over to people everywhere, and also to the great city of Alexandria.
By then people's hearts had also grown numb, and there was no longer any weeping or mourning dances.
But people were dazed, like those stupefied by wine alone; they were stricken in their hearts and fell silent. Only this was necessary:
to drag the corpses outside and throw them away. People would fasten iron hooks onto the dead, as onto a dead animal, and drag them out and throw them away.
They were dazed and bewildered. As Scripture says, “The burial of a donkey”—so it happened to everyone here as well.
From then on, just as in Alexandria, no one went outside the gate without a written label hanging around his neck or on his arm. Chapter Five.
A continuation of the sorrowful account: concerning wills and inheritances. As for wills and inheritances, there was no one to speak about them.
If anyone happened to pursue such matters in a worldly manner, or appointed heirs, they would quickly die before those leaving them the inheritance.
Likewise, if anyone, poor or rich, or whoever he might be, came upon an open treasury, a large shop, or any portion of it,
and was tempted by the hope that perhaps he would survive and acquire possessions, and reached out his hand and took something, immediately, as though the angel of death were standing behind him,
he would faint and collapse. Because of this, even if someone wished to distribute his gifts among the needy, they would not look at him or accept anything from him.
Those who did accept anything perished. For there were some needy people who were still alive, and they thought, “Perhaps we will survive.
If someone gives us something, let us ask for and accept charity. After all, we are not entering anyone’s house and taking anything belonging to those who have died.
We will only ask for charity.” So they went to a large silversmith’s shop.
They found an old man sitting at its entrance; all his people had perished. They approached and said to him, “Please grant us a blessing.
Perhaps we will live and remember you.” He said to them, “Look, my children, the whole shop is before you. Go in, and whatever you desire,
pick it up and take it out. Do not be afraid. Take as much as your hands can carry, and go in peace.”
For if someone said that there were only a thousand pounds of gold and silver in that shop, he would still have said very little.
So these men went in, having been given permission. They looked and marveled, and set their eyes on great quantities, especially of gold.
They loaded themselves up and turned to leave. When one crossed the threshold and the other came to go out, it was as though a sword passed between them and struck them both down,
one here and the other there. They fainted, fell, and breathed their last, and their [?] was scattered. And so a great terror
fell upon those who remained. From then on, gold and silver, and indeed all worldly possessions, became worthless in everyone’s eyes.
A single terrifying, relentless onslaught was seizing everyone. Because of this, no one any longer put his trust in gold or in any other wealth.
Instead, everyone’s face was turned toward the grave, ready for it. Those who remained healthy carried corpses and bore them away.
Some did so for high wages paid by others, some for a little, treating the payment as unimportant, and some made a point of accepting nothing at all.
Those who were healthy and greedy for gold had days when, if they wished,
they could collect as much as a pound of gold, or as much as a hundred denarii, for themselves, since they could charge whatever they pleased.
Those who had no fear of God took things in this way. Two of them were strong young men, and these carried their loads vigorously.
They demanded payment greedily and without fear. In the end they kept demanding payment from the royal referendary for one day, two days, and three.
When he took account of how much they had taken from him alone, he said to them, “Go, my children. You have enough.
Why are you contending like this? Go and [?] what you have taken. Do not set a bad example for others.”
But they told him, “We will not stop.” He did not force them, but said to them, “You know best.”
Those unfortunate men ran off, took up their loads, and came to the pits where the corpses were being piled up. When they reached that place, both of them fainted and fell.
They died suddenly. When that man saw this, he wept over them, saying, “Woe to you, greed of Adam!
This very hour has shut your mouth!” Then he ordered one of his servants, “Go over and see whether they have on them what they collected.
Take it and give it to others who will go and carry bodies in return for it. As for these men, let them go down headfirst with the rest.” Again, three others.
They collected four hundred and fifty denarii. Finally they said to one another, “We have enough. Let us take this and leave this city.”
They went to divide it among themselves. As they sat, they took it out and counted it on a marble slab: one hundred and fifty denarii for each of them.
When their shares had been separated, just as each was about to reach out his hand and take his earnings, each of them fainted where he was, and they fell down and died.
Thus each man's earnings were found before him, divided and laid out, while their owner lay fallen opposite them.
This, then, was the instruction given to the angel appointed over that scourge: to fight against human beings
until they despised all the possessions of this people—if not willingly, then unwillingly.
Thus, whenever anyone remained rebellious in his thinking and still coveted worldly things, he quickly deprived him of his life as well.
And so this city, once so populous, became increasingly ruined and deserted day by day.
What more is there to say about those pits in which people were piled up and packed down? Men stood below, as though in a deep abyss,
and others stood above. Those above dragged the bodies and threw them down like stones thrown into some chasm, while those below caught them and piled them up on top of
one another, alternating one row this way and another that way, as men and women were packed down.
Young men and children were stamped into the gaps between them, trampled underfoot, and crushed like spoiled grapes.
In this way they were also thrown headfirst from above, coming down and breaking apart below:
free men and free women, old men and old women, young men and virgins, young women and children.
How could anyone speak or tell of that hideous pit? Who could look upon that burial and still have his soul remain in his body,
without its departing amid bitter groans? How powerfully wickedness can destroy the children of Adam!
How, and with what [voices], with what dirges, and with what dances and laments would he dance—
the one who remained alive and watched that winepress of destruction, ruin, and wrath, while those doing the trampling stood there, and whenever a man or woman was laid down,
or a young man or a baby, they trampled them underfoot to flatten them and make room for the rest. The one being trampled went down and sank into the sludge of those underneath,
sometimes for five or even ten days, and only then reached that basin of destruction.
What mind could bear and endure the suffering of those gray-haired elders? They were not even buried with a donkey’s burial, as it is written.
Who would not be seized by anguish of heart, trembling, and grief as he stood watching the lovely young men, like flowers,
who were seized by their hair and dragged along, then thrown from that height into the depths of the lowest Sheol,
falling with their bellies bursting open, while the sight of their youthful bodies lay exposed below, amid great horror and grief
that was bitter and beyond consolation? How could an eye endure seeing these heaps of children and babies,
piled in heap upon heap like dung on the face of the earth? Who would not weep for us who witnessed it more than for the dead? To what a spectacle our sins have brought us!
Even if the wise should afterward reproach us for our lack of understanding, it is fitting for us, my brothers, at the sight of these things,
to raise dirges and laments for ourselves, rather than for these people, and say: “Woe to you, our eyes! What are you seeing?
Woe to you, our bitter lives! What destruction you have experienced, falling upon your own flesh while your eyes looked on!”
It would have been far more [?] for us who witnessed it to have been among those who drank the cup of wrath, who completed their journey without experiencing this destruction,
rather than to have been witnesses to these things, which darken the heart along with the eyes, the mind, and the understanding.
With what words, or with what mouths and tongues, what voice and speech, could anyone adequately recount these things?
And how am I, wretched as I am, who wished to relate these things, not like someone who has fallen into the depths of the sea and is battered this way and that by the waves,
unable to touch bottom and nowhere near reaching a harbor, but driven and tossed among harsh and mighty waves,
and now close to drowning and destruction? What more is there to say or relate about these unspeakable events,
which happened in this city more than anywhere else, to the point that even the wise lost their understanding, and the skills of the skillful, as it is written, were undone and rendered useless?
No one of sound mind could any longer readily be found. Rather, as the saying
is written, “They reeled and staggered like drunken men, and all their wisdom perished.” This, then, is what happened.
Like people drunk on [?], so each person [?] spoke with his companion, bewildered and babbling,
while people were also easily led into foolish thinking through the intoxication of chastisement—as indeed happened in this city.
And when the demons wished to lead people astray and mock their madness, a report from someone or other spread among those who were still alive.
For if, they said, jars were thrown from the windows of the upper dwellings into the street and smashed below, death would flee from the city.
And when foolish women in one neighborhood [?] gave their minds over to this foolishness and threw jars [?], word spread from one neighborhood to another throughout the whole city.
And everyone gave themselves over to this delusion, so that for three days none of the people who remained could be found in the streets.
For anyone who had escaped death, however many there were, was busy inside the house trying to drive death away by smashing jars.
Again, he acted through some of the demons who habitually [?] among people. And when those who had foolishly smashed jars grew weary,
having lost the hope their delusion had given them, as day by day they continued toward utter destruction, the demons appeared to them,
seeking to mock the appearance of godliness—that is, the appearance of tonsured men, monks and clerics. And from then on,
wherever a monk or a cleric appeared, they would howl and flee from him, thinking that he was the death that was destroying them.
Thus this delusion spread: that death came in the form of tonsured men. It particularly afflicted the city's simple people and common folk.
Consequently, someone wearing this habit could scarcely appear in the street: when people saw him, they would fall over one another,
fleeing, rushing away, and shouting, “Where are you coming? We belong to the Mother of God! We belong to such-and-such a martyr! We belong to such-and-such an apostle!”
Even afterward, this delusion persisted among a few people until the end of two years.
Whenever they saw a monk or a cleric, they would shout, “We belong to the Mother of God!”
By then, only a very small number of people could be seen in this great, world-ruling city, out of its countless tens of thousands and thousands.
These things, then, are for a remembrance of the mourning and afflictions that took place before our eyes. From the outset we began with that outline recalling them,
and, recounting them in sequence, we recorded them one after another at the end of three years afterward.
While these same afflictions still held sway in the eastern regions and had not yet ended, we left this account as a remembrance for those who would come afterward,
so that, when they hear of the chastisement of us foolish people who provoke God's anger, and of the [?] judgment for our sins, they may restrain themselves, as it is written,
and cease provoking the one for whom everything is easy to do, and repent and seek mercy at all times,
lest this chastisement be sent upon them too. Here ends the account of the sudden plague, as written by the holy John of Asia.
Also, which patriarchs were recognized at this time. In Antioch, Ephraim son of Appianus, from Amida, was recognized.
For Alexandria, the patriarch Zoilus; for Rome, Agapetus; for Constantinople, Menas; for Jerusalem, Macarius [?].
The orthodox and persecuted were these: Theodosius, patriarch of Alexandria; Sergius, patriarch of Antioch;
Anthimus, patriarch of Constantinople; Theosebius of Ephesus; Thomas of Damascus; Jacob of Edessa, from the monastery of Phasilta;
and Theodore of Hira of Naaman. The kings recognized were these: Khosrow, king of the Persians; Justinian, emperor of the Romans.
Harith son of Jabalah, king of the Arabs, and a Christian. Abraham, king of the Himyarites, and a believer. Andug, king of the Ethiopians,
and a Christian [?]. Ahudemmeh, catholicos in Persia and martyr, is mentioned, as is John, catholicos of Armenia.
Eunomius, bishop of Amida. John of Pergamum. Photius of Smyrna. Sergius, bishop of Harran. John, bishop of Qenneshre.
John, bishop of Callinicum. John, bishop of Asia, who himself wrote these things. The priest of the island of Chios.
John and Bar Sahde, bishops in Persia, are mentioned. Saint Constantine, bishop of Laodicea, is also mentioned.
He fought vigorously against patriarchs, emperors, and bishops, and against the wicked council at Chalcedon.
Although the emperor and his entire senate repeatedly urged him to enter into union, he would not be persuaded. The emperor pronounced his decision against him on
Saturday, saying with many oaths, “On Monday you will not leave here until you do this.” But that holy and great man of God,
strengthened by the power of the Holy Spirit, saw the emperor’s decision, took courage in his Lord, and said, “If Christ acknowledges me,
Monday will not overtake me so that I should see your face.” And so he finished his course on Sunday, in accordance with his own words, the words of that blessed man.

The Lord glorified those who glorify him. When the emperor learned of the saint’s death and saw that it had happened just as he had declared, he trembled and was alarmed, and abated his persecution a little.
At this same time, great distress befell these kingdoms because of the shortage of priests: the Ethiopians, the Himyarites, and the Indians.
Every year they sent envoys with magnificent gifts to Emperor Justinian,
begging him to give them a bishop who did not accept the Council of Chalcedon.
Although they repeatedly pleaded with him, the emperor, because he was fighting in support of the council,
advised and urged them to accept a bishop from the man who upheld the council and occupied the see of Alexandria.
But they insisted that they would not accept anyone from the council’s party, but only someone from those who did not accept the council.
He ordered that this should not be granted to them as they wished. And so they returned empty-handed.
Every year envoys went back and forth from all three of these kingdoms,
until about twenty-five years had passed, more or less, and the priests among these peoples had died out and disappeared.
After exhausting themselves with repeated efforts and being unable to obtain a bishop who did not agree with the council, they too came to the point of going beyond the prescribed order
of the canons and considering how the priests might assemble and place a Gospel book on the head of one of their number: “There,” they said, “he has been made a bishop.”
In this way, as they supposed, they performed the rite of episcopal ordination, though they did not even remain in the rank of laypeople.
For most of them took offense and did not consider this an ordination or accept it. Instead, a great division arose among them.
Thus, because of the lack of a bishop, another heresy arose there too, and the error of the Melchizedekians took hold. They were the ones who brazenly used to say:
that Melchizedek is the Messiah. Thus, from [a single people?], not only would the church be divided, but the kingdom as well.
For this reason it would be divided into two, and wars, divisions, and disputes would persist in these regions for a long time.
Finally, Phantasiasts, followers of Julian and Gaianus, entered all these regions and devastated them.
In the year eight hundred and fifty-eight, famine and pestilence began to rage and spread in the regions of Mesopotamia.
This great and severe pestilence, which occurred throughout the whole land, lasted from the year eight hundred and fifty-five
until the year eight hundred and fifty-eight—that is, three years. From here we will say a little about the wrath
that was sent upon the regions of Mesopotamia. Furthermore, it is good and right
that we also bring into the record of our history the things that happened at this time in Amida, a city of Mesopotamia, together with the other cities.
To begin this history of ours, filled with bitter sufferings, calamities, and terrors like those of the dreadful pestilence, we would now need the blessed, sorrowful prophet Jeremiah,
who was well practiced in sorrowfully raising laments over the cities of his people.
Learning from the prophet ourselves, let us say: “Who would give my head water and my eyes fountains of tears? Then I would weep day and night
without ceasing over the destruction of the daughter of my people.” It is now time for us to say this over the affliction of the city where we were brought up,
namely, the city of Amida, together with the other cities around it, and over the chastisement of upheavals and calamities
that was sent especially upon this tormented city, after all its severe hardships and bitter sufferings,
and the blows of its prolonged persecution, lasting no less than forty years.
Throughout all these afflictions of persecution that it was suffering, it endured the stumbling blocks placed before it by its betrayers,
and, without murmuring, treated the plundering of its possessions as nothing. For the truth of its faith, in a heroic struggle, the whole city together,
small and great alike, was handed over even to a few of its own children who had turned and become its persecutors.
It fought resolutely, mightily, and heroically. In its struggle it was brought not only to trial, but also to the crucifixion of its children
and the burning of its priests. It suffered merciless, bitter tortures of every kind and endured them with thanksgiving.
Throughout this whole period it was also handed over to two savage beasts, one after the other, instead of true shepherds: to the deceitful one and to that man from among the foolish Galatians.
These men were cruel, furious, and savage, thirsting for blood, eager for plunder, and bent on persecution more than all those who had arisen in every region and city.
After all these resolute struggles and heroic battles that it suffered and endured for the orthodox faith, whether because of sins
or as a disciplinary trial, the ordeal of famine was first sent upon it, distressing and bitter,
and upon its entire region, for about eight years. It came little by little, until it reached the point where [?] would seize.
So that scarcely three or four measures of wheat [?] could be found for sale. The fields now lay fallow, because no seed remained.
Even when people who had the means and were wealthy found a little out of a large quantity to sow, the earth hardened over it,
and it did not come up. Or if it happened to sprout and come up, it would suddenly be scorched and dry up.
Thus people were driven into distress, and many fled from region to region and from city to city because of the suffering caused by that bitter and severe famine.
Then again, after eight full years, when God's mercy was revealed toward his creation, and he looked upon its afflictions and suffering,
especially those of the poor, the widows, and the orphans, who had been brought to the point of death, the grass of the field began
to sprout properly. People began bringing seed from other regions and sowing, and it sprouted properly and produced many times what had been sown.
Through divine grace, vegetation began to grow. Everyone rejoiced and, having eaten their fill, gave thanks to the good Giver,
who had not withheld his mercy from his creation or from all those who trusted in him and awaited the hope he offered.
Then again, in the year designated in Greek as [?], which was the year eight hundred and seventy-one of Alexander the Macedonian,
along with the fearful chastisements and terrible signs that were continually appearing everywhere, in heaven and on earth, suddenly, at this very time described above,
the ordeal of another fearful, dreadful, and disgraceful plague was sent upon the city of Amida: madness, derangement, and demonic possession.
Along with these came an evil delusion. At first, as though through the action of rebellious demons, bewilderment and terror would suddenly fall upon many people,
as a false rumor spread among them: “Look! The king of the Persians is entering the city with his entire army! He is destroying the whole city!”
As a result, people fled and left the city in a great rush, scattering in every direction and toward every quarter.
They spread the news, terrified others, and fled, making everyone they encountered flee as well,
whether on the roads, in the villages, or in all the neighboring cities—wherever they passed through.
Thus panic and confusion arose in all the regions and cities through which they passed, as they spread the news and insisted that Amida had been

conquered by the Persians, taken captive, and [?]. “You must flee!” they said. And so the inhabitants of the regions suddenly went into exile, and great confusion and destruction prevailed everywhere for many days,
until the ordeal that had overtaken those wretched people became known and clear.
After this, people began barking like dogs, bleating like goats, crying like cats, and crowing like roosters.
They imitated every sound made by every speechless animal. Men and women seized one another,
especially young men and young women. Most went astray, so that few escaped this chastisement.
Finally, they would gather in groups, confused, bewildered, agitated, and disordered, and run here and there at night into the cemetery.
They acted like mad people and [?], sang, behaved wildly, and bit one another.
They would cry out as though with horns and trumpets, and speak empty and contemptible words as though speaking in the person of demons.
They indulged in lewd [?], filthy talk, and shameful blasphemies. They would also leap up, cling to the walls, and hang themselves upside down.
They would fall down and roll about naked, and do other things like these, so that none of them even had enough awareness to recognize his own dwelling and home.
But those who had escaped that madness devised ways to gather them into the churches amid commotion, using force and threats.
Consequently, all the churches and martyrs’ shrines in the city became packed with them from end to end. Even when they were gathered together in those churches,
some of them could be seen behaving wildly and foaming at the mouth in various ways, while others chattered and spoke contemptible words, as
though speaking in the person of demons, saying, “Look, [?] we numbered tens of thousands!
If the holy apostle Thomas had not come out against us, we would have taken the whole city captive, devastated it, and killed and strangled its people.
But the apostles and martyrs who are buried in this city confronted me and restrained us from wreaking destruction. Otherwise,
we would not have left a single human being alive in it.” Some of them would bend down as though to pray
and kneel, while others would leap up, climb onto them, and ride them. Sometimes three or four would mount one another through the working of demons.
If any of those who had not gone mad happened to enter the churches to pray, they would stand up and ridicule and mock them.
They would address obscene and filthy words to them, so that many would flee in shame and leave the church.
Then again, many of them would become bewildered together and cry out, saying, “Look, the governors are coming!
Look, kings are entering! Let us run out to meet them!” And so they would become bewildered
and rush out in a great surge, many of them together, running frantically back and forth throughout the city,
wandering, dazed, running about, agitated and confused. Some of them would also laugh shamelessly and speak filthy, contemptible, and obscene words.
Others would weep with choking sobs and then speak obscenely again. Still others would blaspheme and utter ugly, strange cries of madness.
And so those who had not been struck by this bitter affliction of derangement would go out, gather them together again, and bring them into the churches.
They would prepare many different kinds of food, having compassion on them
and grieving for them, and bring it in to them. Some had their wives bring food to them, and they were sustained. This illness of madness and derangement lasted for a year,
especially in the city of Amid. Although in the other cities—Tella, Edessa, and the rest—
only a few [?] were chastised by this scourge, this battered city was chastised especially severely.
God alone knows for what reason and because of what sin this abandonment occurred, so that the Christian people should come under such chastisement,
and foul demons should gain such power, especially over the young, to the point of throwing them upon one another inside the churches in shameless impurity.
So, when this became known, they stopped them from eating oil and drinking wine.
They provided them with bread and salt, or groats without oil, to eat, and vinegar-water to drink.
They also appointed guards over them so that they would not defile themselves in the churches and do the demons’ will.
After these people had suffered this strange scourge for some time, they began, one by one, to return gradually to their senses.
They grieved, wept, and sighed, and devoted themselves to prayer and [?] of continual supplication.
Those who had recovered their senses now also came in groups to Jerusalem and the other holy places to pray.
Grieving and dressed in black, they went about offering supplications, praying, and weeping.
And so, through the help of the grace of our Lord’s mercy toward his creation, he brought deliverance to his people and drove away from them
the evil powers. That great plague occurred in the year 855 and lasted three years.
In the year 858, famine began to come, and it lasted eight years, until the year 866.
Three years, however, were severe: no one reaped or gathered a harvest. In the year 867, this madness described above occurred, and it lasted one year.
In the year 869, there was another plague in that very same city of Amida in Mesopotamia.
Now death was the third scourge, following these two severe chastisements.
A great plague struck immediately, so that nearly all those who had gone mad perished along with the rest. Thus, within three months,
thirty-five thousand were counted as having been carried out of this afflicted and miserable city during its plague, until it was left, in its bitter suffering, a desolate ruin.
We have briefly recorded these things concerning the chastisement inflicted by these three bitter scourges that occurred at this time because human sins provoked wrath, so as not to weary the reader.
We have set them down as a reminder for those who come after us, to awaken the remembrance of all those who come after us to repentance and prayer.
As our Lord also taught us in his Gospel: “Pray that you may not enter into temptation.”
So let whoever has ears to hear listen, as it is written. And again: “Whoever is wise will heed these things.”
The holy John, bishop of Asia, wrote these things, for he witnessed them himself. In the year 857, there was confusion
over the beginning of the fast in the imperial city, in Alexandria, and in all the eastern regions. There was great confusion throughout the whole church.
This was when the Council of Chalcedon held sway. Some began the fast two weeks early,
while others began one week later. In the imperial city, while we were there, after the fast had been observed for one week according to the rule,
the emperor reversed course, and he and his officials decided that the fast would begin after another week. Once the fast had begun, meat had also been prohibited in the city.
Then afterward, by a stern command from the emperor, the butchers were required to slaughter animals and bring out meat for sale, on the claim that the fast had not yet begun.
Under compulsion, and against their will, they slaughtered sheep, cattle, and pigs and hung them up for sale, while the whole city regarded the meat as something dead,
and looked at it as sacrificial meat. No one approached it except those few who were inclined toward gluttony and debauchery.
There were many, however, who scooped up dust, ashes, and rubbish and scattered them over the meat wherever it was hanging.
When it rotted and no one bought it, the meat sellers were again required to slaughter animals. They went and complained before the governor of the city,
who was requiring them to slaughter them. That governor informed the king, who ordered them to slaughter the animals, and, if they suffered losses and the meat did not sell,
they were to receive payment from the public treasury. Thus they were not to stop, and they were to receive the price of the sheep and cattle from the public treasury.
Thus there was great turmoil, not only on the eve of the fast, but also at the holy Feast of Unleavened Bread. Again: On the unlawful ordination by the hand
of a dead man, which took place in the city of Ephesus at the hands of the Julianists, in the year eight hundred and sixty of Alexander.
Since Paul, the wise architect and builder of the Church, warns us, saying, “I ask you, my brothers,
to watch out for those who cause divisions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching you learned, and to keep away from them.
For such people do not serve our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own bellies, and with pleasant words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent.”
Again he instructs everyone, saying, “Examine everything and hold on to what is good; flee from every evil thing.” And again: “Beware of evil workers; beware of dogs.”
Therefore, while guarding against the godless error of the evildoers who teach the phantom doctrine, we thought it right, O lovers of truth, not to wrong your zeal
and conceal in silence the evil offense, the destruction of human souls, the violation of all the rules of Christianity,
and the opposition to all the Church’s canons on the part of the followers of the error and fanciful doctrine of Julian of Halicarnassus.
This was wickedly and misguidedly perpetrated in the Church of God by those who were in the city of Ephesus and adhered to this very heresy.
It had taken a particularly strong hold and spread there because of four lawyers from that region who had shared Julian’s opinion and doctrine in the city of Alexandria.
These men, together with the others, acted fancifully against the honorable order of the priesthood.
They dared to do a shameful thing, far removed from every rule of proper conduct—something alien and shameful, as it is written, even
to speak of. For in this aforementioned city, apparently through the efforts of the lawyers,
a certain bishop named Procopius, who belonged to this fanciful error, had come and settled.
He had been misguidedly drawn toward the fanciful doctrine of the Phantasiasts. After some time, however, he learned from many people
that, as a consequence of the error of Julian and all who shared his doctrine, the entire hope of Christians was henceforth nullified, made false, and destroyed,
and had become an illusion and dreamlike hallucinations. When he was rebuked by many people for this, he subsequently repented and turned away from Julian’s doctrine.
He anathematized him and drew up a written statement of repentance, which is preserved to this day in the monastery that is the head of all the monasteries in the region of Asia.
Afterward he went astray again and returned like a dog to its vomit—to this same heresy. He came and settled in Ephesus,
for a number of years, until the end of his life, holding fast to this doctrine of an illusory appearance.
When his adherents pressed him to appoint a bishop in his place, since he had reached extreme old age, he nevertheless observed proper order in this matter.
He refused, saying, “The canons do not authorize it. I will not appoint a bishop and be anathematized along with him.”
Thus he would not agree to do it by himself. When he became mortally ill, they again pressed him, but he would not be persuaded to appoint a bishop for as long as he lived [?].
After he died, however, seven presbyters reportedly assembled. Of these it would almost be right to say that gall
was what they drank, and they became drunk, lost their reason, and had their understanding blinded by the maddening spirit of error. Entirely outside the order prescribed by the church’s canons,
they took counsel together and brought another man, a monk named Eutropius, and bent him over that corpse.
They lifted the dead man’s hand and placed it on his head. In the dead man’s place, they themselves reportedly recited over him the prayers for ordination as a bishop.
And so [?], they say, he became a bishop—one who had transgressed the law and was outside all the church’s established orders.
But for this wretched Eutropius, who had become a useless instrument, one act of destruction, empty error, and trading with a bag full of holes was not enough—
the profit he imagined he had gained through a dead man’s hand. Rather, his own understanding was also blinded, and he was left in darkness concerning all canonical and ecclesiastical order.
Although he had himself become an instrument of corruption through a dead man, he added disaster to his former wickedness and went beyond eleven
bishops, they say, who themselves also came into being as mere phantoms. The fool had forgotten
what the dead man had refused to do while alive and well: to appoint a bishop by himself, contrary to the canons.
He too ought to have recoiled, trembled, and been afraid of daring to appoint bishops by himself, quite apart from the fact that he had himself come into being through a dead man’s hand.

He too proved to be dead and useless with respect to the church’s orders, a cold corpse without spiritual perception, together with all those who derived their office from him and those who would afterward derive theirs from them.
Not only we, but all the regions of Asia bear witness to the truth of these things. He sent
them out—this same man sent those who had derived their office from him—in every direction, to become advocates of their error.
Those who belonged to the heresy of a phantom and an illusory appearance carried this out zealously, going out to the east and the west,
to the imperial city, to Alexandria, and throughout Syria, even crossing over to Hira in Beth Nuʿman and into Persian territory.
One of them, whose name was Sergius, also hurried to the lands of the Himyarites. He had previously been an ascetic.
He turned aside and himself became an arrogant instrument, going about disturbing, corrupting, misleading, and ruining all these regions,
appointing priests in name only. Reportedly, he too appointed a bishop in his place, a man named Moses.
That is, an instrument of corruption and destruction, just as both he and the man who appointed him had been. He died, however, in the land of the Himyarites.
When not even four years had passed, others among them directed their journey toward the regions of Sophene and Arzanene.
They also entered Armenia, so that even now many of them remain in these regions, going astray and leading others astray.
They especially corrupted the regions of Arzanene and Sophene and led them completely astray through their heresy, and [?]. This lawbreaking destroyer of souls committed offenses there.
But [?], when they understood these things, took offense at this ordination and realized that it was fraudulent and not genuine.
They reproached one another, fell into conflict, split apart, and became thirty factions. When they understood the ordination of the dead,
which they had wickedly performed, they rejected it completely and established a separate church in the city of Ephesus itself.
And so they received communion from the former priests, as they themselves confirmed to us more fully concerning these things that had been done by them in this way.
Otherwise, since we were not close to these events, we would not have undertaken to complete an account of them from outside hearsay.
But now, since I have treated all these things in this way with careful regard for their truth, let them be accepted by you and by everyone without doubt or dispute.
Stand firm in our Lord. Concerning the flood that occurred in the river flowing through Tarsus in Cilicia. The year eight hundred and sixty-one.
Most of Tarsus, the great city of Cilicia, was swept away, submerged, and uprooted by floodwaters from the river flowing through it.
The other villages of the region, even those very far away, were also swept away. Fields, vineyards, and the other cultivated properties were ruined,
uprooted, and left dry, and earth covered them. At this time the destructive heresy of Montanus was exposed to ridicule and uprooted.
Its history and how it arose have been recorded by us in the account of the time of the apostles.
Now, through the efforts of the holy John, bishop of Asia, the bones of Montanus were found,
who used to say of himself that he was the Spirit, the Paraclete, as well as those of Crates and of Maximilla and Priscilla, his barking women.
He burned them in fire and tore down their temples to the foundations.
In the year eight hundred and sixty-two, there was a great earthquake in the imperial city, on a Sunday.
On the seventh of the month of August, there was a fearful, severe, and violent earthquake in the imperial city, in the middle of the night, as Sunday was beginning.
Many houses were overturned in it and became dreadful tombs for their inhabitants. Many churches also fell,
along with bathhouses and city walls, especially the wall of the imperial city called the Golden Gates.
Many lives were also lost everywhere in the earthquake, and many cities were overturned and laid in ruins.
Thus Nicomedia, the metropolis of Bithynia, was overturned and utterly destroyed, and most of it was swallowed up by the sea.
The rest were buried in the rubble, and many were found alive in the rubble.
Some came out unharmed, while others were injured. These fearful earthquakes continued, coming one after another, for forty days.
While the mercies of the compassionate God were present among them and were calling people, they persisted in prayer in the churches and remained in them.
With sorrow and tears of repentance, commemorations of these earthquakes were held in a large, spacious field seven miles from the imperial city.
Every year, on the days when they had occurred, many supplications were held, with practically the whole city assembled.
101. The dignitaries too eagerly went out to the field for these supplications. At this time, the following were recognized among the faithful:
These bishops: Theodosius, patriarch of Alexandria, in exile; Anthimus, patriarch of Constantinople, in exile;
Paul, patriarch of Antioch, in exile; Jacob, bishop of Edessa, from the monastery of Psilta;
John, bishop of Amida, from the monastery of Qartmin; Theodore, bishop of al-Hira of Nu'man.
The following patriarchs were recognized among the Chalcedonians: Vigilius of Rome; Eutychius of the imperial city; Apollinarius of Alexandria;
Domninus of Antioch. The year 863. The Jews and also the Samaritans rebelled in the region of Palestine.
At this same time, the Jews and Samaritans together formed a secret plot against the Christians in Caesarea in Palestine.
They rebelled and united under the names of the Greens and the Blues, and went into battle against the Christians.
They ravaged and killed many—everyone they encountered. They rushed to the Christians' churches, plundered them, and insulted and mocked the holy things.
When the city's proconsul came out to turn them back and drive them away, they gathered and surrounded him. When he saw the multitude of people gathered against him,
he fled to his headquarters. They ran after him, caught him, and killed him. They cut him into many pieces, and his entire staff as well. They also killed
many newly baptized people while they were wearing their white garments, and took a great deal of plunder. When Emperor Justinian learned of these things, he became very angry.
He gave orders to Amantius, the military commander stationed in the East, who was a Christian and zealous for the Christian faith.
He went to Caesarea and throughout the land of Palestine. He seized some of the rebellious Jews and Samaritans and crucified them, burned others, and put others to the sword.
He cut off their hands and feet, and they were subjected to various tortures. In this way he exacted retribution from them.
Terror and ruin came upon all those of them who escaped. The year 864.
There were great and powerful earthquakes, and many cities and [?] in the land of Syria were overthrown by them.
In the month of June of this year, there was a severe and violent earthquake in addition to the others.
Many cities were overthrown by it, including the cities of Phoenicia and those of Arabia and Palestine:
Beirut, Tripoli, Tyre, Sidon, Zarephath, Byblos, Antaradus, and the remaining cities, villages, and their surrounding districts fell and were overturned.
Many people were buried in their houses, along with livestock and everything else, in the wrath brought on by sins. The year 865.
Large gatherings of patriarchs, bishops, monasteries, solitary monks, and laypeople assembled from every region.
In the imperial city, concerning the faith. We cannot, then, give a precise and detailed account of these assemblies, whose members burned with zeal
and hastened to the emperor, one after another at different times, over the question of the unity of the church.
This initiative came first from all the persecuted bishops, especially those of the East.
They gathered together, brought along, and pressed into service monks, men of the wilderness, men perfected in holiness, and workers of miracles,
and others skilled in knowledge, discourse, and the divine Scriptures, who knew the doctrines of the true faith.
They came, entered, debated, stood firm, and fought courageously for the truth. Yet it was also revealed through the Spirit to the holy men who were with them
that nothing could be accomplished at that time. So they secretly boarded a ship and departed from the imperial city.
This greatly distressed even the faithful Empress Theodora herself, and she sent people in every direction.
But not one of them was found, nor was it known where they had settled. Those of them who reached their own places,
however, could not be persuaded to respond again and leave their places. Thus they ended their lives, and the assembly too was dissolved,
without anything at all having been accomplished. The year eight hundred and sixty-six.
The burning by fire from heaven of the great and mighty temple of idols that stood in Baalbek, the city of the sun, which is in Phoenicia, between Lebanon and Senir.
Again, during this same period in the reign of Emperor Justinian, a great marvel occurred through the burning
by fire from heaven of the great and mighty building of the temple of idols in Baalbek, the pagan city that is called in Greek the City of the Sun.
In this city there was a great and strong temple of idols, which, they say, was one of those mighty buildings that Solomon built.
Its length measured one hundred and [?] cubits, and its width seventy-five cubits.
It was built of whole, dressed stones, each twenty cubits in length [?] ten cubits, and four cubits wide within the course of masonry.
Besides the craftsmanship of its construction and its tall, mighty columns, which were also wonderful to see, its roof was made from the strong cedars of Lebanon
and covered with lead above. Its doors were of bronze, and there were bronze rams' heads overhead, beneath each of the timbers of its roof,
projecting three cubits into the building. The other features of that building were also marvelous.

The misguided pagans were greatly carried away with pride and boasted of the strength of that building, and countless sacrifices, votive offerings, and burnt offerings to demons were continually made in that temple.
Indeed, no one had been able to demolish it or put an end there to the error of the idol worshipers.
But God, who saw the waywardness and error of the people caused by the grandeur of that temple, suddenly
sent fire from heaven into it. The fire blazed within it and consumed it, completely destroying its timbers, its bronze [?], its lead, and the idols within it.
It even baked its stones like pottery, along with the statues arranged within it for the false worship of paganism.
And it licked down to the soil of the ground, leaving a few stones in it as
a sign, baked hard by the blaze. Thus a great calamity suddenly overtook all the worshipers of the idols, especially those of that temple, with weeping, lamentation, and bitter mourning
for the entire pagan community. They gathered and came from every direction on hearing of the calamity that had overtaken them
