and their gods—deaf, dead, and without sensation—along with the temple in which they had been arranged. They gathered and stood around it, weeping bitterly,
for many days. The temple burned until it became a mass of flame.
But all the Christians who saw and heard what had happened to that temple were filled with joy and gladness.
As they marveled at the wondrous sign God had performed, their mouths were filled with praise and their tongues with thanksgiving throughout the whole church of God.
They rejoiced and offered praise because of the great wonder God had performed in the sudden destruction of that temple by the force of a blazing flame from heaven.
In the year 867, the great church of the imperial city collapsed, on the third day of the month of May.
In the great church of the imperial city, half of the eastern side—that is, the dome—was suddenly shaken and fell.
Through the providence of God's mercy, since he does not desire the destruction of his creation, it was closed and no one was found inside.
Otherwise, it would have crushed thousands and tens of thousands. For it had already been cracked and damaged by that terrible, violent earthquake.
Its collapse brought great distress to the emperor and the whole city. The part that had not fallen proved more difficult
to bring down than the part that had fallen, because it was a great, strong vault.
It remained suspended in place, and the craftsmen [?] could not work out how to bring it down. They were afraid
that it might fall and strike the columns and the [?] below, bringing down the entire church. For the eastern part that had fallen
had crushed and shattered the whole magnificent canopy and all those marvelous columns surrounding the entire screen of the sanctuary,
the altar itself, all the standing fittings, and the rest. The emperor gave orders, and with fear and much labor the other part was brought down.
He then rebuilt it firmly and solidly, raising it twenty feet higher than before; some say as much as thirty.
He spent much gold on it. Its construction was so strong that nothing in the world is thought to be stronger. In the year 868,
there was a violent earthquake, and the city of Botrys collapsed in that earthquake. A great mountain called Rock Face split apart and fell into the sea.
When Botrys in Phoenicia, which lies on the seashore, collapsed in the violent earthquake,
a great mountain adjoining it, called Rock Face, was suddenly shaken and torn apart by the violence of the earthquake.
A great mass broke off from it and fell into the sea. The earthquake hurled it far out into the sea,
where it settled and formed a barrier opposite the city over a great distance. The sea lay inside it, and an entrance remained on one side, making a great and remarkable harbor.
which hundredweights of gold and the efforts of kings could not have made the like of.
And so it became a large, spacious harbor, capable of receiving great ships within it, so that everyone was amazed and marveled at God's providence.
He whose anger itself is mingled with mercy. Now Emperor Justinian had sent a great deal of gold to all the cities that had been overthrown by the earthquake.
Little by little they were rebuilt and their walls restored, although the wicked disposition of those who survived had not greatly changed or diminished.
In the year 869, there was a gathering of Egyptian monks concerning the faith in the imperial city.
Burning with zeal, they gathered and came, spoke, debated, rebuked, and pleaded. When they saw that there was no relaxation, they turned back
and boarded ships and went to their own country, having accomplished nothing. In the year 870, there was a great earthquake.
Brogus [?] was overthrown, along with many other cities on the seacoast, and villages in Galilee, Arabia, Palestine, and the territory of the Samaritans.
The sea also withdrew and retreated inward about two miles along the whole of Phoenicia. For the terrible calamity
and the great and astonishing sign that occurred in Beirut, a city of Phoenicia, when the earthquake took place and the cities fell, we wish to put on record
for the knowledge of those who come afterward. For when the terrible earthquake suddenly occurred, the sea, away from the city of Beirut and the other cities on the seacoast of Phoenicia,
was checked, turned back, and restrained. At God's command it fled inward for a distance of two miles.
The dreadful depths of the sea were exposed, and many great and astonishing things could be seen there:
ships that had sunk while full of various kinds of merchandise, and others that suddenly, when the sea withdrew inward from the land,
including those that had been moored in the harbors, descended and slid onto the ground, were shaken and broken when the sea left them and fled at its Lord's command.
This calamity was meant to shake people and bring them to sorrow and repentance,
so that, at the sight of this terrible wrath which they witnessed, they would hold in contempt not only these worldly things but even their own lives.
But they were like Pharaoh. It was not God, as is written in that case, but Satan who here hardened all their hearts, like Pharaoh's.
Those who were found in the cities and villages along the seacoasts rushed with the impetuosity of arrogance and hardness of heart
and entered the great sea to seize the treasures, namely the fearsome and hidden ones in the depths of the sea, misled by greed that would destroy their lives.
Thus, as thousands of people rushed headlong to destruction into the depths of the sea
and began carrying merchandise and running to bring it up, others, seeing these people loaded with the wealth that would destroy them,
rushed with great eagerness so that they would not miss out on the hidden treasures that had suddenly been laid open by the earthquake. While these were running down into the depths,
and others were hurrying upward, others were scrambling in between, and all were stumbling over one another in confusion, then, at a hidden signal,
the force of the terrible sea suddenly surged back to its former depths, covering and burying them in the lowest depths of its abysses.
All these wretched people, who chased after wealth from the depths of the abyss, went down into the deep like Pharaoh.
They sank like stones, as it is written: “The Lord brought the waters of the sea back over them,” when he broke through the barrier and it surged back to its former fullness.
Those who were still on its outer shore were themselves pressing forward in a frantic rush to go down.
When they saw the mighty height of the sea as it returned to its former place, those who were near dry land fled ashore.
When they had escaped, as far as their own efforts went, a violent earthquake struck, shaking down the buildings of the cities, especially those of Beirut.
It came down and crushed those who had escaped from the sea, so that none of them remained. While the sea stood towering behind them,
the earthquake shook the city down in front of them. Because of their wicked greed, they were caught between two disasters.
In their case the sacred saying was also fulfilled: “Though they escaped from the sea, justice did not allow them to live.”
Thus those who went down in pursuit of wealth were brought to utter destruction. They lost the breath of their lives, and their corpses were found floating like dung on the surface of the water.
Then, when the city had been overthrown, fire broke out among its ruins at God's command. The fire continued burning
and blazing among the ruins for two months, until even the stones were burned and reduced to lime.
Afterward the Lord sent rain down from heaven for three days and three nights.
Thus the fire that had broken out in the city of Beirut was extinguished. Those within it who had escaped drowning in the sea and the city's collapse
lay there wounded, their wounds festering, and tormented by thirst for water, because the city's aqueduct had collapsed.
When the compassionate Emperor Justinian heard, he sent gold and trusted men from his own service. They cleared away the debris and brought out countless human corpses.
They also rebuilt a little of the city. In the year eight hundred and seventy-one, an order came from the emperor
that lawyers, grammarians, monks, and shipowners [?] from Alexandria, Misr, and Egypt should assemble in the imperial city for a debate about the faith.
For all the shipowners who transported the public grain were believers.
They assembled before Emperor Constantine, who knew that they opposed the council, and he raised the subject of the faith with them.
After much had been said, they told him, “Since we are men who struggle with the sea and are not trained in debate,
if you please, issue an order that, when we return after two voyages, the monastic fathers, lawyers, and grammarians should come with us,
those who are well versed in the Scriptures, along with the other leaders of the city. Then all these matters concerning the faith can be examined and discussed.”
This proposal pleased the emperor. He did not delay in carrying it out, but immediately issued a firm decree authorizing and ordering them to come.
They took it and departed. When they had gone down to Alexandria, they assembled, and the decree was read. They agreed among themselves
that, since this was a struggle for the truth of the faith, they must not be negligent, grow slack, or be afraid. Thus a large gathering of monks and young men assembled.
They boarded ships and came together in the imperial city. They entered and bowed before the emperor in our presence, and matters for debate were raised.
They proved so well prepared that the emperor himself was astonished, although he too was practiced in debate.
He had thought that there was neither a bishop nor anyone else who could meet him in debate. But when he realized that they could meet him,
he dismissed them and appointed a meeting two days later. So they assembled again and spoke at length for many days.
Again he neglected the matter and began putting them off and delaying them, until a year had passed.
And so, when they saw that he showed no sign of being prepared to do anything, they too returned to their own country,
having gained nothing. In this way he was continually convening gatherings of this kind.
Some of these people lived in the city itself. Many of the faithful also lived in the palace itself through the care of the late empress.
Thus they would assemble, debate, and plead their case many times. They received promises and were dismissed, while absolutely nothing was done.
In the year 872, a council assembled in the imperial city by order of Emperor Justinian.
Meanwhile, in the twenty-sixth year of Justinian’s reign, he convened a council of patriarchs and bishops in the imperial city.
When it assembled, it examined and confirmed the condemnation of Origen, which had originated with Emperor Justinian himself.
It also confirmed the condemnation of these Three Chapters: namely, Theodore of Mopsuestia, the letter of Ibas, and what Theodoret had written.
Because of this, the whole region of Italy—that is, Rome and all its surrounding territories—was thrown into turmoil.
It was for this very reason that Vigilius, the patriarch of Rome, had come to the imperial city.
At first he showed himself opposed and fought fiercely against the condemnations of these Three Chapters.
In the end, however, he agreed and accepted what this council had done. From then on, great divisions and disputes throughout all the western regions
increased, and there were also many persecutions, calamities, and schisms. At this council, however, something happened that had never happened before:
three patriarchs were present: Eutychius of the imperial city, Apollinarius of Alexandria,
and Domninus of Antioch. Vigilius of Rome, although he was in the imperial city, did not sit in the council.
Thus, from then on, all four patriarchs met together with all the other bishops and metropolitans.
Although this council issued decisions on many matters, it was not accepted by everyone. For want of a name, since it lacked one, it was called the Fifth Council.
We have given this brief account of it. Concerning the great gathering of the heads of monasteries and the other eastern monks who were with them,
which took place in the imperial city after the death of the late empress, in the year 874 of Alexander.
After the death, then, of the faithful Empress Theodora, who had cared for and strengthened the party of the faithful, gathering them together, sheltering them, and providing for them.
Some of Justinian’s advisers gathered and said to him, “Now that the empress, who is among the saints, has died—
she who used to care for those who do not agree with you, and whose support made them insolent and contemptuous of you—if you now send for them, gather them, and bring them here, they will all
agree with you and accept the council, because they have become afraid and have lost their resolve.”
When the emperor heard this from his advisers, he became eager and firmly decided that it would certainly be advantageous for this to happen.
First he began urging my humble self, John of Asia, to send immediately and gather all the monasteries of Syria,
promising honors and authorizing generous expenditure for provisions, litters, and the other transport animals,
and for everything needed for the journey. As he was now insistently pressing me with his command
to set out and travel to the regions of Syria, with great promises and generous funds, I began speaking to him about these plans,
asking why he had decided to send and trouble men of venerable old age, making them leave their monasteries to fall into disorder and neglect during their absence,
especially since they were in various places of persecution. He gave many answers to these objections,
but he also heard that I declined to act as an intermediary and agent in this undertaking,
giving as my reason that I feared the denunciations and curses of such holy and perfect men.
Thus, weary of me because of my refusal and unwillingness to comply [?] in these matters, he left me alone and dismissed me.
He sent for another man who was eager to undertake these things, and dispatched him.
Thus they assembled and came, a great and imposing gathering of venerable elders, about four hundred men. Even the
large and spacious courtyard called Isidore’s was given to them, and they lodged there. Most of the city’s people flocked to see them and receive their blessing.
Thus they entered the emperor’s presence. He looked at them and was amazed at their appearance, and he began questioning them.
He saw that they were firm in their truth and powerful in speech. He did not find them weak, as people had led him to expect and had told him.
A whole year and more passed in this way, with them coming and going, speaking and debating, but they were neither brought down nor weakened.
They asked to be released and were allowed to leave. They departed without accomplishing anything either. In the year eight hundred and seventy-five,
on the sixth of September, at the third hour, while the Gospel was being read, there was a great, violent, and terrifying earthquake.
It was so violent and severe that the man reading the Gospel in the Great Church fell down.
Many places were damaged by it. Half the city of Cyzicus collapsed, as did parts of other cities.
In the year eight hundred and seventy-six, in June, there was another great, violent, and severe earthquake. Many cities were overthrown by it,
including the cities of Phoenicia, that is, those of Arabia and Palestine, and Beirut, Tripoli, Tyre, Sidon, Zarephath, Byblos, and Antaradus.
And the remaining cities and villages and their districts fell and were overthrown. And many people
were buried in their houses with the rest, in the wrath that scourges sinners. In the year 877, the holy Theodosius of Alexandria died on the nineteenth
of July. He had lived in exile for thirty-one and a half years. In the year 879,
there was a severe earthquake in January, on the fourteenth, at midnight before Friday dawned. It was more severe than all those that preceded it,
so that both walls of the imperial city were shattered and split: the inner wall of Constantine
and the outer one of Theodosius. Many large houses collapsed and became heaps of rubble over their inhabitants.
The rest remained standing, cracked and shattered, so that there was no building whatsoever that did not bear a sign of the destruction caused by the earthquake.
Many churches also suffered in this way. Many of them fell completely to the ground,
while others remained damaged and standing precariously. These things happened not only within the city,
but throughout its surroundings as well, including many of the sturdy buildings on the splendid estates of the imperial officials,
especially in the region of the Hebdomon outside the city gate, and throughout that whole region along the seashore,
as far as the city called Rhegium. This Rhegium [?] was turned upside down by the great wrath,
together with its wall and all its other buildings, so that it could not be recognized that a city had stood there.
The remaining churches and all the surrounding places were also affected, extending far into the region of Thrace. For even the emperor’s great porphyry column,
which stood before the palace of the Hebdomon, with his statue standing upon it, fell in that earthquake.
The force of the earthquake lifted it upward; it turned headfirst and came down, embedding itself eight feet into the ground.
Likewise, countless cities, villages, and houses were overthrown and destroyed. Countless houses were buried.
As many were being searched, many people came out of them alive. For an earthquake as severe and terrifying as this
had never occurred among all the earthquakes that preceded it. The earth trembled and shook this way and that, like trees before the winds,
and was convulsed by night and day for ten days and their nights. The rest of the people who had escaped offered sorrowful supplications.
The cities that remained persevered in fasting and prayer, pleading lest they too perish in the wrath.
Such was the horror of the severe earthquake that the merciful emperor himself, in his distress, did not put the imperial crown on his head for thirty days.
Even when the holy feasts of the Nativity and Epiphany arrived, he went out from his palace without a crown and went to church before everyone.
In the year 882, the Chalcedonian patriarchs are recorded: Anastasius of Antioch,
Apollinaris of Alexandria, Vigilius of Rome, and Eutychius of Constantinople.
Macarius of Jerusalem, whom Eutychius deposed. Afterward Macarius returned and deposed Eutychius [?], and sat in
his place. In addition to these were Paul, patriarch of Antioch, known as Bar Ithutha, and Jacob of Silta,
and John of Amida. In the year 883, Eutychius of Constantinople was deposed.
John succeeded him. In the year 884, the emperor went astray and departed from the orthodox faith.
He fell into the fanciful error of the Phantasiasts, into which the wretched Julian had also fallen previously. Perhaps it is not improper to say that he went far beyond him.
For he said that our Lord’s body was not corruptible, nor had it come from anything corruptible.
For, he said, even the body of the Virgin Mary, who bore him, was itself neither corruptible nor subject to suffering.
And anyone, he said, who says that the body of our Lord, or that of the blessed Mary, was subject to suffering and corruption falls into error.
Thus he began writing letters and sending them to all the patriarchs. He required each of them to assemble the bishops under his authority,
and everyone was to sign the edict he had written. He issued a stern command that anyone who would not sign and assent
should be cast into merciless exile. But while his threat was fierce and harsh, his end [?], and he and his threat came to nothing,
along with his heresy. In the year 885, a great and terrifying fiery comet appeared in the northern region,
on [?] of the month of May. Its beginning—that is, its lower end—extended from a star, and it stretched a great distance.
At first it rose and appeared around midnight, and afterward from evening onward. It appeared with its head inclined toward the east.
Little by little it straightened and stood upright above, like a great spear. Then, toward morning, it again tilted and inclined toward the western region.
For a period of two or three months it continued to rise and appear regularly in this way.
Afterward it turned and appeared again in the southern region. Then, at the death of Emperor Justinian, it disappeared and was never seen again.
We provide these things as a record of events for those who come afterward, so that, as they read, they may consider their final outcome.
In the year 885, Emperor Justinian died, and Justinian [?], his sister’s son, became emperor. In the year 889,
Mar Jacob of Pesilta died, as did Mar John, bishop of Amida. The holy Mar Cyriacus succeeded him.
At Edessa, Mar Severus succeeded Mar Jacob. The holy Mar Peter succeeded Paul of Antioch.
This reckoning—that is, this historical account—begins with the very beginning of creation.
It proceeds as far as the birth of Abraham and the reign of Ninus, who built Nineveh and reigned there for fifty-two years.
In the forty-second year of Ninus, Abraham, the patriarch, was born, as Eusebius attests.
For we have taken from him the material for this historical account down to the years of the faithful Constantine. From here, however, down to Theodosius
A little from Socrates, who belonged to the religion of the Novatians. But from Theodosius down to Emperor Justinian, from Saint John, bishop of Asia.
This is the year eight hundred and eighty-five. But from this point down to the present year in which we now live,
which is the year one thousand and eighty-six of Alexander, and the year one hundred and fifty-eight of the Hagarenes,
we have found no accurate written account of events like the earlier accounts. Nor, concerning the evil and bitter times that have passed over us and our fathers,

have we found any written account of anything. Nor concerning this time of distress and bitterness, which has come upon us because of our sins, when we were handed over into the hands of Assyrians and barbarians,
have we found anyone who wrote anything. But to leave a remembrance of this evil time and the bitter distress that the earth suffered in our days and in our time,
at the hands of those Assyrians whom the prophet also names when he says, “The Assyrian is the rod of my anger,
and the staff in their hands is my scourge. I will send him against a perverse nation, and I will commission him against a spiteful people.”
This rod and this staff of the Lord, which he stretched out and gave to the Assyrian to chastise the earth with it, was also seen in the sky, rising and remaining visible for many days.
This was our wish, so that perhaps those who come into the world after us may hear, tremble, and fear the Lord,
and walk uprightly before him, lest he hand them over too, as he did us, into the hands of this destructive wolf.
It is written, “Instruct your children,” and again, “Ask your father, and he will show you; your elders, and they will tell you.” But when
we traveled around many places, we found nothing accurately written, except scattered details.
There were also things we heard from very old men, which they themselves had seen and experienced,
and also events of which we ourselves were eyewitnesses. We wished to collect them and set them down here, one by one, in this sequence.
But anyone who comes across these accounts and wishes to reject them should know that it is not in one place, or in one kingdom,
or in one region that incidents and events of various kinds occur. So here too, if he comes across a written account that does not agree with this one,
let him understand these things: even the earlier historians do not agree with one another. One gives less detail and another more.
One writes about the church, and another about other matters. But this does no harm at all to discerning and God-fearing people,
if a date is one or two years earlier or later. Rather, let it be enough for those who fear God to see the scourges of former generations,
and turn away from wrongdoing themselves, so that those scourges do not fall upon them too. It says, “Be on your guard and fear the Lord your God,
lest he bring these scourges upon you too.” We begin with the year eight hundred and ninety-eight.
The year eight hundred and ninety-eight. Emperor Justinian died, and Justinian “of the four” [?] became emperor, and Tiberius became Caesar.
The year nine hundred and one. That Justinian died, and Tiberius took possession of the kingdom. In the year nine hundred and two, Saint Peter, patriarch of Antioch, died.
The year nine hundred and five. Tiberius died, and Maurice succeeded him for eight years. The year nine hundred and twelve. There was a great darkness in the middle of the day.
The stars rose and appeared as they do at night, and remained for about three hours. Then that darkness lifted again [?].
Daylight appeared as it usually had before. In that same year Maurice died, and another Maurice became king,
together with his son Theodosius, for twelve years. In the year 614, Narses, the commander of the Persian army, conquered Edessa.
He entered it, seized Severus, the city's bishop, and stoned him to death. In the year 615,
Saint Athanasius became patriarch of Antioch. In the year 916, Edessa was captured.
In the year 924, Maurice and his son Theodosius were killed, and Phocas reigned for eight years.
In the year 928, King Phocas ordered all the Jews under his authority to be baptized.
He sent George the prefect to Jerusalem and the whole land of Palestine to compel all the Jews to be baptized.
When he went down and gathered all the Jews in Jerusalem and its surroundings, their leaders came before him, and he said to them,
“Are you servants of the king?” They said, “Yes.” He said to them, “The lord of the land has ordered you to be baptized.”
But they remained silent and did not answer him a word. He said to them, “Why do you not give
an answer?” One of their leaders, whose name was Jonah, answered, “We carry out and obey everything the lord of the land commands.
But we cannot do this, because the day of holy baptism has not yet arrived.” When the prefect heard this, he became very angry.
He stood up, struck Jonah [?] in the face, and said, “If you are servants, do you not obey your master?”
He ordered them to be baptized. Thus, whether they wanted it or not, he had them all baptized. At this time Jacob the Jew was known,
as were Athanasius, patriarch of Antioch, John, bishop of the Arabs, Simeon of Harran, and Cyriacus of Amida.
In the year 932, the Arabs conquered the land of Palestine and as far as the great river Euphrates.
The Romans fled and crossed to the east of the Euphrates. The Arabs gained control there. The first king to rule over them was a man of their own named Muhammad.
They also called him a prophet, because he turned them away from worship of every kind and taught them that there is one God, the maker of creation.
He also laid down laws for them, because they were deeply attached to the worship of demons and idols, especially the worship of trees.
Because he showed them the one God, and because they defeated the Romans in battle under his leadership, and because he laid down laws for them that suited their desires,
they called him a prophet and also the messenger of God. They are a very lustful and carnal people. Any law, whether from Muhammad
or from some other person who feared God, that was laid down for them but did not suit their desires, they despised and abandoned. But whatever conformed to their wishes
and fulfilled their desires, even if it was laid down by the most contemptible among them,
they held firmly to it, saying, “This man has been appointed for us as a prophet and messenger of God, and God has commanded him to do this.”
He governed them for seven years. In the year 933, Phocas, king of the Romans, died.
Heraclius reigned in his place for thirty-one years. In the year 934, Mar Cyriacus, bishop of Amida, died.
Mar Thomas succeeded him. In the year 937, the stars in the sky fell.
They were all darting northward like arrows, giving the Romans a terrifying sign of their defeat,
and of the conquest of their lands by the Arabs. This indeed happened to them shortly afterward, without delay.
In the year 938, Muhammad, king of the Arabs—that is, their prophet—died. Abu Bakr became their ruler.
For five years. In the year 940, Heraclius, king of the Romans, began to build the great church of Amida.
In the year 943, Abu Bakr, king of the Arabs, died. Umar succeeded him for twelve years.
In the year 944, Heraclius, king of the Romans, went down to Edessa, and the battle of Gabitha took place.
The Persians were defeated, and he left Mesopotamia. In the year 948,
the Arabs crossed into the Jazira, and the Romans were defeated. ʿIṣ entered Edessa. In the year 952, the Arabs attacked
Dara and fought against it. Many people on both sides were killed, especially among the Arabs.
Finally, he gave them his word, and they opened it. From then on, no one was killed. In that same year, he attacked Dvin.
Many people were killed there too, as many as twelve thousand Armenians. In the year 953,
the Arabs conquered Caesarea in Palestine. In the year 955, the Roman commander Valentinus, the patrician, came
to wage war against the Arabs. But he became afraid of them and fled, leaving behind all the possessions he had with him.
The Arabs took them. In that same year, Procopius and Theodore marched out and entered Batnan of Serugh in great fury.
They plundered, looted, took captive all they wanted, and returned to their land. After Athanasius the patriarch, his disciple, the holy John, succeeded him.
At this time the holy John, patriarch of Antioch, was known, as were John, bishop of the Arabs,
and Simeon of Edessa, and Matthew of Aleppo, from the holy monastery of Zuqnin, and Mar Thomas, bishop of Amida, from the same monastery.
In the year 950 and [?], Umar, king of the Arabs, died. Uthman succeeded him and reigned for twelve years.
In the year 960, Muawiya entered Cyprus. In that very same year, Arwad was conquered. In the year 961,
the holy Mar John, patriarch of Antioch, died and was buried in Amida itself. He was laid in the holy sanctuary of Mar Zʿura. And in that very
same year, the holy Mar John, bishop of the Arabs, died. He was laid in the church of Mar John the Baptist in Amida.
In that very same year, the holy Mar Simeon of Edessa also died in Amida itself. He was laid in the church of Mar Zʿura.
In the year 962, Mar Theodore became patriarch of Antioch.
In Edessa, meanwhile, there was [Cyriacus]. In the year 963, there was a battle between the Arabs and the Romans at Tripoli.
In the year 964, Habib entered Jazira, and Procopius came to make peace with the Arabs.
In the year 965, Heraclius, king of the Romans, died, having reigned for thirty-one years.
Constantine the Younger succeeded him for one year. In the year 966, this Constantine died.
Another Constantine succeeded him for twenty-seven years. In the year 967, Uthman, king of the Arabs, died.
Civil strife broke out, the land was thrown into turmoil, and the Arab people fell into confusion. There were many evils in the land.
There was great bloodshed at their hands and among them, because they would not submit to one leader. Instead, each of them rushed to seize leadership,
each wanting to reign himself. The army commander in the western land, whose name was Muawiya, wanted to reign.

The people of the West also loved him, pledged allegiance to him, and submitted to him. But the land of the East and Jazira rejected him and submitted to another army commander, whose name was Abbas, and pledged allegiance to him
as king. From that time, battles and bloodshed began among them. They shed one another's blood and drenched the land with one another's blood.
They fought many battles against one another everywhere, and about five years passed in disputes and clashes.
In the year 968, the battle of Siffin took place between Abbas and Muawiya. They shed much of one another's blood on both sides.
In the year 973, Abbas was treacherously killed by some of his leading men, on Friday at the hour of prayer, while he was kneeling and praying.
Muawiya [?] sole rule for twenty-one years, including those five years during which civil strife and turmoil raged between him and Abbas.
In the year 976, the holy Mar Theodore, patriarch of Antioch, died. The holy Mar Severus bar Mashqe took his place.
In Edessa, Mar Jacob succeeded Cyriacus. At this time Aaron the Persian, the Persian interpreter, was known.
In the year 988, Muawiya, king of the Arabs, died. Yazid succeeded him for three and a half years.
In the year 990, on the third day of the month of Nisan, a Sunday, there was a great and severe earthquake. In it Batnan of Sarug collapsed,
and the old church of Edessa. Many people died in it. In the year 992, Yazid, king of the Arabs, died.
Marwan reigned for one year. In that very same year, Constantine, king of the Romans, also died.
Another Constantine succeeded him for sixteen years. In the year 993, Marwan, king of the Arabs, died.
Abd al-Malik succeeded him and reigned for twenty-one years. In his days civil strife raged for nine years, because the Arabs would not submit to one leader.
Throughout those nine years, they did not cease from battles and evils. In the year 994,
the holy Mar Severus bar Mashqe died. Because of a dispute among the bishops, the patriarchal throne remained without a head for five years.
In the year 999, the holy Athanasius became patriarch. In the year 1002, there was peace.
The whole land submitted to Abd al-Malik, and he took his seat on the throne [?]. In the year 1003, this Abd al-Malik carried out a tax assessment of the Syrians.
He issued a strict command that everyone should go to his own region and to the village [?] of his father's household. Everyone was to be registered by name, along with whose son he was,
and his vineyard, his olive trees [?], his property, his children, and everything he owned. From this point onward, the poll tax began to be collected on men's heads.
From this point onward, all evils began to pour down upon the Christian people. Until then, kings had collected a tax on the land, not on men.
From this point onward, the descendants of Hagar began to subject the descendants of Aram to Egyptian slavery.
But woe to us, because we have sinned! Slaves have gained mastery over us. This, then, was the first tax assessment that the Arabs carried out.
In the year 1014, Abd al-Malik, king of the Arabs, died. He had reigned for twenty-one years, including the nine years in which he waged civil war.
Walid reigned in his place for nine years. In the year 1015, the holy Athanasius, patriarch of Antioch, died.
The holy Mar Julian succeeded him. In the year 1016, there was a great and severe plague in the land.
It reached the point that people could not keep up with carrying one another out. It was especially severe in the region of Serugh.
In this same plague, seventy-two people from the monastery of Mar Shila died. In the year 1008, Constantine, emperor of the Romans, died.
Justinian reigned in his place for ten years. In the year 1017, a synod assembled at the monastery of Mar Shila.
Its prominent leaders were Julian the patriarch, Thomas of Amida, and Jacob of Edessa, the interpreter of the Scriptures.
The holy Mar Jacob, bishop of Edessa, was renowned. In the year 1018, Justinian, emperor of the Romans, died.
Leontius succeeded him and reigned for (four) years. In the year 1019, the holy Mar Julian, patriarch of Antioch, died.
Mar Elijah succeeded him. In the year 1020, there was a tax assessment, and the first assessment was confirmed.
It also greatly increased the evils. In the year 1021, the holy Mar
Jacob, bishop of Edessa, died. Mar Habib succeeded him. At this time, the holy Mar Thomas the Stylite of Tella was renowned.
In the year 1022, Leontius, emperor of the Romans, died. Tiberius Apsimarus succeeded him for seven years.
In the year 1023, Walid, king of the Arabs, died. Sulayman reigned in his place
for two and a half years. In the year 1024, the holy Mar Thomas, bishop of Amida, died.
Mar Theodotus succeeded him. After Apsimarus, emperor of the Romans, Justinian reigned for six years.
After him, Philippicus reigned for three years. After him, Anastasius in turn reigned for two years.
After him, Theodosius Constantine reigned for one year. He was the one reigning when Maslama entered Roman territory.
These are the remaining years of the reigns of the Roman emperors, amounting to twelve years.
This is what I noted earlier: one shortens the reckoning and another lengthens it. The Arabs, too, count only by moons; they do not count months as the Syrians do.
Nor do the chroniclers generally record anything but the days during which the emperor occupied the throne.
They leave out the years of turmoil. Although I have done this for my own use, I have arranged them in order as follows so that the reader will not become confused.
In the year 1028, Maslama entered Roman territory. When countless Arab forces had assembled and begun to enter the land
of the Romans, all the regions of Asia and Cappadocia fled before them, as did all the land extending from the sea
and over the Black Mountain of Lebanon as far as Melitene, and along the river Arsanias as far as Inner Armenia. All this land was adorned with settlements containing many people.
It abounded in vineyards, crops, and all kinds of desirable trees. From that time onward it was devastated, and these lands were never inhabited again.
When the emperor saw that a vast army had advanced against him, and that his own commander, whose name was Leo, had given them his word, his heart trembled.
His hands grew weak. He abdicated, laid aside his crown, and shaved his head.
It is an established custom among the Roman emperors that if one of them abdicates, he shaves his head and stays in his house.
From then on, no one remains with him at all. This emperor did just that. Although Leo himself, the commander, sent him a message saying, “Take courage and do not be afraid,”
he was not persuaded, but resolutely abdicated. This Leo was a brave and mighty man, and also a warrior.
He was Syrian by birth, from those border regions. Because of his prowess, they had made him commander.
Through his wisdom, this man spared the land from drinking human blood.
He gave Maslama his word that he would bring him into Constantinople without any fighting. Trusting his promise, Maslama neither fought nor took anyone captive.
Instead, he advanced in force directly toward Constantinople. He arrived and attacked it. Leo, meanwhile, entered the city
and saw that the Romans had lost heart and that the emperor himself had abdicated. He encouraged the Romans and told them, “Do not be afraid.”
When they saw his courage, and also feared that he might rely on the man who had been emperor, they took him and made him emperor.
Once he had put on the imperial crown, he clothed himself in strength and courage. They strengthened the city wall.
He also sent troops and cut off the roads that brought provisions from Syria to the army. He also destroyed the ships and cut off the crossing.
The Arabs and the entire army with them were shut in as though in a prison. Maslama gave orders and planted a vineyard.
A great and severe famine came upon them, until bread disappeared from their entire camp. They even ate their livestock and horses.
Maslama kept demanding of Leo, “Where is that promise in God’s name that you made me, that you would bring me into Constantinople without a battle?”
Leo would answer him pleasantly, saying, “Wait a few days, until the nobles of the empire submit to me.”
Under these circumstances, the one group remained outside and the other inside, without any fighting, for about three years.
The famine also became severe among the Arabs, until they ate their own dung and even ate the flesh of the dead.
They also attacked one another, until a man was afraid to walk alone.
Meanwhile, Maslama demanded of Leo every day, “Either give me what you promised, or I will attack.”
News reached them that Sulayman, king of the Arabs, had died and that Umar was reigning after him. Umar himself also sent them a letter:
“Leave that place, so that you and everyone with you do not die of hunger.” When they received the letter,
Maslama asked Leo for permission to enter the city and see it. He entered with thirty horsemen and went around it for three days.
He saw the works of the emperors. Thus they broke camp, and he left that place without their having accomplished anything. When he reached a city called Tyana,
the governor of the city saw that they were hungry, exhausted, and weak, and regarded them with contempt.
He sent word to Leo: “Send me an army, and I will attack them secretly.” But this plan was not concealed from them either.
Instead, when they became aware of the army behind them, one of the commanders, named Abbas, a prominent man in the kingdom, asked Maslama:

“Give me an army. I will go and meet them before they come, surround us, and wipe us off the face of the earth, so that our end becomes worse than everything that has happened to us on this expedition.”
He took a large army and went to meet them. While they were advancing slowly,
not yet ready for battle, and unaware even of the Arab scouts [?] coming against them,
Abbas went down and reached a large meadow ahead of them, where they were preparing to camp that day.
He concealed the whole army in ambushes, in the ravines, and in the clumps of reeds there. When the Romans arrived and went down into the meadow,
not knowing or even suspecting what the Arabs had done, they made camp. They also sent their livestock out to graze, as was customary
for the army. The others rose from their ambushes and from the hollows where they had hidden themselves [?] all around that meadow, according to the signal agreed upon among them.
They descended on them, surrounded them, and slaughtered them all with the sword. Not one of them escaped.
There were about sixty thousand of them. Then they stripped the dead and returned to their companions.
Another Roman army, which was following behind them, heard what had happened to the first army, became afraid, and turned back.
The Arabs took captives and plundered everything they found before them, then departed [?] and came to Syria.
In the year 1032, which was the first year of Umar, king of the Arabs, and the fourth year of Leo, emperor of the Romans,
Maslama left Roman territory, having also devastated the whole land between the frontiers and made it like a desolate wilderness.
To avoid making this account too long, I am leaving out many of the things that happened to them on this expedition.
At this time, Elijah the patriarch, Mar Habib of Edessa, Simeon of Harran, and Theodotus of Amida were well known.
On the miraculous sign that took place through the holy Mar Habib, bishop of Edessa, at this time. It is right to conceal a king’s secret.
But it is altogether right to proclaim God’s wonders and reveal them to everyone. Nor is this strange or in any way harmful to the ears of those who hear,
if we include in this account the miracle that God performed in our own days through one of his apostles, by this same power. There was an Arab man, and when they wanted
to enter the land of the Romans, he came and stayed at the monastery of Mar Abel in the territory of Edessa.
When he saw that the monastery’s gatekeeper was a man who feared God, humble and kind, and adorned with every divine virtue,
he entrusted a large amount of gold to him, saying, “Keep this for me. If I return alive, I will take back what is mine.
But if you learn that I have died, distribute it among those in need.” Then he departed from there. When that chaste man received what had been entrusted to him,
he took it, dug into the ground, and buried it, without letting anyone else know. The Arabs remained away for about thirty years, and he did not return.
By the Creator’s command, it happened that before they came out from the land of the [?], that gatekeeper departed from this troubled world,
without having told anyone this secret, even then. When the owner of that deposit arrived and asked about the man, they said that he had died. He said to them,
“Give me what I left with him.” They answered and said to him, “We know absolutely nothing about this matter you are speaking of.
He never told any of us about it or left us instructions saying, ‘Someone has something deposited with me.’” But because the man was one of the prominent people,
he put severe pressure on these monks, saying, “Either give me what is mine, or I will destroy your monastery.” And because that gold was no small amount, severely
“Either give me what is mine, or I will destroy your monastery.” And because that gold was no small amount, they were put under severe pressure. The authorities ordered them
to sell all the monastery’s property and give him the proceeds. If this was not enough to repay him, some of the monks belonging to the monastery were to be sold,
and in this way he was to be repaid. When all the people of the city and the entire region saw this bitter sentence pronounced against the chaste monks,
they were overcome by bitter grief, because their brothers and sons were to be
sold into slavery and brought down from apostolic service in the world to slavery among pagans.
When the city’s chaste bishop, Mar Habib, saw his brothers being led into slavery, he was overcome by bitter grief and turned toward the Savior with sorrowful tears.
He mounted and went to the monastery to persuade that man, accompanied by a large crowd of leading men from the city and the region.
They pleaded with him at length to wait until they could collect contributions from everywhere and gather his money for him, but he would not be persuaded. He said, “My money is with them.
Let them give me what is mine, and I will leave.” Although they assured him with many oaths and sorrowful tears that they knew nothing about his gold,
he did not believe them. The holy Mar Habib was pressed on every side, since these men said, “We know nothing,” and the other man would not accept it.
He put on the strong armor of true faith in his Lord and followed in the footsteps of the one who asked in Bethany about Lazarus, “Where have you laid him?”
He took incense and a censer in his hand and went down to the monastery’s cemetery, allowing no one to go with him.
He went and stood over the grave in which that blessed man had been laid. He knelt and prayed, then rose and set down the censer.
He offered before the Savior the sweet fragrance of the tears of his heart. He stood at the entrance to the tomb,
with unwavering faith, which even performs mighty deeds like God, and called out, saying, “So-and-so, rise in the name of our Lord!”
At the sound of his voice, the man straightened up and sat facing him with a cheerful expression, as though he had never experienced the decay within graves.

He said to him, “My son!” He answered, “Yes, my lord.” “Did so-and-so, the Arab, leave anything in your keeping when he entered Roman territory?” He said, “Yes, my lord.” He asked, “How much?” He said,
“Such-and-such thousands [?], in full.” He asked him, “And where is it?” He answered, “I have it buried in the monastery’s gatehouse, beneath such-and-such a bench.
If you command it, I will go and give him what belongs to him.” He asked him again, “Is there anyone in this monastery besides you who knows where it is?”
He said, “No, my lord.” Then the chaste man said to him, “The resurrection of the dead has not yet come. Rest until your Lord’s command orders you to awake.”
At that very moment he returned to his former condition. When the holy man had learned the whole truth from the dead man, he went down and ordered them to bring him a pickaxe.
He went and stood in the place that the dead man had told him about. He ordered them to remove the bench and dig beneath it.
They did as he said. He uncovered that gold and gave it to its owner, and so delivered his holy monastery.
In the year 1034, Umar, king of the Arabs, died. He had occupied the throne for two years and four months.
Yazid became king after him and reigned for four years. In the year 1035,
this Yazid ordered all images to be erased wherever they were found, whether in a sanctuary, a church, or a house.
Thus wretched men went out from him and destroyed all the images wherever they were found. Again, in the year 1036, this Yazid ordered
white dogs, white pigeons, and white roosters to be killed. Thus a harsh decree went out, and the speechless animals,
though innocent, were being destroyed. The streets of the cities and villages stank because of them. Instead of “Be fruitful and multiply
and fill the earth and subdue it,” and “Let birds fly across the face of the sky, and let animals multiply on the earth,” they made themselves opponents of creation.
What he had formed and arranged in the womb according to his will, by his creative command, they wished to destroy through their wickedness.
They wished to obstruct the Maker’s command, so that the world would no longer proceed according to the limits established for it by the Creator.
This same man also ordered all blue-eyed people to be killed. But this order was annulled through the efforts of God-fearing men, and he harmed no one.
He also ordered that a Syrian’s testimony against an Arab should not be accepted. He set an Arab’s value at twelve thousand and a Syrian’s at six thousand.
These destructive laws also began at this time. He further ordered that a thief’s foot [?] should be cut off instead of his hand.
The Arabs rejected this and did not put it into effect. In the year 1038, this Yazid died.
His emirs of the Jazira were: first Aburin. He was dismissed, and Mardas came. Then Mardas was dismissed, and Aburin himself came again.
In the year 1039, Hisham son of Abd al-Malik became king over the Arabs, for nineteen years and four months.
In the year 1040, the holy Mar Habib, bishop of Edessa, died, and Constantine succeeded him.
At this time the holy Mar Elijah the patriarch, Simeon of Harran, and Constantine of Edessa were known,
and Theodotus of Amid. Concerning Theodotus, bishop of Amid. Now this holy Theodotus, bishop of Amid, because in solitude
and in the humble labors of the solitary life he had grown up, and continually practiced them
and longed for them, and was a quiet, gentle man, adorned with every divine virtue,
asked to be released from his office as bishop of the city. He left his episcopal seat, abandoned the city, and went down to the region of Dara,
into the borderlands between Dara and Amid. There he built himself a pillar and climbed onto it, imitating Mar Thomas of Tella.
He also built a monastery there, which still stands today beside the village called Qaluq. There he ended his life.
The holy Mar Cosmas then took up the episcopate. Again, concerning the holy Mar Cosmas, bishop of Amid.
This holy Mar Zama too was a great monk, zealous for everything good.
He also performed astonishing miracles, like Elijah the Tishbite and the first apostles. But because he was zealous and admonished the great just as he did the lowly,
he was not loved by the city's leaders, because he rebuked them severely, speaking openly and without favoritism,
about the corrupt deeds they were continually committing. And because they feared that he might open his mouth and curse them,
since he was a stern man, and they were afraid to oppose him openly,
they stirred up the villagers not to receive him when he went out to visit them. Through this they would have grounds against him for driving him out of their city.
But this did them no good, nor those who had advised them. Now when it happened, according to
the rule established by the elders, that he went out to visit the region, he was unaware of the plot that had been devised against him.
When he reached a village in that region named Tella d-Kum, whose inhabitants were also [?], and the wooden gong was struck as customary and they assembled, they decided not to receive him.
They would not even consider him worthy of a message delivered by a man, but sent word to him through an old woman: “Take your dignity with you and go on your way.
Otherwise, be warned that you will leave here in a very bad state.” But these wretched people neither knew nor understood, because they walked in darkness,
that the word spoken by our Savior to his disciples cannot be set aside: “Whoever receives you receives me.
And whoever does not receive you, shake off the dust of your feet against him as a testimony. It will be more bearable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for that place.”
But when that modest man learned of their insolence from the old woman, he ordered his disciple to draw along the carriage in which he was sitting and take it past the southern side of the village.
Those wretched people, in whom the prophetic saying was fulfilled: “The fool does not know, and the senseless person does not understand.”
One sin alone was not enough for them; instead, they went up to the gate of their church, which stood on a height.
He stood there while they mocked him and watched to see what he would do. But this courageous man, though he saw all their contempt, was not intimidated.
Instead, strengthened by faith and trust in his Lord, he continued on and passed through their village. When he reached the eastern edge of the village,
he ordered the carriage to stop, and they took off his shoes. He turned toward the village and shook them out against it, saying, “Because you do not welcome
your bishop, you idol, Kum, God's wrath will overtake you swiftly and speedily.”
Then he quickly continued on and passed into the village east of them called Great Tarmal, for he had been coming from the west.
It was the season of the barley harvest, and there was not even a single patch of cloud in the sky that day.
But God's wrath swiftly and speedily overtook the wretched village that had chosen to defend the wrongdoing of the city's leaders.
This was to bring fear and terror upon the whole region, and upon all those who wished to treat their bishops with contempt,
and to become a story for generations to come. He entered Tarmal, while clouds gathered over the other village. While its people were still turning this way and that,
a storm gathered over it, with a blast of winds that tear mountains apart. Hail like stones fell upon it and struck their vines and fig trees.
It also broke the trees within their territory and destroyed all the green vegetation in their fields. It reduced their crops to something like dust, leaving them unrecognizable.
The storm cloud also scattered their heaps of grain, and they could not be gathered again. All hope of their livelihood vanished from the face of the earth.
When those who had shown contempt saw what had happened to them—that while their words were still in their mouths, God's wrath had risen against them—
and it seemed to them that the wrath was rising against their own persons as well, they awoke as though from a deep sleep, like a drunken man whose wine has worn off.
They remembered what they had done to their bishop and recognized that these things had come upon them because they had treated him with contempt.
They were all the more firmly convinced of this because that wrath had not passed beyond the boundaries of their village. So they came out, from the least to the greatest, and went
barefoot and weary, weeping bitterly with shame on their faces, to the village where he was staying.
When the holy man saw them, he too grieved bitterly for them, like Elisha over those children whom the bears had torn apart.
He grieved especially because that wrath had destroyed everything they possessed. So he joined them in their sorrow and prayed for them.
From that time, God cast fear and trembling before him over the whole region, and also over the city's leaders.
Even before he left the village where he was staying, the people of the other villages, small and great alike, would come out to meet him with entreaties.
After the holy Mar Elijah, patriarch of Antioch, came the holy Athanasius.
In the year 1042, Maslama entered the gateway to the land of the Turks and committed great atrocities in the land of Armenia.
And throughout this whole northern land. Maslama invaded their territory with vast, countless armies.
For they used to come out like this every year and do a great deal of harm. When he invaded their territory, they came out against him.
He fought a battle with them and slaughtered a great many of their people. When he had shaken them,
they came to his feet and asked him for peace. He granted it to them, after receiving their binding promise.
In that same year Maslama tore down [?] the gate in the land of the Turks, because they had fought a battle beyond that gate and were also trapped inside it.
He feared that they might go into that unfamiliar country, which belonged to the Turks, and that the Turks would gather against them and wipe them from the earth.
For they are a people who have no God and are Magians. For this reason Maslama was compelled to give orders, and that gate in the land of the Turks was torn down.
It had been built by Alexander the Macedonian. First the entire camel train was released and went out, then the donkeys, and after these the stonemasons. Finally they themselves went out.
They also scattered caltrops behind them along the entire road. In the year 1043, Maslama gathered a great many people:
craftsmen, carpenters, and stonemasons. He carried out all the work needed for construction, then went in and rebuilt the gate in the land of the Turks that he had torn down.
When he had rebuilt it, he made an agreement in God's name with the Turks that no one on either side would cross into the other's territory. Then he left.
But since they do not know God, do not understand that they are his creatures, and do not even acknowledge that there is a God in heaven, they did not keep their word.
Instead, they despised God himself and scorned his word. They treated it with contempt, crossed over, invaded, and committed great atrocities throughout the land outside their borders.
Hisham sent Jarrah, the army commander, against them with a great force of cavalry. When he entered, since it was harvest time,
he made the whole country suffer greatly during his advance, because he was an undisciplined man and did not restrain his army.
He destroyed all the farmers' crops, besides the many other hardships they inflicted on the poor people as they passed through.
They all came and wailed before him, but not one of them received any relief from him. And when everyone was oppressed in this way
by his advance, he received a supply of prayers from them all alike, as he deserved. When he went in and fought a battle with them,
they killed most of his army. They also captured many others and took them into their own country. When this happened, he sent word to Hisham to send him help.
Maslama followed him into the country with an immense, countless army. But by the time he entered, Jarrah and his army had been put to the sword.
For the Turks had overwhelmed them from every direction and put them all to the sword. Not one of them escaped.
The Lord repaid the evildoer according to his wickedness. The Lord repaid him for all the evil that he and his army had done to the farmers,
wherever he went. He brought it all down together upon their heads. But when Maslama entered, they trembled and were terrified before him.
For they feared his name more than the sight of him. He fought a battle with them and poured out their [?] like water over the face of the earth.
He filled the birds of the sky and the wild animals with their flesh. When he had defeated them, he put Marwan son of Muhammad in charge.
the one who later also became king over the Arabs—over Armenia. And he departed, leaving a large army with him as well.
This man, however, destroyed them more than all his predecessors. In the year 1029, there was a great and terrible earthquake.
It devastated many places, temples and churches, together with large buildings. It caused especially great destruction in Maʿda, and damaged the old church of Edessa.
It also brought great, tall buildings down upon their inhabitants. Even those that remained and did not fall in the earthquake—
he placed a mark on them, so that their inhabitants would tremble before the Lord whenever they saw that mark left by the earthquake.
At this time Hisham also dug the Zaytun canal and built cities and fortresses along it, together with many villages.
He adorned it with many plantings of every kind. He also dug the Beth Balash canal, built a fortress along it, and planted plants of every kind there.
He also dug the Hani canal. Along this one he made fortresses and gardens of every kind. His brother Maslama also dug the Beth Balash canal.
He too built fortresses and villages along the river he had dug, and adorned it with every kind of beauty.
In the year 1040, Neocaesarea was conquered by Maslama. He carried off its entire population into captivity and sold them into slavery like property,
except for the Jews, who were the ones who handed over the city itself. They had secretly gone out to Maslama and obtained his promise.
Through their treachery they also directed him [?] to the entrance of the city. These he took captive but did not sell; instead, they went away with him.
In the year 1045, Sulayman invaded Roman territory, conquered Pluzonia, and carried off its entire population into captivity.
For Artabasdos, the son-in-law of Constantine, king of the Romans, emerged as a usurper. He seized the city of Constantinople and put on the royal crown by usurpation.
For King Constantine himself was fighting the enemy nation with his entire army. But this usurper Artabasdos—
he had left him in the city to guard it, together with a large army from Pluzonia. When this man had seized the city,
he secured the kingship for himself, forgetting the covenant he had made before the Lord with Leo.
When this man had seized the city, and the king’s army and the king himself were encamped outside the city, and the entire army
of Pluzonia was fighting against the king from within, Sulayman invaded. Leo sent him this message: “Do not come against me,
so that you do not come to harm at my hands. Instead, go to Pluzonia, take captives and plunder, and do whatever you desire.
For there is no one to stand against you.” So he went, took captives, and plundered as he wished. He carried off what no one else like him had ever carried off before.
Leo seized the usurper himself and put out his eyes. He also threw the army that was with him down from [?]. In the year 1046,
Malik ibn Shabib, emir of Melitene, and Abdallah al-Battal invaded and attacked Synnada. While they were encamped in the meadow of Synnada,
many armies, beyond counting, gathered against them to take revenge on them for what the Arabs had done in Pluzonia the year before.
While these Arabs, who numbered about fifty thousand, were encamped without concern, the Romans suddenly surrounded them on every side.
They slaughtered them all with the sword. Only a few of them remained, because the day was drawing toward sunset.
Even these were struck with swords and [?] and bows. In this way they fled and traveled throughout that whole night.
Barely five thousand of the fifty thousand who had gone up escaped. Their leaders, too, fell by the sword along with them.
Never before had such wrath come upon the Arabs. At this time a certain deceiver appeared in the land of the West.
He led many of the Jews astray and destroyed them as well. Satan, who from the beginning has been a destroyer and an evildoer against all Adam’s children,
does not direct his warfare against only one people or one language group, against one but not another. Rather, it is against them all
equally. For each people or language group, he becomes a source of deception through whatever he knows they love.
Satan takes his name from his deeds: “Satan” means “adversary.” He has never stopped or rested from disturbing and misleading all peoples in every generation,
without being checked or ceasing from his earlier evil deeds, the things he devised to harm the ancestor of our race.
At this time he led away from the land of Jazira a certain man from the region of Mardin, from a village called Such-and-such.
He brought him across to the land of the West, to the country of the Samaritans. He gained access to the house of a prominent Jew.
When he entered, he violated that Jew’s daughter. When those Jews learned of this, they beat him almost to death,
subjecting him to many tortures because he was a Christian. But when he found an opportunity and escaped from their hands,
he set his heart on doing them every kind of evil. He went down to the land of the Arameans, which is stained with all the evils of sorcery.
He devoted himself to sorcery and to all the devil’s arts. He was trained in every kind of evil and became fully accomplished in them.
Then he left and went up to that land, saying before them, “I am Moses, who long ago brought Israel out of Egypt
and was with them in the sea and in the wilderness; and to bring them out into the wilderness, and then bring them in again, to give them possession of this promised land,
just as they possessed it before. Just as the Lord [?] all those nations in it before your ancestors,
so now he will destroy them all before you. You will enter and possess it as you did long ago.
All the scattered people of Israel will be gathered, as it is written: ‘He gathers the scattered people of Israel.’”
As he made them hear these pronouncements every day, and continually amazed them with his sorcery,
they all followed him astray. At times he led them around in the mountains, and even hurled them from the crags and killed them.
At other times he confined them in caves and openings in the earth and destroyed them. And [?] he made them suffer terrible evils.

He killed and destroyed many of them. He also took an immeasurable amount of gold from them through his sorcery and deception, constantly giving them hope that he would lead them away into the wilderness.
And when he had had his fill of the evil that he made them suffer every day through his sorcery,
He deceived them and took all the gold, property, and slaves that he had acquired from them, and fled home.
But when they came to their senses and saw the evils he had done to them, they all went out after him in all four directions,
asking questions and searching for him. When they found him, they brought him to Hisham, the Commander of the Faithful.
He handed him over to them. After they had subjected him to every kind of torture and torment, they finally crucified him on a wooden stake, and he died.
The Lord repaid him as he deserved. In the year 1047, Atiq rebelled and declared his independence.
When this Atiq rebelled and declared his independence, following the Arabs’ custom when they go out,
of divorcing their wives and giving up everything they own, he did the same. He went out to the country below Sinjar with twenty companions.
When Hisham learned of him, he sent word to Quliyu and Zuhayr, who commanded the cavalry in Sinjar, to go out and fight him.
When they received the command, they gathered a large army and went out after him. When they caught up with him in the desert belonging to Sinjar,
he asked them to wait until morning and then fight one another.
Because they had a large army, while these men were few in number, they treated them with contempt. Moreover, their thirst had become severe,
because water was scarce in that desert. The day was also nearly over. While they were treating him with utter contempt,
Atiq, who was a mighty man, as were those accompanying him, acted cunningly against them in this way.
When darkness fell and those unsuspecting men had eaten, drunk, and gone to sleep, Atiq and his companions armed themselves and attacked them during the first watch of the night.
They slaughtered them all, as the Lord turned each man’s sword against his companion. Atiq’s men passed through them like woodcutters and like plowmen through a field.
Except for a few of them who mounted swift horses and escaped, not one remained whom they did not put to the sword.
The army commanders Quliyu and Zuhayr also fell among those killed [?].
In the year 1052, Leo, emperor of the Romans, died, having reigned for twenty-five years.
His son Constantine succeeded him and reigned for thirty-five years. At this time the bridge opposite Callinicum was built,
the one over the Euphrates, by King Hisham. In the year 1053, there was a great and violent earthquake on Sunday.
It rumbled throughout the whole night of that Sunday, like the powerful sound of a bull
bellowing: that was how the sound was heard. When the time for the Eucharist came and all the people had entered the church,
the church of Marq collapsed and crushed everyone inside it, because of the force and violence of the tremor that came suddenly.
No one escaped from it alive except the priest who was offering the Eucharist in it at that time.
The hill on which the church of Marq was built also kept bellowing and rumbling for about thirty days.
In the year 1054, the great bridge over the Tigris near Amida was swept away.
For the winter was harsh, and heavy snow fell from the sky and lay thick on the ground for many days, until all living creatures were close to perishing.
The animals in particular, and all the birds, perished in it. Afterward there was again harsh and violent weather, with storms and rain for days.
The snow melted, and the ground became saturated with the abundant water that had fallen on it, and also with water from the snow.
There were great surges in all the rivers, especially the Tigris. It rose in a great flood, with powerful torrents.
It killed many people and also devastated countless places. Large timber also came down with it, and it was so powerful and violent
that large walnut logs struck even the great bridge beside Amida. They piled up against it, one upon another, for five or six miles upstream from it.
Thus, because of the pressure and weight of the timber and the force of that flood, the bridge broke apart and collapsed before the waters. From that time onward it was never rebuilt.

For Hisham gathered stonemasons, craftsmen, and the entire workforce to rebuild it. But while he was pressing ahead with rebuilding it, his end overtook him, and it was left unfinished. Now at this time
Edessa too was overwhelmed. The river called the Daisan, which passes through the city of Edessa, experienced a great and powerful surge.
The waters rose high, and the water outlet in the wall on the eastern side became blocked.
The water submerged it, backed up, rose, and overflowed into the city's streets. It ruined all the shopkeepers' goods.
Many houses also collapsed in it. Because it happened during the day, no people were killed by it, since they fled and abandoned their houses.
It also broke through the water outlet and caused great destruction throughout the plain of Edessa and Harran.
In the year 1055, Hisham, king of the Arabs, died. Walid reigned after him for eight months.
The usurpers Yazid, Abbas, and Ibrahim, who were brothers, together with their brother Abd al-Aziz, the sons of [?], rose against him
near the city of Quri and killed him with the sword. Yazid reigned after him for six months, but the land did not submit to him.
Nor did he appoint officials in Jazira. Yazid died, and his brother Ibrahim took his place. In that same year, civil strife broke out throughout the land.
Because of the rebellion that Abbas and his brothers carried out against Walid, killing him with the sword and taking power although the kingship did not rightfully belong to them,

the Arabs did not submit to them, especially the people of Jazira. Instead, everyone held his own position and looked after himself. Civil strife and the taking of captives spread throughout the land,
and no one could [?] leave his own place. On the drought and the great famine that also appeared throughout the land at this time.
At this time the Lord sent upon us all these evil and bitter afflictions: the sword, captivity, famine, and pestilence,
because of our sins and the evil deeds our hands had done. He says, “Even if Moses
and Samuel stood before me, I would have no desire for this people. Send them away from my presence, and let them go. And if they say to you, ‘Where shall we go?’
this is what the Lord says: ‘Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; and those destined for captivity, to captivity.’”
“I will appoint four scourges against them,” says the Lord: “the sword to kill, dogs to drag away, and the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the earth to devour and destroy.”
“And I will make them an object of horror.” Jeremiah, who was rich in revelation, left us these words. And again, he himself says, “Jerusalem’s outcry has risen before me.”
Their nobles sent their underlings for water. They came to the cisterns and found no water. They brought their containers back empty.
They were ashamed and humiliated and covered their heads. Because of the deeds of the land, there was no rain. The farmers were ashamed and covered their heads.
Even the does in the wilderness gave birth and abandoned their young because there was no grass. The wild donkeys stood on the paths, panting for air like jackals.
Their eyes grew dim because there was no vegetation. Truly, everything the prophets spoke has been fulfilled in this time.
Look at the sword of the Arab armies that turned against one another: they drenched the earth with their blood.
Birds and wild animals, and even dogs, ate their fill of their flesh. People also took one another captive, and then plague came upon them as well.
If anyone went out into the countryside, the sword would destroy him; whoever stayed at home would be seized by plague and famine. On every side, distress and bitterness could be heard.
First, the rain that usually fell on the earth in winter was withheld and did not fall. All the seed dried up,
without producing even [?] at all. There was a great famine throughout the land, until wheat reached a price of eight qafizes for a dinar,
and even at seven, none was available. Those in authority sent men, and wherever they found wheat, whether in houses or in the ground, they confiscated it and put it under seal.
People were pressed to the point of death because of the famine, especially the owners of grain, since they had not been weighed down by the distress of famine.
The authorities seized their wheat, and they perished from hunger. From then on, famine gripped poor and rich alike.
The famine was equally severe in every land, so that not a single place was better supplied than another.
Instead, there was distress everywhere. Even the wild and domestic animals that eat grass died for lack of grass.
Great distress came upon people and all living creatures because of the famine, the like of which had not occurred in our time or in our fathers’ time.
Even the springs and fountains failed, and the rivers dried up. At Hisham’s death, many afflictions appeared on the earth.
All these evils overtook us because of our many sins, especially plague and famine. Again, concerning the great plague that occurred at this time.
Here the prophet Jeremiah is very useful to us, for he knows best how to lament the afflictions that have surrounded us on every side.
“Who,” he says, “will make my head [?] and my eyes fountains of tears? Then I would weep day and night over the ruin of the daughter of my people.”
And again he says, “I will raise weeping and lamentation over the mountains, and a lament over the pastures in the wilderness, which lie desolate because no one passes through.”
“Let our eyes shed tears,” he says, “and let our eyelids flow with water. Therefore, women, hear the word of the Lord, and let your ears receive the word of his mouth.”
“Teach your daughters lamentations, and let each woman teach her neighbor a dirge, for death has climbed through our windows
and entered our palaces, to destroy the children in the streets and the young men in the squares.”
“The corpses of human beings,” he says, “fall like dung on the surface of the earth, and like sheaves behind the reaper.”
“And there is no one to gather them.” Let us now come and weep, not for one people alone or for one city, Jerusalem,
but for all the peoples, and also for the many cities that wrath has made into winepresses.
Within them it has trampled and pressed all their inhabitants like fine grapes, without pity.
For the whole earth, over which the decree went out like a reaper against standing grain, cutting down and removing people of every stature, every size, and every rank together, without distinction.
For the corpses that rotted and fell apart in the streets throughout the world, their fluids poured out like water in the streets, with no one to bury them.
For the houses, large and small, beautiful and delightful, that suddenly became tombs for their inhabitants.
Servants and masters alike suddenly fell dead in them, and no one escaped to carry their corpses out of the houses.
For the roads that have become deserted. For the many villages whose inhabitants all perished together.
For the courtyards that used to resound to one another. For the adorned bridal chambers in which dead women were suddenly seen.
For the virgins who were kept in their rooms, awaiting the joy of their weddings, but were suddenly carried into the grave.
And for many things like these, which surpass the speech and narration of all who can speak. For these things, then, the prophet ought to have wept
and said, “Woe to me!”—not for the shattering of the daughter of my people, but for the ruin of the whole inhabited world, and for

the entire earth, which death destroyed because of its sins. He also ought to have used the prophetic words of his fellow prophets, bringing them forward and saying to the remnant of those who survived:
“Beat your feet and wail, ministers of the altar; come in and spend the night in sackcloth, ministers of my God”—not because fine flour has run out in the house of the Lord,
but because human beings have vanished from the world. Along with this: “Let the earth sit in mourning, and let all its inhabitants lament.”
“Call for the mourning women to come, and the women who beat their feet, so that together they may make [?]”—not for one only child or for one corpse,
but for peoples and kingdoms. “The earth will surely totter; the earth will surely reel; the earth will surely quake.
The earth will be utterly ruined; the earth will also be utterly plundered. It will sway like a hut, and its wrongdoing will weigh heavily upon it.
It will again become fuel for burning, like a terebinth whose leaves have fallen, and like an oak that has fallen from its base.” All these things have been fulfilled in this time.
Great earthquakes and violent tremors, together with armies, wars, and conflicts among the Arabs over rulership.
There was also famine that afflicted human beings, so that the entire population of the south and east was uprooted from its land
