and settled in this northern and western land. There was also strife, along with every kind of calamity. “And I will send after them,” says the prophet,
“the sword and captivity, famine and pestilence as well.” All these things happened in our days, with nothing lacking. Look at the sword of the Arabs against one another!
And look at the captivity: no one could travel without being plundered and having his servant taken away. And look at the famine that afflicted people both within and without!
If someone went inside a house, famine and pestilence met him. And if he went out into the countryside, there again he encountered the sword

and captivity. From then on there was bitter distress on every side, suffocating anguish and bewildering sorrow. As it is said, they were drunk, but not with wine, and staggered, but not from strong drink.
People began wandering and roaming from city to city and from one region to another, reeling like drunkards and looking for bread, but there was none, as the prophet said.
At first they began falling ill with dysentery and sores, and those who died were mostly heads of households.
This continued throughout the winter days, and people could not keep up with burying them.
People lay abandoned in the streets, porticoes, towers, palaces and all the courtyards, wasting away from the severity of the disease
and the terrible intensity of the famine. Those killed by hunger were more numerous than those killed by disease.
Those who had enough bread to satisfy themselves suffered even more severely from this disease. When the days began to grow warm, swellings appeared on those who were sick.
They began falling in the street like dung on the ground, with no one to bury them. This pestilence began among the poor who lay abandoned in the streets.
They were being shrouded by everyone with honor and songs of praise and were properly laid to rest. And [?] the poor were nearly all gone.
The pestilence grew stronger and raged fiercely among the inhabitants of villages and cities. When the priests intended to go to a single funeral bier,
fifty or sixty biers would gather there. Even as many as ninety or a hundred biers
would gather in one place in the morning, with two or three, or even four small children on each one.
Thus, throughout the day there was no rest or pause in carrying out people's bodies. The Arabs filled the ground with burial pits,
and the Jews did the same. The Christians' tombs were all filled, until they too had to dig in the ground.
In a single day, more than five hundred biers went out through one gate. All day long these gates had no respite from the constant going out and coming in,
as people carried bodies out and deposited them, then returned to collect others. By then, no funeral service was performed for them anymore,
except for a few, because of the rapid succession of deaths, the small number of priests and the countless multitude of biers.
In the morning the priests would order everyone who had someone dead to come with the deceased to the nearby four-pillared gateways,
and [?] a place or street, they were to gather there in one place. Thus the priests would divide up in the morning
and go in every direction, performing the funeral services and taking them out in batches. More than a hundred biers would go out in a single procession.
On these biers there were more than two hundred people, sometimes even two hundred and fifty. These processions kept meeting one another without interruption throughout the day.
There was no distinction here between a slave and his master, a slave woman and her mistress, or a slave's son and the son of a [?].
Instead, the same winepress of destruction and wrath was mixed for everyone, and slaves and masters suffered equally together, without favoritism.
Ordinary people and leaders lay abandoned opposite one another, groaning, so that everyone would marvel at God's sentence of judgment and remain in astonishment and amazement.
On the judgments of God, which cannot be investigated, understood, or measured by mortals.
“The judgments of the Lord,” it is said, “are a great deep.” The destroyer stretched out his hand against those who held power
and those renowned for wealth and living luxuriously in high rank. The houses of many of them were left without an heir; not even a servant or a master remained in them.
Their possessions, their wealth, and their cultivated fields he suddenly left to their companions, along with their splendid houses.
How many great houses were renowned for wealth! And how many families perished, with not even a single heir left to them!
As for the land west of the Euphrates, the human tongue is inadequate to recount the calamities and astonishing things that happened there.
Likewise in the other cities of Palestine, and in the north and the south,
as far as the Red Sea, together with the rest of Cilicia, Iconium, Asia, Bithynia, Lusonia [?], Galatia, and Cappadocia.
The distress of this bitter suffering came upon the whole world as well. Like rain falling over the whole earth,
or the rays of heaven spreading equally everywhere, so now this plague spread equally over the whole world.
Nevertheless, it afflicted especially severely those regions specified above. In them, many villages and places suddenly became ruins,
with no one passing through or living there. They were filled with [?] corpses stretched out on the ground like dung on the face of the earth, with no one to bury them.
Not a single person remained in them. People lay thrown down within them, swollen, oozing, and stinking. Their houses too were [?], like tombs,
with their owners inside, oozing with decay and maggots. Their belongings, their gold, their silver, and everything they had made lay abandoned in the streets,
with no one to gather it up. Gold and silver were despised there. Their possessions lay scattered everywhere, with no owners. Old men and old women too, honored for their gray hair,
who were [?] to be buried with great honor by their heirs, lay thrown down in the streets, in houses, and in public squares, their mouths open, falling apart and stinking.
Lovely virgins and beautiful young women, who had been looking forward to joyful bridal chambers and the adornment of costly clothing,
lay exposed and abandoned, their putrefaction mingled together. They became a pitiful sight to those who saw them—and not in tombs,
but in houses and in the streets. Handsome, cheerful young men lay piled up and abandoned, their putrefaction mingled with that of their parents.
These things happened in these lands, and everywhere else as well. Those who remained, a few out of many, carried the bodies
and brought them out all day without stopping. They would go out and throw them down, like someone throwing a stone onto a heap, then returning to take another
and going out again to throw it down in the same way. Many who had no relatives left
could be seen lying abandoned in the streets and being eaten by dogs, with no one to bury them. Each person could attend only to his own household.
They even hired many people simply to collect them from the houses and the streets because of their stench.
Here too that saying was fulfilled: “He brought the smell of their decay into their nostrils,” together with the saying, “The earth mourned and lamented.”
There was no longer any weeping or distress or grief, because everyone was already knocking at the grave’s door. Gold and silver were despised like dung.
Wherever married women or virgins wore gold and silver or costly jewelry,
no one would reach out his hand and strip anything from them, nor would even parents take anything from their children. Rather, they even expected to go down to Sheol with them.
Their [?] was also mingled with their own. With what tears could I weep at that time, my dear friends? What lamentations would be enough
for me? What heartbreak, what mourning dances, what laments, what dirges, what sorrows would suffice,
when we saw the elderly and people of every stature and size felled and laid low like cedars?
Great mercy was also revealed in this scourge, for at first it overshadowed those poor people who lay in the city streets.
Everywhere it began with them first. But when they had reached their end, this terrible scourge then turned upon the rich and all the leading men of the cities.
Through this mercy of God, two things happened and were accomplished, so that both groups benefited from what took place.
First, those who inhabited the cities demonstrated through them their zeal for righteousness.
Through their care for the poor, they accumulated great benefit for their own souls, tending them, clothing them, bringing biers, and carrying them out.
They buried them with great sorrow, and also with diligence, reverence, and zeal. There was also another benefit: if he had mingled them with the rest,
they would have lacked people to care for them. Instead, they were [?] first, while everyone was healthy, standing ready and eager,
carrying out and burying those who had no one to bury them. Then those who had relied on graves and gravediggers
were left outside the grave, so that not one of them even received a funeral service. When the poor had come to their end,
the scourge passed to the leading men. In some cases the plague began among them with the least and continued to the greatest [?], and no remnant of them was left at all. Even
those who escaped this affliction and did not die dragged themselves outside the city as best they could.
Finally, those who did not die were struck by a terrible, painful affliction in their groins—some on one side, others on both.
This same thing happened both to those who died and to those who survived: their groins were suddenly struck.
At this sign, a person immediately gave up hope for himself. Even anyone who escaped death endured something worse than bitter death.
His groins would swell, fester, and burst, becoming large, deep ulcers that discharged blood, pus, and fluid
day and night like a spring. Afterward they would remain in profound weakness, some for a month and some for two,
and others for five or six, or as long as a year. Many remained so for two years, and many of them became permanently disabled.
Then the prophetic saying was also being fulfilled: “All knees will run with water, and every human heart will melt,”
along with the saying, “Baldness [?] upon all their heads.” So it also happened at this time that only an occasional individual escaped from a household or a family.
Thus he would fall into this weakened state. It happened that both his knees discharged fluid, blood, and pus, to the point that even his head became bald.
Later, the few who survived could not be recognized. Unless they could be recognized or distinguished by their clothing, no one could distinguish the priests and monks.
For they were all bald. Moreover, just as a swelling appeared in the groin, so it also appeared in the armpit and on the neck.
Most recovered from it fairly easily, some after a time, while some
never recovered completely. While this affliction was striking the land from every side, like labor pains striking a pregnant woman,
the Arabs did not stop their wars and their acts of violence against one another. Then Marwan came out from the gateway of the land of the Turks, while the whole land was in confusion and turmoil.
In the year 1057, Marwan came out from the land of the Turks. It is written in the prophet Jeremiah as follows:
“Therefore, this is what the Lord says: Look, I am placing stumbling blocks before this people, and they will stumble over them, fathers and sons together.
Neighbor and friend will perish.” All these things happened among the Arabs: brothers and nephews fell over the stumbling blocks of rulership.
Those of the house of Abbas and the house of Hisham, along with nephews, neighbors, and friends, attacked one another and perished.
They caused many people to perish with them. Jeremiah himself also spoke about Marwan’s advance: “Look, a people is coming from the land of the north,
and a great nation will rise from the ends of the earth. They are armed with bows and spears. They are cruel and show no mercy.
Their sound is like the raging sea. They ride horses and are prepared like warriors for battle. We have heard the news of them, and our hands have grown weak.
Distress has seized us, and pains like those of a woman giving birth. Do not go out into the fields or travel on the road, because of the enemy’s sword.”
Isaiah also spoke about them as follows: “I have stirred up one from the north to come from the rising of the sun, and he will call on my name.
Rulers will come and trample as a potter tramples clay.” And again: “From the north disaster will be unleashed upon all the inhabitants of the land.”
When Marwan came into Jazira and it submitted to him, he appointed officials [?] there in all the cities,
including Mosul. He assembled a large army and equipped it, with metalworkers and craftsmen to accompany it. He crossed over to the west against the house of Abbas.
Yazid, the one who had killed Walid, died after completing six months, and his brother Ibrahim took his place.
When he learned that Marwan had crossed the Euphrates with a large army and that Jazira had submitted to him, he trembled before him.
“They reeled,” it says, “and staggered like drunkards.” He immediately sent Nuaym ibn Thabit against him with a large army.
They say that this man had seventy sons. When they approached one another and fought, Thabit’s entire army was killed, and he was routed before Marwan.
When those of Ibrahim’s house saw that he had defeated them in the first battle, they trembled. He assembled vast, countless armies.
They also gathered villagers to throw stones with slings. When they approached one another and the armies met, they clashed at Ayn al-Jarr.
They fought many battles against one another, and countless men fell on both sides. In the end, Marwan defeated them and put them to flight.
Ibrahim and his brothers fled, as did Sulayman ibn Hisham. Such a massacre had never been seen anywhere in the world, nor had blood ever been poured out in one place as it was there.
More than five thousand villagers were also killed in it. When Marwan had won, he attacked Homs, captured it, and demolished its wall.
He also brought Yazid out of his grave and hung him upside down on a wooden stake. He took four hundred thousand in gold from a certain Jew.
Concerning the shepherds who served in the church, those known at this time. After Saint Athanasius, patriarch of Antioch,
came Saint Mar John. In Edessa, the holy bishop Constantine was known, and in Harran, Saint Mar Simeon from the holy monastery of Qartmin.
In Samosata there was another Constantine, and in Maypherqat, Saint Mar Athanasius, who was called Sandalia. He also later became patriarch.
In Amida, after the [?] Mar Cosmas, there was Mar Saba, from the holy monastery of Zuqnin in the district belonging to the city.
When he had completed about twenty years, he died. Severus, from his own monastery, succeeded him.
This man too, after about one year, died in this same plague while it was raging. Then another Severus, again from the same monastery, succeeded him.
At this same time there was also a small disturbance in the church on account of Saint Mar John,
because not everyone was willing to submit to him, over the bringing of the royal treasury from the West to the Jazira.
When Marwan learned of the plotting of the westerners around him and wanted to bring that royal treasury to the Jazira, the westerners opposed him fiercely.
They began to turn against him. When he realized that they would not surrender it to him without a battle,
he deceived them by saying, “I want to take it to Damascus, not to the Jazira, because the royal seat is established there.”
When he did this, they allowed him to bring it to Damascus. They also came with him. He brought it in there and dismissed everyone to their homes,
after a few days had passed. When he had waited about two or three months, he secretly removed it without the westerners noticing and brought it to Harran.
He himself came and lived there. From then on, wars against him never ceased throughout his reign.
In the year 1058, Dahhak rose up as a Harurite in the Jazira. When Marwan came to the Jazira, and still
his troubles had not ceased, another evil growth sprang up against him from the land of the Jazira.
At this time a usurper appeared: Dahhak from Mount Izla, along with Jacob and Khabari, and also Saqsaqi.
These men rose up and fought many battles against Marwan, killing many of his people. After they had fought many battles everywhere,
he finally fought a fierce and violent battle at Tell Mashrita. Dahhak and his entire army were killed, and those who remained were routed and fled.
In the year 1059 there was a great tremor and earthquake in the land of the West. The earth shook violently, and the earth reeled,
swaying like a hut. These things, and things like them, and things far worse than these, are brought about by the injustices, sins, and evil deeds that we commit every day.
What cause can we point to for these tremors occurring, except the sins of human beings?
Is the earth perhaps coming loose, and then, when it shakes and trembles, does it call its maker to come and strengthen it? I do not think so.
Rather, it groans as it trembles because of the wicked people upon it, as it plainly demonstrated in an actual event [?]. There was an earthquake at night.
A sound like the bellowing of a bull could be heard from a great distance. When morning came, the bishop issued a firm order
that everyone should gather and fall down in supplication, saying that this event had occurred because of sins. When everyone had come for supplication,
they all went together outside the city to the church outside the city called the Church of the Mother of God—that is, the one at Mabbug in the western region.
They too were Chalcedonians, and their bishop himself went out at their head. When they arrived and reached the church, they all went inside,
like goats in a pen, and cried out together in prayer. Suddenly there was an earthquake,
and that building collapsed upon them and crushed them all, together with their bishop. They died in it, and no one escaped from it alive.
Instead, suddenly they were all together in one winepress of destruction and wrath. The righteous also perished with the sinner.
In the year 1060, the Persian people advanced against the land of Syria and also subdued the Arabs.
They ruled over the land in their place. Isaiah had prophesied about these people beforehand, saying, “Look, the Assyrian is the rod of my anger,
and the staff in their hands is my scourge. I will send him against a perverse nation, and commission him against a spiteful people.”
And again he said, “On that day the Lord will whistle for the flies at the lower reaches of the rivers of Egypt,
and also for the bees in the land of Assyria, and they will all settle in the desolate valley and in the clefts of the rock.”
These truly are the rod of anger, and the staff of scourging is in their hands, just as the prophet said.
They carried staffs in their hands, and at the end of each one was an iron spike. They resembled people going out to kill dogs.
As for his also calling them flies and bees: truly, just as flies buzz and settle on everything, making a swarm and also a foul smell,
so these people too are sorcerers, thieves, adulterers, and murderers. Wherever any one of them stayed,
he promoted wickedness, as well as strife and turmoil. They were stirred up from their own land
and advanced in great numbers, like a swarm of bees that look insignificant and do not turn back. In this way they gathered and advanced against the land.
The Arab army came down to confront them near Aqola, but it could not stand before them, because they devastated it. The survivors fled
and scattered. They took weapons, horses, and great wealth from them, for they had all been foot soldiers and had possessed nothing
except those staffs in their hands. Joel also spoke about them in this way: “Like the dawn spread over the mountains,
a numerous and mighty people, whose like has never existed before and will not exist afterward through the years of successive generations.
Before them fire devours, and behind them a flame burns. Before them the land is like the garden of Eden, but behind them it is a desolate wilderness.”
And no one escapes it. “Its appearance,” it says, “is like the appearance of a horse, and they run like horsemen.” The prophet rightly described it as the appearance of horses.
Like the mane that a horse has on its head and neck, they too have long hair like a horse’s mane.
And again he said: “They run like horsemen, and like the sound of chariots jolting over the mountaintops.”
“And like the sound of a flame of fire consuming stubble, and like a mighty people drawn up for battle. Before it the nations will tremble.”
“And every face will turn black like the soot on a pot. They will run like warriors, and climb walls like fighting men.”
And again: “They will climb into the cities, run along the walls, climb onto the houses, and enter through the windows like thieves.”
“Before it the earth was shaken and the heavens trembled.” Nahum also said: “Their appearance is like fiery torches, and they run like lightning.”
“They will seize their rulers and stumble as they go. They will hurry to the wall, and [?] will be prepared.”
And again: “All their faces are black like the soot on a pot.” It is not only their faces that are black,
but all their clothes are black as well. For his entire clothing is black. For this reason they were called
“Musawwida,” which in Syriac means “the black ones.” When they had conquered the lower land, Marwan again sent Ibn Hubayra against them at Nisibis.
He too was unable to stand against them; they defeated him as well. Then Abdallah son of Marwan came down in turn, and he too was defeated.
Marwan also came. They fought many battles, and on both sides they killed many of one another.
Finally they fought a harsh and fierce battle, and the earth was soaked with the great quantity of blood they shed upon it between the Zabs. Marwan was defeated and fled.
His army was scattered. He fled and crossed the Euphrates, and all the cities were shut against him. The westerners also wanted to fight against him.
From that point they disappeared, and neither he nor any of his men could be found. Of those they captured, he killed some, and they put some in prison.
When the Persians had defeated Marwan, they swept through the land like evening wolves and like an eagle hungry for food.
Habakkuk also prophesied about them when he said: “Look, I am raising up the Chaldeans, a bold and bitter people,”
“who march across the breadth of the earth to take possession of dwellings that are not theirs. They are mighty and fearsome, and their judgment proceeds from themselves.”
Indeed, they were marching across the breadth of the earth. “Their horses,” it says, “are swifter than leopards and fiercer than evening wolves.”
“They will swoop like an eagle hungry for food. They all come to plunder.” This prophet rightly compared them to evening wolves.
For the wolf, because it stays out of sight all day and cannot allow itself to be seen by people or dogs,
is hungry in the evening, since it has not eaten all day. “At the rising of the heavens [?],” it says, “they gather together,”
“and lie down in their dens. A person goes out to his work and his labor until evening.” Just as those are hungry and famished, so were they.
And like an eagle that cries out when it is hungry, so they cried out. Wherever they arrived, they seized the products of people’s labor like wolves.
As he said, “They all come to plunder. He mocks kings, scoffs at rulers, and laughs at every fortress.”
How aptly the prophecy says that he laughs at fortresses, since all the walls of the cities were torn down by their hands!
What capable and wise kings had built at great expense in gold, for protection against enemies, they destroyed.
He said, “He mocks kings and scoffs at rulers.” How did he mock or scoff, except by tearing down their fortifications?
The first conflict took place over the island of Akki. They issued an order that their supporters should blacken their clothing.
In the year 1054, the stars in the sky fell at the beginning of January,
on a Friday. They looked like balls of fire moving in every direction,
giving advance warning of the afflictions that afterward came upon the earth—war and plague—and of the coming of the Persians.
The year 1061. The Arabs rebelled. When the Arabs saw the evils that the Persians were inflicting on them,
and that they had no pity on them, killing them like sheep and taking them captive, they could endure it no longer and rebelled.
For he said, “He scoffs at kings and rulers.” And again, “The contemptible will rule over the great, and the dishonored over the honored.” They rebelled,
the Arabs. He killed a great many of them, and also drove them away, and they went down to their own land, although he had not reigned for a full year.
He stirred up rebellion, and Burika came forward as a Kharijite. In the year 1062, the Arabs of Maypherqat rebelled against their own region.
They began committing great atrocities against the inhabitants of the mountain and the surrounding country. Qura son of Thabit advanced against the district of Qulb.
He seized its leaders and killed seven of them. Then, when these things happened and they heard that men had been killed, their brothers, the inhabitants of the district of Phis,
took precautions so that they would not suffer harm from their brothers. A courageous, faithful, God-fearing man made preparations,
a man named John son of Dadi, from the village of Phis itself. He gathered all the inhabitants of the district of Phis
and spoke with them, saying, “Today you know that there is no king to exact payment for our blood from these men.
If we leave them alone, they will gather against us and sweep us and everything we have from the earth.” They readily listened to him and followed him.
They made him their leader. He also brought them into the holy church, and they swore to him by the divine mysteries that they would obey him in everything he commanded them,
that they would not disobey his word, and that they would not plot against him in any way. He acted with great courage, making God his leader above him.
He took his company and appointed for it commanders of armies, commanders of thousands, commanders of hundreds, commanders of fifties, and commanders of tens.
He also stationed guards at all the passes leading into the mountain. A man named Suda came forward, promising all the Arabs of
Maypherqat that he would bring them the severed heads of the mountain’s leaders and put all the rest in chains.
After making such promises, he took a large force with him and marched out against them, supposedly seeking peace.
But when they learned of his deceitful scheme, he suddenly attacked him and killed many of his people.
The rest fled and were killed by the horses beneath them, and he entered the city. From that time onward, great trouble arose among them.
Now both sides, the Arabs and the Christians, wanted the wretched man who had been living in the fortress of Qulab for two years

to come down from the fortress, but he would not agree. Instead, they stirred up trouble against him. The Arabs wanted to bring him down from there for fear that he would rebel against them together with the mountain people.
The Syrians also wanted him to come down, for fear that he would plot against them. But when he defied both sides, they drove him to rebellion in the fortress.
He also gathered reckless men around him and became their leader. He would take his whole band down to raid the villages and bring their people up to the fortress.
He suddenly attacked Alul and Pashpasht. He and his force committed every kind of outrage in them. He bound all their inhabitants and plundered everything they owned.
While they were mistreating the village's inhabitants, a message was secretly sent to John: “Come to our rescue, so that we are not carried away into captivity.”
When John heard about the distress of his brothers, he hurried, quickly took his force, and came down against them.
While it was still night, they surrounded the village where those men were. He sent them a message: “Come out of the village and go in peace.”
But he would not be persuaded. Instead, he took his armed force and went out to fight them. John attacked him, and he was killed,
along with his force. The Lord turned his wickedness back upon his own head, struck him down before them, and he died.
Now on that mountain there was a man who was one of their leaders, called Stephen son of Paul, one of the mountain people. He was an oppressive and deceitful man.
This man trampled on the oath to God that he had sworn to John before the divine mysteries, and continually dealt deceitfully with them,
while his heart was set on surrendering to the Arabs. He treacherously sent for an Arab force, and Awf came to him with a large force, to the village called Hadu.
In his deceit, he made a secret agreement with them to bring John and deliver him into Awf's hands.
Indeed, he acted and carried out his plan as he wished. But God did not grant the wicked man his desire, and the plot that he devised against the innocent man
came down upon their own heads. They filled with their own bodies the pit that he had dug. They brought Awf and his two companions inside the house,
and he hid them in an inner room. He agreed with them that when they brought John and led him into the house to meet him,
they would come out of the inner room and kill him. He also stationed the force [?] in ambush around the village.
He quickly sent for John: “Hurry and come without delay. Let us see what we can do, for an army surrounds us on every side.”
In his innocence, John arrived quickly, like a lamb to the slaughter, knowing nothing. But as he was about to enter the house where the ambush lay waiting for him,
a faithful and God-fearing man who knew about the secret plot was made available to him, as though by God's will.
He revealed the plot to him, and John quickly turned back. While they were waiting for him to come so that they could carry out
their desire against him, he sent a force against the troops with them while they were still unaware, and surrounded them on every side.
Not one of them escaped. Instead, he impaled them all on stakes, while Stephen was still unaware, as was Awf, their commander.
When he learned what had happened to their companions, he mounted the swift horses they had with them and tried to escape.
But even so they did not escape, because swift men pursued them, overtook him, and killed him and his companions with the sword [?], and he died.
But when Stephen saw that his deceit and that of Satan his father had been exposed, he fled and escaped to the city and did not die. He never went up to the mountain again, because he was afraid.
From this point onward, evil upon evil increased between the mountain people and the Arabs. Every day they committed countless killings against one another.
The mountain people seized the gates, and not a single Arab was seen anywhere on the mountain. But another plunderer arose against them from within their own territory.
He was a man from Urta named Gregory. He marched against them with a large force and fought the people of Nahr de-Harre.
He killed a great many of them, and they captured the rest and mutilated their bodies.
He cut off the ears of some and the noses of others, and he burned out the eyes of others with fire.
All the people of the Dry Mountain restrained themselves and submitted to John. In the eastern regions, however,
Burayka rose in rebellion. In the region of Edessa, Ubayd Allah son of Bukhtari also rose up.
This man inflicted great evils on many people, especially in Beth Ma'dma. He seized its leading men and roasted them like
fish over a fire for the sake of gold. He killed many, took captives, and devastated them. As for all the monasteries in the territory of Edessa, Harran, and Tella,
he devastated them and took everything they had produced. He also roasted their superiors in the fire, and they died.
These are the monasteries he destroyed, along with many villages: the monastery of Qubbe, and the monastery of Rishmath, which is in Tishpa,
and the monastery of Qatra, the great monastery of Hasmi, the monastery of Saint Lazarus, Beth Ma'da, and the monastery of Saint Abel,
and the monastery of Saint Migas, and the monastery of Sanin, along with many villages. This wicked man's entire fury was directed against the monasteries.
Satan also stirred him up against the churches. Every day he threatened the eastern and northern monasteries
with carrying out against them the vengeance of Satan his father. On the three severe winters that occurred one after another, and the heavy snow that fell during them,
and the destruction of livestock, wild animals, and birds that died [?] because of the intense cold during those winters.
In this same year there was unrest. Heavy snow fell and piled up on the ground to a depth of five spans.
It remained on the ground for ninety days, and in the plains it remained for seventy days, until all living creatures were close to perishing.
Many people who owned livestock also had wheat. When all the livestock's supply of feed consisting of [?] had run out,
they brought out their wheat and poured it out before their livestock so that it would not die of hunger. Yet their livestock could not survive on their wheat.
Instead, it all perished like locusts. People could not even eat their meat. There was intense cold, ice, and severe frost. It froze solid.
Darkness lay over the earth for many days, so that a person could barely see the path before his feet.
And it settled on the trees, vineyards, and olive trees like snow, until it dried up all the trees, vineyards, olive trees, and gardens.
There was hardly anything that was not affected by the severity of the ice and frost. The rivers froze solid.
Horses could even cross them at a gallop, and the ice beneath them did not move.
Even the Tigris itself froze, so that a large caravan of camels could cross it without the ice beneath their feet moving.
All the wild animals and the birds of the sky perished. Thus there were snow, cold, and frost, together with famine, strife, sickness, and pestilence,
for three successive years, until the whole northern land was close to destruction.
On the famine that occurred during these years, and on the Armenian and Urtian peoples who came out into the land of Syria.
Now snow covered the whole earth for many days. Days passed, and the surface of the earth remained hidden.
All the seed that had been sown spoiled beneath the snow as it rotted; it was weakened by the ice and dried up. And when the snow disappeared,
nothing grew except brush and thorns. The prophet’s saying was fulfilled upon us: “Cursed is the ground because of you.
It will bring forth thorns and thistles for you. When you cultivate it, it will no longer yield its strength to you.” And another says:
“You have sown wheat and harvested thorns. You have toiled but gained nothing. Be ashamed of your harvests.”
The earth brought forth thorns, thistles, and brush for us. Instead of wheat, darnel grew; instead of barley, thistles grew.
Instead of beans, lentils, and chickpeas, thorns grew for us. When a little happened to sprout and grow up,
mildew and blight descended on it and ruined it. If it escaped the cold, ice, and blight, caterpillars and weevils attacked it and ruined it.
If you took ten ears of grain and rubbed them in your hand, not a single grain of wheat could be found in them. Thus, because of the blight,
many fields remained unharvested, visibly red as they stood. The poison that had descended on them was red.
It descended and remained on them like frost that remains on trees in winter. Even the color of the wheat itself changed to red.
Concerning these things, the prophet Amos cries out to us: “I struck you with blight, mildew, and hail.
The locust devoured the abundance of your gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees. Yet you did not return to me, says the Lord.
I sent pestilence among you. I killed your young men with the sword, [?] your old men. I made the stench of your decay strike your faces.”
During this year, wheat was being sold at one griba for a dinar, and the quantity fell to seven qafizes for a dinar.
On the weevils and caterpillars with which the earth swarmed during these years. When harvest time was approaching and everyone was waiting for [?],
the earth swarmed with a great multitude of creeping creatures. They climbed onto the wheat, barley, and all the green plants, though the place where they fed could not be detected.
Every ear of grain that it reached was ruined. And if the grains of wheat were nearly ripe, they would suddenly
dry up, leaving nothing in them but the husk alone. This showed those who could discern
that it was sucking the moisture out of the ear of grain. The ear’s strength was also drained away, and it quickly changed color.
People called it a tick and a weevil, because it was not just one species or one form. It was round and patterned—
the one they called a tick. The weevil is likewise round and small, and its snout is long, like that of a [?].
But it was a mixed swarm, mottled with many colors. In the opinion of the wise, this was the very plague sent upon the Egyptians through Moses.
For it was the crawling locust, the cricket, and the mixed swarm. This plague attacked nothing except wheat.
It clung to the stalk of wheat or barley from its root to its head, and to the leaves. Concerning caterpillars.
There were also great numbers of caterpillars, which ruined vineyards, trees, and all the fruit. There were so many that people could not even walk on the ground.
They were spread everywhere, for the earth itself was spewing them out and bringing them forth. Thus the vineyards, trees, fruit, and crops were ruined,
along with everything people depended on for their livelihood. Concerning locusts. It is written in the prophet: “He gave their crops to the locust and all their labor to the crawling locust.”
This is the locust that travels on foot, having no wings with which to fly away. Its destruction is great and worse than that of all the other scourges of wrath.
As for the weevil, it was said that if it settled on a heap of wheat, it ruined it. Evidence of
this was that when it settled on a field [?] that was ripe and nearly ready for harvest, the wheat was ruined.
Although the grains looked plump and fine on the outside, when they were broken open, their insides had become like flour.
Even if they were sown, they did not sprout, because they were ruined. Not even the lower country escaped this affliction.
The whole earth spewed out locusts. They spread and ruined their crops, vineyards, gardens, trees, and every green plant.
The prophecy spoken through the prophet Joel was fulfilled against us: “Hear this, elders, and listen, all inhabitants of the land:
Has anything like this happened in your days or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children about it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.
What the caterpillar left, the flying locust ate; what the flying locust left, the crawling locust ate; and what the crawling locust left,
the cricket destroyed.” Here still more came upon us beyond what was in the prophecy: snow and frost, which ruined all the trees.
Whatever escaped these was overtaken by blight, mildew, locusts, crawling locusts, crickets, mixed swarms, and caterpillars,
until famine bore down on people beyond measure. Wheat began to disappear from the storehouses, and the amount available fell
to one griba for a dinar, and then to seven qafizes for a dinar, and there was none. Concerning the Armenian and Urtian people,
who came into the regions of Syria because of the famine; and concerning the wasting disease, dysentery, pestilence, and various illnesses that entered the land when they came.
Now God sent many afflictions upon the wheat, the barley, the vineyards, and everything that sustained human life, because of the sins and wrongs committed by us every
day. Famine grew severe in the land, especially in Armenia and Beth Urtaye, because all their crops had been ruined.
Nothing could be found to sustain them. For when he wishes, he dries things up with cold; and when he wishes again, he waters them with love.
Here, then, he dried them up with cold. All Armenia went into exile because of the famine that had come upon them, and they departed for Syria,
fearing that they and their children might die of hunger. Yet even in this way they did not escape the wrath.
“I will give them bitter water to drink and gall to eat. I will scatter them among nations that did not know them.
I will send the sword, captivity, famine, and pestilence after them, until I destroy them.” These things the Spirit said. And all these things happened.
They went out, and the whole land was filled with them: cities, monasteries, villages, and farms. They sold everything they owned and bought themselves bread.
Famine prevailed in the land. They were also afflicted first by a disease of boils and an intestinal illness, and then by dysentery.
Wherever any of them managed to reach, they lay prostrate: in porticoes, halls, churches, towers, and everywhere else. Pestilence also took hold of them.
Most of them died, until people could no longer keep up with burying them. For wherever they went, the hand of the Lord was against them to bring disaster.
This affliction of famine, boils, and dysentery also took hold of the Syrians themselves and destroyed them.
Those killed by famine were more numerous than those killed by disease. In this same year, there also died from our monastery
of Zuqnin, from this very dysentery, forty-two people, not counting outsiders. This disease and pestilence grew severe everywhere.
The year 1060. The Persians returned against the land with large armies. They fought and defeated everyone who met them in battle.
They carried out a great slaughter among the Arabs of Mosul and Aqula, putting great and small alike to the sword.
Abdallah ibn Muhammad, the brother of the king of the Persians, advanced and fought Burayka near Dara. He defeated him, and Burayka fled before him.
When Abdallah heard about all the evil that the Arabs of Maypherqat had done to the Syrians of their region, and about what the Syrians had also done,
he sent messengers to summon John, who went down to him at Harran. He received him gladly, honored him, and also gave him gifts.
He appointed him governor over his region and sent him there. Meanwhile, Salih ibn Sabih went up, entering Armenia.
He took hostages from the whole mountain region and placed them in Maypherqat before John [?] from Harran, from Abdallah’s presence.
He also brought up with him a letter ordering that his hostages be handed over to him. When he arrived, he released all the females among them.
But because the Arabs of Maypherqat had given Salih a bribe to take revenge for them on John and his companions, he put him off with words, saying,
“Today or tomorrow I will release the rest.” So a long time passed, and various illnesses took hold of them.
Many of them died in prison, while this man continued putting him off with words for many days.
He wanted to find grounds against him, so that he might destroy both him and them, to please the Arabs of Maypherqat. Then there sent
John messengers to Abdullah, who was emir over the Jazira.
On the day when Salih was due to crucify John on a wooden cross, at [?] of the day, a messenger arrived to fetch him.
He brought him out of prison. He went down to Harran with Stephen son of Paul. There the Lord struck Stephen, and he died.
The Lord brought his wickedness upon [?]. John, however, sent a letter and quickly released all those whom Salih had imprisoned while he was emir.
In the year 1061, Constantine, emperor of the Romans, marched out with large armies. He demolished Melitene and scattered it.
He expelled its inhabitants without killing anyone or taking any of their possessions as plunder. Instead, he drove them out and expelled them from it.
They all went out to the Jazira. He demolished its wall and burned its houses. Then he took his army and returned to his own land. In the year 1064:
The Persians demolished the cities. When the Persians returned a second time, conquered the land and its fortresses, and ruled over it,
the king gave orders and demolished all the walls of the cities of Syria.
They gathered many stonemasons and craftsmen and demolished all the walls. He burned their gates
and took the bronze and iron in them. What capable and wise kings had built at great expense for protection against enemies,
these men, in their tyranny, demolished and razed to the ground. Jeremiah's words were fulfilled concerning them: “The broad walls shall be utterly demolished,
and her high gates shall be burned with fire, and the peoples shall labor in vain.” Again he said, “The Lord resolved to destroy the walls of daughter Zion.
He stretched out a measuring line and did not withdraw his hand from destroying her. He brought her ramparts into mourning, and her walls became desolate together.”
Let this prophet Jeremiah come and lament, not over Zion alone, whose walls were demolished, but over all the cities of the Jazira and the West.
Ezra the scribe also spoke about the destruction of the walls and about this crooked seer who razed them: “The walls—”
And about this crooked serpent who razed them: “He will bring low the walls that have not sinned against him.” “One builds,” he says, “and another tears down.”
In the year 1065, the whole northern land was plundered by Kushan. This man was an Armenian from Fourth Armenia.
When Marwan was defeated and fled, he took all his possessions and his household and entered Roman territory. Because he was a brave and powerful man,
Constantine made him commander of the army. In that same year he marched out with a large army and attacked the whole of Mount Sahya.
He took captives and plundered all the villagers living there. He took their property and everything they owned. He left nothing that they did not take,
except the bare lives of the people who remained, which he did not take. Thus he took everything
and entered Roman territory. In the year 1066, Kushan the Armenian again marched out into the land of Hanzit
with large armies of Romans and Urtaye [?]. When Akki, who was emir over the Jazira at that time, heard,
He gathered a large army of Persians and Arabs around him. He also put his son in command of them and sent him to fight Kushan.
When the young man advanced in pride and with great arrogance in his heart, and the armies encountered one another, he despised them. For youth is prone to disorder, and when it does not
exercise judgment or listen, it falls into the depths of misfortune. Older men who had grown up in warfare,
and who also knew the many circumstances that arise in war and its changing fortunes, advised him and told him not to rush into fighting him.
For he was a man experienced in warfare, strong and not one to turn back. He also knew the land and its features, since he had been born and raised there.
But he rejected the advice of the elders who counseled him—a second Rehoboam, a foolish son—and followed the advice of the young men who had grown up with him.
As he hurried to gain a name and victory for himself [?], he suddenly acquired a dishonorable name, full of disgrace and shame, for many generations after him.
He advanced rashly, intending to fall upon him swiftly and wipe him and everyone with him from the earth,
and also to bind the rest, plunder, take captives, and come away with a great victory. But when Kushan saw the young man and his behavior,
he stamped his [?], curled his lip, shook his head, and said, “This is the day the Lord has made for taking revenge on my enemies.
Come, then, let us rejoice and be glad in it!” When he drew near to fight, and the slain began to fall on both sides, Kushan pressed hard against the Persians.
They began fleeing before him, and they all fell before them by the sword. They hunted down many, took captives, and stripped the slain.
The son of Akki fled, stripped of his equipment, on the swift horse beneath him. He escaped, leaving all his baggage in the hands of the Romans.
Except for a few of them who were riding horses and abandoned everything they owned and fled, not one of them escaped being put to the sword.
While the young man was hurrying to gain fame and victory, he brought a foul reputation upon himself and his father’s house. Instead of what he had intended—
to plunder, take captives, and bind many—he was plundered [?], and they were bound and went into captivity. Orthodox shepherds known in the church at this time:
The holy Mar John, patriarch of Antioch, and the holy Mar Michael [?], patriarch of Alexandria the Great;
and the holy Mar Timothy of Edessa; Constantine, bishop of Samosata; Dionysius, bishop of Harran; Sergius [?], bishop of Madra;
David, bishop of Dara, who later also became patriarch. In Maipherqat [?], Athanasius, who was called the Sandal-maker, was known.
He built the famous monastery on the mountain of Tel Beshme. It is also called the Monastery of Mar Athanasius. He too later became patriarch.
In Amid, the holy Mar Abai, from the Monastery of Mar Habib in Arzanene, was known. As for the holy Mar Severus,
whom we mentioned above, from the monastery of Zuqnin, he was relieved of the administration of the city while he was still alive, because his eyesight had grown dim
and he could not see well. The holy Mar Abai took his place. John, bishop of Callinicum, was also known.
He caused disturbances in the church, which we will also recount in their proper time.
After the holy Mar John, patriarch of Antioch, there was a monk named Isaac from the monastery of Qartmin. He established a dwelling for himself in Edessa.
And because, it is said, he practiced the alchemy of silver and gold, he became friends with Abdallah, the emir of Jazira, who later also became king.
When he wanted to honor him for his friendship, he made him patriarch of Antioch after Mar John. But very evil are the offices
acquired through disorderly means. When this man had greatly exalted his friend, he soon reached out and gave him the noose of Judas.
He was not well received by the people, nor did his leadership last very long. For the very man who had exalted him overthrew him and also destroyed him.
The people did not even know what had happened to his body, and he was not granted even a burial by human hands.
This is the fine reward Satan is accustomed to giving those who run after him in this world. After him came the chaste Mar Athanasius Sandalaya, bishop of Maypherqat.
But this man too did not last many days, since he also soon perished and died. Others, however, tell different accounts.
We do not dare to say anything about hidden matters. Instead, we leave them to God, before whom everything is revealed and laid bare.
They took him and brought him up from Harran to his monastery, where he was buried. After him came the holy Mar George, from the holy monastery of Qenneshre.
Concerning the synod assembled during the tenure of George, patriarch of Antioch, in the city of Mabbug on the Euphrates River,
in the church of Mar Thomas the Apostle outside the city. During the tenure of Isaac the patriarch, there were many occasions for scandal,
and also during that of Athanasius Sandalaya, who was likewise patriarch, which caused the faithful to stumble. Many members of the church stumbled because of them.
This was especially because they had been appointed by the emir of the tyrannical government, along with other troubles that followed them, which there is no need to set down in this book.
After the death of the venerable Athanasius, all the shepherds of the holy church wanted to appoint a head for themselves before Satan should cast among them a love

of leadership, and they should fall into the hands of the tyrannical government, and the latter state become worse than the former, with division, strife, and turmoil arising in the holy church in their days.
This indeed happened to them, as was said by the righteous man: the fear that he feared came upon them.
They had no peace, nor was there quiet, and turmoil entered. What they had dreaded quickly overtook them.
All the shepherds together, those of Mosul, Jazira, and the western regions, agreed, and they quickly assembled with one soul and one good purpose,
and in complete agreement. All the bishops, together with respected and faithful men, agreed to meet in the city of Mabbug, in the church of Mar Thomas.
They sat for a day or two, and much was said among them about many candidates. When one praised someone, another came and objected. This continued for many days.
Then, finally, it happened that there was a man at Beeltan, from the holy monastery of Qenneshre, who lived chastely in that place.
He was adorned with a God-fearing way of life. He was also a well-known and renowned man, a teacher of doctrine and a zealous advocate of everything good.
His name was George, and he had been appointed to the order of deacons in his monastery. All of them, equally, in complete agreement and concord,
chose and approved him while he was far away. They then quickly selected some of the respected men there and sent them to bring him to them.
They all went in and greeted him. They also put their agreement in writing, affixed their signatures to the document, and gave it to him. At their head was John of Callinicum.
Timothy of Edessa; David of Dara; Abai of Amid [?]; Sargona of Mardin; Stephen of Khabur; and Constantine of Samosata. Page 213. Cyriacus of Tur Abdin.
Dionysius of Harran; Elijah of Sinjar; and, from Mosul, Paul of Tikrit; Zakkai of Karma; Jonah of Beth Nuhadra; together with many others.
These also came from the West. When he had written, completed, and sealed the document, and they were all about to lay hands on him according to the established order of the church,

Satan saw that peace was about to come to the whole church. He did not neglect the matter, remain quiet and still, or rest even from this. Instead, he quickly made arrangements and brought a certain monk there.
He made him his dwelling place. For he himself could not appear openly, stir up trouble, cause disorder, and sow divisions among them,
just as he had been unable to speak to Eve in his own person, lest his deception be revealed and exposed.
So here too he acted and accomplished his purpose. There he chose the serpent, entered it, and dwelt in it, and through it carried out everything he desired. Here,
he chose a monk as his advocate and through him accomplished everything he desired. His name was John. His residence was in Shuharta, with the name reversed [?].
He had been going about for a long time under the guise of living as a stranger. Claiming to know this George, he approached these bishops of Mesopotamia,
especially those of Qartmin, and said, “How can you wish to make a man your patriarch who has threatened your monastery,
saying, ‘If I gain authority in the church, I will wipe the name of Qartmin and of the monastery of Athanasius from the earth’?”
When he had greatly disturbed and unsettled them with these things, they, having no confidence in the holy George,
believed that man’s words, without realizing that all their force came from Satan. They got up, mounted quickly, and secretly took
themselves away, departing for their own country. When those who remained saw that their companions had departed, they became still more alarmed and afraid.
First, they feared that they might bring division and disorder into the church if they appointed him while their companions were absent. Second, they had already put the man forward,
and he was now in danger of being disgraced and becoming a cause of stumbling in the world. For those who do wrong do not recount a matter as it really happened,
especially at a distance. Those who remained, after considering both the good and the bad, and especially because their conscience caused some hesitation [?],
came forward and appointed him. The notable men among those from Mesopotamia were these: Matthias of Edessa; Abai of Amid; Constantine of Samosata;
John of Callinicus; together with all the others from Mosul and the West. But those who had departed earlier were leaving no stone unturned.
When everyone had departed and gone to his own country, Satan still did not remain quiet or cease sowing disorder among them. He incited them in this way:
many of the Mesopotamians gathered and made John of Callinicus, from the holy monastery of Qarqaphta, their patriarch.
He violated the agreement, the covenants, and his own written pledge, fell prey to the love of power, and became patriarch.
From then on, the whole dignified and chaste monastic order suffered mockery, insults, and abuse.
Many anathematized the one and everyone who accepted him, while many anathematized the other. Thus this disorder in the church has continued down to the present.
From then on, what insults, what mockery, what denunciations, what evils did not arise among them! They even went as far as imprisonment at the hands of the tyrannical authorities.
See what evils came upon the church and its shepherds through that evil monk, who took the place of the deceitful serpent
and crooked, and brought turmoil into the church through his words and counsel. In the year 1065,
Abdallah son of Muhammad, king of the Persians, died. Then his brother Abdallah contended for the leadership,
as did another Abdallah, son of Ali, his uncle. From then on there was nothing but bloodshed and many killings among them.
All the westerners and the Arabs of Mesopotamia supported the son of Ali, pledged allegiance to him, and wanted him as king.
And all of them [?] and went out after him. The Persians and the people of Khorasan, however, supported Abdallah son of Muhammad. They fought many battles everywhere,
and much blood was shed on the ground by one another. Finally, they fought a battle on the River Masha, below Nisibis.
After they had fought there like this for many days, and many people on both sides had fallen, Abdallah son of Ali was finally defeated
by Abu Muslim the Persian. He was routed, fled, and perished, on the twenty-sixth of November, on Tuesday as Wednesday dawned.
The son of Ali was defeated, and Abdallah son of Muhammad took possession of the kingdom for [?] years. On that very evening of the defeat of the son of Ali,
God performed a great wonder: a certain great, alarming, and terrifying star
flew across and cleaved the sky and the air. At sunset it descended into the middle of the army of the son of Ali, in the form of a ball of fire.
When the Arabs saw this, their hope was shattered and lost, and their eyes grew dark.
They could no longer stand their ground, because they knew clearly that this had come from the Lord, and they could endure no longer.
In the year 1066, the trees bore apples, peaches, and all kinds of fruit
in October and November, as they do in the season of April and May. In that same year there was abundant grain throughout the land. In the year 1067,
on the third of March [?], a Tuesday, there was a great, alarming, and terrifying earthquake at midnight in the land of Mesopotamia.
Three villages on the [?] were overturned by it. And the people—and three villages on the Khabur were overturned by it.
Many people within them were crushed inside them like grapes in a winepress, and perished, along with many places that the earthquake destroyed.
It happened because of the great abundance of our sins. For it says, “The earth will surely reel, and the earth will surely totter, and sway like a hut.” Our sins can do these things:
shake the earth beneath us. In the year 1070, there was confusion over the Easterners’ fast. Some of them began the fast on the eighteenth of February
and ended it on the sixth of April. The others began the fast on the twenty-fifth of February and ended it on the thirteenth of April.
Thus all the Christians were thrown into confusion: in one place they celebrated Easter, while in another they celebrated Palm Sunday;
in one place they observed the Passion, while in another they celebrated Easter. They did the same in the cities: in one church they celebrated Easter, while in another they celebrated Palm Sunday.
Many of those inclined to gluttony fasted for only six weeks, beginning with the later group and breaking their fast with the earlier group.
But many others who were caught in the middle perished because of the stumbling block that arose among them: they entered with the first and settled with the last.
In the year 1071, in the month of Adar, a white sign appeared in the sky before dawn.
It was in the northeast, in the constellation called Aries, north of the three stars that shine most brightly in it.
Its shape resembled a broom. At that time, two of the wandering stars were also in Aries, at its beginning, in the first degree:
Saturn and Mars, a little to the south. This was on the twenty-second of the month. The sign remained for fifteen nights,
until the dawn of the feast of Pentecost. One end of it, the narrow one, was brighter, and a star could be seen in it; it inclined toward the north.
The other end, broad and dimmer, inclined toward the south. It moved gradually toward the northeast.
Its shape was as follows. On the eve of Tuesday after Pentecost, it appeared again at evening, in the northwest.
It remained for twenty-five evenings, moving gradually southward. Then it disappeared again. Afterward it reappeared in the southwest,
and remained there in this way for many days. At this time many divisions arose in the church over its leadership.
The eastern monasteries made John patriarch, but the cities of Mesopotamia did not accept him, nor did all the monasteries.
The westerners and the people of Mosul, however, accepted George. Because of this, the whole church was thrown into turmoil.
In the year 1072, the holy Mar Timothy, bishop of Edessa, died. He was succeeded by a certain monk, a recluse,
who lived in a village in that region called Beth Qedona. His name was Simeon.
Because of his chastity and virtue, and because he was adorned with every excellence, especially love for strangers and the poor,
the entire community of the faithful in Edessa, unanimously and in agreement, wanted him to become the shepherd of their souls.
So they forcibly broke open his cell, seized him, and brought him to Patriarch George to make him their leader.
But this chaste Simeon loved the quiet, chaste, and restful labors of monastic life more than becoming a bishop and standing at the head of the people.
He was unwilling and would not accept this burden of leadership. Although the venerable George pressed him greatly, and the people of Edessa wept before him,
he remained unwilling and would not accept. So they seized him by force and ordained him entirely against his will.
The venerable George also called heaven and earth, God and his angels, to witness against him, charging him not to leave the city and his flock and move elsewhere.
Thus, after binding him under many anathemas not to move away or flee, they took him and brought him to Edessa.
All the people of Edessa came out and welcomed him with great splendor. After he had been in the city for a day or two,
without eating bread or drinking water, until he was close to losing his life,
he persuaded them to allow him to leave and stay in one of the monasteries on the mountain of Edessa, for he said, “The air here is oppressive to me.”
the city. And so he settled in a monastery south of the city, called the House of the Mother of God.
Every day the clergy and leading men went up to him there, urging him to enter his city and take charge of it.
But he would not agree to this on any account, saying, “Even if I must die or be crucified,
I will never do this. Leave me alone, for God’s sake, and appoint whomever you wish as your bishop.”
But the people of Edessa would not even consent to hear this with their own ears, because of their love for him.
And so the whole winter passed, while he refused to be persuaded either to enter the city or to perform an ordination for them,
or to celebrate a feast for them. Nor would they let him leave them, because their hearts longed for him.
Even the Arabs and heretics of the city loved him.
Finally, when they saw that they were achieving nothing, they pleaded with him: “Find us a God-fearing man to take your place, and let us complete the arrangements for the episcopate,
provided that you do not go far away from us.” But he would not agree even to this, saying, “You are a stubborn people! Choose a bishop for yourselves,
and do not burden me with any trouble.” Because they did not want him to leave them, they laid this whole responsibility upon him.
But he would not accept even this at all. When he saw that nothing was helping and that he could not escape their hands,
he said to them, “Place the word of God before me: you must accept whomever I bring, while I too will not [?] from you.”
They all went in and swore to him. Now there happened to be a man who was humble, kind, and quiet, and adorned with every divine virtue,
in the holy monastery of Zuqnin, in the territory of Amida, who was called Anastasius the Cushite. This was the man whom Simeon chose above everyone else
to entrust with his position. He also took upon himself the risk concerning him and, though far away, testified about him: “There is no one like him today among the monks.”
Such was the testimony this holy man gave about this virtuous man, although he had never seen him in person.
He then proceeded to write letters with a stratagem to this chaste man and to all the honored elders of his monastery, as though he wished to see him and speak with him.
He sent some of his own respected men to fetch him. But when he received the letters, he knew that they were full of guile,
and he would not come down. Nor would the members of his monastery hand him over. Thus his messengers went up and came down empty-handed many times.
Finally the members of his monastery persuaded him, since Simeon did not cease sending letters and appeals, and because they did not want to slight the venerable Simeon.
He and his disciple came down to him at Edessa, and then went up to him on the mountain where he was living.
He came out and welcomed him with great joy. He quickly sent a secret message to the members of the church and the leading men of the city,
without the chaste Anastasius knowing anything at all, saying, “The man I promised you has now arrived.”
At this, everyone, great and small, quickly came out and went up to him. They saw him and rejoiced greatly over him.
First of all, they all placed him under the same obligation: he was not to turn aside in either direction at all until they gave him permission.
When the modest Mar Anastasius heard these things, he trembled and became alarmed. His face changed color, and he became like a dead man.
He severely reproached the members of his monastery, [?] for bringing him into such a situation, and especially the holy Simeon. And when he had pleaded with him
for many days and he had not agreed, they devised a plan against him: they would seize him by force, take him to the patriarch, and have him ordained.
But when he learned of this plan that the people of Edessa had devised against him, he got up during the night, took his disciple, and departed for his monastery.
The holy Simeon also asked their permission to leave when he saw that the honored Anastasius had departed. He said, “I have done for you what you asked of me.
Now let me go.” So he left them and departed for the mountain of the Samosatans. There he lived until the end of his life,
welcoming the strangers and afflicted people who came to him, for he was a haven for all who were in distress.
Zechariah, from the monastery, became bishop there in his place. He too was brought down from a pillar.
In the year 1075, there was a great epidemic among horses throughout the land. This epidemic spread over the whole earth.
It began at the outermost ends of the earth and gradually advanced and spread throughout the land. The animals perished from it so quickly, in the blink of an eye.
This destruction was so swift that when a horse herder drove a herd containing three hundred mares down to a watering place,
twenty or thirty would fall at the watering place itself and perish there. The valleys, hills, ravines, and roads were full of them, and they lay rotting.
Its appearance resembled that of the plague swellings that had broken out among human beings, for it took hold in their necks.
Not one of them could withstand this disease for even a single hour. If, however, one of them happened to feel its effects
and survived for two hours or half a day, it would escape death. Barely one in a hundred escaped among those
that were stricken. Mares, mules, and donkeys died of it, one after another. This disease spread among all the peoples and kingdoms of the earth, until people were left without horses.
The work of that broom which had appeared a short time before was plainly demonstrated in what happened, as it swept the world
like a broom sweeping a house. Discerning and God-fearing people also believed that this bitter scourge had been sent against human beings,
but that through God's mercy, his abundant grace, and his love for humanity, he had diverted it from human beings to animals.
This bears witness to us that the animals had not sinned or angered the Lord by the work of their hands and by their sins.
“I killed your young men with the sword,” Amos says, “along with the capture of your horses. I made the stench of your decay rise into your faces.
Yet you did not return to me,” says the Lord. Micah also said, “On that day,” says the Lord, “I will destroy the horses from among you, and I will destroy your chariots.”
Truly, he destroyed horses and chariots from the earth, just as the prophets said. Our sins brought this about, so that creatures without speech suffered in our place.
In the year 1072, Abdallah son of Muhammad, king of the Persians, sent Ibn Wahb with a large army and troops from throughout the Jazira.
And he rebuilt Melitene in Cappadocia, which had remained in ruins for eight years.
They brought people and troops into it, and it was inhabited and enjoyed greater peace than before. In the year 1076, the stars in the sky fell.
In the month of January, on the fourth, a Friday, when darkness began to fall and the stars began to rise,
two stars appeared in the middle of the sky, fighting with each other, like people fighting or engaging in battle with
one another. They continued moving in this way, fighting as they descended toward the east. When these had descended and gone out, all the stars in the sky began to fall,
darting like balls of fire shooting in every direction. This falling continued throughout that whole night.
And the words of our Savior were fulfilled, which say: “The sun will be darkened, and the moon will turn to blood. The stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken.”
“But,” he says, “the end is not yet.” Let the reader understand the things that happened afterward in the world and judge:
whether it was because of the turmoil and divisions that arose in the church on account of the patriarchs George and David, when all the Christians turned against one another,
or, again, because of the afflictions people suffered under tyrannical rule, and their flight from city to city, from one country to another, and from village to village.
He says again: “There will be great affliction, the like of which has not occurred from the beginning of the world until today.”
“Pray,” he says, “that your flight will not be in winter. Woe to those who are pregnant and those who are nursing in those days!”
Read, discerning reader, and go on to see what evils happened afterward in the world. Look, we have recorded them at their proper times.
What afflictions! What evils! What divisions, torments, and blows! What flights! What acts of plunder!
What [?]! What apostasies of sons and daughters, and separations of wives from their husbands! What famines!
What diseases! What pestilences! Consider all these things, discerning reader, which came after that falling of the stars.
Besides this, all peoples, nations, and kingdoms were brought low and fell before this tyrannical power. No human being could stand against it.
At this time, the religion of the Manichaeans in Harran, a city in Mesopotamia, became an object of ridicule. They happened to have a monastery east of Harran,
about a mile away from the city. In this monastery they held a great and terrible festival once every year.
There they offered sacrifices, and their wicked bishop lived there. That great festival took place there, and there they performed [?].
When their festival was approaching, they had a custom of seizing a man and keeping him imprisoned from one year to the next.
At their festival they sacrificed him. They would take his head, it is said, put a coin in its mouth, and place it in a niche. They worshiped it and used it for divination.

Now, when the day of their wicked festival drew near, they wanted to bring in the man whom they were preparing to imprison, so that he would be their sacrifice for the festival following the one that was about to take place.
The leaders of the Manichaeans wrote a letter and went out into the marketplace of Harran. When they found a man of the sort they wanted,
they took hold of him and said to him, “Take as much payment as you wish, and go and deliver this letter to such-and-such a monastery, to its abbot.”
But he did not know about Satan’s scheme, which was intended to destroy the poor man. In his cleverness, he hurried along like a lamb to the slaughter.
When he quickly reached that monastery and approached its gate, he asked those who came out to meet him about their abbot, and urged them to call him.
They hurried inside and told him. When their abbot heard, he quickly came out and welcomed that man with honor and great joy.
He said to him, “Come in, rest a little, and eat some bread. You will receive the reply to your letter and go
in peace.” They led the man into one room after another—one, two, three, and still more, six and seven—
until they reached a man who had been imprisoned since the previous year. He was being kept ready to be brought out for sacrifice at the approaching festival.
He instructed him, “Sit here beside this man.” When he sat down, he said to him, “Sit here beside this man.” When he sat down, that man said to him,
“Woe to you! What has happened to you?” He replied, “Why?” The other said, “He did the same to me. When I came here, I found another man sitting here.
At their festival they sacrificed him. Look, his head is in this niche. A lamp burns for them in front of it, and they bow down to it and practice divination through it.
And now they are preparing to kill me at this festival. Then you will sit in my place until the next festival, and then you too will be brought out for sacrifice.
But if you want to escape from here, listen to me, and it will go well for you. Look, when they are ready to kill me, stand beside me.
When my head falls to the ground, pick it up quickly while my blood is spurting, and make for the gate.
If they approach you, whether they plead with you or offer you many gifts, do not put it down. If they try to seize you, sprinkle some of that blood toward them, and they will run away from you.”
That man took to heart what he had told him, with a fine fury, and carried it out completely, leaving nothing undone.
When they killed him, he picked up his head and ran toward the gate. They pleaded with him and wailed, telling him to put it down.
But he would not yield either to their gifts or to their pleas, nor did he shrink back in fear of them. They, however, could not approach him.
And so he carried it away barefoot and went before Abbas, who was the emir of Jazira at that time.
Abbas learned what had happened and sent men who captured and imprisoned them all—the men, the women, and the children. He seized everything
they possessed, subjecting them to various tortures. He took from them more than four hundred and five hundred thousand in money. The year 1076.
On the fourteenth of the month of March, a Friday, the holy Severus, bishop of Amida, departed from this world and was buried in his monastery. And in this same year,
a synod of bishops assembled and established peace and unity with Patriarch George, after the death of John, bishop of Callinicum,
whom the people of Jazira had made patriarch. At this same synod, they deposed from the episcopal rank all the bishops
who had been appointed by Patriarch John. This was not, however, because of their faith, but because their appointments had not followed proper order or God’s law.
Nor would the places to which they had been appointed accept them. Nor, to speak truthfully, were they worthy of the episcopal rank.
For they were [?] men, ravenous wolves who had no pity on the flock. The apostle Paul warned us about such people beforehand.
These were the evil trees that produced evil fruit and fed it to the church. We recount their deeds in their own time.
At this synod he handed over to George the people of Jazira, Mosul, and the West, together with their monasteries and cities.
Its leaders and prominent members were George, patriarch of Antioch, and David, bishop of Dara;
Abai, bishop of Amida; Sargon, bishop of Mardin; and Constantine, bishop of Samosata.
In the year 1077, there was a large and formidable gathering of Nestorians at the monastery of Beth Kula, in the mountains of Qardu.
They held a festival, as they customarily did at the place where the ark had come to rest.
While a large crowd was gathered there on [?] in November, lightning flashed from heaven, and fire came down from heaven.
It swept through that sanctuary and burned it and the people inside it. The fire reduced its stones to lime.
Even those outside it did not escape the burning fire. It consumed them all, and no one escaped.
More than seven hundred and eight hundred human lives were lost in this fire, along with a great many livestock.
The stench of decay from that place spread as far as two miles, and for two years people could not approach the surrounding area.
That place, which had provided deliverance from the waters of the flood for people, livestock, wild animals, and creeping creatures,
now became a place of destruction for people and the livestock with them, through the flame that descended from heaven.
Just as the ark of the covenant did not save the priests Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, or even itself, so here too the ark [?] did not save
the sanctuary built in its memory, the priests, the vessels used in celebrating the mysteries, those inside the sanctuary, or those outside.
Instead, they all perished together in one winepress of destruction. Not one of those who had assembled on the mountain at that gathering escaped.
The clouds and the sky could be seen raining fire and sulfur from heaven, just as the Lord had rained them upon Sodom.
From a distance, that mountain looked like the smoke of a furnace.
Hardly anyone escaped from it alive. If anyone did escape, he came out with half his body burned.
