The foul smell of the sulfur that cloud was raining down, and of the burning, spread as far as two or three miles.
Our Lord did all this to the Nestorian people in our days. In the year 1074,
in the month of March, there was a great flood in the river Tigris. It broke through its boundaries and caused great destruction along all its banks.
It swept away houses, mills, villages [?], people, and livestock, along with many possessions. It caused especially severe destruction in Mosul.
It struck the city during the first watch, rose, and swept across three streets. It carried away houses, possessions, people, and everything. As for the areas of dry land,
some boats and rafts could be seen floating above them, and even the groves of tall date palms there were covered by the flood.
Even ships passed above them. He did the same throughout all the lower regions there.
In the year 1078, all the armies of the Persians and the Arabs advanced and descended upon the northern land.
Abbas, who at this time was emir over Jazira and was also the king’s brother,
advanced against Edessa, Abdin, and Tella d-Kum. Hasan ibn Qahtaba, another commander, and yet another commander,
who had been appointed over the king’s own army and was called Ibn Ashath, advanced against the Tigris
and also against Amid, with vast, innumerable armies. While they were attacking Amid, the city in Mesopotamia,
the king’s commander, Ibn Ashath, died. There were various peoples in this army.
Some of them worshiped fire, others the sun. They would rise early at dawn and worship toward the east.
At midday they would worship again toward the south, and in the evening they would worship toward the west. Others worshiped the moon, others the stars, and others horses.
Others had various other kinds of images of idols made for themselves, which they carried with them and worshiped.
Thus everyone among them still held to, and practiced, the erroneous worship that prevailed in his own land and among his own people.
For this army was a mixture of all peoples and was called the king’s mawali.
It included Sindhis, Alans, Khazars, Medes, Persians, people of Aqula, Arabs, Kushans, and Turks.
So we may say that it was a swarm of every variety. There were also many different sins among them, beyond counting.
Because of their immeasurable wickedness and uncleanness, and also so that we ourselves do not defile the reader’s tongue
or the listeners’ ears, we pass over them, for it is degrading for the mouth to speak of them.
But, as I believe, God himself stirred them up and brought them out of their land because they offered what is owed to God alone to various images of creatures like themselves.
And because they did not acknowledge God their maker, nor understand that he was the God of all peoples, and that his name existed before the sun—
and he commanded light to exist, and also said that there should be two great lights in the firmament [?],
one to rule the day and the other to rule the night, and he also gave fire to serve the needs of human life—
they made these things into gods for themselves and worshiped them. They made him jealous with foreign gods and angered him with their objects of worship.
They also sacrificed to demons that were not gods, gods they had not known.
God brought them to cast them down among the northern mountains through various diseases, and also through the sword, plague, and famine,
and to give their flesh to the wild animals and the birds of the sky. They advanced and prepared to enter Roman territory.
They found this land between the borders adorned and bearing stones of every kind [?], for it was the fruit season.
Especially because the land was uninhabited and was adorned with stones, many trees, and vineyards as well.
When these lawless peoples found these things, they seized them far beyond what necessity required.
They ate insatiably from them, and they all fell ill with various diseases,
especially abdominal pain and hemorrhoids, so that everywhere they camped or fled, one could see human corpses lying unburied,
on the roads, the heights, and in the valleys, thrown aside and being eaten by wild animals. All their livestock also died.
In particular, all the camels that had come in behind them perished. Of the fifty or sixty that had come in with one man,
not five or six came out—and sometimes not even one. When the whole army had entered, they attacked the fortress on the frontier called Kamakh. For there were many builders
who had come in with them from throughout Mesopotamia. Abbas left some of them to build a fortress called Ziyad,
while others went in with them. Abbas himself sent for Armenian wagons and had them brought to him, and with them he hauled many cedar timbers.
He ordered the carpenters to make mangonels from them and set them up on the crag opposite the fortress, so that they could launch missiles into the fortress with them.
The Romans inside the fortress also assembled mangonels to oppose them. These Romans who were shut inside
forged for themselves an invincible weapon and set up for themselves an impregnable wall: God himself, their Maker.
They said, “There is no deliverance except from the Lord, and it is better for us to trust in the Lord
than to trust in a human being or a ruler. Indeed, all the nations surrounded me, but the name of the Lord our God will destroy them.”
The commander who was in the fortress at that time was called Sergius. This man was kind, gentle, and God-fearing,
and compassionate toward the poor. This testimony about the man came from all the villagers who used to go in search of madder and happened to be captured by the Romans.
They brought them into the fortress, and they appeared before him and experienced his compassion, generosity, and kindness. They themselves testified about the man before us and before everyone.
For at that time taxation had become unbearably harsh upon the Syrian people, and they had no relief,
because their lands had been sold to the Arabs. The Arabs themselves, because they were not being given their customary payments, bought lands and farms for themselves
and became farmers themselves. As a result, the villagers’ trade ceased, and they would gather
in large groups and go into Hanzit in search of madder. Often they would cross over and go beyond the frontier,
either because of the negligence of the official in charge of the guard, or because of the merciless hardship that pursued them as a result of greed.
They would be captured by the Romans and brought to Kamakh.
When this man saw them, he treated them with great compassion, saying to them, “If you wish, stay with us.
But if you wish, leave and go home in peace.” If they chose to leave, he would send them away with provisions.
Truly, my brothers, God rewarded this man by rescuing him from the hands of the Assyrians, together with everyone who was with him inside the fortress.
When this man saw the great army surrounding him on every side, and that his own men were few in number,
and that, like the Rabshakeh, they were taunting those standing on the wall, saying, “Who among all the nations has escaped from the hands of Abdallah ibn Muhammad?
Have you not heard what he did to Marwan and [?] the house of Hisham, wiping them off the earth? Where is the king of Egypt, Africa, the Nubians, and the Moors?
Where are the kings of Armenia, Bishan, Media, and Persia? Have you not heard what he did to the kings of Sindh and India?
Which of all the kings of the earth has been able to rescue his country from his hands, that you should escape from his hands?”
But this faithful man, like Hezekiah, put on the helmet of faith and strengthened himself with great hope in his Lord.
He ran to the refuge of prayer, where the sound of their cries moved even those outside. The good God did not disregard their petition, but
through their faith they heard: “He shall not enter this town. Instead, I will put a hook in the nostrils of this Assyrian and send him back in shame along the same road by which he came.”
Although those Persians were attacking by every possible means, all their devices proved useless.
He made movable wooden shelters so that they could fill the hollow beside the wall with earth and stones.
This too proved useless. The Romans who were throwing stones from inside, because they threw accurately,
were killing many of the people outside. They were also breaking the Persians’ mangonels. Since one side of the fortress could be climbed,
the Romans brought long, large timbers, tied large round stones to their ends, and placed them at the mouth of that ravine.
When the Persians clambered up, the Romans sent down one of these timbers, sweeping everyone before it and knocking them down,
even tearing them limb from limb [?]. One night, when the Persians noticed that the Romans had fallen silent,
they thought that they had fallen into a deep sleep. An immense, countless multitude climbed up against them.
When the first men clambered up and reached the top, they shouted, “God is great!” in their joy, thinking that they had already captured the fortress. But the Romans who were keeping watch woke up.
They boldly killed these men and also sent down those timbers with their stones, which swept before them everyone who was on the ascent,
and [?] them into a single heap of corpses. Thus all their efforts came to nothing, because the Lord was the Romans’ helper.
He appointed two army commanders, and they entered Roman territory with a large force, about
fifty thousand, to plunder, take captives, and devastate all the Romans’ lands. They entered, but since they were unfamiliar with the country
and had no guide who knew that land, they were afraid to travel through frequented country,
lest the Romans become aware of them, gather against them, and wipe them off the earth.
But what Job said happened to them: “The fear I feared has come upon me, and what I dreaded has overtaken me.”
They did not stop or rest, and the wrath of God overtook them. He swept them away as a sheaf is gathered in its season.
Like an acorn falling from its cup, they first devastated [?]. Their provisions ran out, and they suffered from hunger.
Then they fell among parched mountains and were perishing from thirst. They and their livestock were close to dying from thirst,
and to perishing without a sword or a drawn blade. They went down and found a desirable meadow. They dug with their spears and soon found water there.
They drank and gained relief from death by thirst, both they and their livestock. Because they had gone far inland,
they were not heading straight toward inhabited country, but were in a ruined and desolate land between the Romans and the land of the Armenians.
After wandering in the mountains for many days, they headed toward Caesarea. They found a fertile land and all the people in the villages
threshing and living there, with no one to alarm them. Suddenly they fell upon them, and no one was able to stand against them at all.
They penetrated far beyond Caesarea and fulfilled all their desires in that land, taking captives, plundering, and laying the land waste.
They also carried its inhabitants away into captivity. They drove all the livestock out before them and took away an immense haul of people and livestock,
ornaments and utensils, as well as a very great quantity of gold and silver. But their joy did not reach its fulfillment.
With the measure they had used, it was measured out to them. They filled the pit they had dug with their own bodies, and the trap they had spread caught them.

The Lord repaid them according to their deeds. Because they had taken captives, they were taken captive. Because they had plundered, they were plundered. Because they had wanted to acquire male and female slaves,
they themselves became slaves. Because they had wanted to devastate lands, they themselves were devastated, and they drenched that land with their blood.
What happened to them came about in this way. When they invaded that land, because it was very prosperous,
they plundered, took captives, and bound its inhabitants without pity or mercy. They wanted to set out for Syria with an immense body of captives,
with great renown [?] and a mighty victory. Just as they wished, they had already acquired great wealth, along with male and female slaves.
The wretched people did not know that they were walking in darkness, and that in a little while they themselves would become captives.
Truly, here one may sing and say, “The Lord rescued the poor and afflicted from the one who seized them by force,”
along with, “He brought them out from between the teeth and brought them back from the depths of the sea.” When the Persians thought that they had now arrived and emerged into the land of Syria,
they were now free from fear. They reached [?] the meadow of Syria, and they were now free from fear.
They reached a large meadow and wanted to camp and rest there. This meadow has a narrow entrance, and on every side there is sloping ground descending into it.
After they had camped, rested a little, and sent out their livestock, they wanted to rest there, still not knowing the lay of the land.
Then God, who does not neglect those who call upon him, directed and brought a Roman commander who had with him twelve
thousand cavalrymen. This Roman force was coming from another place, from another battle.
While he was enjoying a great victory, they reached that meadow outside the gate where the Persians were encamped.
They too wanted to camp and rest there, without even noticing the danger farther in beyond them or knowing what had happened in their land and among their people.

For they had come from a great distance. When they made camp, some of them went up to the top of a hill and saw the great army, the captives, and the great quantity of plunder from their land, encamped farther in beyond them.
They trembled and were dismayed. They quickly came down and informed their companions. The commander did not disregard what he heard.
Instead, he sent others, about three hundred more horsemen, armed, to discover the truth: whether it was real, or whether some apparition had appeared to these men through mirages.
When those who had been sent went up and took a careful look, they informed the man who had sent them. He too went up with four or five thousand men.
When the Persians saw them standing at the gate through which they wanted to leave, and realized that they were shut in as though in a prison,
their hearts trembled, and they melted within. Their hands grew weak, and they shook and staggered like drunken men. All their wisdom vanished.
The Persians themselves sent messengers to see how large the army was and whether they were preparing for battle.
For there was a great height between them, and a narrow gate. When the messenger came and told them the truth,
that they were a great army and appeared to be preparing for battle, the Persians wanted to speak peaceably with them, using pleasant words.
First they released all the captives they had taken, along with the possessions and the plunder—
all that they had plundered—saying, “Only let them spare our lives, and we will leave just as we entered, without anything extra.”
But the Romans did not delay over this. They quickly sent word to the cities and to the other army commanders, and assembled a great army against them.
They divided it into four units and descended upon them from the front, from behind, and from either side.
Because it was still night, they agreed on a signal: when they had come down and were ready, they would sound the horns.
All the people were also to shout together, “Lord, have mercy!” When they had come down and made ready, the horns sounded, and the people too shouted like thunder, “Lord, have mercy!”
When the Persians heard their voices, they trembled and became like the dead, like slain men lying in graves. Their eyes grew dark, and they could not see.
Their hands grew weak, and all their hope of survival vanished. Even before the sword struck, they counted themselves dead.
They wanted to flee but could not muster the strength, because the Romans had surrounded them like a ring. The Lord thundered against them from heaven
and threw them into confusion before the Romans. Here one can see that the Lord arose and openly brought deliverance. The snare was broken,
and those who had fallen into it escaped, and [?] caught those who had set it. Those who an hour before had considered themselves masters of slaves
were themselves seen to be prisoners and slaves. Their end was evil, because they had not remembered to do good,
but had pursued the poor and the wretched, and those whose hearts were in pain, to put them to death. Thus they fought all day long. The Persians were crushed before the Romans.
They inflicted a great and exceedingly severe defeat on them, as the Persians themselves testified.
before us, with solemn oaths. Those who escaped wounded from the battle itself said that they had never seen or heard of blood in one place as there was there.
They said that the blood and corpses in that meadow reached up to the horses’ bellies. Now, because there was so much water in this meadow,
that blood was not absorbed into it. Truly, it is fitting here to say with the prophet: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon,
and all her carved gods have been shattered.” They did not help their worshipers. And let us say: “Terror, the pit, the snare, and the sword are upon you, Assyrian!
Whoever flees from the sound of terror will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs out of the pit will be caught in the snare. And whoever escapes from the snare,
the sword will devour him.” As the day drew toward evening, only a few of them remained. Some of them escaped their grasp, but the sword devoured the rest.
Raddad, the commander of the army, fled stripped bare with his horses, leaving all his baggage in the hands of the Romans.
Only about a thousand escaped with him, and these too were wounded. In this way he escaped to Melitene.
I pass over another battle that he encountered, in which Raddad himself received three sword wounds but did not die.
Malik ibn Tawq, another commander, fled toward Qaliqala with five thousand men. Thus he returned to the one who had sent them, with great shame and disgrace.
He had also lost all their baggage, and whoever escaped from among them came out with nothing but the clothes stripped from him.
Let us also describe what happened to those at the fortress: how they acted, how they withdrew, and how they departed in greater disgrace and shame than their companions. The villagers,
who had been hauling wheat and flour for them from Syria, saw that this journey brought them great loss and not even a little profit,
because, as we said above, this entire route was full of harm and losses,
especially since all the livestock had perished. Because of this they stopped and brought them no wheat or flour, and a severe famine came upon them,
until they were all close to perishing for lack of food. A qafiz of millet came to cost three and a half zuzes, and none was available.
They remained like this for about twenty days. Then Abbas sent word to Syria, and a great supply of provisions came in.
The villagers too had had no work of any kind. But when they heard, the whole population of Mesopotamia and the western region stirred into action,
and the land of Inner Armenia also headed there. Everyone among them who could brought supplies in, until everything there became cheap.
Merchants, shopkeepers, cloth dealers, and others like them bought wheat, barley, flour, and the other crops needed to sustain human life.
They heaped them up in limitless piles, expecting to amass great wealth for themselves. The wretches did not know—for the eyes of their understanding were blinded by the love of money—
that they would soon lose even what they had acquired, and that this entire venture was full of losses, without even a little profit.
Meanwhile, they were attacking the fortress night and day with many methods of warfare, but each day they gained nothing except their own destruction.
The Romans’ mangonels killed many of them every day. But Abbas, being a compassionate man,
also showed kindness to these poor men who had become involved in [?]. When he saw that some of them were perishing from the stones of the mangonels, which
which was being hurled from within by the Romans. He assembled his army commanders and ordered that each day one of them should provide men to hurl stones from mangonels,
while the villagers were to perform other tasks that did not expose them to death.
When they had spent a long time there, Abbas even said, “Even if I remain here ten years, I will not leave here until I have conquered it.”
They rounded up people from every region, and he entered there. After he had fought using every means of warfare and accomplished nothing, they resorted to threats,
saying, “Perhaps they will be frightened and open the gates for us.” But they were like an eagle soaring through the air on its swift wings:
just as it is not disturbed by anything on earth, neither were these people. Finally, they approached them with intimidation and persuasion,
urging them to abandon the fortress and leave it peacefully. But this too came to nothing.
Instead, they stood there mocking them. Winter had already arrived, and the weather was beginning to grow cold in that country.
They feared that snow might overwhelm them, that the roads might be cut off, and that they might perish there from hunger and cold.
He also feared that armies might gather against them and drive them out of the country, and that they would suffer greater disgrace than their comrades,
of whom, out of fifty thousand who had entered, not even five or six thousand came out—and those were wounded.
Moreover, since they could accomplish nothing, a herald suddenly proclaimed that they should mount and leave.
The merchants, shopkeepers, buyers, and sellers quickly lost all their merchandise.
For they had bought and piled up wheat, barley, and flour without restraint, but they could find no pack animals to hire and load with their goods.
Because the terrain was difficult for pack animals to travel over, villagers used to bring their loads as far as the crossing of the river called Salqat, and then return from there.
They would take only one or two animals out of a hundred across to the north side of the crossing. It often happened that they hired pack animals
but did not take their own across. For this reason, pack animals were scarce there. When the herald proclaimed throughout the army that they should load up,
and the Persians saw that all the merchants’ goods remained behind, they went out, set fire to them, and burned them, lest they remain and the Romans come down and benefit from them.
Yet even after he did this, much remained. Another army also went out toward Qaliqala.
As for all those carrying and bringing cheese, oil, honey, utensils, and other produce to the army,
wherever they encountered them, they threw down their loads and drove the men and the unloaded donkeys before them.
Thus, in a single hour, poor people lost everything they owned.
So everyone gained only losses and harm from this expedition. Even the [?], after Abbas departed—
he gave orders concerning all the laborers under his authority, and the wages they had received on entering, including the hire of the donkeys, were taken back from them.
Thus they broke camp, and Abbas departed. He went down by the same road on which he had come, with shame, disgrace, and countless heavy losses.
Other troops went down to Amid and the Tigris and went on into Persian territory, destitute, hungry, and exhausted.
Not even half of them got out, much less their possessions and their slaves, who fled and entered Roman territory.
One could see how, just as they had been proud and boastful when they entered, they were humbled and despised when they left,
hanging their heads, miserable, and possessing absolutely nothing. Yet this army’s advance brought great profit to the whole northern region,
because of the coins they poured into it, especially since they were newly minted. From then on, anyone who wanted to mint coins
did so without fear. Newly minted coins multiplied, especially debased ones, and people suffered losses because of them.
The whole land of the Jazira was adorned with vineyards, fields, and abundant livestock.
There was not even one lowly poor man in a village who did not own a yoke of oxen, donkeys, and goats.
There was no place capable of yielding anything, little or much, that was not sown or visibly planted as a vineyard.
It was the same throughout the mountain region: every place where a plow could pass was planted with vineyards.
Their greed grew so great that they seized property that earlier generations had given to churches and monasteries.
Wheat and wine were abundant. Because of the abundance of the harvests, there were many fights, disputes, and quarrels over boundaries.
Many times they even went as far as murder over boundaries. Many times they went as far as murder.
Even the workers in the cities were overwhelmed by their lawsuits against one another. The land was also full of livestock herders,
because of the abundance of their herds. We have written these things now because we wish to make known the distress into which the land fell, along with this people who grew fat and kicked,
and forgot God who made them, and even reviled God, who gave to them.
And from what greatness, wealth, possessions, and teams of oxen—from being owners of male and female slaves—to what degradation they came!
A man who had owned a thousand goats and a thousand sheep, teams of oxen, camels, mares, and male and female slaves, and who used to ride Arabian horses,
with slaves riding mules and [?] like pagans before him—such men and others like them could be seen carrying their children on their shoulders,
bent over, stripped of their clothes, hungry and thirsty, going from door to door for a scrap of bread. They were also driven from one region to another and from place to place.
Women who had lived in private chambers, stripped and ill-treated, carried their infants on their necks and were tossed from region to region and from city to city.
In this year, from the time the army came down, wheat sold at twenty-five gribs to the dinar,
and even as much as thirty. Wine sold at forty measures to the dinar, or forty-five. Everything else was similarly priced,
because the land was enjoying great abundance at this time. They also began once more to build sanctuaries and renovate churches.
On the causes, disputes, and disturbances that arose in the holy church and among its shepherds in this year.
Of the year 1078, and especially concerning George, patriarch of the apostolic see of Antioch.
When the chaste John died—the man whom the bishops of Jazira [?] had made patriarch because they had broken away and separated from George and the Westerners—
as we explained above, the chaste and God-fearing bishops wanted to cast all the troublemakers out from among them and become one people,
and to submit to one head, according to the rule established and confirmed by the holy fathers. They also feared that some schism or disturbance might arise in the holy faith.
Moreover, all the cities supported George, proclaimed him, and loved him.
They agreed, and all the people of Jazira and all the Westerners assembled in the territory of Serugh. The chaste George himself was also
with them, in the year 1076 of Alexander. Much was said by both sides about the grounds for their various disputes with one another.
The chaste patriarch George, however, loved peace more than schism and division, and did not want the ordinances and rules to be changed during his lifetime—
those handed down by the 150 holy fathers who assembled with the Holy Spirit in Constantinople,
who defined and established the patriarchates: for Nectarius of Constantinople, after the patriarch of Rome; for Timothy of Alexandria and Egypt,
and also of all the western territories; and for Meletius of Antioch and the whole East. He feared that during his lifetime there might be [?]
in that see of Antioch. He accepted and agreed to all the demands made by the bishops of Jazira.
But when it came to the bishops ordained by John, whom those from the monastery of Qarqaphta had made patriarch, he neither agreed to this nor accepted it.
Instead, he wanted to place them outside the entire priestly order. The bishops of Jazira complained about this, because many of them were from well-known monasteries.
Yet the chaste man was not unyielding even in this matter. Rather, he said that the priesthood should be granted,
and even the episcopate, to anyone willing to go to the lower territories of Sijistan and Harb [?]. This too greatly pleased the bishops.
For the holy man said, “How can I remove from his city a bishop who is better than I am, and whom I did not even appoint, and bring these men in,
when he shepherds the flock entrusted to him with every praiseworthy practice of virtue, and has already spent more than thirty years as a bishop? Nor are there
any cities that want one of them or will receive him. But anyone among them who is willing and fears God
should go to the lower territories.” He ordered that those who agreed should receive help from everyone and go. Truly, my brothers,
even if the chaste George had wanted to accept them, there was no one among them worthy of the rank of bishop. For they were arrogant men,
boastful, disruptive, quarrelsome, crafty, learned, speaking twisted things, and not keeping God's judgment before their eyes.
The apostle's words apply to them: “I know that after I leave, fierce wolves will come among you, not sparing the flock.
Even from among your own number, men will arise who speak twisted things, to draw the disciples away to follow them.”
Our Lord himself also spoke about such people when he warned his disciples: “Beware of false prophets who come to you in sheep's clothing.”
But inwardly they are ravenous wolves. You will know them by their fruits. “Do people,” he says, “gather grapes from thorns,
or figs from thistles? Thus every good tree produces good fruit, but a bad tree produces bad fruit.
A bad tree cannot produce good fruit. You will know them,” he says, “by their fruits.” Truly, these were bad trees,
and they made the church and the people of God taste bitter fruit. From this I show what a great extent the land had reached.
But let no one blame the holy George and the bishops because he expelled them from the church. My brothers, I am astonished
at the chaste John: although he was an ascetic through the chaste labors of monastic life
and was praised by everyone, how could he present men like these for the laying on of hands, even for the priesthood? There was not even a city that wanted them.
For the city of Amid, which already had two or three bishops, he appointed more than three or four, supposedly for it,
although its bishops were far superior to those he appointed. One of them was Mar Severus, from the holy monastery of Zuqnin,
a great and God-fearing man. Because his eyesight had weakened, he asked to be released from the administration of the city, and he lived in his monastery until the end of his life.
In his place came Mar Abi, from the monastery of Mar Habib of Arzon, a gentle and humble man, adorned with every divine virtue.
At Tell Beshme there was Sargon, a godly man from the monastery of Mar Athanasius. They were all venerable and holy elders.
Although the city had these men, he himself appointed others as well, one of whom was from the monastery of Kharbaz.
I have written these things, my brothers, because I wish to make known the evils that befell us afterward. But let no one blame the writer
until he has also seen the fruits of these bad trees. For, as the saying goes, a man’s appearance reveals his deeds, and his footsteps testify about him.
Here are the men, with their deeds before them. When that synod was dissolved and everyone went back to his own country, the chaste George also went down to his monastery.
These wretched men also departed in great disgrace and deep shame—not like men who concealed their dishonor and stayed in their monasteries,
but they moved every stone, disturbing and agitating many people.
They also sought a way to take revenge on George and those with him.
George, having experienced the affair and also fearing what had happened before, went to his monastery,
having also resolved not to enter a city, village, or monastery unless those in charge of that place first came
and brought him there. That very year it happened that the people of Harran came and brought him
because of a certain dispute between them and their bishop. When he had finished the business for which he had come,
the people of Amid went down after him with Mar Abi, their bishop, so that he would not be reluctant to come and visit them.
But he, so that he would not be reluctant to come and visit them [?]. He, however, like a gentle shepherd,
He granted their request and went up with them. As he passed through the villages and towns along his route, everyone received him with honor.
The people of Amida themselves also came out and welcomed him with a great procession, as was fitting for a man like him.
After he had spent some days there, the monks of the monastery of Zuqnin came—all the honored elders of that monastery—
with the chaste Mar Autel, their abbot, and Dionysius, their visitor, who later also became bishop of Harran.
They took him to their monastery, because the chaste George had long desired this:
to see this monastery and pray in it. When he had fulfilled his desire and enjoyed the love of the monks of that monastery, he passed on to Hah and entered Tell Qum.
As he was intending to journey to his monastery, Satan, who had hated good things from the beginning, stirred up his disciples,
who are his instruments, fully prepared for destruction, because he had seen that everyone welcomed him
and knew that peace was about to reign in the church and that turmoil and contention would disappear from it. Some of those whom we mentioned above went down to the king.
He also spoke evil words about the chaste George and all the bishops. He even said, “He is the king, not you!”
Very rightly did the prophet say about these people: “Your rulers are rebels and companions of thieves. They all love bribes
and hurry to repay injuries.” Look at the oleander: it has put down roots, displayed blossoms, and produced deadly fruit.
Come, look at the trees, and recognize them by their fruit. When the king heard these things, his anger rose like smoke.
He roared like a lion bent on destruction and sent swift messengers breathing fire after him and after all the bishops of the Jazira.
While he was still in Tell Qum, they took him from there to Harran, without even allowing him to enter his monastery.
All the bishops assembled there, and from there they went down to the king in Baghdad, where he was living at that time.
This king, whenever he heard of anyone raising his hand or foot anywhere in the land under his rule, could not—
whether the person was Persian, Arab, or Syrian—remain quiet or rest until he had destroyed him. Anyone who came to him and informed him about someone who possessed anything
he considered a great friend. When they reached him, entered his presence, and he saw them, he growled at them like a bear intent on destruction.
After speaking harshly to them, he drove them from his presence. But as for the chaste George,
he confined him in prison and put him in irons. After they had spent many days there, he commanded them:
“Appoint as your head whichever of you is [?], and go back up,” supposedly treating them mercifully.
They all wanted to appoint David of Dara, saying that all these things were his doing, and also that he was an elderly man.
They said that even if there were someone else, he would not yield to him. The ship would survive a long time, and this man would depart to his own place.
These things were not hidden from him either. Whether willingly or unwillingly, he came.
The king also gave him written orders authorizing him to imprison, beat, and destroy anyone who appeared and would not submit to him. George remained confined in prison.
From this point, strife arose in the church and among the people of God, and insults and mockery were directed against the monks and bishops,
until not one of them could pass through the city streets because of the insults and mockery. They even called them murderers and shedders of blood.
They went so far that they would not even receive the Eucharist offered by any one of them,
saying that David’s name was commemorated [?] over it. These are the evil seeds of weeds that the Evil One sowed through his disciples.
When the venerable David and the bishops with him went up to Mosul and Tikrit, instead of welcoming the patriarch,
they came out to meet him with insults and mockery. They even called him a murderer and a shedder of blood. But he paid no attention to any of them and did not complain.
Instead, he entrusted everything to God and called God as his witness concerning the matters under dispute, saying:
“If I have any part in George’s case, may a terrible punishment come upon me.” And although, with many oaths and anathemas, he delivered
addresses in the churches, no one believed him, for they said, “These things happened at his command.”
Thus he was not accepted by even a single person, because of the affair of the venerable George. Nor did he demand redress from anyone for the insults against him.
He did not compel anyone to proclaim his name, but said, “Whoever wishes to proclaim it may proclaim it. As for anyone who does not wish to proclaim it, I have no quarrel with him.”
By this he showed that he had been falsely accused, for although he held great authority, he compelled no one, even while hearing insults and mockery to his face.
If he happened to send one of his bishops to one of the cities, they would go so far as to attack him.
If he happened to offer the Eucharist, they would not receive it from him, but treated both him and his Eucharist with contempt.
If there happened to be a God-fearing person who admonished them and said, “Wrath will come upon you because of this deed,”
they treated him worse than the other. They also went from church to church, saying, “We will not receive the Eucharist from so-and-so,
because he proclaims David’s name.” The honored habit of monks and bishops was especially despised in their eyes.
If there happened to be a monk whom neither David nor George had ever seen, they would mock him until he anathematized and cursed both of them as well.
In the end, people were asked to proclaim the name of neither one nor the other. Thus this strife continued to wreak havoc in the churches until the death of the venerable David himself.
See what evil fruit these evil trees produced! Wait and hear [?] what wrath came upon us after these things.

Know, my brothers, that whenever the church is thrown into turmoil, the affairs of the state are also thrown into turmoil. It happened that the former was thrown into turmoil first, and afterward the latter.
In the year 1079, the fortress of Arsamosata, on the Arsanias River, was built.
When the builders and stonemasons had begun its construction, and it had risen to about the height of a person,
a large Roman army came and encamped on the riverbank beside the fortress. It did not, however, cross over.
For it was the holy day of Sunday. They had not even been instructed to make the offering. But when they began, he presented the offering and also ate the bread.
All the people of the fortress abandoned everything they owned and fled. Then the Romans entered, took everything, and fled.
Then the Romans entered and took everything. They also burned what remained and demolished the building itself.
They took everything they found and went back to their own country. Then the Arabs, architects, and masons assembled again and rebuilt it.
Abbas sent letters to all the cities, ordering all the Arabs of the Jazira, great and small alike, to come down to Harran.
When they assembled and went down, they even left their crops unharvested, because they were under pressure over the money. All the people rose early and went down,
great and small. Nothing was gained except loss, for it is difficult for an evil man to become good.
Instead, he detained them there for many days, until their crops too were lost and they were ruined.
After enrolling about six hundred of them in these fortresses, he dismissed the rest, who carried home the returns of a losing venture.
In that same year, Dionysius, bishop of Harran, died. Another Dionysius, from the monastery of Zuqnin, succeeded him.
Again, in that same year, Stephen of the Khabur died, and in his place there was [?]. In the year 1080, Bishop Zechariah departed from
Edessa, and John from Tella. Elijah, from the monastery of Qartmin, succeeded Zechariah in Edessa. He was a brokenhearted and troublesome man,
with no place for God in any of his thoughts. It was not because he was worthy of the rank of bishop that he became one,
but because the people of Edessa appointed him. Yet he was not accepted and did not succeed. Instead, he brought in his wake occasions for accusations,
which there is no need for us to record. Thus Edessa remained without a bishop. In Tella, Sabina succeeded John.
At this time the following were prominent: Sergius of Mardin, David the patriarch, Mar Abai of Amid, Constantine of Samosata,
and Paul of Tikrit. Everything was very cheap: thirty qafizes of wheat and forty jars of wine for a zuz,
and eight pounds of oil. The land was adorned with vineyards and fields. Livestock were as plentiful as sand. Zayd came concerning the [?].
They assessed a zuz for him on each dinar. He took it and went away, causing no further loss beyond this. Again, in that same year,
stones fell from heaven—black stones. Many people saw them and picked them up, and they still remain to this day.
Whether a cloud had carried them up, or where they came from, God alone [?]. Moreover, the ground on which they fell
had no black stones in it at all. But the reader should be assured that the Lord does whatever he wishes in heaven and on earth.
The year 1081. A governor was appointed over Mosul, an evil and bitter man. His name was Musa ibn Mus'ab.
The prophet prophesied about this man when he said, “He laid waste the earth with his words and made the inhabited world desolate like a wilderness.”
Neither among pagan kings, nor among Magi or Manichaeans, did this man find his equal. He brought upon it [?].
Upon the land, great distress: from the creation of the world until today, it had never seen distress like what it suffered from this man.
If anyone wishes to call this man Antichrist, and his officials the messengers of the son of destruction, he is not mistaken. Rather, he is calling him by his own name: the wicked king.
All his servants are wicked. As we said above, how the honored monastic habit was despised!
Bishops and monks were mocked, and they even attacked the Eucharist. The insults made monks afraid to enter the marketplace.
This came especially from the people of Tikrit, Arsido [?], and Mosul. And this wrath first fell heavily upon them.
He even went out after them to hunt them down in distant regions. This king had no man after his own heart except this one.
Elsewhere it is written, “I have found for Jesse a son after my own heart.” Abdallah son of Muhammad found in Musa a man after his own heart, who would walk wickedly before him all his days.
When he became governor over Mosul, he roared like a lion bent on destruction, saying, “I will pursue my enemies and overtake them.

I will not turn back until I have finished them off. I will strike them down, and they will be unable to rise. They will fall beneath my feet. They will cry out, but there will be no one to save them.
They will appeal to the Lord, but he will not answer them. I will grind them like dust before the wind, and trample them like mud in the streets.”
He persecuted the land and destroyed the people upon the face of the world. He struck them down, and they could not stand before him.
They fell beneath his feet, and he trampled them into the mud of the city streets. He made them like chaff before a whirlwind.
As they fled from place to place, they cried out to the Lord, but he did not save them from his hands or deliver them from their distress.
Their eyes failed as they waited for a deliverer. He asked the king to allow him to send and bring back the people,
the fugitives from Mosul, from every region, supposedly because he wanted to restore peace to the land.
He wrote to the whole country that no one should oppose him or any of his officials.
He sent one man to every three cities of Jazira, with a large force accompanying him. To Amida, Arzan, and Maypherqat there came
a wicked man, like the one who sent him, named Adam son of Yazid—a greedy man who did not keep God before his eyes.
These people from Mosul who lived in this region of Jazira were extremely rich at that time, so that all the fruits of the labor of the people of Jazira
were consumed by them through [?] and interest. Although the Lord said, “Do not charge your brother interest, and do not lend your money at interest,”
they did the opposite: they charged interest and lent on [?] and fixed terms. They became owners of male and female slaves.
They acquired garments, vineyards, and fields, until they were very close to possessing the whole land where this language of the Arameans was spoken.
Indeed, nearly all Jazira was about to belong to the Narsibdians [?]. They also sat in the marketplaces like officials and masters of the land.
They also took control of the churches like rulers, claiming that they were managing them. They did not remember that they were foreigners, strangers, and temporary residents in this land.

If they had ruined their own land, how could they make the land of their neighbors prosper? The prophetic saying was fulfilled concerning them: “Do not envy the wicked, and do not be jealous of those who do wrong.”
For they quickly dry up like grass and wither like green vegetation, which sprouts and grows anew in the morning, but withers and dries up in the evening.
Truly, they were proud and exalted beyond measure. As it is said, “The Lord uproots the house of the proud.” It was brought low, uprooted, and destroyed.
They became like a flower before the sun. When the man we mentioned above came, entered, and seized these cities, they all fled before him.
For they were all shopkeepers and cloth merchants. They did not own much property.
They hid their possessions, carried their children on their shoulders, and fled. There was cause to weep over them,
as they struggled among the mountains, naked, hungry, and exhausted, like chaff before a whirlwind. Others went into room after room,
and shut themselves up like dead people in dark inner rooms. They trembled, and their complexion lost its human color and became like that of the dead in their graves.
It was summer, and this made things very hard for them. Those who fled died of hunger, both they and their children,
in the mountains and caves, as they wandered from one mountain to another. Those who hid in houses perished from fever,
and also from fear, distress, and heat. Even those with whom they were hiding were more frightened than they were.
For wherever one of them was found, they subjected them to severe torments,
and also the household in which he was found. A herald also proclaimed: “Whoever hides a man from Mosul shall have everything he owns sold and shall pay a fine of [?].”
This frightened people, and everyone drove out whoever was staying with him. He also said: “Whoever catches a man will receive forty silver coins as his reward.”
When the brutal and godless people—the vile, drunken Arabs—heard this, it became a business for them, and they rejoiced whenever one of them was caught.
Even if one of them went out at night, they would catch him and mercilessly make demands of him,
saying, “Either give us something, or we will take you away and collect the reward of forty silver coins.” Whether he was willing or unwilling,
they took from him and then let him go. Sometimes he would then fall into the hands of others who were worse than the first.
Because this man was crafty and cunning, not even the whereabouts of anything any of them owned were hidden from him.
Rather, it was as though the property itself were calling out to him, “Here I am! I am such-and-such!” And as though he himself had hidden and stored it,
he found out about everything so easily, and everything was revealed to him, just as it is written concerning the son of destruction.
There were men who had married women, fathered Syrian children, and mingled with the Syrians, so that they could not even be distinguished from the Arameans.
Yet he readily found out about them. He seized the headmen of the village where they lived and inflicted severe beatings on their bodies,

until they provided guarantors that they would bring them to him. When he had caught them all in this way and made them stand surety for one another, he also sold their property—everything they owned—and took it as his own.
Thus he stripped them all as bare as a finger. He took them away and brought them to their own country, where he imprisoned them.
Hunger, various diseases, and pestilence took hold of them, and only a few of them remained alive.
The wealthy and powerful among them sold everything they owned and gave it to him, and were left stripped bare. Nothing at all remained to any of them.
But this wicked man, because he had bound himself by oaths not to take a zuz or a follis from any of them, demanded dinars
of gold. Even when one of them sold everything he owned, he could barely raise the amount demanded of him.
Concerning the sign shaped like a broom that appeared in the sky. In the year 1080, in the month of Iyar, something shaped like a broom appeared in the northeast.
It appeared at this angle, rising darkly, as though it were sweeping up some dust in a house.
At dawn it appeared with its tuft inclined toward the earth. It moved forward little by little until it entered the axis of that wheel in the sky.
It was swallowed up in it and disappeared. Its appearance was like the drawing above. It was very aptly and rightly called a broom.
For just as a scraper and a broom enter a house and scrape and sweep it, so this too swept the world
and destroyed everything in it. First, in this same year, all the livestock perished, especially the sheep and goats. There was a great and severe snowfall,
and the earth was covered. The snow remained for many days, until the livestock perished from hunger. There was also severe frost.
In various places the snow fell and buried the flocks and their shepherds, and the flocks perished along with their shepherds.
Again, it blew upon the flocks and their shepherds, and the flocks perished along with their shepherds. Again, a wind blew from the south and east for three days and three nights,
with heavy snow. This killed many people and livestock, especially sheep and goats.
Many people whom it overtook on the roads also fell down dead, both they and their donkeys.
Concerning the people who came up from the lower land, who are called giants in the ancient language, in the year 1078.
At this time the king sent a certain people from the land of Persia, brought them up, and settled them on the Roman frontier.
These people were naked and unclothed, both they and their wives and children. And because
they practiced no trade and taught none to their children, nor did their wives know how to work wool,
their trade was instead to lie in wait along the roads, both by night and by day,
killing, robbing, and waylaying travelers. Because they lived in rugged mountains, no one could withstand their power.
They even went so far as to attack the king himself and waylay the treasury of the Commander of the Faithful.
When they did this, and that whole land was in turmoil because of them, the king sent a large army against them.
He took them captive, plundered them, and put them in chains. He gathered them all together, intending to put every one of them to the sword, while he crucified their leaders.
When he was intending to do this, God-fearing men advised him to send them to the frontier to face the enemy, so that there they would either be taken captive or be killed by the Romans.
They quickly acted on the advice he had received. He sent for them, brought them up, and settled them in the land inside the fortifications opposite Kamakh.
They numbered about three hundred thousand. But they fled and scattered throughout the land, and only a few of them remained.
Since this land was nearby and they were naked, most of them died in the first winter that overtook them.
Not even those who remained had abandoned their former evil ways. On the restoration of the great church of Amida. At this same time,
the people of Amida carried out a great and remarkable renovation of their great church, which had been built by the God-fearing, faithful king Heraclius.
For this church had not been renovated since its original construction. Care was taken
over its restoration, because it was damaged and close to collapse, by Abus [?] Mar Abai, the bishop of the city,
and the honorable Mar George, the visitor, and Thomas the archdeacon. He devoted great care to it, at considerable expense,
and replaced all its decayed material, putting new material in its place. They restored it to its original condition.
Again, on the order that came from the king, requiring the property of churches and monasteries to be registered. Satan, who always hates good things,
did not cease even now from stirring up divisions and disturbances in churches and monasteries. “I will set a man against his father,” it says,
did not cease even now from stirring up divisions and disturbances in churches and monasteries. “I will set a man against his father,” it says,
“and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man's enemies will be the members of his own household.” At this time an order came from the king
that the heads of monasteries and the heads of churches should be arrested and should register the property of their monasteries, churches, and sanctuaries.
The reason for this was as follows. Satan, who had chosen Judas Iscariot as his disciple from that pure company of apostles,
now also chose a man named Ze'ora from the holy and pure monastery of Mar Matthew in the region of Mosul. Because of some dispute that had arisen
between him and the head of his monastery—just as Judas had acted toward his master by betraying our Lord for [?]—this man too fell in no way short of the other.
Satan put it into his heart to act not merely as the other had done, but many times worse: to bring about not one killing,
but many; to destroy not one place, but many. Nor did he wish to uproot just one monastery,
but many. He separated himself like a wolf from among the lambs and went down to Ja'far, the son
of the king. He told him, “All the gold belonging to the house of Hisham and the house of Marwan is there in such-and-such a monastery.”
He left nothing in the monastery undisclosed to him. Ja'far sent ruthless men to this monastery,
and took everything in it, including all their vessels used for worship. He bound all the monks with harsh fetters and brought them to Ja'far.
He severely oppressed and imprisoned them, demanding from them the things that this second Judas had told him about.
For this reason an order went out throughout the land that everyone should register the property of their monasteries.
But although everyone thought that they would certainly confiscate it, as they had done with that monastery, Ja'far fell in no way short of what had happened with Belshazzar.
Because this man had treated the vessels of the divine mysteries with contempt and wanted them to belong to him and his concubines, even then God did not neglect his church and his people.
Instead, God sent an evil spirit upon Shaphar, which began choking him. He released those monks, took their property, and returned to their monastery.
Thus this affair came to an end and was not investigated again, because that evil spirit destroyed him.
On the prosperity of the land and the evils that were being committed in it. Since we wish to describe the afflictions that the land endured,
let us also describe its prosperity, and show from what heights to what depths the rich and glorious land descended. At that time the land was prosperous,
especially Mesopotamia and the whole northern region. It was adorned with crops, vineyards, and abundant livestock. The whole land was filled
with herds of horses and flocks of goats. People acquired such an abundance of grain that wine lasted until the next wine harvest [?], and wheat until the next wheat harvest.
Truly, Israel grew fat and kicked. They did not say, “Blessed is the Lord, who has made us rich.” Instead, they attacked
the property of the monasteries and churches, saying, “What does the church have to pay? We have to pay the poll tax,
and we have children.” For they had many children and had also become very, very rich. They enjoyed every good thing.
They also became haughty, boastful, envious, adulterers, sexually immoral, drunkards, robbers, and false witnesses.
They were close to perishing in the abundance of all their wickedness, had he not sent that evil angel upon them and made a breach among those wicked, overfed people.
If someone had a lawsuit against his neighbor and the judge required witnesses, he would go to the marketplace and meet an acquaintance.
He would say to him, “So-and-so, testify for me.” The other would readily answer, “By the word of God!”
About what? He would swear oaths before knowing. What did such a people deserve, if not what happened?

“Let the work be made harder for the men,” it says, “so that they occupy themselves with it and do not occupy themselves with empty words.” Moreover, there would no longer be any leisure for words [?].
Every day, the people of the same village brought lawsuits against one another over the boundaries of fields, and one village against another.
The wretched people did not know that wrath would soon come upon them, and that they would not even retain possession of their vineyards, houses, and fields.
Instead, these would be left desolate, with no one passing through or living there. Even those in the honored monastic order transgressed its proper obligations.
Instead of following the command, “Take up your cross and come after me,” they acquired horses, herds of cattle, and flocks of goats and sheep.
Each of them took on tax obligations heavier than the public tax. They went out into the countryside to acquire vineyards and houses at auctions,
to ride horses with saddles like the pagans, and to live according to their own desires, without submitting
to the superior appointed over them by God. Do not think, discerning one, that I recount these things because I like accusing people.
Rather, I wish to show God's goodness, compassion, kindness, and patience.
After all these things, stay and listen to the depths into which we slipped and the afflictions that befell us.
On the slaves who rebelled in Harran, a city in Mesopotamia. At this time, many slaves formed a conspiracy.
About five hundred men—Moors, Sindhis, and Khazars—gathered together, armed themselves, and entered the city of Harran at midday.
They headed straight for the treasury, killing everyone they encountered with the sword. They wanted to break into the treasury
and seize its wealth. When Abbas heard this, he hurriedly gathered a large force and met them in battle. When they fought a fierce battle,
men were killed on both sides. Finally, the slaves lost their nerve and fled. Many of them were killed, some were captured, and the rest escaped.
He also seized their masters, beat them, and put many of them to death. On the king's advance into the northern land, and on the building of Callinicus,
and how all the calamities came upon the land from this. Since we have described the land's abundance and splendor, and all its blessings,
and also the rebellious people, we will show where the calamities began. It is written in the prophet: “Behold, the Assyrian is the rod of my anger,
and the staff in their hands deals my blows. I will send him against a godless nation, and commission him against a spiteful people, to take plunder and carry off captives,
and make them like mud in the streets.” And again, because he said, “Behold, the princes are all kings together.”
“Therefore the Lord will not rejoice over their young men, nor will he have compassion on their orphans and widows, because they are all godless and wicked,
and every mouth speaks foolishness.” And, he says, “There will be none who flaps a wing, opens his mouth, or chirps before him.” “He has come,” it says, “to Anath,
and laid down his equipment at Michmash. He crossed the pass of Geba to our lodging place. Ramah was afraid, and Gibeah of Saul fled.
He waved his hand over the mountains of Zion and over the heights of Jerusalem.” The prophet spoke well when he saw with the eye of prophecy
this deadly serpent moving about. In this year, the king fled from the place where he had been living, together with all his nobles.
He advanced into the northern land with vast, uncountable armies. He came to Mosul, and the great and small from all Mosul gathered together.
They lamented before him about the calamities, captivity, oppression, and slaughter that Musa ibn Musab had brought upon them.
But because he delighted in slaughter more than in peace, he drove them all away from his presence.
He even inflicted great suffering on their leading men. He was pleased with Musa and delighted in him, as someone who had found a man after his own heart.
He said, “I have found a man after my own heart, who will carry out all my wishes and do everything that is in my heart. From now on he will walk before me in wickedness all my days.”
As he pressed on to enter Jazira, Abbas, who was his brother and also the emir of Jazira, heard about him.
He knew that the man favored slaughter more than peace. And because the land of Jazira had flourished with vineyards, crops, and settlements in the days of Abbas,
for he was a compassionate man who desired peace, he quickly sent word to all
the districts that they should flee and leave their villages deserted before him. But the villagers did not take heed
or understand what had been told them. Instead, they stayed where they were, undisturbed. When he entered and saw that the land was abundant, splendid, beautiful, and full of every good thing,
For it was the month of Iyar, and all the land’s crops were still in it.
But when he saw these things and surveyed the land, flourishing with its large population, he did not treat his brother as he should have.
When he saw this peace within his brother’s territory, instead of showing gratitude for it, he roared against him like a lion when it wants to maul.
When his brother came out to meet him and welcome him with the ceremony appropriate for kings, he drove him away from his presence and cast him aside like a despised rag.
He would not even allow him to appear before him, saying, “What about your claim that Jazira was devastated?” And he removed him from his position of authority.
He seized his wealth and treated him with every kind of cruelty. After doing these things to his brother, he came against Nisibis and Kaphartutha.
He advanced to Callinicum. On the second building of Callinicum. For this man’s soul was inclined toward sorcerers and diviners.
Whatever they told him, he followed and carried out. When he spoke to them about the times and the kingdoms,
they cobbled together foolish, insipid words and handed them to him, as demons habitually lead astray those who approach them.
They told him, “A man will become king and build a city beside Callinicum.
He will also go to Jerusalem and build a mosque there. This man will reign for forty years.” But the wretched man said, “I am he.”
He sent and brought lime burners from throughout Jazira. He ordered them to mold bricks and the builders to build a wall.
On the flight of the Armenians from Roman territory, and on the slaughter that the Arabs inflicted on the Romans.
While the king was in Callinicum, Armenians left that territory and went to the interior fortresses.
They asked him to go out to meet them, saying that they wanted to come out to Jazira. These were among those who had entered with Kusan.
When they had gone in, gathered their families, and come out, and the Arabs had also come to meet them, the commander of Kamakh heard about it, took a force, and hurried after them.
He caught up with them and their wives while they were encamped in a meadow. But because the Armenians have been deceitful from the beginning and conduct themselves deceitfully,
some men slipped away from them and came and told the Arabs where they were encamped, for they were not very far away. While these Romans were encamped and sleeping without concern,
the Arabs came upon them during the second watch of the night. They fell on them suddenly and slaughtered them with the sword.
He captured many of them and brought those he had taken alive, together with the heads of those he had killed, down to the king at Callinicum.
They wanted to receive a reward from him, along with renown and triumph. But instead of a reward, he gave them a hostile reception.
They say that he even took their slaves. On the assessor whom he sent throughout the land. Again, when he saw that the land was rich in inhabitants, he wanted to carry out a tax reassessment.
He did not desire compassion, settlement, or peace, but to add many people to the poll-tax rolls and to increase the land’s tribute and afflictions.
He sent and brought himself cunning and crafty men, made them officials, and sent them to the districts to register everyone.
On the crown-land officials and tithe collectors whom he also sent throughout the land. Again he appointed ruthless men over the crown lands and the tithes.
And because this official whom he had appointed over the crown estates was a Magian, he was godless and also merciless.
He went through all the cities of Upper Mesopotamia and registered the marketplaces and every place where anything was sold.
Every shop in the marketplaces that had not been included in the tax assessment he seized for the king. He did the same with the mills.
He measured the marketplace with a rope, from one city gate to the other, from east to west, and likewise from north to south.
Beyond the marketplace he measured forty cubits on either side. Whether houses or shops, he took possession of whatever fell within these forty cubits and registered them.
Every place that had not been recorded in the tax assessment—whether a garden, a mill, or cultivated land—he registered among the crown estates,
as belonging to the king. He also registered the wall all the way around, together with its outworks. He registered a strip forty cubits from it all the way around.
He did this to all the cities of Upper Mesopotamia and the West, for he himself traveled through Upper Mesopotamia and the West,
and also through the four Armenias. Other men took over these places from him under fixed-payment contracts.
He himself went down to Harran. From then on there was nothing but raiding and plundering: anyone going out was seized, and anyone coming in was seized as well.
He was stripped and everything he had with him was taken. Whether he sold anything or did not sell, they seized anyone who had anything with him and took his merchandise.
They also went out into the fields and onto the roads, seizing everyone who passed along the road. Concerning the tithe collectors.
He also appointed another official over the tithe and sent him out to devastate the land. When this man arrived and entered the cities,
he entered the marketplaces and went through the shops, recording the merchandise inside each one. If it was worth a hundred coins, he recorded it as worth two hundred. He would collect
the tithe at five coins for every hundred, and, if he could, ten for every hundred. They also went out onto the roads again.
They stripped everyone passing by, both those going and those coming. The wretched men in the cities also went out [?], roaming the roads at night.
They would enter and spread out in the vineyards through which the king’s highway passed. When people passed by—merchants, poor people,
and those coming in search of bread—they seized them roughly and said, “Either give us [?], or come with us to the emir.”
In this way they took as much as they wanted from them and only reluctantly let them go.
They seized poor people who were coming in search of bread and took everything they had with them.
When they begged them to give them [?] so that they could get away, they said, “Go and dig for three or four days for one coin.”
He settled accounts with them as though someone had been digging in his garden. In this way, everywhere, people were robbing the poor.
Even the thieves, wherever they found poor travelers, pretended to be tithe collectors and robbed them.
Thus they had no need to lie in wait on the roads at night, since they carried out their wishes and desires in broad daylight.
They also registered people’s grain. When someone had fifty garibs, they recorded a thousand.
They wrote whatever they pleased. But in this very year he omitted nothing.
On [?] and brands. He appointed other officials to [?] and brand people on their necks like slaves.
“And everyone,” says the prophet, “who does not bear the [?] of that beast between his eyes.” Here, however, they bore it not only between their eyes,
but on both hands, on the chest, and also on the back. When this man came, his arrival shook the earth more than that of all his predecessors.
For he had ordered them to be branded on their hands with a brand that would neither disappear nor be erased from its place throughout a person's lifetime.
When he entered the cities, everyone was thrown into turmoil and fled before him. The shops were shut, and buying and selling ceased in the markets.
Traffic on the roads also ceased, both coming and going. Those coming in stopped because they feared the evils. Those going out also stopped,
because he had seized the gates and allowed no one to leave the city. After he had done this for about a week, and no one remained in the marketplace,
and no one from the countryside was entering the city anymore, he sent the tax officials to the man who had been appointed in place of Abbas to collect the tax.
They said, “The people have fled because of this man. Unless he leaves here, you will not be able to collect the tax.” When he heard this,
he sent a letter after him, and he went down. The people had a brief respite from this man, because he stopped during this year. On deportations.
He also appointed another official to send everyone away to his own country and his father's home. This man likewise appointed officials and sent them to the cities.
It was not one official for each city; rather, he would send the official of each city to another city,
so that officials would gather in a single city—one official in charge of deportations for every city in the Jazira.
And [?] there was no escape on either side, but only plunder, evil, injustice, wickedness, every kind of evil conduct, denunciation, and oppression,
and people taking revenge on one another. This came not only from outsiders but also from those within. A brother would plot against his brother, and one would betray the other.
He appointed a Persian man over Mardin to take away its deportees and collect its tax, because its people had fled more than those of any other place.
The whole country had become Arab, and all the Syrians had fled from among them. His name was Khalil son of Zadan.
This man made the Arabs suffer many evils. Neither before him nor after him was anyone found equal to him in hostility toward the Arabs.
He sent his own commanders to all the cities. Anyone reported to have come from Mardin, whether he himself, his father, or his grandfather,
forty or fifty years earlier, he uprooted from his house, his village, and his inheritance,
and brought him down. With this man no bribe was accepted, nor was any plea received. Nor were they greatly fleeced.
In this way he gathered people into that country until there was no place, village, or ruined settlement that he had not filled and packed with people.
But he drove the Arabs from one region to another, taking everything they possessed.
He also filled their cultivated lands and houses with Syrians, and had their wheat sown for the Syrians. Even those among them who were wealthy,
He seized them and treated them mercilessly, subjecting them to tortures and beatings of every kind.
He would bring one of them forward and pass a razor over his head and beard. He would make him a crown of dough and put it on his head. Then he would seat him
facing the sun and pour oil onto his head so that it would run down little by little into his eyes. His head would also blister and crack.
There was also the crushing of shins, fingers, and arms, and the iron balls that he placed over their eyes.
He treated them with such merciless tortures and killed many of them. The rest fled, passing from one region to another.
As for the other evils that occurred in all the cities, let us call upon the great Joel, who saw them beforehand, and let him recount them to you.
Hear this, elders, and listen, all inhabitants of the land: has anything like this happened in your days or in the days of your ancestors?
Tell your children about it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.
What the flying locust left, the crawling locust ate; and what the crawling locust left, the cricket ate. When the prophet saw this time
and these evils that were destined to come upon humanity during it, he said these things. And so his words were fulfilled in actual events.
Whoever escaped Ṣawfi [?] was caught by the tithe collector, and whoever escaped the tithe collector was caught by the poll-tax collector.
Whoever fled from the poll tax was caught by robbers. But the villagers were worse to them than all the others.
They robbed them under all sorts of pretexts. And because of the tax officials with whom the whole land was filled,
they were afraid to appear before the authorities. Those unjust tax officials themselves would catch anyone they saw.
Either they stripped him and took his earnings, or they led him away and handed him over to the tax official of his own district.
Thus no one could speak of just one evil, for they were hunting people down for one another. They did not care very much about their escape,
but stripped a man as bare as a finger and then relaxed their watch over him a little, so that he would flee from them rather than accompany them and accuse them of having seized his earnings.
And if they happened to catch him again, they treated him worse than before. This wrath was equally severe throughout all the regions of Mesopotamia.
He also ordered that no one should reap, neither Arab nor Syrian. This order was issued before he entered Mesopotamia: no one was to reap or thresh.
For he wanted to inspect the entire harvest. That year the grain came in abundantly everywhere.
When he came and inspected everything, and had inflicted every kind of evil through Abbas [?], he appointed other officials over the zakat, that is, the alms-tax on property.
He sent them throughout the regions. Having received their orders, these men acted mercilessly. They would enter the Arabs’ estates and everything in them,
whether it belonged to Syrians or Arabs, they would register. But they did not merely record what was actually there—the piles, heaps, and stacks of wheat or barley.
If one of them contained a hundred gribas, they would record it as containing three hundred.
Thus, whether something belonged to Syrians or Arabs, nothing was left unregistered: everything situated on the Arabs’ estates was recorded.
Whether a garden, a crop, or property. They would go up to the city and demand money from them for it.

For many of them, even when their grain, ox teams, and wine, if they had any, were sold, the proceeds did not cover what was demanded of them. For they would register a man as having so many ploughlands,
with so many gribs sown in them. Even if he had sown no more than five gribs,
they assessed him for a full ploughland. Thus the Arabs suffered oppression and bitter treatment even more than the Syrians. As for the Syrians, he gave orders to the collectors
of the poll tax, and they assembled. He demanded guarantors from them for every village and sent them to proceed against the emirs, scribes, registrars, district heads, and governors.
While he had not yet left Nisibis, he ordered every emir, scribe, registrar, district head, or governor who had held office in the days of Abbas
to come down to him, together with the local [?]. Even if there were twenty governors in a village, they all came down in response to their written summonses.
Thus the tax collectors who had been handed over to him came down to him at Nisibis. He put them in irons, and they went on with him.
The scribes and registrars also went on with him. They kept paying and suffering losses until they consumed their own flesh, yet they did not escape.
The people of the region remained with him for a long time, but he did not question them about any matter, because they had gone up without orders [?].
Thus they were not questioned, not even after he went up. After doing all these things in Jazira, he stationed his servant at Callinicum.
As Isaiah also said about him: “He deposited his equipment at Michmash. He crossed over to Beth-bethan.
Ramah trembled, and Gibeah of Saul fled.” He stationed this servant of his at Callinicum and crossed over to the west to go to Jerusalem.
He shook it, uprooted it, terrified it, and devastated it more than Jazira. He acted as Daniel prophesies concerning the Antichrist.
“He built,” it says, “the temple as a place of worship.” For the little [?] that remains of Solomon’s temple is a mosque of the Arabs.
“He took,” it says, “a Hittite woman as his wife.” “He rebuilt,” it says, “her ruins.” [?] their slaves and their property, especially buffalo cows. Not one
did he willingly leave to anyone. After doing every kind of evil there, as he had in Jazira, he crossed over and came back as winter approached.
Let us return to Jazira and show what happened. Before his return from the west, he appointed a Persian man to investigate the poll tax,
called Abu Awn, along with other collectors for other revenues. From this point the troubles began.
Like ravenous animals, each of which clings to its own side of a carcass, so these men would enter a single village—five tax collectors in one day,
[?], or six or seven, and sometimes as many as ten. Each of them, for his own share, would pluck away at the inhabitants of that village.
Whether the villagers had the means or not, before leaving there they made them taste death rather than water, along with great losses.
Whenever they finally mounted and rode away, others took up quarters there in turn. By then the villagers could not even provide their bread.
