What, then, can I say except the words of the prophet? “I became to them,” he says, “like a lion and like a bereaved bear. I became to them,” he says, “like a lion
and like a bereaved bear, and like a leopard on the road to Assyria. A lion will devour them there, and a wild beast will tear them apart.”
If anyone calls these people wild beasts, he is not mistaken, because they were worse than birds and wild beasts.
And the same prophet also said: “And [?], and his springs will dry up, and his fountains will become parched. He will plunder the treasury of all its precious objects.”
“Samaria will be condemned,” he says, “because she has rebelled against her God.” Another prophet said: “Wake up, you drunkards, and wail, all you wine drinkers, over the wine
that has disappeared from your mouths. For a nation has come up against my land, mighty and beyond counting. Its teeth are like a lion’s teeth, and its fangs are like the fangs of a young lion.”
You see how the prophets call this wicked people wild beasts. “It has laid waste my vine,” he says, “and stripped my fig tree.
It stripped it and threw it down, and its branches turned white.” Truly, wine disappeared from the vineyard workers. They even began fleeing from village to village,
though even in this way they could not escape. Whoever escaped one man was received by another, who stripped them.
Even if they escaped the depredations of thieves, the masters of the village they entered acted in place of thieves and robbers.
Whoever there bore the title or was recognized as chief and governor was himself the chief of a robbers’ den.
When the poor went to seek shelter with him, he dug pits of every kind for them. And every evil
flowed from him upon those far away and those nearby, those within and those outside. In this respect, all the local chiefs were alike.
“Her rulers,” he says, “are rebellious and companions of thieves. They all love bribes and hurry to repay injuries.
They do not give justice to orphans and have no compassion on widows.” Nor was God’s judgment before their eyes.

If the prophet bears witness to these things, what blame can those who love God place on us, who have seen and felt them with our own hands, for putting them in writing so that they may be known to the generations after us?
It is written: “Ask your father, and he will tell you.” And it says: “Tell your children, and let their children tell another generation.” Concerning how people began to plunder graves.
But when evils multiplied and struck against one another, beating wing against wing and reaching out hand to hand, and from every
side the sound of lamentation could be heard, no one among the living was able to escape this distress.
It grew so severe against people still living bodily lives that they even went out in bands against those sleeping in the dust.
And those who had a desire for theft and for plundering [?]—and that instrument of sin was revealed, that son of destruction,
that advocate of the devil, who exalts himself above everything divine and worshiped, whose root and origin are from that rebellious house,
from that people who wanted to stone Moses. From them an evil shoot sprang up against us at this time because we had sinned: namely, Musa ibn Mus'ab.
People had not yet been greatly oppressed, but only the poor of the lowest classes and the resident foreigners who were in the land.
These were oppressed, ruined, and destroyed that year. They began carrying their children on their shoulders and moving from village to village.
In this year, shocking reports reached us from distant regions: in such-and-such a place, people were opening graves and, it was said, taking silver and gold out of them.
We could not accept what we heard, because the deed was so appalling—that people could do this to the dead.
Although everyone who came said this, and reported that gold was being extracted from them, we do not venture to affirm that this is possible.
But the matter was not long delayed, and we saw it with our own eyes in our lands and among our fathers and brothers who had previously died.
This too we set down here in its proper time, just as it was, as it happened.
Concerning our Lord’s rainbow, which appeared inverted in this year, and concerning the white rod that appeared in the middle of the sky.
It was directed toward the curve of the rainbow like an arrow. Again, in this same year,
in the month of May, the rainbow that is regularly seen in the clouds appeared with its curve below and its arms pointing upward.
It resembled a bow drawn in a man’s hand for battle, displaying a threat and a warning against the inhabitants of the earth.
It appeared on holy Sunday, at the third hour of the day, as the honored elders who saw it before us testified.
If anyone is unwilling to believe this, let him examine the earlier chapters, and he will find something like it. The things that happened afterward also bear witness.
Again, something appeared like a white rod, stretching from the western edge of the sky until its tip pointed eastward in the middle of the sky.
It was as thick as a rope. This too was not seen by many, for it continued rising for many days.
Many people said many things about it. Some said that it was a rod of wrath.
Others said that it was a comet, one of those that rise in the sky, and that it meant nothing. But discerning and God-fearing people,
when they saw this sign, were filled with great fear, because they knew that this was on account of sins,
and a threat full of wrath. Fools did not even give it a thought. As it is said, “The wise person looks into the distance, but the fool does not even look at what is before his eyes.”
As it is said, “The wise person’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness.” This rod pointed directly toward the middle of the drawn bow.
It showed its effect and did not delay long, but carried out the work for which it had been sent by
God. Perhaps someone will say that God has no bow and arrows. Whoever wishes to say this should listen to what the psalmist says:
“God will rise up and suddenly shoot an arrow at them. Their tongues will grow weak, and all who see them will tremble, and all people will be afraid.”
And again he says, “He sent out his arrows and scattered them.” People were scattered and became refugees everywhere. Lands were devastated; villages [?] were deserted.
The people went from place to place. Concerning another sign that appeared again in the northern region in the same year.
Another sign appeared at the northern horizon. Its very appearance testified to God’s threat and warning against us.
It appeared during the harvest season, covering the whole northern side, from the eastern corner to the western corner.
Its appearance was like this: one red band, one [?], one black, and one saffron-colored. It rose from below upward.
As one band faded, another rose. While someone watched it, it changed into seventy different forms.
To the discerning, it was a sign warning of a threat. Many people said many things about this, saying that it foretold bloodshed.
Others said other things. But who knows the works of the Lord? “I will give signs in heaven,” he says, “and mighty deeds on earth.”
On how the poll tax was collected, and on the imprisonment in the churches. When they demanded payment from everyone, and people could not find the means to pay it all,
the emir seized these guarantors and apportioned among them as much as he could, assigning everyone
an equal share. They then apportioned it among their villages [?]. Since these troubles caused by Abbas had not yet begun,
and the root of all evils had not yet arrived, the demand was not issued oppressively or beyond what was rightfully due. Rather, they demanded the revenue in full from its districts.
But when even this did not suffice, he again apportioned it among them—that is, among the guarantors. And when even this did not suffice,
although those guarantors had also plundered the poor, orphans, and widows in their districts, he showed no pity for the orphans and no mercy to the widows.
This was not done on the government's orders, but on their own initiative. As the saying goes, “The wild asses in the wilderness are food for the lion, and the poor are food for the rich.”
Such was their situation. Yet many of them rejoiced in this lurking danger and darkness that had settled over the land. The wretches did not know that before long
wrath would sweep over them too. Instead, each hurried to buy the utensils, property, and belongings of the poor people in their village
and stockpiled them in their houses. Now they had become rich, just as they wished, making advance loans [?] and lending at interest without mercy.
They were close to achieving their desire of acquiring even the children of the poor as male and female slaves. The wretches did not know
that the end of the wicked is destruction. They would pay a dinar for fifty grivas of wheat, some for sixty, and others for seventy.
For anyone who produced a zuz, they would write down as much as he wanted. For wine, they would pay a dinar for fifty measures,
others for sixty or seventy, and even eighty. Wheat was selling in the market at thirty grivas for a dinar,
or thirty-five, and the amount rose as high as forty. It was the same with wine. A sheep cost a zuz,
a goat a zuz, an ox five zuzim, and a donkey four zuzim. Low prices for everything
prevailed. When the business remained unfinished and the amount had not been raised, the emir assembled the local inhabitants.
Now this emir was a man who hated oppression and injustice. He would not even accept a gift from anyone,
nor would he send a policeman into the district. He assembled the local inhabitants and imprisoned them in the great church. On the imprisonment in the church.
When the herald called for them to assemble in the church, the policemen also went out to [?] a fire. They rounded up everyone who had a reputation for having even a little money.
What can I say now except the words of the prophet? “O God, the nations have entered your inheritance and defiled your holy temple.
They have made your holy temple a latrine. They have handed over the bodies of your servants to beatings and tortures,
and the flesh of your righteous ones to be torn by whips and rods, their feet to the stocks, and their hands to suspension.”
and their fingers to their wrists. For all the freeborn men had been gathered together, as well as the freeborn women.
Those whose husbands were far away, or somewhat removed from this evil affair, he brought out of their houses and dragged through the marketplace.
He brought them down and imprisoned them in the church itself. Women who had never been seen in the marketplace were brought down in humiliation among the men.
He did the same to the Arab women. All the Arabs, too, were brought down without distinction. If a man was absent, he dragged away his wives or his daughters.
As they seized people one by one, village by village, they either borrowed and brought the money, or were killed with blows and the crushing of their feet and fingers.
The wicked men who made these threats went up and sat on the elevated seat before the table of the divine sacrifice.
He even dared to do this: for the prostrations of their prayer, which provokes God, onto the table
that was holy they would climb to pray. With unclean feet they trampled that holy table.
In the sanctuary itself they performed that unclean washing of their private parts, along with the other filthy acts they committed there. And all the people, men and freeborn women,
relieved themselves inside it, in front of one another, without concealment. And [?] they remained there for three days and their nights. A bitter outcry rose from it.
Instead of the sweet fragrance of choice spices, the stench of decay rose from it, together with the bitter outcry of those being punished there.
Because of the oppression, they turned against the possessions of the churches and monasteries,
so that even the distant churches might feel the humiliation being inflicted on the city's glorious church, which was also the head of all those in the region.
Although the foul stench did not spread its odor through them, their possessions, vessels, and altars were stripped from their inhabitants and pledged into the hands of pagans.
"I will begin with my house," he says, "because the priests have defiled the sanctuary and violated the law." "What use to me," he says, "are your many sacrifices?
I have had enough of burnt offerings of rams and the fat of fattened animals. I take no pleasure in the blood of bulls, lambs, and goats.
When you come to appear before me, who has required this from your hands, that you trample my courts? Bring me worthless offerings no longer.
Incense is detestable to me. At the new moon and on the Sabbath you gather an assembly. I cannot endure [?] and confinement.
My soul hates your new moons and your festivals. They have become a burden to me; I am weary of carrying it. When you spread out your hands, I will turn my eyes away from you.
Even if you multiply your prayers, I will not listen. Your hands are full of blood." And as, upon all the evils of our many sins,
the prophet looked with the eye of the Spirit, he said these things: "From now on there will be no delay in my words, says the Lord. I have spoken, and I will act."
After the oppressor had dealt with them using every torment and affliction, he compelled everyone to contribute, each one of them, as he saw fit in the matter:
Arabs and Syrians, merchants together with the shopkeepers of the marketplace. For during those days buying and selling had ceased in the marketplace,
and the roads were empty of people coming in and going out, because the city gates had been shut. And when the God-fearing people saw
all the filth that these unclean men were committing inside the holy sanctuary, they clothed themselves in deep sorrow and cried out to the Lord, saying, "Why, Lord, have you forgotten me like this?"
And your anger grew fierce against the sheep of your pasture. Remember, Lord, your church, which you acquired with the precious blood of your Only Begotten.
And you redeemed it through your life-giving sufferings. Your enemies boasted within your church. As though it were a thicket of trees, they split its gates with axes,
along with its timbers. The dwelling of your name was defiled on the ground, while they said, “Let us destroy them all together,
and abolish all God’s festivals from the earth.” How long, God, will the enemy taunt you and provoke your name forever?
Why have you withdrawn your hand and your right hand from within your church? Why, Lord, has your anger blazed against your people, and why have you rejected your inheritance?
You handed us over to the nations. Those who hate us gained power over us, and our enemies enslaved us. We were subjected to their hands.
In response to these things, the Lord himself says, “I rescued you many times, but you embittered me through your deeds.”
When they put pressure on everyone, money was collected. He did not even spare what his associate had lent to the villagers, down to the last dinar [?], for they went out and demanded
it from Cyrrhus. Thus the tax collector [?] the region and went down to Nisibis to meet the Commander of the Faithful, after making the rounds of the West.
This round of collections took place in all the churches of the cities. More than all the others, the church of Edessa was plundered, and its possessions were carried away.
Let us too say with the prophet, “Despite all these things, the Lord’s wrath against us has not subsided,
but his hand is still raised.” Concerning a deceiver who appeared in Jazira in the year 1081.
For we have desired to relate everything and leave a record for those who come into the world after us, so that, when they see the sign that has been set up, at which their predecessors stumbled,
they may take care not to stumble over it themselves. “The fool is struck,” it is said, “and the wise person takes warning.” Let them see the stumbling blocks over which their predecessors stumbled
and turn away from them themselves. For each day its own filth wells up with it. Our Lord commanded his disciples, “Beware of false prophets,
who come to you in sheep’s clothing.” He said, “They will lead many astray, and, if possible, even the elect.”
And again, “See that no one leads you astray. Many will come in my name. If someone tells you, ‘Look, the Messiah is here,’ or ‘He is over there,’
do not go. Many are going to lead people astray. If someone tells you that he is in the wilderness, do not go out.
And if they tell you that he is in the inner room, do not go in.” Although Christ himself revealed all the stumbling blocks to us,
and the prophets also proclaimed them to us beforehand, and the apostles cried like trumpets in my ears about the coming of the deceiver and the false prophets who come before him,
we listened neither to the prophets nor to the Lord nor to the apostles. Instead, we shut our eyes and stopped our ears
and buried our hearts in the mire of error, so that we would not see with our eyes, hear with our ears, or understand with our hearts the words of the holy Scriptures. Instead, we forgot them all
and followed our own desires. As for the one Daniel called “the sign of desolation,” Christ “the false messiah,” and the apostle “the son of destruction”—as for the Antichrist, we
have grasped him with our hands and touched him. One of the messengers of the one who is written to be coming at the end appeared in our own days.
His disciple has shown us everything that he will do when he comes, now through deeds and not through hearsay.
At every dangerous and frightening place where a murder has been committed, discerning people put up some sign, so that when people who do not know come and see that sign,
they may understand in their hearts that the sign proclaims a warning. From then on, it teaches them about what happened in that place before.
We too have set down here these things that happened in our time, so that, if you too should happen to encounter him, you may beware of that bitter one,
who mixes his bitterness with honey. Now it happened at this time that a certain man came from the region of Tikrit, from the village of Beth Rama.
Having lost his parents while he was young, he longed for the chaste life of monasticism. He left and entered the holy monastery of Mar Matthew in the region of Mosul.
After he had been there for two or three years, the evil one enticed him to return again to his former vomit.
For he had not yet distributed what his parents had left him. Just as he tempted Judas through the love of money, so he tempted this man too,
setting great things before him through love for the poor and strangers, the afflicted and the distressed, along with many other things.
But in exchange for his splendid promises, he reached out and gave him a noose, just as he had given that other man. Now when
he went home, instead of monastic conduct and love for the poor and afflicted,
he attached himself to young men his own age and joined them in everything they did. Instead of distributing his earnings to the needy, as he said he would, he squandered them on drunkenness.
He lived dissolutely, behaving disgracefully, and in the end he even turned to paganism and became a pagan.
As he continued living so dissolutely, all his wealth was squandered. Nothing remained that had not been squandered through his loathsome conduct, except a rope.
He came to his senses and said, “Woe to me! What have I done to myself?” He left and went into the desert of Sinjar, to the virtuous hermits there.
When they received him, he chose great and severe labors for himself. He subjected his body to fasting, along with many prayers.
He continued in these practices for about five years, until his body wasted away and he became like an Indian, his complexion changed by the harshness of the sky.
Even now the devil did not leave him alone. Instead, he began appearing to him, it is said, in the form of angels who praised his labors.
They also told him, it is said, about things to come. But when the holy Mar Zeora heard these things, he said to him, “My son, beware of the deceiver’s cunning.
All these things come from the evil one.” For this chaste man, Zeora, was at that time the head of the ascetics there.
Every day that chaste man warned him not to be deceived by any of these things,
but to despise them all, because they came from the evil one. Yet he did not stand firm, but surrendered himself to them. And [?] he drew people after him,
saying, “Such and such will happen. So-and-so has also had such and such done to him. Today people are coming to me from such-and-such a place.”
Discerning people know that this is not difficult for a demon: when he induces someone to do
something, he arranges for his counsel concerning that person to be revealed publicly. He does not speak of something that does not happen, but of something that happens through his counsel.
For this reason he is called the slanderer, because he reveals secrets. It is written, “A slanderer reveals secrets.”
Nor, again, if someone sets out on a journey and a swift messenger comes and says, “So-and-so is coming here today,” has he said something that will not happen,
but something that will come to pass. In this way this wretched man, too, went astray, fell into error, and departed from what was right,
through demonic visions in dreams. A great crowd began gathering behind him, because he himself had gone astray and lost his mind.
But when the blessed Mar Ze‘ora heard these things, and they saw that he would not accept their advice,

but had even begun to despise them, saying, “You are simply jealous of me,” he seized him and [?], and they drove him away from there. They also excommunicated him, forbidding him to remain anywhere in Mosul.
He left and came to Jazira, to the territory of Dara. Now in the territory of Dara there is a large, strong village,
with a large population. Its inhabitants are simple people and exceptionally hardworking farmers, more so than all their neighbors.
They are also more devout than all the others in their region, and are deeply attached to the monks.
They honor their priests as they would angels, because they are far removed from all worldly cunning
and concern themselves only with their work. It was to such a devout people that the devil led his servant.
When he entered the village and they saw him in shabby clothing, with his appearance filthy and blackened, they welcomed him as they would an angel.
He began telling them that he had been sent by God to proclaim to them
that their village was soon to be overthrown and swallowed up in the earth, that a plow would pass over it, and that it would never be inhabited again. In their simplicity,
they accepted him, and in the purity of their hearts they listened to everything he told them. The name of that village is Hah, in Tur Abdin.
Every day he proclaimed, “Repent, pray, and fast before the earth opens its mouth and swallows you,
for the measure of your sins is full, and your wickedness has become greater than that of Sodom and Gomorrah. Now nothing remains but a sentence without mercy.”
When the pure-hearted people heard these things and saw the honey mixed with poison, the wholesomeness of the honey kept them from recognizing the bitterness of the deadly poison.
They did not listen to our Lord, or to the prophets, or to the apostles, or even to their own bishops. Because of the words “Fast and pray,” they did not recognize the evil one’s deceit.
Instead, whenever anyone said, “Fear God! This man is a deceiver,” they would reply, “What evil thing does he say?
He only says, ‘Fast and pray.’” They would not listen to anything from anyone, but went astray and led the whole region astray after him.
They clothed themselves in mourning and tears, abandoned their work, and left their crops and vineyards untended. They devoted themselves to supplications.
From then on they began saying about him, “He performs every kind of miracle, just like our Lord.” His messengers—that is, the demons—went out
and spread his fame throughout the whole land of Jazira. People from the north and south, east and west, flocked to him, all wandering off to greet him.
When a group was coming from one direction and met another group going away from him,
those who were coming would ask those who were leaving, “How did you find the man?” And they would say:
that nothing like what he was doing had been heard of anywhere in the world. They would also show their limbs and say, “This man
was paralyzed; this man’s arm was withered; this man had leprosy; and this man was blind. But now, as you can see, we have no defect or pain of any kind.
Look at our eyes, which are open, our hands, which are stretched out, and our legs, which are healthy. Do not question us, but be strengthened through faith and go to him.
You will receive from him everything you ask for.” And so they continued on their way to him.
Others like these would also meet all the caravans coming to him: “He drives out demons, opens the eyes of the blind, and makes the deaf hear.
He makes the paralyzed walk.” And [?] they would say to others, “We [?] as he raised a dead person. They performed all the miracles before us.”
Be assured, reader and listener, that those who appeared to people as they went there and met them with donkeys, mules, horses, and a large crowd,
and who would also show their limbs, claiming that he had healed them, were not human beings, but demons.
We can know this from the fact that not a single [?] was ever seen returning from him in good health. They would appear to others and say to them,
“We are angels, bound by the prayer of Mar Marutha”—for they called him Marutha—“and if he lets us, we will bring rabies along with locusts.”
They would appear to others and say, “Flying serpents are coming upon the earth, and they will leave no one alive, if Mar Marutha lets us.”
Voices like these were heard throughout all the regions of Mesopotamia, coming from rebellious demons.

From then on, there was no interruption in the traffic on the roads leading there. Understand, discerning reader: even when that son of perdition comes, he will act in just this way, as his servants go out
and spread his fame throughout the earth. They will show themselves bodily to everyone, saying, “This man was paralyzed; this man was blind; and this man had leprosy.
He healed them.” They also make one another dead, paralyzed, leprous, blind, and afflicted with every kind of sore, and bring them before him.
When he commands the paralyzed man to walk, he walks. And look: he is like someone who was truly paralyzed, and now, look, he walks!
The wretched people who abandon the Holy Scriptures and follow him do not know that these are demons.
No one who approaches him is healed by him unless his affliction comes from the evil one himself. When that demon leaves him, he appears healthy.
He says, “You are not being healed because you have no faith.” We ourselves have seen [?], and we testify to these things:
Of all those whom we saw going to him and returning, whenever one was asked, “Have you recovered?” he would say, “I am well,” although he had received no benefit from him at all.
That man would say, “If you believe, you will receive healing in forty days.” And on this condition—“At the end of forty days you will receive healing”—
he would dismiss them. Thus people from all the regions rushed out and went to him. They also brought him many deeds,
along with gold, silver, and splendid vessels. He reportedly gave alms and offered many prayers. [?] He would stand and sprinkle ashes on the people,
saying that God was being appeased. He stood on a raised platform like a bishop, although he had been appointed to the rank of deacon.
Yet the apostolic canons command that a priest is not to be blessed except by a fellow priest or a bishop, nor is he to receive a blessing.
But apart from these things, this insolent man not only used to bless the priests; he would even, they say, pass a cross and his hand over
the priests’ heads. He also used to prepare oil of prayer while many priests were gathered around him, and give it to them.
He prepared the oil in this way: he would, they say, recite a prayer [?], and afterward spit into it. With his spittle he would consecrate it.
No bishop or monk could enter there and say anything against him without being killed by the inhabitants of that village.
They would say, “You are simply jealous of him.” But the holy Mar Cyriacus, the bishop of that region,
when he saw that his flock had been taken captive by the Evil One, and that they would not listen to anything he told them, but even subjected him to abuse,
hurried to the venerable Patriarch David and informed him of everything. When the venerable David heard these things, he had the man seized and imprisoned in Harran.
Even then they did not abandon his error. Many people would even come to visit him in prison.
He would, they say, prepare oil and give it to them, and that filthy man would even consecrate it with his spittle.
Passing over many things, we turn to other matters, wishing to describe the years of distress that the land endured.
Concerning the first year of distress, which was the year 1084. First, concerning the scribes, tax collectors, and fiscal officers.
When the king returned from the land of Jerusalem, he seized Abbas and stripped him of everything he possessed. In his place he appointed Musa, [?] Mus'ab,
whom we mentioned above. He handed over to him the tax collectors, scribes, and fiscal officers who had served in the days of Abbas, so that he could audit their accounts.
He himself went down to Baghdad. When this tyrant received the order, he sent for everyone who had been a tax collector, fiscal officer, or scribe in the days of Abbas.
Since he had not yet left Mosul, he took them down to Balad and imprisoned them there, weighed down with heavy iron shackles.
Without auditing their accounts or making inquiries in the districts so that they could disclose what they had collected, this man, skilled in evil, sent and brought to himself
from each city men who were informers and greedy, men who had no thought of God at all.
Such were the men this son of destruction chose for himself—slanderers like himself. He honored them in word and deed,
even promising them great things, like Satan promising those who follow him.
After all this, he repaid them with an evil end and hell. With these words he would win each of them over.

Each would disclose information about those from his own city, whether a scribe, tax collector, or fiscal officer: what he possessed and what he did not, and his circumstances regarding wealth, houses, or [?].
When he had learned about everyone and had also become informed about their activities, not even those informers received a good outcome from him.
Instead, God handed them over to that wicked man whom they loved [?], and they suffered worse than anyone.
They harassed those who had served under Abbas for about five or six months, until he had learned all their activities
from these wicked men whom this tyrant had selected from their cities. He did not accept information from only one district.
He brought each of them out one by one. According to what he learned about each person from informers, he mercilessly assessed the gold they were to give him.
For some it was two thousand, for others four thousand, for others ten thousand, for others fifteen thousand, for others twenty thousand, for others thirty thousand, and for others forty thousand.
As we said earlier, he assessed them according to what he had learned from informers—not because
they owed it, but to satisfy his own greed and appetite. And so he tortured the feet and hands of each of them,
until he accepted the amount assessed against him. Once he had agreed and accepted it, he would send him in irons to his city, accompanied by horsemen and Arabs, to collect that sum from him.
He also ordered the assessors to come and record everything they had left. Now this man, so skilled in evil, saw that the king had promoted him and increased his former honors.
He also knew that the king himself delighted in devastation more than a wicked man did. He roared like a lion bent on destruction and began devising schemes against the land,
just as Pharaoh had against the Israelites. First he ordered the assessors to assess their regions.
These assessors, too, had learned every kind of greed from him. Nor did he order them to assess the land out of any desire for its welfare,
but for appearances, so that word would spread that he was collecting according to a new assessment.

This is clear from what happened in the end: from anyone whose assessment the assessors increased, he collected according to the new assessment; from anyone whose assessment they reduced, he collected according to the old one.
The assessors themselves openly demanded gifts and promises, without shame or fear of anything.
Thus they assessed the land, producing no benefit, but only the great losses caused by their theft and greed.
On the tattooers and the lead seals. Along with these men, he also sent tattooers and lead seals.
They were also instructed to tattoo everyone they caught with the name of his region and city. Then he was to be sent off to his region and his own locality.
But they paid no attention to this. Instead, they hurried to satisfy their greed. Moreover, they would fasten these
seals on them for [?], and they themselves imposed many additional charges on them. First he seized the leaders of the region,
saying, “Let everyone bring his own people into the city, so that I will not have to go outside and become a burden to you.” When everyone had brought in his own people, he tattooed them,
writing the name of each man's city on his right hand and “Jazira” on his left. Around his neck he hung two seals,
one stamped with the name of his city and the other with the name of his overseer. At the outset he also collected one zuz from every three men.
He also recorded the man's name, his appearance and distinguishing features, and the village and district he came from. This greatly disturbed the people,
because he caught many people who were strangers. He tattooed each with the place the man said he came from,
even though it sometimes happened that the man had never entered that village. If this registration had actually been completed,
it would have harmed the world more than anything that had happened on earth. When he saw that his work was not completed, he went out into the region, and they caught everyone coming and going.
Although he passed through that same region more than twenty times, it was not enough for him, until he had exhausted the people. No one escaped him.
And then, as the prophet Daniel and the apostle John said, all people were taken, and no one escaped him.
And then, as the prophet Daniel and the apostle John said, all people received the mark of that beast on their hands, their breasts, and their backs.
On the tithe collectors. He sent other workers to collect the tithe, and these too threw the land into turmoil.
When he entered the cities and passed through [?], he would also show what was in it. If a poor man had property there worth a hundred coins, they recorded it as five hundred.
And if it was worth a thousand, they recorded it as five thousand. He passed through the houses of the Syrians and the Arabs. Wherever there was
wheat or barley, or anything like these stored away, they sealed it up. And without even looking inside,
they would write, “[?] thousand charged to so-and-so.” They also demanded from him one jarib for every ten jaribs, saying that he must deliver them to them in Baghdad.
Had this been carried through, it would have devastated the land. For there were many of them who had ten thousand recorded against them,
though they did not possess twenty jaribs. For those wicked informers whom we mentioned above had become their teachers in wrongdoing.
Musa himself also continually sent for them, and they came down to him, so that he could learn everything that was in each one's city.
From then on, people bribed him personally and paid him honors, so that he would keep his mouth shut about them. And when the tithe collectors did these things,
the poor people suffered losses [?], and also at the hands of the informers, in great measure. Only with difficulty did they put a stop to this evil from them.
After that he went out to the roads and the crossings, and they stripped everyone who came and went. They also lay in ambush on the roads at night,
and like thieves took people's earnings, including those of people fleeing the tithe and the crown-estate levy, saying, “We are tithe collectors.”
When this limitless evil began devastating the land, and the roads were cut off from people coming and going,
they went down and cried out before Musa. He ordered that they were not to harass anyone outside the marketplace. Then, only with difficulty, they stopped their evil deeds.
On crown estates. Every shoot that sprang up after another was worse than the one before it.
For these shoots sprang from an evil, bitter root full of wrath. It is written, “Their planting is from an evil plant,” and again,
“The love of money is the root of all evils.” The greedy man can never be satisfied. Even if he acquires the whole world,
he longs to acquire still more that he has not seen. And just as Sheol and destruction are never satisfied, neither is this man, who is a son of Sheol and a son of destruction.
He was not satisfied with all the people, their vineyards, their possessions, and their lands. They worked for him,
but they were not enough for him. Instead, he spread his greed over the roads, the mountains, and the waters flowing in the rivers,
and even to the dead who had been in their graves for two or three thousand years.
He tore their bones from their resting places and scattered them over the surface of the earth like manure. Woe to you, Sheol!
Just as you are not satisfied with the corpses you heap up within yourself every day, so too the children you have borne and acquired are not satisfied, until death itself shuts their greedy mouths.
When those appointed over the crown estates arrived, he seized the marketplaces and the roads, and took all the passersby captive. He also occupied the river crossings so that no one could cross.
Nor could fishermen catch fish from them. He measured the marketplaces with a rope, from north to south and from east to west,
forty cubits on this side and another forty cubits on the other side. He seized houses, shops, and many courtyards.
Every shop that they did not find in the old assessment they confiscated. They forced the inhabitants of the houses to leave them.
When the loss here, at the hands of this man and that ringleader of all evils, became great, this evil was stopped only with difficulty.
He also measured the city wall itself and seized the porticoes and its surroundings, so that by every possible means they might satisfy their money-loving greed.
He sent out a herald to proclaim: “Anyone who wants to rent a shop or a portico must go
to the administrator of the crown estates.” Through these measures too he caused their owners great loss, and he scarcely returned to anyone anything of what he had taken.
They seized the places where there had been trading. And because many people lived by catching fish in the rivers,
selling them and paying the taxes imposed on them in their distress, he sent out a herald to proclaim: “Anyone who catches a fish from the river, or builds a fish weir or a dam in it,
without authorization from the crown-estates administrator is liable to death.” Thus people were prevented from fishing. If they happened to catch someone bringing in fish
or casting a net, they would beat him with deadly blows and take the proceeds of his work.
They also demanded from anyone who wanted to fish half of whatever catch he might make. When the fishermen had been barred everywhere, some of their own number came forward,
and he accepted their undertaking to pay him the tax he had assessed on them. They in turn imposed assessments on the villages situated along the river.
He did the same with all the rivers, specifying the stretch each person was taking over and the amount of tax.
They also seized the ferryboats, and he likewise took half their revenue. From then on everyone was oppressed on every side:
anyone who escaped the tithe would be caught by the crown-estates administrator. Sometimes both would seize him at the same time,

along with the other deportation officers, who left no one anything.
On the deportations and the evils that took place.
This root of persecution produced
a shoot containing more deadly and destructive poison than all those before it. He appointed one agent over the whole of Mesopotamia to deport everyone to his own country.
When this man received this command, he set his face
toward every kind of evil and chose wicked men for himself. Anyone who called them wild beasts and birds of prey would not be wrong. These were the men he chose and sent to the cities.
He also fixed how much gold each of them was to bring him. He appointed and sent many agents to a single city, doing this for every city in Mesopotamia.
He treated each city in this way, so that ten agents might enter a city in a single day or week to carry out deportations.
Thus they descended on people like destructive beasts, tearing them apart without mercy.
They sold everything that any one of them possessed and took it, supposedly as their wages. They brought the people in and confined them in houses until they perished from hunger.
Many of them also died from hunger, cold, and the beatings with which they were tortured to make them bring money.
For everything these poor people possessed was not enough to satisfy the greed of the birds that had gathered over them.
And because these things did not suffice them, he turned against the inhabitants of the region, while they invented pretexts against them.
“We have men staying with you,” they said. And they oppressed people through their expenses and demands, beyond their taxes and other dues.
Thus, if someone entered a village or an estate, he would find more than four or five officials.
And if someone fled from one village to another to escape, while he was traveling along the road,
he would be attacked by deportees, tax collectors, or thieves. For now they were robbing openly, without keeping watch at night.
And if he happened to escape these too, the villagers themselves made up for all the other evils,
without fear of God. Now, then, it is time to say with the prophet Moses: “A fire has been kindled in my anger, and it burns down to the lowest Sheol.
It will consume the earth and its produce, and burn even the foundations of the mountains. I will heap evils upon them, and unleash fanged beasts against them,
along with the venom of snakes that crawl in the dust. Outside, the sword will cut them down, and inside their rooms, terror.”
Do not suppose that by “fanged beasts” or “snakes” the prophet means creatures that are snakes and birds by nature.
Rather, he means those who possess only the outward appearance of human beings, while all the evils of dragons, wild beasts, and [?] are found in their conduct.
As the philosopher also said: “I see a human being, but I do not see humanity.” He saw, that is, the image of a human being,
but he did not see human conduct—only that of beasts and birds. And the prophet adds: “The venom of snakes.”
Know, discerning person, [?] that all these things were found in them, especially venom, for they would accept no persuasion,
but were like fire. Nor did they have any mercy; rather, they were like ravenous wolves falling upon a flock.
The region’s own officials became mute dogs for them, unable to bark.
Instead, they too came to an agreement with the thieves and lent them a hand in every evil and injustice.
And when a poor man whose earnings had been seized came before them, he received no help from them.
For greed had struck them dumb, and they could not speak what was right, because they themselves had departed from the path of justice.
And whatever they agreed upon [?], they contrived every means for their own benefit and seized whatever had been
plundered from the poor. Let us also tell of the evils that befell the Arabs, for not a single person escaped this wrath that came at this time
because of our many sins. Again, concerning the official in charge of the Arabs’ property-alms tax. A ravenous wolf’s entire conduct is full of fury.
So too with this man: all his steps and movements were full of oppression and fury. He also appointed another official over the Arabs’ property-alms tax.
This was like a kind of assessment imposed on the Syrians. He also imposed another burden concerning the Arabs’ tax on wealth [?].
This was like a kind of assessment imposed on the Syrians: he went over them and their estates.
He registered their plowlands, all their property, and the income from everything that each of them possessed.
Whether it was a vegetable garden or a flax plot, he registered it, even if it belonged to villagers. But they, because it was not in their laws—
nor had any of the former kings imposed such a levy—regarded it with contempt and paid no attention to it.
When he had finished registering all their holdings, he sat down, calculated everything, and made it into a monetary tax. He assessed each plowland at twenty-four zuz.
As for the tithe that fell due to him from goats, sheep, cattle, and other produce, he assigned them prices just as he pleased; he did the same with wheat.
For he left nothing of theirs unregistered, down to beehives, pigeons, and chickens.
Even if a villager had sown a plot of wheat or barley, or planted a garden, on the estate of one of them, they registered it against its owner, the Arab.
When they had calculated the entire monetary tax and assessed each person according to his holdings, crooked, insolent men came upon them, worse than a brood of vipers.
They were spiteful, unjust, and merciless, and the judgment of God was not before their eyes. They had no
respect for the elderly, showed no mercy to widows, and plundered orphans. Men like these came to collect payment from them.
From then on, nothing could be seen but distinguished men and elders being dragged about and pulled around, while blows and floggings of every kind were inflicted on them.
With a rope they would suspend one of them by his arm—distinguished men, bearers of [?]—
until they were close to departing from this world. Supposedly, they were taking one-tenth.
Those Arabs even sold everything they owned, but it was not enough to meet what was demanded of them.
They also pleaded with them to collect according to the law laid down by Muhammad, their guide and lawgiver,
and by the former kings: to take from what each one possessed—wheat from wheat, and likewise livestock from livestock. But they would not agree.
Instead, they told them, “Go and sell your holdings however you please, and give us our gold.” Truly, here evil was outdone by evil.
And there is also that secular saying: “Sorcerers overcome sorcerers.” Antidotes too are overcome by other antidotes made from bitter and harmful vipers.
Those Arabs too were burrowing among these wretched villagers like a worm in wood.
He took their lands and houses, their movable goods and their possessions, until they were close to acquiring both them and their children as slaves.
Whatever they owned, they themselves worked it for them like slaves. But against the crooked serpent this did not avail them—that is, against Musa ibn Mus'ab.
Instead, he brought all their schemes to nothing. Nothing but blows and severe floggings could be heard on every side. Besides this,
in some places those Arabs themselves also made the villagers living on their estates taste death.
Because they too were divided over whether to pay along with them, until he uprooted them and took everything they owned. He even fled from their settlement.
And because this was the beginning of the trouble, and he was the first of the plunderers, and there was still something of everything left,
they were not altogether severely distressed. But he was not satisfied even with those unjust exactions. He assessed each plow at twenty-four zuze.
And for every thirty oxen, a heifer fit for the yoke. He assessed the heifer at twelve zuze.
And again, for every forty oxen, a cow. He assessed the cow at twenty-four zuze, although it was not worth even four in the market.
They assessed each beehive at one zuz. Yet even so they did not stop or desist from their evil deeds. As for the other crops,
they imposed an assessment on each one of them just as they pleased. And when they treated them without mercy,
showing no shame before the elders and the respected men among them, they left them and [?] to Musa and wailed before him.
They complained to him about the man. He even remitted twelve thousand of it for them. But as it is written, an evil man does no good,
and if he happens to do good, he does so by mistake. So this man too did good by mistake. But he remembered and went back to demand those twelve thousand from them.
He did not let them keep it. Indeed, it is difficult for what is bitter to become sweet, or for a thornbush to produce dates.
And because that whole [?] of wrath that poured over humanity remained in the collection of the poll tax,
let no one, my brothers, blame the writer because his account falls short of the multitude of evils that have poured over us. For even if all human beings became
writers, and all trees became pens, and all wine became ink,
they would still fall short of the full extent of the evils that had gathered in the land. They would not be able to write down and recount what happened in the land.
Let us therefore turn to other things as well, and leave a brief record for those who come into the world after us.
Concerning that first sign which appeared in the northern region and appeared again this year.
Long ago God spoke through the prophets to that rebellious house. But finally he spoke through his beloved Son
with all the descendants of Adam. But now, to us, children who provoke him, who have the words of the prophets
and these promises that the Savior gave his church, and the preaching of the apostles, yet whose hearts have grown dull, whose eyes are closed, and whose ears are stopped,
so that we do not see with our eyes, hear with our ears, and understand in our hearts the living words of our Savior, and turn from our wickedness and live,
signs appeared to us in heaven, showing threats, as to a disobedient people.

Their very appearance testified to discerning people about the greatness of our wickedness and the wrath that threatened us from divine justice. The sign that had appeared a year earlier in the northern region appeared again this year,
in the month of June, on a Friday. Indeed, throughout these three consecutive years in which it appeared, it appeared on a Friday.
It stretched from the eastern side to the western side.
As someone stood looking at it, it underwent many changes: when the red rays faded, green appeared.
When the green faded, saffron yellow appeared; and when this faded, black appeared, indicating that the earth was enduring not just one affliction
but also afflictions differing from one another, as happened to us [?].
The likeness of this sign, depicted above, concerns the tax demand in the first year of distress, which came through the poll tax.
“My people,” he says, “enter your rooms and shut your door upon yourself and your children [?]. Rest for a little while, until my anger passes.”
Again, the same prophet says, “My people, do not fear the Assyrian who strikes you with his rod, for in just a little while my anger will be fulfilled.”
Another prophet also spoke, seeing with the eye of prophecy this evil time and the terrible destruction that befell the people, the priests, and the holy sanctuaries,
and how joy departed from humanity. He cried out, saying, “Priests, put on sackcloth! Beat your breasts and wail, ministers of the altar!
Come in and spend the night in sackcloth, ministers of my God, because fine flour and drink offerings have been withheld from the house of your God. Consecrate a fast; call an assembly.
Gather, elders and all inhabitants of the land, at the house of the Lord your God. Cry out to him and say, ‘Alas, alas for the day!
For the day of the Lord is near, and devastation will come from God.’ Look, before our very eyes food has disappeared from the house of our God, along with joy and gladness.”
Joy and gladness departed from humanity. Sundays and festivals also ceased. Offerings and drink offerings were withheld from the holy altars.
Our festivals turned into mourning, our joy into lamentation, and our gladness into afflictions. “On that day,” Isaiah said,
“the Lord will humble the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord will expose their figures.” On this very day that has been described,
the Lord took away the splendor of the daughters of the holy church and of noblewomen: their clothing, their ornaments, their braids, and the ornaments in their hair,
their sidelocks, the adornment of their faces, their earrings, their necklaces, their [?], their [?], their bracelets, their tunics, their cloaks, and their fine linen,
their purple garments, their clothing, their blue garments, their scarlet garments, and all the finery with which they adorned themselves.
Instead of their pleasant fragrance, they had sand; instead of belts around their waists, he tied aprons around them; and instead of flowing locks, they had bald patches.
Instead of their blue garments, they were covered in sackcloth and rags, as they and their children wandered from place to place and from house to house,
hungry, naked, and exhausted. Let us turn to that time and show what happened during it. First, the tax collector came to demand the poll tax,
proclaiming peace and saying, “Stay and live here, and do not move away, because I am collecting according to a new assessment. I am not holding one district responsible for another,
nor one village for another, nor one man for another.” Thinking that there was truth on his tongue, they endured and stayed.
“His words,” it says, “are sweeter than honey, but they are [?].” When he had received the poll tax and word went out that it should be collected from everyone in his own locality,
he sent many tax collectors against them and appointed two or three officials over every village.
He appointed one of these officials over every ten men, and appointed two district chiefs for every district, along with other assistants.
And so he went out like destructive wolves when they fall upon a flock of sheep, with couriers coming and going like flashes of fire.
The roads and villages were full of them, so that having ten or twenty collectors in a single village was nothing unusual. Even what they were demanding
they contrived to obtain for themselves. They also cut open purses and took whatever they wanted, and no one called them to account. And when they had plundered
and taken widows and orphans captive, they brought in all the property and sold it. The villagers themselves did evil things to the poor among them.
He settled one installment, although it had not yet been properly settled. Then another tax collector came to undo the work of the first and demand the middle installment.
When the first collector had demanded payment and settled the installment, he brazenly and shamelessly demanded that his own expenses be assessed in full upon the whole region.
And so he took it and went away, like a wind that passes and does not return, although he led them to believe that he would return again.
If someone were to say that the first couriers took a third of this installment, he would not be far wrong, apart from the theft committed by the tax collectors, district heads, and governors.
On the second tax collector. This man was crafty and insolent, a glutton and a greedy man, and a companion of thieves.
He openly and shamelessly coveted the fruits of other people's labor.
Even when people came to him for judgment, whatever escaped the thief's hands he contrived to take for himself.
His words were like honey to our taste, but their outcome was worse than wormwood and bitter.
This man chose men from whose sight the fear of God had been banished, and made them run ahead of him.
He sent them into the region like wolves and ordered the governors that, when they demanded payment, they should first demand what he called the emir's handful.
When the district heads and tax collectors entered a village, they seized the village's governor so that he would bring the tax money demanded of him.
They cut open the purse and took from it as much as they wanted, saying, “This is the emir's handful.”
They also mercilessly beat respected men and elders honored for their gray hair. From then on, from every
side the sound of lamentation could be heard. He also supported all the poll-tax collectors,
by sharing in their theft. He brought them out from their places to the outer gates and imposed the poll tax upon them at three and four times the amount.
They schemed against God's people with every bitter evil. The leading men of the city also supported him, because he promised them great things.
In all his dealings, this man demanded tribute for himself, not for the royal treasury. And when every kind of evil had multiplied upon the land,
including poll taxes and old arrears, they demanded payment for someone who had died twenty years earlier, and mercilessly collected it many times over,
along with many other evils, demands for additional payments, and things too numerous to count.
This man was skilled in evil. Although the first and middle installments had not yet been demanded,
this schemer drew up a document of settlement for the whole region, for both Arabs and Syrians, without anyone knowing about the document.
Except for those few who were skilled in evil like him and ate with him. And this is what he wrote in the document recording their agreement:
“We willingly undertake to pay one hundred and twenty thousand, and no additional levies or outside demands are to come upon us—neither upon us nor upon anyone else.”
In that same document he also wrote the names of all the leaders of the region, together with their agreement.
He sent the document to that root of all evils, Ibn Musab. And it seems to me that this evil sprang from that root himself.
For all his agents acted in this way. And because a letter had arrived ordering the leaders of the regions to go down to him, Musa gathered them
all together and sent them to him. He also made secret arrangements with those who went down from the city,
promising to do great things for them if they would go down and praise him before Ibn Musab.
He also generously gave them money for their expenses out of his own funds. But this too was not concealed from the people of the region.
From then on they became opponents and adversaries of one another. Thus they quarreled with one another throughout the journey.
The people of the city favored him, while the people of the region wanted someone else. And so the party of the people of the region prevailed over those from the city.
This was especially so after the people of the city learned of the evil involved in that document of agreement which he had drawn up and sent to Ibn Musab.
And [?], and they did not follow him. They brought in someone else for themselves, and he made an agreement with them for seventy thousand.
And he went up. Again, concerning the account of the three. This man too, who completed the trio of wrath,
did more evil than his companions, because he sprang from that evil-producing root and received from him power and promises of every kind of evil.
Even if his evils did not exceed those of his predecessors, they were no less. Like his companions, he was a thief and an associate of thieves.
He made poor people endure every kind of evil and oppression. He stripped them of their property and sold everything they owned.
He brought oppressive demands upon many people: they would seize a poor man and torment him to death with various tortures.
And when they knew that his circumstances made it impossible for him to produce anything, because he possessed nothing on earth,
those agents, who were unjust judges, would instruct him: “Go out into the marketplace, and find someone you know has possessions. Say,
‘I have property deposited with him,’ or, ‘He owes me money.’” And when this wretched man was being pressured from
his right and his left, from before him and behind him, from above and below, to testify falsely against someone, he trembled before the Lord.
But if he would not testify, those unjust judges wore him down with tortures. Then he would call upon God as a witness to what he was being compelled to do:
that against his will he was being driven to give false testimony against people who owed him nothing [?], or whom he did not know. And what can be said about these men,
except that they loved evil more than good, and lies more than speaking what is right? Indeed, those judges loved everyone who spoke falsehood.
They favored lying tongues more than truthful ones. They all spoke injustice, and their hands became entangled in unjust deeds.
If there was anyone who did not know or was not practiced in evil deeds, they taught him every evil scheme.
Thus this injustice spread throughout all the cities, the injustice itself testifying that the public treasury had flourished from it.
They brought in goats, sheep, cattle, and all the livestock of poor people and sold them: two pregnant goats for one zuz;
a donkey for two zuzim; a plowing ox for three zuzim; a strong, pregnant cow for three or four zuzim.
The wheat was stunted and clung to the ground because of the drought that occurred, about which we will also leave a brief account.
People became deceitful toward one another. Everyone’s tongue was filled with falsehood, and they conducted themselves dishonestly.
Jeremiah saw these things with his prophetic eye when he said, “Let everyone beware of his neighbor, and do not trust any brother.
For every brother practices deceit, and every friend behaves treacherously. They lie to one another and do not speak the truth. Their tongue has learned
to speak falsehood, and because of this they have become worn out and weary. They would gather and sit together to devise deceit, and through their deceit they did not know the Lord.”
Instead, everyone was a liar; everyone was full of injustice. All their feet ran toward evil. There was no one who did good. They all turned aside and together became corrupt.
For they went from evil to evil, and the rulers ran from injustice to injustice. Like lambs that fall among wolves,
so the poor among them were stripped and plundered. They subjected them to every kind of evil and sold everything they owned.
The poll tax was scarcely paid off, apart from the other evils they suffered from the [?], the garrison troops, the tithe, the crown estates, and the tax assessors.
Anyone whose assessment the assessors increased in the new assessment was charged according to the new one. Anyone whose assessment was reduced from the old one was charged according to the old one.

Thus there was distress and bitterness on every side.

On the settlement payment for that year.
“They will go from evil to evil,” it says. When they escaped one calamity, another overtook them that was worse than the first.
The rulers themselves, presuming that no one would call them to account, imposed assessments on people without mercy or pity.
The rulers of the districts also became their accomplices and were greater thieves than they were. When seventy thousand came to them,
he demanded three times that amount from them and showed no pity, even though they said that such-and-such a village was ruined and could not bear the burden.
Whatever they assessed against it, they and the authorities collected and consumed. When he had fixed each person’s share and went out to collect it,
he took all the poor people captive and seized their livestock, as well as that of the wealthy in their district. Not one of them had
anything left at all. If there happened to be someone who owned property and came from another region, they left him nothing: they took him captive and sold him.
They also attacked travelers. They seized everyone who came and went, took his possessions and livestock, and sold them.
Thieving neighbors also came out and formed bands, supposedly in the emir’s likeness. Whoever they found,
they openly took his livestock, saying, “We demand a settlement payment from you.” From then on, the sound of wailing could be heard everywhere.
If anyone fled from this village, they would strip him on the road. And if he escaped from the road without being stripped,
the village to which he ran for refuge itself took the place of bandits, murderers, and highway robbers for him.
If someone went out into the open country, thieves would meet him like a lion. If he turned aside to safety, others would meet him like a bear.
If he entered a village, the villagers themselves would bite him like snakes. And if he went to the tarkhans to rely on them,
they took the place of a scorpion for him and stripped him. The rulers were three times worse than the officials and the bandits.
For even if they had taken from someone three times what he owed, and told the ruler, “This man owes [?],”
they would beat him to death, saying that he was a pagan. They would not seek redress through the ruler for the robbery committed against him.
Wretched young men, Arabs and Syrians, also went out around the city, onto the roads and along the paths.
They would seize poor people and say to them, “Come and see! The emir wants you. Come, pay the levy.”
In this way they left no one anything without stripping him and taking it. Everyone fled as though from a [?] full of vipers,
away from the city’s surroundings. Another evil befell the poor: when these men who applied the seals arrived, they ran and sought refuge with the rulers and the heads of the districts.
Because they were afraid of the fugitives and the defaulters, they petitioned them, and they put seals on them.
When the levy came, those same rulers seized them and made them take the place of the fugitives and defaulters. Even though a man had not entered his village,
they assessed him thirty or forty. In Edessa, more than in all the other cities, the leaders suffered oppression through this very levy.
A bitter-hearted man named Razin came upon them. Whenever he seized a poor man and examined his case, and learned that he had nothing,

he assigned two policemen to him and instructed him: “Go out to the marketplace, find someone, and say to him, ‘Stand surety for me.’ Then leave him and run away.” The man would accept these instructions,
and go out to the marketplace. “Find someone and say to him, ‘Flee with me.’ Then leave him and run away.” The man would accept these instructions and go out to the marketplace.
He would take hold of someone. They would make him flee and seize the other man. Although that man had not spoken even a word with him, they dragged him to the emir,
saying, “You are the one who stood surety for him. Either bring him to us or bring what he owes.” Though he swore, “I did not stand surety for him;
I do not even know him,” they threw him down and put clamps on his legs until his shins were being broken.
They would not release him until he brought whatever they had assessed against him. “And on that day, the day of the Lord’s sacrifice,
I will punish the nobles and the kings’ sons, and all who wear foreign clothing. On that day I will punish all the plunderers and robbers
who fill the house of their [?] with robbery and deceit.” These are the things that the prophet Zephaniah made known to us when he said, “On the day of the Lord’s sacrifice.”
What is the day of the Lord’s sacrifice, if not the day of our Savior’s holy Passion? For at this very season, throughout all the years of oppression,
evils pressed upon us, so that even the festivals were turned into mourning.
And what nobles and princes, robbers and plunderers, had their houses filled with plunder and goods swindled from the poor, orphans, and widows more than the people of Edessa?
And now what is written has been fulfilled, while their wisdom and understanding have also perished. They sought a single thing from their wisdom, but it could not be found.
“I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,” it says, “and take away their understanding.” And it says, “Their possessions will become plunder, and their houses will be destroyed.”
“They will build houses but will not live in them. They will plant vineyards but will not drink wine. The day of the Lord is near,” it says, “and is coming very quickly.”
“Bitter and harsh is the day of wrath and distress, of affliction, anguish, and destruction, of darkness and gloom,
against fortified cities and lofty towers, when people are driven to walk like the blind because they have sinned against the Lord.”
“This,” it says, “will happen to them in return for their pride.” All these things came upon us, with nothing missing from them.
And while poor people endured many evils, which the whole world would not suffice to record,

and neither the beginning nor the end of the demands made upon them was known, and he was not satisfied with the plunder they had taken, he ordered the entire population to be gathered and confined in the city’s churches.
Again, concerning the confinement in the church that also took place in this year. “Jerusalem sinned grievously; therefore she became unclean. All who honored her despised her,
because they saw her nakedness. She herself groaned and turned away. The oppressor stretched out his hands over all her precious things.
And she saw nations enter your sanctuary, whom you had commanded not to enter the assembly.” “The Lord forgot his sanctuary and rejected his altar.
He handed the walls of her palaces over to enemies. A shout rang out in the house of the Lord as on a festival day. He uprooted her shelter like a garden and destroyed her festivals.
The Lord caused festivals and Sundays to be forgotten in Zion, and in the day of his wrath he rejected kings and priests.” Let the prophet Jeremiah come now,
and see with his own eyes everything he prophesied, which has [?] fulfillment and actually happened. Now, when the wicked official ordered them to assemble,
declaring that anyone who hid a man was liable to death, the officers went out and gathered the entire city, without exception. They even searched the houses.
They left no one whom they did not bring to the church, neither rich nor poor. If the householder was away, they brought down his household.
If they found anyone hiding, they beat him to death, along with the owner of the house in which he had been hiding, and sold everything he owned.
Thus they were confined, from the least to the greatest, Arabs and Syrians. Those wicked men went up and sat inside the sanctuary.
They seized everyone against whom even a single follis was recorded and took it from him. They even made them and their wives provide pledges, and they paid what they did not owe,
while they said that it had been assessed against such-and-such a village. Injustice raised its head because truth had perished. Falsehood circulated openly,
because there was no justice. And after inflicting every kind of evil on the people, they sold everything the people owned and took the proceeds.
They also defiled the inside of the church, because men and women relieved themselves there,
for they remained there for three days and three nights. They befouled it, and a foul stench rose from it instead of a sweet fragrance.
Here the nations entered God’s inheritance and defiled his holy temple. They made the holy church into a latrine.
When the merchants and those from whom money had been taken asked the municipal officials to write receipts for them, he did not
pay them any attention. When they complained bitterly to him about that unjust official, he told the municipal officials,
“If they want them, write them for them.” For those who wanted them, he wrote them; for those who did not ask, he did not write them. Even those who had documents written gained nothing,
because an order was issued and a herald proclaimed that no one should repay any debt, whether old or new, and that no one should be pursued for payment.
So all the merchants and townspeople who had been wronged gathered together and went down to Musa ibn Mus'ab to complain about the injustice they had suffered.
But they were mistaken and had lost their senses, since they sought justice from an unjust man, even supposing that these things had not come upon them from him [?].
He not only failed to give them back what belonged to them, but even became angry with that official for not having taken three times as much from them.
Ibn Mus'ab went down to the king in Baghdad. All the people of the territory of Mosul and of the Jazira set out early and went down after him to the king.
Thus many thousands, together with countless tens of thousands, were there, wailing and weeping before the king over the injustices they had suffered from Ibn Mus'ab,
for more than five or six months. He paid no attention to a single one of them. Instead, abdominal sickness and various other diseases broke out among them.
Not even half of them returned from there. Thus they came back from there having accomplished nothing except harm to themselves and their regions.
An unjust king—all his servants are evildoers. On the various punishments that appeared and that people suffered at this time.
Nor is it improper to include this too in this bitter account. Perhaps the people who come after us will see
our chastisement and themselves tremble before the Lord. It is written, “The fool is struck, and the wise person learns.” “Look, I will feed
this people [?] wormwood and give them bitter water to drink. I will scatter them among nations they have not known.”
Truly, he laid affliction upon our backs through rods that inflicted many blows and carried death. He made men ride over our heads.
He lashed our backs and prolonged our scourging. The Assyrians came upon us carrying rods of wrath in their hands,
and harsh staffs of the Lord’s punishment in their hands. The prophets proclaimed the word beforehand, and it came to pass.
We have seen it with our own eyes, grasped it with our own hands, and endured it in our own bodies. From now on, it is not something heard about, but something felt.
First, he made wooden clubs for them, about four finger-widths wide and smoothed on both sides. They would throw a person face down.
One man would sit on his head and another on his feet, while a third mercilessly beat his buttocks as though beating hides.
Thus the saying was fulfilled, “He laid affliction upon our backs,” together with, “You made men ride over our heads.” Then, secondly:
They would bring two rods and fasten them together at one end with iron. They would place them across a person’s shins,
one above and one below. A man would stand on the other end until the person’s shins were crushed.
Thus the saying was fulfilled, “He put my feet in the stocks.” Thirdly, they would hang people by their arms until their limbs were dislocated.
And women too, by their breasts, until they were torn off. Fourth: they stripped them and loaded stones onto them while they were bent over.
They made them stand in snow and ice, and also poured cold water over them,
until they grew stiff and fell on their faces. Fifth: he made five wooden rods for them. At one end they fastened
them evenly together, and inserted people's fingers between them.
At the other end they pressed down on them until they came together and the people's fingers were broken.
They also made two planks, joining them at one end. One was placed beneath a man's back and the other over his chest.
A man stood on the other end until his ribs were broken and his intestines were about to come out.
They prepared nuts and placed them over his eye sockets until his eyes were about to come out.
They made them stand, stripped and naked, in snow and water until they turned dark like indigo. They made thick clubs
and beat them without mercy as they lay on their faces. Whips lay unused among them. Even imprisonment was unnecessary.
“Princes were hung up by their hands,” said the prophet. Let him come and see our princes hanging here! And not only that,
but hanging between earth and heaven, while others beat them with thick clubs and others put shackles on their feet.
They did not wait for them to endure one torture before proceeding to another. Instead, gnashing their teeth and striking them with their hands,
they wanted to inflict every torture on their bodies at once. They threw them naked onto the snow
and rolled up large stones and placed them on their backs until their bellies burst and their ribs and vertebrae
of their [?] were broken. They heated the bathhouse until it was like fire, filled it with smoke, and shut them inside naked.
They also brought cats and threw them among them. When these cats became hot,
they clung to them and tore their bodies with their claws. They confined them in dark houses
where not a single ray of light entered any of them. It is written in Scripture: “Even the afflictions that are not written in this book I will bring upon you.”
All these beatings and tortures they inflicted on weak people because of the tax.
If only this persecution had not been indiscriminate, involving Christians and pagans, Jews and Samaritans, worshipers of fire and the sun, Magi together with Muslims, Harranians and Manichaeans!
Neither gods nor goddesses were honored in this bitter persecution. Nor was anyone striking people on account of their faith. The very name of worship, in the south as well as the north, ceased.
If Christians alone had been singled out in this persecution, I would have had much reason to praise the martyrdoms of our days above all earlier martyrdoms.
For a swift death by the sword is easier than prolonged tortures that never end. “I have never seen anyone,” said Saint Basil,
“being taken to prison or to be beaten because of his poverty.” Let him come now and see thousands and countless tens of thousands of Arabs and Syrians.
of the guilty and the innocent, of the poor and the rich, all together. A cup of poison and a meal of bitter herbs had been prepared equally for everyone.
For the great and the small, the rich and the poor, as the prophet said. The rich man ate bitter herbs every day because they were unjustly taking everything he owned, and they were breaking
his bones with blows. The poor man suffered because they demanded from him what he did not possess. There was no one to lend him anything, nor anyone seeking a worker for his field or vineyard.
Because of these things he ate bitter herbs and also drank bitter water. “He gave gall as food,” it says. My brothers, let no one suppose that I have set down exaggerations here.
Rather, let him know that all the parchments and [?] in the world would not have been enough to record on them the calamities that befell people in our time.
Nor should he criticize the omissions, since we cannot record everything. Nor were those afflictions seen in only one city.
