On the thirst and famine that occurred in this year, and on the migration of the southern and eastern peoples to the northern land.
The prophets call to us in every way like trumpets and proclaim in our ears like horns that we should always turn to the Lord and seek him.
But our hearts have become heavy within us like stones. We have closed our eyes and stopped our ears against the ways of the Lord,
while we follow our own will. Each one of us loves the desires of his own heart, rather than what pleases the Lord. It is written in the prophet:
“Thus says the Lord: Because my house lies in ruins while each of you runs to his own house, the heavens have withheld their dew because of you,
and the earth has withheld its produce. I have called for a drought upon the land and the mountains, upon the grain, the wine, the oil, and everything the earth brings forth,
upon people and livestock, and upon all the labor of your hands. You look for much,” he says, “but it comes to little.
You bring it into the house, but I blow it away. You sow, but you do not reap.” All these things came upon us in that bitter time.
The rain that usually fell in winter was withheld from heaven. There was no dew, and the seed
did not sprout at all. Whatever did sprout dried up, especially in the southern and eastern lands and throughout the wilderness. There was, however, a little at the foot of the mountain.
And so all the peoples went out to offer supplications. Each language group and people gathered separately, crying out in great distress.
For when people saw that the rains had been withheld, their compassion [?]. They would not bring out even for sale wheat kept from long ago; they rejoiced and exulted.
These are the people against whom the prophet cries out, saying: “Listen, you who despise the poor and destroy the needy of the land,
and say, ‘When will the new moon pass, so that we may sell grain, and the Sabbath pass, so that we may open the storehouses, make the measures smaller, and make the weights heavier,
and buy the poor and needy in exchange for [?]?’ The Lord, the Mighty One of Jacob, has sworn: ‘I will never forget their deeds.’
And again: “I will turn their festivals into mourning and all their songs into laments.” When the owners of the grain learned that the heavens were withholding rain,
they clenched their hands and would not sell wheat, while waiting for the rains to fall. The people were hard pressed, and the authorities ordered
every people and language group to go out in supplication: “Perhaps the Lord will be willing to have mercy on us and open to us the door of his compassion.”
And so the Christians went out with their bishops at their head, and the Jews with their trumpets, and the Arabs likewise.
The Lord was pleased to have mercy on us, and there was rain and sowing in some places, as the prophet Amos said: “I too withheld from you
rain three months before the harvest. I sent it down on one city but not on another. Rain would fall on one plot,
while the plot on which no rain fell dried up. Two or three cities would gather at one city.”
Now when this wrath overtook Mosul and all its crops dried up, and likewise in the east and south, since they had also been devastated by the wickedness of Ibn Mus'ab,
the people of all these regions migrated and descended upon this northern land. All the Taghlibites and Ma'addites came up,
with their sheep, their camels, their wives, and their entire households. They filled the land and laid it waste until nothing remained for the livestock to graze on.
Rather, it was as though the land had been swept with a broom. Because of this, all the livestock of the north perished during the winter that followed.
Lands and cities were devastated. These were in Mosul: Beth Garmai and Hazza—lands and cities. These were in Mosul:
Beth Garmai, Hazza, Marga, Kanishapur, Dasen, Qum, and Salakh, along with many others. Their entire population migrated, together with the villagers, and went up to the northern regions.
There were so many of them that there was no room for people to walk in the cities and villages. They nearly caused a famine because of their great numbers.
What is written was also fulfilled against them: “I will send famine, captivity, and pestilence after them.” All these things came with them and after them.
In due course we will also recount the calamity that overtook them through starvation and captivity, and the pestilence that came upon them.
In the year 1084, the holy Paul, bishop of Tikrit, died, as did Zakkai of Karma and Jonah of Beth Nuhadra. Because of the dispute with David, they did not
accept his appointment of successors to them. Thus they remained without a bishop, while awaiting George's release from prison.
In that same year, the king ordered that a wall be built for Kufa. This man, however, who was crafty in wrongdoing, had fallen in love with gold.
For it is said, “The love of money is the root of all evils.” People, vineyards, lands, wild animals, and livestock did not satisfy him,
nor did the mountains that poured out gold and silver and gave it to him. Instead, he continually dealt deceitfully with everyone,
above all so that not a single coin would leave his possession. When he ordered the wall of Kufa to be built, he devised a scheme against its inhabitants and sent some of his own men.
He ordered them to measure each person's house—its length, width, and height. The owner of the house was then to go out and build a section of the wall of the same length, width, and height,
with the entire expense borne by the householder. In this way he surrounded all of Kufa with a great, strong wall,
without contributing a single copper coin to it, in addition to the evils he committed [?] against people in their graves: he overturned them and scattered their bones over the ground.
As evils multiplied and followed one upon another, striking wing against wing and joining hand to hand,
the oppression of the people grew beyond measure. What people owned was sold beyond measure; what people owned was sold and taken away.
They did not know what to do, because their oppressors demanded that they bring and give them even things that neither their fathers nor they themselves had ever possessed.
And this oppression extended over all living creatures, even the wild animals, the birds, and the fish in the sea.
Because of the rulers’ great injustice, people rushed on, so that they too came to
great and terrible wickedness. They attacked the graves of those who had been dead for a very long time and overturned them.
They disturbed their bones, brought them out of their resting places, and scattered them like dung over the ground.
What we used to hear about from far away has reached us. Now we see it with our own eyes, rather than merely hearing about it.
People flung onto the ground those who had been lying at rest in their graves since before the coming of Christ, rushing to take gold and silver from them.
They overturned graves like this, some of which contained more than five hundred corpses, and threw their bones outside.
There were also many places containing ancient graves that had been covered with earth and were unknown. Satan revealed them to these people.
So they dug up and brought out their bones and scattered them from their resting places. Even elderly people who had been born in these places declared under oath:
“Neither from our fathers nor on our own have we heard or known that there were graves in these places.” They declared under oath:
“Neither from our fathers nor on our own have we heard or known that there were graves in these places.”
This made it clear to discerning people that Satan was drawing people on and setting them against them.
Satan himself also spread the story everywhere that in such-and-such a village they were bringing up gold and silver amounting to [?] thousands,
and that so-and-so [?] had found jewelry, so as to make everyone rush into this transgression.
The wise are not unaware of this: in a grave containing a thousand people, something is bound to be found that was brought in with one or another of them,
whether because of a great epidemic or because the gravediggers did not know about it—a bracelet, an ornament [?], or coins at a man’s waist.
Among a thousand, something small out of the many is certainly found. And when it happens that a bracelet is found
made of bronze, Satan turns it into a gold one—not a small one, but a large and marvelous one—and proclaims it throughout the land. Likewise, if it is made of iron, he turns it into silver,
so that everyone will eagerly press on with overturning graves. And through all these afflictions suffered by human beings,
the wild animals, the birds of the sky, the fish in the sea, the trees, and everything on the earth, and even those beneath the earth,
the Lord’s anger did not turn away from us; his hand was still raised. In this same year, a plot was made against the patrician of Greater Armenia, and they killed him with the sword.
It is said of this man that he had more than a hundred thousand servants. Thus his entire household was seized and brought down to the king.
On the evils that multiplied in the world through false testimony; on deceit; on borrowers and lenders; and on slander.
And on God’s mercy, which bears and endures our offenses. These things too are not unworthy of being set down in this bitter account.
When those who come after us see the many stumbling blocks over which we stumbled, and the afflictions we suffered because of our wickedness,
perhaps they will turn away from them and will not walk into an untracked wilderness as we did, where destructive beasts will surround them as they surrounded us.
It was not because God needed Abraham's compassion that he [?] to him about the sins that the Sodomites committed against strangers passing along the road.
Rather, it was so that he might show his children these evil practices that anger God and bring wrath upon those who commit them.
It is written in the book of the Law: “Am I hiding from my servant Abraham what I am doing?” And again: “For I know him, that he will command his children and his grandchildren
to keep the ways of the Lord after him and to practice justice and righteousness.” He says, “The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has come up before me, and their sins have become very great.”
Did God show Abraham their sins so that Abraham would plead for mercy for Sodom? Rather, it was so that he would continually set them before his children, saying, “Keep away from these things.”
Just as David also said to his son: “Know the God of your fathers and serve him.
And if you abandon him, he will abandon you completely.” This is what happened to us. When we left the path of righteousness, no one noticed.
But when God let his hand fall upon us, all creatures felt it with us: wild animals and livestock, the fish in the sea and the birds of the sky.
Even the dead in their graves, and even stones and trees, suffered with us. It is written: “Love the Lord God with all your heart and with all your soul, and your neighbor as yourself.”
These two commandments, on which the Law and the Prophets depend, together with all the authority possessed by the New Testament—we have opposed them in all our conduct.
And again: “Do not murder. Do not steal. Do not give false testimony. Honor your father and your mother. Do not covet anything belonging to your neighbor. Do not lend your money at interest.
Do not accept a bribe, which blinds the eyes of the wise. Do not join hands with a guilty person to be a false witness for him. Do not pervert justice for the poor. Do not commit adultery.”
All these things have not merely reached our ears: we ourselves have committed them to the full. And so that people may not blame God
for these afflictions that have [?] upon us, let us recognize that he has not even dealt with us as our sins deserve. Let us praise his mercies, which cannot be measured or weighed,
for he bears and endures our [?] and the evil deeds of our hands, because of which wrath comes upon those children who do not
obey. What sins have there been in the world that have not been found among us? If it is the strife of Cain's family, here it is among us.
All the wickedness of Sodom is among us. Deceit, hatred, the Israelites' grumbling and their tyranny—here they are among us.
Robbery, plunder, murders, false testimony, and all the evils of the house of Lollianus—here they are with us.
We wish to point out all these things, one [?], so that our children may see our punishment and not act as we have acted,
so that this bitter rod may not reach them too. First, concerning the false testimony that existed among us.
It is written: “The deeds of human beings have not passed over my lips.” And again: “I would destroy anyone who secretly slandered his neighbor.”
Nor do we wish, my brothers, to recount people's shameful deeds to you or to slander them.
Rather, we wish to show you the practices that caused this affliction, so that you too may turn away from them [?]. For faithfulness has vanished from the earth.
People spoke to their neighbors with deceitful lips. Whenever a man had a lawsuit against his neighbor, he would go into the marketplace
and call to someone: “Sir, so-and-so, testify for me.” The other would immediately answer him emphatically, saying, “By the word of God!”
“And peace be with you.” About what? He would swear oaths before knowing. It was not only pagans who did these things,
but Christians too, and elderly men. Whatever the case might be, anyone who wanted could hire as many false witnesses as he wished for a coin.
They did not keep God’s judgment before their eyes, but would wipe a poor man off the earth in a single hour.
Again: On borrowers and lenders, and on falsehood. “Look,” he says, “you all speak wrongdoing, and wrongdoing entangles
your hands.” “Their mouths are full of evil; deceit and treachery are beneath his tongue, wrongdoing and mischief.” “You must not,” he says, “lend your money at interest,
nor profit at your neighbor’s expense. If you lend money to a poor person among my people who is with you, do not act toward him like a creditor,
and do not take interest from him.” David also said, “He does not lend his money at interest”; “He swears to his neighbor and does not lie.”
These things were disregarded among us. When country people were under pressure because of harsh demands for payment,
they would enter the cities, carrying gifts to people who lent money. When these people saw them, they would say, “Welcome!”
With pleasant words they would tell them, “I will give you as much as you need. Do not worry: as long as I am alive, I will give to you. Will you need to depend on anyone?
I do not require witnesses from you, or guarantors, or a pledge. I do not want interest or any extra payment.
Just take it, and as soon as the harvest comes in, bring me what is mine. Or give me wheat or wine at the price current at that time. Go now,
and come back in a few days.” When that distressed man heard these sweet words, he would go home with great joy, rejoicing.
He did not know that Satan would not let the other man fulfill what had come out of his mouth.
“His words,” he says, “are sweeter than honey, but they are [?]. Their end, however, is bitter gall.”
That distressed man, relying on these empty words with which the lender had reassured him, did not exert himself, run about, and gather the money for his poll tax.
Instead, he sat at home resting until the collectors came. When they seized him, he said to them, “Give me a little time to go in
and bring it to you.” Then he would go in [?] to the man who had assured him that he would give it to him.
He would say to him, “Please, sir, give me that amount I asked you for, so that they do not humiliate me.” But the other would say, “Wait for me a little.”
Or he would leave him and run away. Or he would put him off with words, saying, “Go away today; come back tomorrow morning.
I have no time for you just now.” He would treat him this way for many days. When the man was being pressed to the point of death,

even bringing many people to plead with him, the lender would either tell him bluntly, “I will not give you anything, because I have nothing to give you,” or say to him, “I require a written agreement from you.”

The man would say, “I will make one.” Then, when he had drawn up a written agreement binding himself, the lender would dismiss him with words, saying, “Go away this evening and come back tomorrow morning.”
When these men came early, he would say to them, “I will not give you anything unless you give me a pledge.” Then, when they had also given him a pledge,
he would say again, “How much will you give me as a fee for this money? And settle with me how much wheat you will give me, because I will not accept it at the going price.”
Because of their distress, they gave him whatever he opened his mouth to ask for, and even put it in writing for him. Then he also asked them for guarantors.
And so, after all his earlier statements had proved false, he took collateral from them, drew up a document, and stipulated interest.
He demanded guarantees and required sureties from them. Only with difficulty did he relent and give them the money.
They not only kissed his hands but even licked the soles of his feet, saying, “If, so many days from now, we do not bring you what belongs to you,

we are liable for everything written in the document he drew up for them.” They would gather the money for him. But when a borrower had collected it and went in to redeem himself and enjoy a welcome freedom, there came
Satan, the enemy of everything good. He stood fiercely against him, battling with his thoughts and saying:
“How can you give this money now? They will demand payment from you, and you will have nothing to give them, since all your property has been sold.
That man lacks nothing, and he cannot do you any harm. Your collateral is also safe with him. Even if you take it back from him,
you will pledge it to someone else. So it is better off with him.” See what disastrous advice the evil one gave borrowers,
so that they would not keep their word and the lender’s mind would be put at ease, and afterward he would give them relief. They would also repay him for the deceit he himself had practiced on them.
This wicked advice also came through a woman counselor, a daughter of Adam’s woman. Then, at this time, the saying came true:
“Women have gained mastery over us.” They managed the men’s affairs, and they advised them, “Do such and such.”
The man would say, “You have advised me well,” without setting before his eyes those agreements and oaths sworn before God.
Nor did they consider what they were doing to themselves: they would ask again and receive nothing. Instead, the advice of Satan and of a man’s wife pleased them more than anything else.
Sometimes one of them would even be holding that very money in his hand,

while his creditor pressed him, saying, “Give me what is mine!” Yet he would stubbornly refuse, with Satan standing over his heart, saying, “I have nothing.” He would even be imprisoned and humiliated, yet would not repay.
It is against such people that the psalmist cries out, saying, “The wicked borrows and does not repay.”

The lender went back and forth to the borrower’s door and pleaded with him more often than the borrower had gone to the lender’s door. If he happened to recover half, he thought he had found a windfall.

Thus deceit had gained complete mastery over everyone.

On slanderers and oppressors, and on people robbing one another, together with false testimony.

Again, when the people
of the region went in to levy the poll tax, they would form gangs like those of the household of Caiaphas and go around the towns.
They would find out where someone had something stored away, whether wheat, wine, or household goods. Then they would go to the emir and say, “So-and-so is liable for our poll tax,
and he has such-and-such an amount with so-and-so. Look, he has not paid his poll tax for so many years.” The emir would order, “Go and sell his property.”
But if the man himself or someone else objected and tried to stop them, the authority would say to them, “Do you have witnesses against him?”
Some of their own number, people from their own village, would come forward and testify against him, although he had never even seen them.
And so, while he wailed, they would sell everything he owned, not even allowing him to come near his property.
Others say, “You stood surety to us for a man.” Others say, “You have a vineyard or a garden or an olive grove in our village, and for so many years he has not paid you its tax.”
Although these people swore, “I have never entered your village, nor do I have a garden among you,” they would not let a man go by any means until they had sold everything he owned.
The authorities themselves also supported them in these pretexts. For this reason, people were afraid to be seen in the streets.
Yet even this way they did not escape these wicked men. Instead, they would make inquiries after them.
Whenever one of them caught someone, he would say to him, “Either give me such-and-such an amount, or I will take you to the emir.”
For many men from the city, however, this pretext became a great business. They also filled their houses with plunder and fraud.
It was about them that the prophet Micah spoke, he who rebuked kings to their faces: “The godly person has perished from the land, and there is no one upright among humankind.
They all lie in ambush, and each hunts his brother to destroy him. Their hands are ready for evil, and they do not
do good. The ruler demands gold, and the judge says, ‘Bribe me.’ The powerful man speaks the desires of his soul.
They have discarded their goodness like a moth-eaten rag.” And again: “Do not rely on your relatives, nor trust your friends.”
David also said, “They sharpened their tongues like a sword, and their speech like an arrow, to shoot secretly at the innocent.
Suddenly they shoot at him without being seen. They plotted and also hid snares, thinking that the Lord does not see.” And again he said about them:
“They will return in the evening and howl like dogs, and go around the city.” They loved curses more than blessings.
They put on curses as armor, and these entered into them like water and like air in the city [?], from the wild dogs of the villages and the city.
Their mouths stood open like foul graves, so that they would also seize one of these poor people.
Whenever he escaped from these men, others caught him, and after these, still others. Isaiah said about them:
“How the faithful city has become a prostitute! It was full of justice and righteousness, but now of murderers.
Your silver has been rejected. Your tavern keepers mix in water. Your rulers are rebellious, and they are all partners of thieves.”
And again he said, “Mockers will rule over them. The people will fall upon one another, each upon his neighbor. The young will rise against the old,
and the despised against the honored.” “Her rulers within her roar like lions, and her judges are like evening wolves. Her prophets are reckless.”
“Woe to those who plan violence and do evil on their beds! They also rise early in the morning and do what they have planned, and they raise their hands
toward God. They covet fields and houses and take them by force, and they oppress people.”
Micah said these things about the plunderers and the wicked. And again he said, “Her rich people are full of violence, and her inhabitants are full of falsehood.
Their tongue is deceitful in their mouths. I too will begin to strike you, and I will destroy you because of your sins. You will eat but not be satisfied, and dysentery will be within you.
You will take hold but will not save, and whatever you save I will hand over to the sword. You will sow but will not reap. You will press olives but will not anoint yourself with oil.
“You will press, and wine [?],” so that the laborers might find relief from them. Even money was struck by a wrath worse than that which struck anyone else.
In the first year, the poorest people and the foreigners perished, as we noted above. In the second year, those above them perished.

In the third year, those above these perished. In the fourth year, those devourers and plunderers themselves perished. Neither their own possessions nor anything they had plundered and accumulated remained to them.

These things, others like them, and things greater than these, which the prophets had proclaimed beforehand, people carried out and fulfilled against one another. The villagers, especially, went to greater lengths.
At first, the townspeople and merchants began the wrongdoing, rushing to buy the villagers’ produce, their vineyards, their fields, and everything they cultivated.
But they did not enjoy it, because those villagers turned against them. If anyone had wine or wheat in the village of any one of them,
they brought it out and sold it or consumed it, while the authorities supported every kind of wrongdoing and held no one accountable.
As for those merchants, it was not enough that their produce had been plundered and lost: they would seize the man and bring him before the authorities, saying, “All
our produce has been taken by this man. Order him to impose a levy on the village.”
So the authorities would torment him until they destroyed him from the earth, and they took everything he owned. They took it from those who had plundered and those who had not.
The rich, too, fled before the villagers like goats before wolves and wandered about. They even disclaimed the vineyards and everything they had acquired from them.
It also happened that [?] people would go out freely and buy wine from them at the winepress. They would go in and complain to the emir.
If it was stored in their village, the authorities sent someone and had it carried away. If it had been brought into the city, the authorities likewise took it.
Thus the buyer lost both the wine and its price. But however much we multiply our account of the evils that occurred, which those people also committed against one another,
we remain far from reaching the full extent of the evils. No one can write them down, so numerous are they.
But let these few things suffice for discerning readers. Concerning these things, let us say with the prophet Jeremiah: “My people have become foolish, and they do not know me, says the Lord.
They are foolish children and are not wise. They are skilled in evil, but they do not know what is good.”
“I looked at the earth, and behold, it was waste and empty.” Truly, all of them together broke the yoke and snapped the bonds.
“Therefore a lion will crush them, and evening wolves will tear them apart. A leopard will lie in wait around their villages. Everyone who goes out from them will be crushed,
because their offenses have grown grave and their sins have multiplied.” They displayed their wickedness like the people of Sodom.
On the second year of the distress, which is the year 1085.
Since we have already written and reported above about the bitter afflictions and the merciless theft that arose among people because of the hardships that occurred
during them—namely, the property tax of the [?], the [?], the tithe, and deportations,
along with many other things that we noted above—there is no need to explain them again to discerning readers,
since they understand that this year multiplied its evils many times over those of the earlier and later years.
And not only from the earth and from human beings, but also from heaven, even from the Lord. [?] demanded two for one, without mercy.
The tithe collector went out to the roadsides like a mad dog, and they stripped everyone coming and going without pity.
The tax collectors were more eager for some poor person to fall into their hands than vultures are for a carcass to fall.
Like vultures around a carcass, they plucked at poor people. But what can I say about the overturning of graves, except what Jeremiah said?
For he tells us about the overturning of graves and the scattering of their bones like dung over the surface of the earth, with no one to gather them.
It is written: “At that time, says the Lord, they will bring out the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem from their graves.
They will spread them out before the sun and the moon and all the hosts of heaven, which they loved and served and followed, which they consulted and worshiped.
They will not be gathered or buried, but will be like dung on the surface of the earth.” These things happened in our time, and we have already written about them above.
Yet this year added evils beyond all the years before it and after it, especially the overturning of graves. Jeremiah also said about those living at that time:
“All who remain of this evil family will choose death rather than life, in every place to which I have scattered them.”
Jeremiah also said: “The corpses of this people will become food for the wild animals and the birds of the sky, and there will be no one to rescue them.
I will put an end in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem to the sound of rejoicing and the sound of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride,
because the whole land will become a wasteland.” These things were fulfilled when human corpses were given as food to the wild animals and the birds of the sky.
He compares this godless people to wild animals and unclean birds. The sound of gladness and the voices of bridegroom and bride ceased,
since even those who had married dismissed their wives and gave them certificates of divorce because of the abundance of evils. For it is said, “Because of the abundance of lawlessness,
the love of many will grow cold.” We do not need to write these things down again, but pass over them quickly,
turning to the additional evils that this year suffered beyond its fellows. On the harsh winter,
the severe cold, the shortage of pasture, the difficulty of keeping stall-fed livestock alive, and the destruction of all the livestock;
on the famine, the bitter illness, and the pestilence in which people and animals perished like locusts;
on the taking of children captive, as the villagers took one another captive; on the plundering of people and the killings that occurred because of the shortage of bread;
on the blocking of roads, and on Christians eating meat during the fast, and even eating the corpses of the dead for lack of bread.
I will speak about these things. I will recount these things and write them down for those who come after us. First, about the harsh winter and the destruction of livestock,
wild animals, and birds, and the violent winds that occurred during it. It is written: “I will turn your summers into winters.”
This is what happened to the world in this year. In this same year, however, the wine harvest was abundant,
so that God might provide relief for the poor, enabling them to curb the greed of these judges, whose mouths stood wide open.
Like open graves that are never satisfied with the corpses brought to them every day, so the rulers of this age were never satisfied with the produce that the whole earth yielded to them.
But God gave abundant harvests from his rich storehouse, so that they might fill their foul mouths with them and leave poor people alone,
until their day of reckoning came, their debts fell due, and the measure of their sins was full.
Winter came early, in October, and heavy snow buried the vineyards with their grapes still on them.
It remained for days. Even with the snow piled over them, people went in and gathered the grapes into [?].
Because of the severity of the great cold that overtook the land, they all fell off and were lost in the snow.
The cold and snow continued like this, without the usual rain falling, from October until nearly the beginning of June.
One day there would be a snowstorm, and another there would be winds that tore mountains apart, with ice and severe cold.
Thus God willed that wrath should come upon the land that year from every direction: from heaven and from the earth, and also from the four winds of heaven.
Heaven brought snow and hard ice, and the earth below brought cold that split rocks.
The regions also suffered the great evils that people inflicted on one another, too numerous to count. On the destruction of livestock and pack animals that occurred that year.
And on the shortage of sustenance for feeding livestock. When the drought occurred, as we have already mentioned above, the people of Taghlib and Maadd migrated
with their flocks, their camels, and their wives. They came up into this northern land. All the Arabs of the south also came up and laid it waste.
They also bought all the grain that had been brought down, and all the open pastureland was filled.
The whole land was swept clean, as though with a broom. Straw and fodder were also scarce.
Because there was no pasture outside, and the harvest stored inside was also small, all the livestock, both those at pasture and those in stalls, perished: goats, sheep, and pack animals.
For whenever something happened to be available to eat—since there was absolutely nothing but dust, and not even a leaf on a tree that had not been eaten since summer—
the livestock outside ate what had been stored for the livestock inside. Then both those outside and those inside perished.
For winter dragged on and lasted a long time, and the cold grew more intense: cold outside and hunger inside.
Because of this, all the livestock of the north died: sheep, cattle, horses, and donkeys, so that [?] stank from the carcasses,
until those [?] were worse in their stench than graves. On a violent wind that occurred that year. This too was added.
A harsh and violent wind arose, the like of which had never been seen either in our days or in the days of our fathers.
Many people perished in it, and the small livestock, pack animals, and birds all perished in it. Much of the sown crop was also uprooted.
It even swept the soil of the earth into drifts like those formed from snow. It lasted two days,
one after the other, between Christmas and Epiphany; and again on February 14, on the first Sunday of the fast, and on Monday at the beginning of the fast.
And because the ground had been loosened by the frost and there was no moisture, all the seed in the gardens and the soft soil was uprooted and dried up.
Darkness and gloom also gathered from the fine dust. All the birds perished too, especially the doves.
It was not known what had happened to them: whether they had gone ahead of it, or had fallen in the wilderness and perished from the cold.
In the dovecotes they died in countless numbers, and only a very few remained in them. Just as the birds of inhabited places perished, so too did those of the wilderness.
Concerning the hail that fell again in this same year. Hail also fell again in this same year, the like of which had not been seen in our days.
For it was large, like [?]. It came in shapes of every kind, and there were also [?] as sharp as a sword.
Some had two, some three, and some four. It broke trees and vines, and uprooted the crops as well.
It did great damage to all the houses because of the large lumps in it. The wind blowing in the cloud picked up the water that had fallen to the ground
and lifted it up against what was coming down from above, so that it seemed to those watching that the earth itself was lifting it up and throwing it straight toward the sky.
Concerning the return of Musa son of Moab to the land, the exactions he imposed, and the distress people suffered because of them.
As we mentioned above, when the year 144 of this era of the wicked one had ended, an appeal was made
by all the regions of Jazira and Mosul, and they went down to accuse him of the wrongs he had done among them.
But they were mistaken in thinking they could find justice with a crooked man who loved thieves. Instead of the good they hoped to find, they kindled evil against themselves.
Not only did he refuse to accept what they said, but he gathered together all the petitions that the poor people had presented to him concerning their distress
and handed them over to him. He also increased his honors and placed him above all his other officials.
He also ordered him to impose exactions on the cities themselves and within them, each city's exactions being drawn from it and imposed within it.
When he received this order and returned in great triumph, he roared like a lion intent on destruction.
Just as a destructive beast, when it falls into a pit and escapes, adds to its former evil deeds,
so this man too multiplied his former evil deeds many times over, since the king had supported him with his command.
God himself also stretched out a hand to him, just as he said to Jeremiah: “Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath,
and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it. They will drink and stagger and be driven mad because of the sword that I am sending among them.”
“I took the cup from the Lord's hand and made all the nations to whom the Lord sent me drink it.”
And again he said: “Drink, become drunk, be driven mad, and fall, never to rise again, because of the sword that I am sending among you.”
And again he said: “And will you go unpunished? You will not go unpunished, for I am calling down a sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, says the Lord. The Lord, from on high,
will roar, and from his holy dwelling he will raise his voice. He will roar mightily against his fold. ‘Hey! Hey!’ he will shout like someone treading grapes, against all the nations of the earth.”
The uproar reached the ends of the earth, for the Lord has a case against all the inhabitants of the earth.
Truly, the Lord had a case against all the inhabitants of the earth in this year, for not a single people or kingdom was at peace.
Instead, afflictions fell upon them all alike, because they all drank from the cup in the Lord’s hand, and [?].
The Persians were thrown into turmoil because no remission was granted them; the Arabs suffered exactions, and the Jews and Christians along with them.
The Egyptians, Armenians, people of Sind, and all the peoples were harassed with harsh taxation.
This therefore makes it clear that they drank from this cup. As it says, “You showed your people hard things, and you also gave them bewildering wine to drink.”
Not even the land of the Romans escaped this bitter affliction. Rather, the rulers of the peoples all alike fell into the love of money,
ours as well as theirs, because the mixture in the cup is the same for all peoples. Habakkuk also said, “You have had your fill of disgrace instead of honor.”
“Drink, you too, and be thrown into turmoil. The cup in the Lord’s right hand will come around to you, and disgrace will cover your honor. For the violence done to Lebanon [?] will cover you,
and the destruction of the animals will terrify you, because of human bloodshed and the violence done to the land, the city, and all its inhabitants.”
See, this prophet showed that the first cup, which the earth and its inhabitants drank in the year before this one,
came from the Lord’s hands, declaring and saying, “The cup in the Lord’s right hand will come around to you, and disgrace will cover your honor.”
“Look,” he says, “I am placing in Zion a stone to stumble over and a rock to trip over. Everyone who falls upon it, it will scatter; and everyone upon whom it falls will be shattered.”
These were [?]: if they accepted, they brought wrath upon themselves; if not, the sword—and drought on every side.
Again, as we said above, the Lord placed a stumbling block before all the peoples and brought them low through nakedness and cold,
and through snow and ice, so that they could not go out and flee from him because of the extreme severity of the cold.
If one of them happened to flee, he would turn back without delay, although there was no one pursuing him. It seemed
as though he were someone in chains, easily caught by his pursuers, who then came home. The prophet did not hide this from us either,
but said, “If you set your nest on high, I will bring you down from there. And if you go down even to Sheol, I will bring you up from there,
and hand you over to those who seek your life.” And again: “They will trample him like mud in the streets and like [?] on the face of the earth,
with no one to rescue him.” This makes it clear that it came upon us from the Lord. Then this man returned and roared like a lion intent on destruction.
He asked and inquired about harsh and merciless men and made them officials in their cities. This was worse than everything else for the poor.
For he was able to keep them from betraying him, since he was a native of the region, and nothing was hidden from him.
He also chose for himself leading men of the city and the region and made them his associates. From then on they stole openly,
they and the officials, with no one holding them accountable. They too became poor under great oppression, and he grew weak.
Their hands, and their hearts were shattered. Their backs were broken when they heard of the wicked man's arrival, and their hope perished. For the terror that he feared
came upon them, and what they dreaded overtook them. They had no ease, no quiet, and no rest, and wrath came,
as Job said. He appointed those tax collectors, one for each village, though each also had many others with him.
Their demands for the poll tax they were collecting were also harsh, for they were thieves, robbers, and highwaymen.
These were the men they chose and appointed as judges. It is written: “When kings are unjust, all their servants are unjust.”
And so, with cruel oppression, blows, and bitter floggings, they demanded payment from poor people.
They themselves took more than half the amount demanded as their fee. Then they came back again, after taking money from them as their fee.
He forced them to sell their produce at a loss, and they themselves bought it with the fee [?] he had taken from them.
In this way they filled their houses with the produce of orphans and widows. He also bought their goats, their oxen, and everything they owned.
When one of them first came out into the district, he owned nothing. First he demanded his fee; afterward he put pressure on them and bought their produce himself.
What injustice could be worse than this? The district heads and officials were also partners in this wickedness.
For theft was more prevalent among them than anything else. As it says, “Your rulers are rebels and partners of thieves.”
Through these bitter measures he demanded a third and two [?], with neither a beginning nor an end being known. They did not disclose what they were taking, nor
was it known what they assessed and imposed, for all their dealings were those of thieves, robbers, and highwaymen.
He seized prominent men and freeborn people of the district, sold all their property and everything they owned, and ruined them and wiped them off the face of the earth.
It was not enough for them that he took everything they owned; they also demanded from them what they did not possess.
He appointed tax collectors for the many revenues owed to the Arabs' treasury, and demanded these many times over. He assessed old arrears.
For every ten silver coins assessed, they demanded thirty, and sometimes forty. They devised additional assessments out of these and on top of them.
They went out and imposed them throughout the district, along the roadsides. Sometimes they devised and imposed additional assessments on the district's own estates,
and on the Muslims, and then imposed them on the Christians. They did not go around out of concern to make payment, but to satisfy their greed in their love of money.
They assessed and mercilessly imposed fixed levies on the district and on the Arabs' estates,
although their yields were unknown, while the foundations of evil [?] lay underneath. The tax collectors also kept adding similar charges.
He also added district heads, couriers, and officials over them. Thus merciless theft, oppression, and injustice prevailed among them all.

Against these people the prophet Isaiah cries out, saying: “Woe to me! The wicked have acted wickedly; the wicked have acted wickedly [?]. Terror, the pit, and the snare are upon you, inhabitant of the earth. Whoever
flees from the sound of terror will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs out of the pit will be caught in the snare, for the floodgates on high have been opened.”
The foundations of the earth shook. The earth will reel violently; the earth will totter terribly. The earth will stagger like a drunkard and sway like a hut.
Its wrongdoing will weigh heavily upon it, and it will fall and never rise again. They brought in wrongdoing without shame, and the earth shook and tottered.
People went from village to village and from one place to another. Humanity’s wrongdoing grew strong. The earth was ruined, its surface was overturned, and the law perished.
There the slave became like his master, and the priest like the people. The borrower was harsher than the lender, and the debtor more powerful than his creditor.
Isaiah also spoke about these things: “Look, the Lord is devastating the earth and breaking it apart. He overturns its surface and scatters its inhabitants.
The people will be like the priest, the slave like his master, the maidservant like her mistress, the borrower like the lender, and the buyer like the seller.
As with the creditor, so with the one who owes him.” He says, “The earth will be utterly devastated and thoroughly plundered, for the Lord has spoken.” The world lamented, sat down, and mourned.
The earth became like its inhabitants. The law was abolished. Good commandments were exchanged for evil ones. The upright, everlasting covenants were abolished.
In their place came wrongdoing and wickedness, together with theft. Satan said concerning the wicked, “Look, [?] my eye [?] among them.”
He said to his workers, “Pursue him and catch him. Let no one get away. Let no one escape from wickedness, small or great.”
He spread his net, and all Adam’s children were caught in it. His hand found the gathering of the nations as though it were a nest.
No one was delivered from sin—not even bishops, priests, or judges—or from
betrayal, or robbing one another, or slander, insults, blasphemies, hatred, and grumbling, or theft, adultery, or plundering graves.

All the seeds of the Accuser were now sown among everyone. According to his rank and his strength, everyone [?] was pressing forward; according to his rank and his strength, everyone was pressing forward to do evil.
When the prophet saw these things, he said, “Because of these things the earth will waste away in mourning, and all its inhabitants will be found guilty.
The grain sat in mourning, and the vines lamented. All the joyful-hearted will sigh. Joy and tambourines have ceased, and the sound of rejoicing has fallen silent.
Joy, lyres, and song have ceased. They will not drink wine. Strong drink will become bitter to those who drink it. The town has been plundered, and every [?] house has been shut.
There is wailing over wine in the streets. All joy has ceased, and rejoicing has passed away.” Into their laps came destruction, sorrow, and bitterness.
These things have not reached us through hearsay; rather, we have seen them before our own eyes. People inflicted every kind of evil on one another.
They attacked the solitary monks, the recluses, and the pillar-dwellers. They brought many down from their pillars and brought the recluses out of their places of confinement.
Those monks who gather humbly and in holiness in the holy communities, in the dwellings of the monasteries,
suffered more than anyone else: afflictions, persecutions, and bitter beatings because of the judges’ demands. Let the reader know and understand
that never has a persecution harsher than this year’s been seen in the world. If this persecution were not indiscriminate,
since all peoples were afflicted and persecuted in it, more than in any that preceded it, I would have reason to praise the martyrdoms of today.
Nor could someone who owned anything and wanted to flee do so: he was bound as though in chains until he was stripped bare. And not
Something was still left. He was released only when he had been stripped of everything and fled. While any one of them still had anything,
he could not flee. Even if he fled, the road itself would strip him. And if he were to [?] and put his possessions in the ground,
that very place would cry out against him: “Here are so-and-so’s possessions! Come and take them!” And if he entrusted them to other people,
the very person who sheltered him would take the place of thieves and robbers for him. About these things the prophet Obadiah says:
“Even if you rise as high as an eagle, and even if you set your nest among the stars, I will bring you down from there, says the Lord.”
And again he said: “How Esau has been searched, and his hidden treasures sought out!” Here one could see how something hidden by someone was quickly discovered...
Hosea also said: “Because of the abundance of injustice, insolence increased.” And again: “Insolence is in the house of God.” Insolence increased among everyone,
along with injustice, deceit, and favoritism. “My people have become foolish; they do not know me. They are foolish children, skilled in evil, but they do not know how to do good.”
“I looked at the earth, and there it was, desolate and empty,” said holy Jeremiah. The whole earth became desolate and empty, and the darkness of sin and injustice gathered over its surface.
All the property in the land was sold, and its merchants became more numerous than the stars of heaven, just as Nahum also declared to us.
Two or three pregnant goats sold for one zuz, and ewes likewise; an ox for one zuz, a donkey for one zuz,
and a mule for ten zuzim. Whatever had escaped destruction was lost on the road. Their splendid and desirable belongings—
whatever the [?] plundered was plundered, and these things were sold for nothing. That is, an article made for twenty or thirty zuzim
went for two or three zuzim. When the land had been stripped bare and the holy days of the fast drew near,
the weeks called “weeks of delight” began. But we do not call them weeks of delight, but of bitterness and distress throughout the whole year.
And so this affliction continued throughout the holy fast, until after New Sunday.
The festivals and Sundays ceased. The supplications customarily held on the days of the fast, on Palm Sunday, and on Sundays ceased.
The Christians pulled out all the iron and wooden fittings from their houses and sold them. They pulled out their doors and sold them, while hoping for better things.
Finally, they even pulled out the beams in their houses and sold them. Then they abandoned the ruins of their houses and fled stripped of everything,
wandering from village to village and from one region to another. Here we may say with the prophet Jeremiah: “The people ate bitter herbs and drank bitter water.
They were scattered among nations that neither they nor their ancestors had known, and the sword was sent after them until they were destroyed.”
Isaiah also said: “They will be like fleeing gazelles and like sheep with no one to gather them. Each will turn back to his own people,
and each will flee to his own land.” And again: “Their houses will be filled with echoes, and demons will dance there.
Ostriches will dwell there, sirens will answer one another in their courtyards, and jackals in their luxurious palaces.”
We must say not only that fine flour and drink offerings disappeared from the house of God, but that the timbers of the churches were torn out and sold.
What remained was burned in the fire, and their equipment for work was destroyed. The vineyards lay ruined; the vines mourned. The fields produced thorns and thistles.
The fig tree dried up, and the olive tree too was ruined. The pomegranates, palms, apple trees, and all the trees were devastated.
Because joy had ceased among human beings, the farmers fled, and their houses became a dwelling place for wild animals.
On the affliction caused by the devastation and wickedness of the people of Quris [?], the villagers themselves acting against one another.
Nor did it seem right to us to leave this out of this account of woes, sighs, and bitter suffering. I have already written above
that the cause of the hardships arising from the region was worse than all the earlier and later evils.
For his own food alone did not satisfy him. He even made the despised and lowly into runners before him.
He did not leave even a peg in a wall that they did not take, for they stole like wolves in the evening.
They had owned nothing at all, but here they became rich through their theft, as did those with them.
Those who until now have been murderers, highway robbers, drunkards, adulterers, men who lie in ambush at night, and housebreakers—
today they are judges! See, my brothers, into whose hands the punishment for sins casts those who commit them.
As it says, the wicked are punished by the wicked. Look where our sins have thrown us, and into whose hands! See who have become our exactors: violent and merciless men.
When he demanded the poll tax and numerous other levies many times over, everything people owned was sold, and they took the proceeds.
They demanded from a locality not merely its tax, but many times that amount. There was no discernible beginning, middle, or end.
They assessed sums and imposed them on the localities, saying, “Such-and-such a place has a shortfall, and so many thousand remain unpaid.”
When this was paid in, he made another assessment. When pressure had been applied and they had raised this amount too, he imposed another levy. No one could speak.
For everyone was afraid of the judge’s [?]. He also seized prominent men and assessed sums against them without mercy, until he had destroyed many
and ruined them. He gave free rein to evildoers from the villages. They seized people and unjustly took and sold everything they owned.
They would say, “You have a vineyard in our village, or a garden, or a woodland, or an olive tree. Or you stood surety to us for someone, or you are one of our poll-tax payers.
For so many years you have paid us nothing. Now bring us what you owe, because we are under pressure.” With these and similar pretexts,
the villagers seized poor people and ruined them. The judge himself taught them to do this and supported them.
He did not hold them accountable for anything they did. They even seized people passing along the roads.
They would seize a man and produce false witnesses against him, saying, “He is one of our poll-tax payers.” But he would swear, “I have never seen these people,
nor have they seen me.” Yet they would say, “He is one of our poll-tax payers.” They also brought false witnesses from among themselves and presented them against him.
In this way they sold his property, his slave, and everything he owned.
They prowled through the cities like dogs sniffing the ground for the tracks of their masters, or of animals or sheep. They asked who had anything stored away,
whether wheat, iron, or merchandise, and took it. They could be seen going around the cities in bands,
even quarreling over people, saying, “So-and-so belongs to us.” When someone escaped from one, others seized him, and from these he was taken to still others.
Even if someone happened to hide something, either in the ground or with another person, that very place would go into labor over it, like a pregnant woman suffering the pains of childbirth.
This was how people behaved during the holy days of the fast, doing these things and others like them.
Now let us turn to other evils, those that the villagers themselves also committed against one another.
“They will go,” it says, “from strength to strength.” We, however, went from evil to evil, for there was disaster upon disaster and flood upon flood.

“And on the heels of one messenger,” it says, “another messenger will come.” Concerning the bitter suffering people experienced through the tribute assessment, and the captivity the villagers inflicted on one another.
For the Lord brings destruction and decisive judgments upon the whole earth. Here one could see the destruction that came upon everything.
Even then the Lord’s wrath did not subside against us, because we too had not stopped our evil deeds and our many injustices.
Instead, day after day we kept adding to them, like someone carrying a heavy load who, instead of taking something off it,
adds still more to it. The Lord was a little angry, and we helped bring about further evils.
For this reason Jeremiah too cries out to us, saying, “Thus says the Lord: Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me,
I would have no desire for this people. Send them out of my presence and let them go. And if they say to you, ‘Where shall we go?’
tell them, ‘Thus says the Lord: Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; and those destined for captivity, to captivity.
I will appoint four scourges over them, says the Lord: the sword to kill, dogs to drag away, and the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.’”
Here the Lord sent us out of his presence, and neither the holy offering nor acts of atonement nor even the righteous people among us appeased the Lord on our behalf.
Instead, he devastated the regions and drove people from their homes. Dogs fell upon them, dragging them away and tearing them apart, and birds destroyed them without mercy.
Indeed, they were worse than dogs and birds. For when those have eaten their fill, they stop tearing at the corpse. But these did not. “It devours,” it says, “and crushes,
and tramples with its feet whatever remains.” These destructive beasts ate their fill and stored what remained in their houses.
All the evils we have recounted were not enough for them; they added these as well. When the registration of the entire poll tax was nearly complete,
a cruel man was sent throughout the land to impose the tribute assessment. His name was Ruzin, the one we mentioned above. He came against Amida, Arzan, and Maypherqat.
As for Amida, because it contained greedy and contemptible local men, not one of whom spoke about its suffering,
unless he wanted evil to destroy it, those greedy magnates and thieving officials accepted a tribute assessment of seventy thousand.
They sent word to the son of Musab that Ruzin should not come in against them, so that they themselves could satisfy their unbridled greed at the expense of the local people.
This he also did, collecting many times as much. He demanded not only seventy thousand, but three times that amount in addition.
They fixed an assessment and imposed on everyone the share that fell to him. And when each person had sold everything he owned,
he oppressed even the poor and the foreigners, and even travelers [?], and merchants too. He unjustly stripped the people in the city of their possessions,
saying, “You too are in the registers.” The official lent a hand in these things. And anyone whom they found possessing even one copper coin,
they imposed a levy on him and stripped him of wheat, barley, or other produce for trade. Only then did they barely manage to meet the assessment imposed on them.
When everyone had been stripped of their possessions, sorrowful cries could be heard from [?] sides. The officials also noticed every place where a little still remained.
They fixed an assessment and imposed it on them, saying, “Such-and-such a district has fled, and there is no one in it.” And also
they paid for that one. Again they fixed an assessment and imposed it, and they paid this one too. When the poor people saw that this blatant robbery did not stop, and that they felt no shame,
and did not fear God, and that even that chief of all evils did not hold them accountable for the injustices they committed every day throughout the regions,
they rose in resistance, saying, “We have been given [?], and the great ruin of our companions, and our own levy and what is not ours.
When will they have had enough of our flesh? We will give no more, because we do not know where to get it for them.”
When the officials heard these things, they clapped their hands and gnashed their teeth like wolves thirsting for blood. They gathered against them all the thieves and murderers of their city.
He also sent his deputy, and with him thieves and men who shed blood, leading men from the region of the Cyrrhestians,
violent and merciless men. He gathered young men from Cyrrhus, a large force armed with bows and slings.
He went up against them, while those Cyrrhestians themselves surpassed in wickedness all the murderers and thieves among them.
They committed terrible evils against their brothers, evils that the tongue is inadequate to recount.
Now this place that rose in resistance lies among the mountains, in the northern part of the region, and is called Tutis.
It too is mixed, Syrian and Urtian, because they share it with the Urtians, that is, those of Fourth Armenia.
In this region there is a place that produces lead and silver, along with other places where iron is smelted. Because of the great oppression that spread over the whole land,
many people gathered at this place where lead was found, so that a large encampment arose there. It also had an official appointed by the king.
People flocked to this place from all the regions. They dug large, deep pits there for the lead.
It was toward this place we have mentioned that they directed the force of Cyrrhestians that had come up, claiming that they wanted to impose a levy on them.
But their Persian officials were unwilling to accept this from them, saying, “Many of them are from your country, and they pay the poll tax and other levies.”
They were not persuaded, however, but armed themselves for fierce battle and to plunder everything the others possessed.
The Persians ordered their camp to stand and drive them away, so that they would not enter and attack them, though they did not want any killing.
When these merciless men attacked them and began killing them, those who were outside fled from the sword.
And because it was still winter, and there was deep snow in that land,
and ice had frozen over the mouths of these pits, which were also buried in snow and full of water,
and they could not be recognized, people fell into these pits as they fled. Many of them drowned and perished,
sinking into them beneath the ice and the opening of the pit. He also killed many of them with the sword and showed no mercy. He stripped and took captive that entire camp.
Let us lament over these things like Jeremiah the prophet and say: “All our enemies have opened their mouths against me. Fear and trembling have come upon us, the pit and destruction.
My eyes pour out streams of water over the destruction of the daughter of my people. My enemies hunted me like a bird for no reason. They put an end to
my life in the pit and threw stones at me. Waters rose above my head.” Let us also add what was said by another:
“Whoever flees from the sound of terror will fall into the pit. Whoever escapes from the pit will fall by the sword. Whoever survives the sword will fall into captivity.”
None of these things was lacking here. Their fellow Christians did not even take pity on those who had drowned or been killed by bringing them up and burying them.
Instead, if they happened to bring one of them up, they stripped off his clothes and left him naked at the mouth of the pit.
There was no need to recount the evil deeds they committed in that land:
first, because perhaps no one would believe them, so evil were they; and second, so that they would not be exposed before the pagans,

who would say that Christians have no fear of God before their eyes, because their deeds are worse than those of the Magi. But in order to make known that these were the causes that brought this affliction upon us,
so that those who see our deeds may guard themselves, and also to show the mercy of God, who bears and endures our follies and our many evil deeds,
we leave a brief record of them. Now he attacked them, and because of the deep snow that lay in that land,
they could not escape. If they did happen to flee, their attackers followed their tracks. When they found them lying in the snow,
together with their servants, wives, and children, trembling and crusted like salt from the severity of the cold,
instead of showing them mercy, they stripped them all—the men, the women, and the infants.
They left them naked, without a cloak or boots. They even took away their trousers, without concealing their naked
bodies. They also committed filthy acts with their wives and daughters in front of one another, without concealment. That wicked man who had attacked them ordered
that whatever anyone seized should be his, so that he and the thieves who had joined him and accompanied him from the region might satisfy their unbridled lust.
And this he did and accomplished. The villagers and their leaders were even worse than the pagans and showed their brothers not the slightest mercy.
Instead, their wickedness surpassed that of men whom everyone called highway robbers. As for the objects that people used,
they destroyed them all. They burned the wooden ones, smashed the earthenware ones, and took the bronze and iron ones for themselves.
From beds and doors to troughs and basins, he left nothing that they did not destroy by fire. He broke jars, pitchers, pots, and earthenware vessels.
They drank as much as they could of the wine in them. They destroyed the rest, pouring it out onto the ground. And if a vessel happened to be sunk into the ground,
and they had no room around it to break it, one of them thrust his spear into it and pierced its bottom, and its wine drained into the ground.
They did the same with the honey. He ate as much as he could and poured the rest onto the ground. He broke all the beehives,
and also submerged them in water, so that all the bees died. They went so far as to do even this, following Satan’s advice, for he had shown them the way there.
They were more eager than the pagans among them to eat meat and cheese during the holy days of the fast,
along with the destructive acts he committed. So when the news reached us

of what they had done to their brothers, we were filled with great sorrow, distress, and bitter sighing. We also marveled at how greatly the Evil One could make human beings his playthings. They also attacked the churches,
and he plundered and carried off their books and all the vessels used in celebrating the holy mysteries.
Because they had confined their wives in those churches, pagans too would enter and have sex with them inside.
Here there was reason to weep with Jeremiah and say, “All her splendor has departed from Zion”—that is, from the holy church. “Her priests are humbled,
and she is in bitterness. The enemy has exalted himself. The oppressor has stretched out his hands over all her precious things, and she has seen nations enter your sanctuary,
whom you commanded not to enter the assembly.” And also: “They violated women in Zion.” These evil things were done in that land,
while they also brought men in chains like murderers. They plundered all their possessions and carried them off with them.
They did the same to many villages, driving out the villagers, taking their inhabitants captive, and dragging them away. Razin passed through Arzan and Maipherqat.
When he discovered the stolen proceeds of their labors, he punished them with severe tortures and harsh blows, until he became infested with worms and died.
He broke their hands and their feet with [?], and extracted from them the wealth they had stolen. The Lord delivered them into the hands of an evil, unjust man.
And all the filthy acts they used to commit came back upon their own persons. People said of them that they used to hunt [?] came back upon their own persons.
People said of them that they used to catch lepers from the streets and sexually abuse them. Those wicked scribes and registrars themselves, who were Christians,
would shamelessly send for and bring virgins who were daughters of the covenant, and violate them along with freeborn virgin girls and married women.

Truly, the members of the household feel no shame and do not know how to be ashamed—these men who attacked the brides of Christ. God delivered them into the hands of someone worse than themselves. As the saying goes, “An evil man
takes vengeance on an evil man, and the Lord on both.” When this man saw their evil deeds,
he had them brought in, pierced their nostrils, and put bridles in them as with camels. He pierced the space between their eyes and hung a [?] there.
He made chains for them by which they were dragged along. After sentencing a man, he handed him over to the young lepers to make sport of him in the street.
Then he threw them into prison, where he would not even give them bread, but only enough to keep them alive.
The house in which they were confined gave off a stench of decay in every direction, worse than a grave.
I have briefly recorded these things so that, when rulers see them, they may keep God before their minds and not behave disgracefully or contrary to the rightful demands of duty.
They should also know that even the lawgiver has a law over him, and understand that a ruler who behaves unlawfully quickly and easily loses the title of ruler that gives him his standing,

and in its place comes the title of tyrant, full of every disgrace—that is, a madman who has lost his mind.

On the famine that afflicted the people,

and on the severe disease and the great plague that occurred in that year.

It is written in the prophet: “Look, I will feed this people wormwood
and give them bitter water to drink. I will scatter them among nations they have not known, and send famine, plague, captivity, and the sword after them.”
What the prophet said came to pass, with nothing lacking; indeed, even more happened. There was great distress in the southern regions
because of that Sahwan whom we mentioned above. Because of the harshness and persecution of Musa ibn Musab, the population of the entire southern and eastern land went into exile
and came up into Mesopotamia. Villages, towns, houses, and farms were filled with them, until there was no
room for anyone to walk or sit because of them. Their arrival greatly increased the distress of the poor and the laborers of Mesopotamia,
because wages had fallen [?], and one could hire one of them. For if someone wanted work done, he could bring as many men as he wished to work, giving each of them only the bread he needed to eat.
Yet he did not even give them that bread freely [?]. Men and women, children and old people went begging from house to house all day without stopping.
Whenever they saw an open door anywhere, thirty or forty of them would gather at it together.
At first, everyone was openhanded in giving.
But when those poor people, strangers, and displaced people increased beyond measure, people stopped giving,
because they feared that they too might run short and suffer as those people did. Moreover, the grain owners had all their grain consumed by weevils, and they sold it fraudulently and deceitfully.
Not even those poor people remained free from sin. The able-bodied young men among them disguised themselves as [?], disabled people, and blind people,
with deception utterly devoid of shame. They went around bent over like people who had been struck down.
They began calling down curses on anyone who would not give to them. A man would not leave the door until he had received what he wanted.
Because of these curses, people were afraid to open their doors. Those wretches who behaved in this way
would go down to the marketplace and sell the bread they had begged for, buying themselves meat and wine.
When people saw these things too, they again stopped giving to the poor, and great distress befell
those people. For there were wretches to be found who committed these inhuman deeds, treating this as a business,
going about to houses, streets, and everywhere else. The inhabitants of the regions of Mesopotamia also took to begging and came into the towns because of the famine.
For all their produce had been sold, and there was no one to lend to them. They ate meat and milk throughout the fast.
Because livestock had become cheap, people gave them meat wherever they wanted it.
In various places the famine grew severe for the inhabitants because of the great number of foreigners, until they fell upon the bodies of the dead.

The foreigners had fled the famine in their own country so that they would not perish in it. But it went before them, accompanied them, and followed them wherever they went and came, together with war and pestilence.
He ate bitterness and drank bitterness, and was scattered among nations he did not know. And he also sent after them war, captivity, famine, and pestilence,
until he was destroyed. They remained in this distress throughout the winter. But when days that were a little warmer arrived, and fresh vegetation began to appear,
they rushed out to the wild greens and grazed on them like livestock. They also gathered some and brought them into the marketplace,
where they sold them and bought themselves bread with the proceeds. Even their complexion appeared green like the vegetation. Yet they were not satisfied, except as livestock are.
What had been spoken through the prophet was fulfilled among them: “You will eat but will not be satisfied, because there will be a flux within you.”
This now happened: they ate, but even these people were not satisfied, and they all fell ill with a bowel disease.
The porticoes and marketplaces were filled with them, as were the spaces in front of shops, towers, great buildings, and everywhere else.
Then many different diseases began breaking out among them again: skin eruptions, pustules, and abdominal pain,
eye pain, fever without other pains, and [?], which is [?], and pleurisy, along with many other unidentified ailments.
Hemorrhoids and dropsy also became widespread. News reached us that there was a disease in Mosul in which people's heads swelled, and they quickly collapsed and died.
They could not even manage to bury them. We regarded this as merely a story, but before very long it reached us.
It spread little by little through the towns farther down until it reached us. This is how it was: first it took hold of a person's brain,
and gradually spread downward until it reached the heart and took hold of it. Then the mind became confused,
the light of the eyes failed, and the person lost all awareness and sank into a stupor like someone dead.
He would remain like this for many days, deprived of all human awareness. And if, when a man was stricken,
he did not make a will on the first or second day, he could no longer understand enough to do so.
But if, after some days, his mind happened to recover and he could converse, he would awaken as though from a deep sleep, unaware even that anything had been wrong with him.
If his bodily weakness allowed it, he would get up. But the disease would return to a person more than five or six times.
Some died at the first attack, and some at the second. In other cases, after it had worn a person down more than five times, it would return and carry him off.
Among many of them, a white eruption would break out on a person. After remaining for a day or two, it would turn dark.
Then a red eruption would break out on him, and this too would turn dark. Then a bluish eruption would appear. And after all this
distress, which he had endured for many days, when he thought that he had finally recovered, he would die of a bowel disease.
And when he escaped from this as well, pustules and [?] overtook him. Four or five could be found lying together in one place.
Each one of them was dying from a particular disease, though their diseases were not alike.
Others, too, could be found dying from pustules, diarrhea, dysentery, hemorrhoids, and that tormenting pain in the heart.
All these diseases could be found together in a single body. While suffering all these things, he lay dying.
Hunger and thirst also tormented him more than these did. And so they lay in porticoes, halls, churches, towers, and streets.
They were buried in filth and ravaged by various diseases. Others wandered through the cities because of the distress of hunger.
They would also stand together at a doorway, more than ten, twenty, or thirty at a time, some of them covered in pustules.
Some suffered from dysentery, some from diarrhea, and others from various diseases. While these afflictions rested upon their bodies,
the severe distress of hunger and thirst also drove them to go on their hands and feet and seek bread for themselves everywhere.
Even those who wished to give alms could not manage to give to everyone who came to their doors.
Because so many people were coming to the houses, those lying in the streets suffered from hunger and thirst.
They will be [?] cast into the streets of Jerusalem because of sword, famine, and pestilence, with no one to bury them—them, their wives, and their children.
And I will pour out their wickedness upon them. If you go out into the countryside, there are those killed by the sword; and if you enter the town, there are those ravaged by
hunger. When this disease struck the cities and people began to perish like locusts, people were afraid to enter the cities because of the authorities, the diseases, and the pestilence.
They began attacking people, blocking the roads and robbing travelers. They would attack, plunder, strip, and kill.
They did not search and chase after gold and silver as much as they wandered about searching for bread.
Thus many murders occurred because of flour or wheat that someone was carrying home to his family.
They did not hesitate to shed a person's blood for one measure of grain or five. The regions also rose up to cross over and plunder villages in other regions.
They also blocked the roads against travelers. People would come in from the countryside, each one's complexion looking like a green plant.
When someone came in, sold the work of his hands, and bought himself bread, he would eat it without restraint.
He would quickly fall at death's door. Some of them, while holding bread in their hands and eating,
turned black as sackcloth, toppled backward, fell, and breathed their last. This happened to many. When many of them began to die,
people could not keep up with burying them all day long. Even so, God did not neglect the poor, but his grace and mercy sheltered them.
First they themselves [?] and fell ill with this disease, until the streets and every place were foul with them. And so, as the times allowed,
and in proportion to the little that people possessed, each person cared for them as best he could.
Even those among them who died were buried by everyone with great honor. They would bring biers and clothes,
dress them, and go out and lay them in their fine burial places, with services and psalms, as is proper for Christians to do.
He also gathered those who were stricken and lay abandoned in the streets, wasted by diseases, hunger, and thirst,
and brought them to a single hall [?]. He appointed people to care for them, and everyone would take and bring them whatever they could.
Because of the distress that had come upon their land, they were all equally destitute. Those who had owned property—look, they were beggars!
