“Those who used to eat delicacies,” it says, “now lie in the streets. Those brought up in scarlet now lie on dunghills.”
Again the prophet Jeremiah adds, saying: “Their appearance grew darker than soot, and they were unrecognizable in the streets. Those brought up in scarlet now lie on dunghills.”
Again the prophet Jeremiah adds, saying: “Their appearance grew darker than soot, and they were unrecognizable in the streets. Their skin shriveled against their bones;
it dried up and became like wood. Those killed by the sword were better off than those killed by hunger, who wasted away like those struck down and trampled in the field.”
Such was also the condition of those who were suffering and disfigured. And when they began to be removed from the streets and buried,
wrath flared up among the townspeople, and they all fell [?] alike: great and small, children and old people, young men and young women.
It was such that, if you entered twenty houses, you could scarcely find in one of them anyone able to bring water to his companion.
Instead, they all lay like dead people, and not one of them knew [?] anyone who could bring water to his companion.
Instead, they all lay like dead people, and not one of them could distinguish good from evil.
Just as it says there that there was no house without dead people in it, so here too one could say that there was no house, not even one, without sick people in it.
There was also what was said by Jeremiah: “The infant’s tongue stuck to [?] the roof of its mouth from thirst.
Children ask for bread, but there is no one to break it and give it to them.” Even if one or two people in a household remained who were not
ill, they lay prostrate from hunger. They were in even greater distress than those suffering from disease, because there was no one to bake and make bread for them.
Those who lay stricken with various diseases were also tormented by hunger and thirst,
because there were few people able to get up and give one another water. Wrath raged fiercely among them, and a plague began among them,
so that two or three people a day would be carried out of a single house. A mother and her daughter, a father and his son, and two brothers together would even be carried out on a single bier.
Two brothers would also be carried out, one from this side of the city and the other from that side. Their biers would come and meet each other, and they would be taken to the grave together.
They would even be laid one on top of the other. This happened to many: they would settle their final account with their Creator at the same time.
It grew severe among the prominent people and the heads of households. All the priests of the church of Amid [?] also perished in this plague. It began to spread little by little,
and passed out of the cities into their surrounding districts and struck the villages. Just as it had ravaged the city, so it did outside it.
Here too the words of Isaiah were fulfilled: “You drank from the Lord’s hand the cup of his wrath. You drank and drained the cup of staggering.”
“There is no one to comfort you among all the sons you bore, and no one to take her by the hands among all the sons you raised.”
“These two calamities have overtaken you—who will grieve for you? Plunder and destruction, famine and sword—who will comfort you? Your sons have fainted
and lie at the head of every street, like a blackened beet, filled with the Lord’s wrath and the rebuke of your God.”
Like a beet blackened by frost, so was the complexion of everyone who survived this disease. They had also lost their hair,
all of them, so that unless their clothing distinguished them as a monk or a priest,
no one could distinguish a priest from a layman, because they were shorn [?]. The light of their eyes had also gone, as had the hearing of their ears.
Nor did their strength return to them for a long time. The warmer the season became, the more severe the disease grew.
When the harvest days in Beth Arabaye approached, the entire northern population rose early, including the foreigners, and they all went down for the harvest,
just to get their fill of bread. Women and men who had lost their hair also went down, for it was customary for the northern people to send their young men down for the harvest.
But now old men and young men, women and men who had lost their hair went down because of the great distress that had overtaken them at this time.
But when they went down and ate their fill of bread, they all fell ill again with various diseases,
so that the roads and paths, the heights and hollows, were full of them, as were the villages, cities, and every place.
They were also dying off like locusts. There were no wages, only enough bread for each person to eat.
Many said that some of them would go out to the fields, and when they had eaten their fill, they fell down and died,
so that twenty would go out and five would return. When the owners of the harvest learned this,
they would not let any of them enter their fields unless his complexion was healthy and his body well nourished. They also paid them wages of five folles a day,
and at most ten. In this way people reaped their entire harvest, showing no consideration for the strength of the poor.
They would not even give them their fill of dry bread—not because they lacked it, but because of their wicked disposition. We will also describe
the wicked things people were doing in disturbing the graves of the dead. On the plundering of graves
and the stripping of the dead. The prophet Jeremiah told us about the overturning of graves when he spoke of them as follows,
and also about the scattering of their bones: “There is no one to gather them; instead, they will be like dung on the surface of the ground.” “At that time,” says the Lord,

“they will bring out from their graves the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of their officials, the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of their officials, the bones of their priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
They will spread them out before the sun, the moon, and all the host of heaven, which they loved and served, followed, consulted, and worshiped.
They will not be gathered or buried, but will be like dung on the surface of the ground.”
Against us ourselves Satan grew fierce and raged because of our many sins, through many generations, times, and cycles.
He brought it about that we should endure this: people overturned graves and scattered their bones outside their tombs without pity.
Just as someone takes rubbish out of a house and scatters it outside, so they would bring them out and throw their bones outside their tombs.
They did not even have enough pity on them to return them to their places once they had carried out their wanton and cruel desires upon them.
Even if zealous, God-fearing people happened to be there and rebuked them
for this wickedness, injustice, and outrage, they would say to them, “What are we to do about this misery?
Where are we to get anything to pay?” When they were asked in turn, “Do you find anything [?]?” those shameless people clung to
the words of Satan, their father and master, and said, “We do find things.” But when they were questioned, “What have you yourself found?” each would say, “I myself have not found anything yet.
But so-and-so [?] and so-and-so found rings, cups, and gold necklaces. And in such-and-such a village, the gold and silver amount to so many thousands.”
Satan taught them these empty words to use as an excuse for their disgrace.
But when the person who was said to have found something happened to be questioned, his find turned out to be a copper cup or an iron ring.
These were their finds, but through his servants Satan proclaimed them as marvels, as thousands and tens of thousands,
so that everyone would work with him in this wickedness, while he gave them the fire of Gehenna as their wages. And because the faithful generations of old had resisted him,
and he had not carried out his will upon them during their lives, he was now satisfied: his servants fulfilled his desire by scattering their bones.
Here the hater of everything good triumphed over both us and them: over those whose bones were scattered, and over us ourselves, who did this with our own hands.
And just as all these people had died from various plagues, so various diseases also fell upon the living.
And the scriptural saying was fulfilled: “When tombs are opened, many plagues enter the cities.”
Because people had become so bold about overturning tombs, they even dared to strip the dead who were being buried in those very days.
No sooner had the gravediggers buried one dead person and gone back to bring another than, while they were on their way, the first was stripped.
They would even open up the graves of Arabs and Jews. They would strip the dead person and then [?] bury him again, so that no one would notice
them; or they would leave him lying naked, face down, and go away. Thus, when people became aware of this too, and even caught some of these grave robbers themselves,
and found the dead people’s clothing in their possession, they would not leave a dead person unguarded after burial, either by day or by night, until the body had decayed.
They would even coat the fine clothing laid with the dead person with lime before the moth could come, and stain it with pitch.
As a result, there were many guards in the cemeteries of the Syrians, Arabs, and Jews.
Until the bodies had decayed and become bloated, they would not leave a dead person without guards.
Those robbers and thieves did not even scruple to strip a poor man with whom a [?] cloth or a piece of [?] had been laid.
We have found mention in the prophet of overturning graves, but we have found no mention of stripping the dead.
But through our wickedness and injustice we have surpassed every evil, both those recorded in the Scriptures and those not recorded.
But let us give thanks to the Lord for his goodness, which cannot be measured or comprehended by mortal beings, for he bears and endures our outrages and our many evil deeds.
On the end of the plague, and on the destructive beasts that came out after the plague. Although we had fallen into all this wickedness and injustice, involving every kind of abomination:
Lying, robbery, plundering one another, slander, insults, licentiousness, adultery, theft, false testimony, murders, and betraying one another.
And evils began to surround us on every side. We could find no way to repent and return to the Lord, but instead even disturbed the dead who lay sleeping
in their resting places. Then the Lord repaid us according to our deeds. God abandoned us, and every evil poured down upon us.
As the prophet said: “I will heap evils upon them and spend my arrows against them. They will be wasted by hunger.
Evil spirits will be handed over to them [?]. I will deliver them to the birds and unleash ravenous beasts against them.
Outside, the sword will bereave them, and inside their chambers, terror.” Isaiah also said: “They will be left together to the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth.
The birds will gather over him, and the beasts of the earth will rage against him.” Habakkuk also said: “You have had your fill of disgrace instead of honor.
Drink, you too, and be overcome. The cup in the Lord’s right hand will come around to you, and disgrace will cover your honor, because the violence done to Lebanon will cover you.
The devastation of the beasts will terrify you, because of human bloodshed and the violence done to the land, the city, and all its inhabitants.”
Saint Jeremiah also said: “Drive them [?] out of my presence, and let them go. If they say to you, ‘Where shall we go?’

tell them: ‘This is what the Lord says: Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; and those destined for captivity, to captivity.
I will appoint four scourges over them, says the Lord: the sword to kill, dogs to drag away, and the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth to devour and destroy.
I will make them an object of horror.’” Again he said: “If you go out into the countryside, there are those slain by the sword; if you enter the town, there are those wasted by famine.”
For when the afflictions of hardship, deprivation, famine, plague, and various diseases multiplied among the people, they left their houses and went up to live in watchtowers and ravines.
There they perished like locusts, from hunger and from
plague and cold. They were eaten by beasts and birds, with no one to bury them. The plague grew severe in the lower regions and devastated that land.
Many households that had numbered forty or fifty people were left without a single person. In one day, more than a thousand funeral biers were carried out of Mosul.
The people of Nisibis, too, were making some large [?] and dumping them into them.
All the leading men of the land died. This plague was especially devastating to the priests of the cities and villages.
Ninety-five people from the monastery of Qartmin died in this plague, particularly prominent men.
And from the monastery of Mar Saliba too, all its superiors [?]. Estates, villages, and the great mansions of the cities remained deserted.
Along with these things, after this plague, certain terrifying and fearsome wild animals were also seen. They were not afraid of anything.
They did not flee from people or fear them either. They killed countless people. They had some resemblance to wolves,
though they differed a little from wolves, in that each one's snout was thin and long.
They had large ears like a horse's. The hair along the ridge of their backs was like the bristles of a pig:
it was long and stood straight up toward the sky. They caused great destruction among the people in Tur Abdin.
People said that they had eaten more than a hundred people from one village—that they had eaten more than a hundred people from one village—
and from many villages, twenty from some, forty from others, and fifty from others. People could not do any harm to a single one of them.
Nor did they flee from people. Even if people went out armed in pursuit of one of them, they could do it no harm.
It would not flee from them either, but would turn on them, and their hands would lose their grip on their weapons.
It would leap on them and tear them apart. They would enter houses and courtyards, carry off little children, and leave, with no one daring to intervene.
Some of them would climb onto high roofs at night, take little children from among the people there, and come down, with no one daring to intervene.
Not even the dogs would bark at any of them. Because of this, that land fell into distress more bitter and severe than anything it had suffered before.
Even two or three people could not travel together. Livestock were not seen anywhere either, because they had been eaten by these animals.
If one of them entered among goats or sheep, it would carry off a person. What can we say about this bitter scourge except that they were sent against us by God?
Indeed, it was clear to everyone that they had received this power from God, since neither dogs nor people could harm a single one of them.
For he said, “I will heap disasters upon them.” Here are the city's merciless punishments: flight from place to place.
And here again are famine, plague, and various diseases. Here are people plundering and taking one another captive, and the land [?].
Not even all the livestock of the land perished in this year. And here were birds everywhere tearing at the unburied corpses of people.
Along with these things, here too were destructive wild animals. These animals crossed into the territory of Arzan and caused great destruction

in one village, and also in the territory of Maypherqat and on the Dry Mountain. They caused a little destruction in Amid too. Despite all these things, the Lord's anger did not turn away from us; his hand was still raised.
Yet it was not that he failed to turn his rod away from us, but that we did not turn away from our hateful deeds. Instead, we multiplied them many times over.
So disasters upon disasters came upon us anew, and the Lord once again laid his hand upon us in punishment.
[Several leaves are missing from the manuscript.] … People could not pass by or come near that house because of the overpowering stench of decay coming from it.
It spread a very long way as well. But if some necessity compelled someone to approach that house,
For a person who had someone there would remain dazed by that smell for a day or two.
Here we could say with the prophet Isaiah, “As abandoned [?] are gathered, they gathered the whole earth.”
There was no one to lift a wing, open his mouth, and chirp. Arabs and Syrians were gathered together, great and small,
locals and foreigners. There was no one who raised his [?], or even opened his mouth and spoke. Let the prophet David also come and [?],
while the holy temple is being defiled and turned into a latrine, like the temple of Baal, that of Nedu-Bel [?].
And let him say, “O God, the nations have entered your inheritance and defiled your holy temple. They have made your holy church a latrine, and a foul smell has risen from it instead of a
pleasant fragrance.” For Isaiah himself said, “Because of these things the earth will sit in mourning, and all its inhabitants will be condemned.” The earth lamented and sat in mourning.
The world lamented, sat down, and mourned, because all the tables were filled with vomit and filth, leaving no place clean. For the prophet himself spoke to them,
as though from the Lord’s own mouth: “I told them, ‘This is my rest: give rest to the weary; and this is tranquility.’ But they would not listen to me.”
And the Lord’s word became for them filth upon filth, filth upon filth, vomit upon vomit, vomit upon vomit.
Here one could see their filth upon their vomit, and all their tables filled with their filth, leaving no place clean.
What tears, what grief could have been enough, when freeborn and clean people could be seen holding their bread in their hands and eating,
while dung was heaped upon dung in front of them, and others were relieving themselves before them because that place was so cramped?
Over these things the prophet Joel cries out and says, “Priests, put on sackcloth! Lament and wail, you who serve at the altar! Come in and spend the night in sackcloth, you servants of my God!”
Not because drink offerings and fine flour had been withheld from it, but because the church had become despised and abandoned by the Lord into the hands of foreigners.
While the people lay under all this great distress, that wicked man took the register they had written at the beginning of the year,
supposedly as a kind of revised assessment. On anyone whose name was not there, or had been [?] by him, he imposed a levy of forty-eight,
which was worth sixty zuz coins; and levies of thirty-five, twenty-five, and fifteen. In this way he released many of them,
while the poor and needy remained in that prison, suffering misery from hunger and the foul
smell. He also seized the leading men on account of their sons, brothers, and household members who were not entered in the detailed register.
He imposed levies on them. He also seized those who were registered and dealt with them in ways that caused them heavy losses.
He chose reckless men and drunkards and made them his companions. They would denounce the lowly and the powerful,
hunt them down, and bring them to him. In this way no one at all escaped without being made to suffer loss, either on his own account or on account of his household,
or because he trumped up a charge against him. He again seized the local people and pressured them to reach a settlement with him. They argued fiercely over this.
He beat their leaders to the point of death. He assessed and imposed on everyone whatever he pleased.
There was no one to rebuke him or say to him, “What have you done?” Neither a word nor truth was to be found with any of them.
For they seized the inhabitants of the city and pressured them over their sons and their brothers, for two thousand.
Even after he had taken it, he did not stop his wickedness. Instead, he went out into the countryside, fabricating accusations of every kind against them.
They would go out onto the roads and paths, hunting down those who were defaulters [?].
Even those who were not, they stripped and took everything they had on them.
But God, in his mercy, caused this oppression to occur in Iyar. From then on, everyone hid in the mountains,
like doves in [?]. All the roads were closed to people coming and going, because upon all the regions
this wrath had descended. People were perishing from hunger, yet they were afraid to approach a city or a village.
If one of them happened to have something to sell in the city so that he could buy himself bread, when he came near the city walls, they would bring
women with them and send them inside. They themselves would hide among the crops until they were wasting away from hunger,
waiting for those they had sent. One of them might remain for two, three, or four days, or even from one Sunday to the next,
hiding among the tombs and crops like demons, and wasting away from hunger. When she came out, it sometimes turned out that he had sold his goods for next to nothing.
It is time for us to say, “Outside, the sword of hunger bereaves; within the chambers, terror.” And upon the people of Tella, Edessa, and Harran,
this wrath grew severe. For the prophet said, “This is the curse that goes out over the face of the whole earth.”
As for the people of Nisibis, when this bitter scourge reached them and levies were imposed upon them without mercy, they seized everyone who came and went.
They would throw them onto [?] without mercy. All the leading men of the region gathered and went down to Moses, pleading with him to reach an agreement with them.
He refused. They pleaded with him again to sell them these rural districts, to which he had sent [?], provided only that these ravenous dogs he had sent would not roam their land.
He would not agree even to this. Instead, he took them and threw them into prison in Mosul.
He loaded them with heavy irons and bound himself by an oath that, as long as he held authority, they would not be released from there.
Although many pleaded with him on their behalf, he would not relent. So they remained in prison until the Lord brought deliverance.
The tyrant [?] also received punishment, the reward he deserved. Now it is time to move from one evil to another.
Account Ten: Concerning the emirs of the tithe and the emirs of the crown estates. For it is said, “From the root of the viper
a basilisk has come forth for us, and its fruits are flying serpents.” Those whom this viper sent out over the land were worse than basilisks.
When these men came and entered the city, they sent out orders and mercilessly entered assessments against the people.
Against a man who owned neither wheat nor barley, but bought his food in the marketplace, they entered an assessment of a thousand geribs.
Others, two thousand; some, five thousand; and some, ten thousand, and upward, even as much as forty or fifty thousand jaribs.
Although he had not entered the house of any of them or learned what that person possessed, he assessed him for whatever Satan suggested to him.
He did the same to the shopkeepers, cloth merchants, [?], and merchants of the entire marketplace. Mercilessly, [?] against them, he demanded payment from them.
So even when everything in a shop was sold, it did not bring in half the amount they were demanding for it.
While everyone lay under this great oppression—from the excise tax, the tithe, and the poll tax—Sufi also [?] according to his power,
taking captive and plundering those coming in and going out. Here we could say: What the flying locust left, the crawling locust ate.
What escaped this one, the cricket ate; and what remained after this one, the consuming locust ate. In the same way, what remained after the poll tax, the excise collectors took.
What remained after the excise collectors, the tithe collectors took; and what escaped this, Sufi took. As it is said, whoever flees from the sound of terror falls into the pit.
Whoever climbs out of the pit falls into the snare, and whoever escapes the snare is devoured by a wild animal. Concerning the second emir of the garrisons.
When Kili Baz Zadin [?], the emir of the garrisons whom we mentioned earlier in this book, died, and Abu Awn came in his place, he fought against
the officials of Ibn Musab and drove them out of the city. A Persian man came from the king, a harsh, violent, bloodthirsty man.
This man shook the land, and all the Arabs in the land suffered oppression from him, because he began to carry out deeds that the Persians were not accustomed to doing.
For the Persians' practice from the beginning was this: prolonged imprisonment without mercy. This man began killing people with beatings and also crucifying them.
Everywhere he went, he brought oppression upon the Syrians through the requisitioning of livestock and the expenses of his army, since his soldiers were quartered upon the inhabitants.
The inhabitants supplied all the provisions for the soldiers themselves and their animals. For the prophet said, “They all come to plunder.”
Before leaving a city, this man would send his advance officer ahead of him to prepare a place for him and requisition livestock for him.
When this officer arrived in a city twenty days beforehand, he threw himself into every sort of wrongdoing and plunder.
They would go out onto the roads or into the villages and seize mules and horses, even colts, and make a business out of them.
They confined them in houses and courtyards. Whoever gave them two coins for a mule or a horse could take it out, and they released it.
Then they caught another one. They also went out onto the roads and the tracks outside the city and caught the donkeys belonging to the poor.
They took one coin from them for each donkey and let it go. They also went out into the countryside and demanded that people bring them livestock. Once they had brought it,
they demanded in turn that they give them money: two coins for each mule and one coin for a donkey. They beat anyone who did not pay them. In this way they brought in
a great many animals from the countryside, the roads, and the marketplaces, and confined them in courtyards.
The inhabitants were also severely burdened by the expenses of these men and their animals. They remained [?] for many days. Then he arrived.
He also took the animals belonging to merchants and travelers. In this way he held a great many animals belonging to poor people for many days and months.
He did not release them until they had sold everything they owned to cover their expenses, since he was unwilling either to release them or to give them anything.
Scripture says, “They are swifter than evening wolves, and they fly like an eagle hungry for food.” And again it says, “They all come to plunder.”
Let us say a little about the man himself. When his reputation spread through the regions, fear and trembling seized everyone because of him.
He began to beat people without mercy, to kill them, and also to crucify them. In every city he entered, he would crucify two, three, or five people. [?]
People trembled before him. They used to say of him that he was destroying thieves, murderers, and highway robbers.
But we learned that most of those he killed were not such people, but men of prayer, those called zealots, wandering beggars, and men of prayer.
He passed through all the cities of Lower Mesopotamia, beating, killing, and crucifying, and reached Amida.
After staying there for many days and crucifying four men there as well, he went on to Maypherqat. From there he returned to Amida and settled there.
While [?] [Several leaves are missing.] [?] They also seized Arabs and Syrians over inheritances, and deprived them harshly
and bitterly. They would give nothing to a person's close blood relatives, as is written in the law of the kings, [?], except for a son inheriting from his father and a father from his son,
and an uncle from his nephew, or a nephew from his uncle. Even these escaped from those beasts only with difficulty. [?] For the prophet Joel said:
“Its teeth are like a lion's teeth, and its fangs like the fangs of a young lion. It has laid waste my vine and stripped my fig tree.
It stripped it and threw it down, and its branches turned white.” Here, however, it happened that the tax collectors took what was left, and the emir in charge of inheritances demanded what remained.
He stripped the people, and their branches turned white, with nothing left. Chapter Six: On the Death of the Emir of Amida,
and on the document that had been drawn up, and on the relief granted to the leading men of [?] who had been imprisoned.
As for Amida, we have too little time to recount the evils that took place there during this year.
For it suffered afflictions during this year beyond all the other cities.
But since the destruction is still only beginning and has not reached its end, I will speak about the beginning of this calamity.
I also bring forward holy Isaiah, because he saw these evils beforehand and understands the matter better than we do.
I also bring with him his fellow prophet Jeremiah, so that every matter may be established by the testimony of two witnesses. “The city was filled with turmoil; the strong city was filled with noise.
Your slain were not slain by the sword, nor were they killed in battle. All your rulers fled together from this wrath.

Those who remained in you were bound; together they were bound, while the rest fled far away. Therefore I said, ‘Leave me alone; let me weep bitterly over the destruction of the daughter of my people.’
For it is a day of turmoil, trampling, and weeping. On this day the mighty Lord called for weeping and mourning, for shaving the head and putting on sackcloth.”
Let the prophet Jeremiah also come and lament over her, since he is especially skilled in weeping and lamentation. “I am worn out by my sorrow, and my heart is sick within me.
Listen to the cries of the daughter of my people from a distant land! Over the destruction of the daughter of my people I am overcome with grief, and horror has seized me.”
